pericopes.text: And now there was no more contention in all the land of Zarahemla, among all the people which belonged to king Benjamin, so that king Benjamin had continual peace all the remainder of his days.

And it came to pass that he had three sons; and he called their names Mosiah, and Helorum, and Helaman. And he caused that they should be taught in all the language of his fathers, that thereby they might become men of understanding; and that they might know concerning the prophecies, which had been spoken by the mouths of their fathers, which was delivered them by the hand of the Lord.—

And he also taught them concerning the records which were engraven on the plates of brass, saying, My sons, I would that ye should remember, that were it not for these plates, which contain these records and these commandments, we must have suffered in ignorance, even at this present time, not knowing the mysteries of God:

links.text: Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.

provenance.other: “the mysteries of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Old Testament never uses the expression at all; Daniel has 'secrets' and Deuteronomy 29:29 'secret things'. The plural mystery belongs to Paul in the English Bible, and the genitive form to this one verse.
provenance.significance: Recover Paul's sentence and the next one comes with it: 'Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful' (4:2). Benjamin's whole argument in verses 3-7 is a stewardship argument — the plates were kept, they must be searched, and thirteen verses later he hands their custody to his son (1:16). The KJV's one phrase for the things a steward holds in trust is the phrase Benjamin uses for what the plates preserve.

links.note: 'We must have suffered in ignorance, even at this present time, not knowing the mysteries of God.' The five-word run is a KJV singleton and the sense is Paul's rather than Daniel's: not a hidden thing God discloses to a seer, but a body of held knowledge someone is answerable for. Benjamin's counterfactual — without the plates, no mysteries — is the stewardship of 1 Corinthians 4:1-2 argued from the negative side.

links.text: Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.

provenance.alternative: 'At this present time' is unremarkable English and could have been written by anyone in 1829 without a source; the KJV's failure to use it elsewhere may be an accident of the KJV rather than a signal.
provenance.significance: What makes the echo worth recording is not the phrase but the company it keeps. Benjamin uses it twice in two verses and then, at 1:5, states his argument in the words of Isaiah 1:9 — the KJV's remnant verse, the one Paul quotes at Romans 9:29 two chapters before he writes 'at this present time also there is a remnant'. Benjamin's case is that a small preserved group escaped becoming like its brethren, which is Romans 9-11's case exactly, and two of its phrases have come along.

links.note: 'Even at this present time' (1:3), 'even down to this present time' (1:4). “at this present time” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse is about a remnant preserved by grace rather than by merit. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because the phrase carries no argument on its own; it is the convergence with Isaiah 1:9 at 1:5, which Romans quotes, that makes Romans 11:5 more than a coincidence of idiom.

pericopes.text: for it were not possible that our father Lehi could have remembered all these things, to have taught them to his children, except it were for the help of these plates: for he having been taught in the language of the Egyptians, therefore he could read these engravings, and teach them to his children, that thereby they could teach them to their children, and so fulfilling the commandments of God, even down to this present time.

links.text: And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds.

provenance.other: “learned in all the wisdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Old Testament never credits an Israelite with Egyptian learning: Exodus says only that Moses was drawn out of the water and brought up in Pharaoh's house. The claim, and the English frame 'X in all the Y of the Egyptians', exist in the Bible at Acts 7:22 and nowhere else.
provenance.significance: The borrowing is split across two verses in the way CONVENTIONS §9 says the n-gram stream cannot see: 1:2 has the frame — 'taught in all the language of his fathers' — and 1:4 has the object — 'taught in the language of the Egyptians'. Put back together they are Acts 7:22. And Acts 7 is Stephen's speech, which 1 Nephi already drew on at six separate places. What Stephen is doing with that sentence is establishing that the deliverer was equipped by Egypt before he was sent from it; what Benjamin is doing with it is explaining how a Jerusalem prophet could read a record engraved in Egyptian. The same claim carries both: Egyptian learning in an Israelite is providential, not compromising.

links.note: 'He having been taught in the language of the Egyptians, therefore he could read these engravings.' Benjamin's argument for the plates turns on a fact about Lehi that has one biblical precedent and one biblical wording, both at Acts 7:22. 'Taught' replaces 'learned' and 'language' replaces 'wisdom', but the construction and the object are Stephen's, and 1:2's 'taught in all the language of his fathers' preserves the 'in all the' that 1:4 drops. Lehi is being given Moses's education in the sentence that explains why the record survived.

links.text: That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children:

provenance.other: “them to their children” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “declare them to their children” in exactly one. Deuteronomy 6:7's 'teach them diligently unto thy children' is the other candidate for the teaching chain, but it has one generation, not the relay of three that Psalm 78:5-6 and Mosiah 1:4 both build.
provenance.significance: Psalm 78:5-8 is the KJV's one sustained statement of exactly Benjamin's thesis: a testimony was appointed, fathers were commanded to make it known to their children, so that the generation to come might know and declare it to theirs, 'that they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God' — and so that they might not be 'as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation'. Verse 5 of Mosiah 1 supplies the failed branch of the relay from the same psalm's supply: the Lamanites, who 'know nothing concerning these things' and do not believe them, are Psalm 78:8's stubborn generation. Benjamin is running the psalm's argument with the plates in the place of the psalm's testimony.

links.note: 'To have taught them to his children, that thereby they could teach them to their children, and so fulfilling the commandments of God.' The relay of three generations, the verb of teaching, and the exact clause 'them to their children' are Psalm 78:5-6's, and the clause is a KJV singleton. Psalm 78 is also the psalm that gives the reason for the relay — that the children not forget the works of God and not become as their fathers — which is the reason Benjamin gives in the next verse.

pericopes.text: I say unto you, my sons, were it not for these things, which have been kept and preserved by the hand of God, that we might read and understand of his mysteries, and have his commandments always before our eyes, that even our fathers would have dwindled in unbelief, and we should have been like unto our brethren, the Lamanites, which know nothing concerning these things, or even do not believe them when they are taught them, because of the traditions of their fathers, which are not correct.

links.text: Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah.

provenance.other: “we should have been like unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Romans 9:29 quotes Isaiah 1:9 and is the mediation test: it reads 'we had been as Sodoma, and been made like unto Gomorrha'. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points, both for Isaiah — the Book of Mormon has 'should have', not Romans's 'had', and it lacks Romans's 'made'.
provenance.significance: The whole of Isaiah 1:9 is the shape of Mosiah 1:5, not just its clause. Isaiah: except the LORD had left us a remnant, we should have been like Gomorrah. Benjamin: were it not for these things, kept and preserved by the hand of God, we should have been like unto our brethren the Lamanites. Both are counterfactuals of preservation, both name what the speaker's people would otherwise have become, and both make the preserved thing — a remnant there, a record here — the sole reason the sentence is contrary to fact. The substitution is the finding: the Lamanites stand where Sodom and Gomorrah stand.

links.note: 'And we should have been like unto our brethren, the Lamanites.' Six words in sequence from the KJV's one verse that contains them, in a sentence built on the same counterfactual as its source. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because a complete clause is reproduced from an identifiable verse. Mediation is decided rather than assumed: Isaiah 1:9 is quoted at Romans 9:29 in different words, and every point of difference falls on Isaiah's side.

links.text: And profited in the Jews’ religion above many my equals in mine own nation, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers.

provenance.other: “traditions of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the plural is Paul's and only Paul's here. The KJV's other ancestral-tradition phrase is 1 Peter 1:18's 'vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers', in the singular and without 'traditions'. Matthew 15 and Mark 7 have 'the tradition of the elders', never of fathers.
provenance.significance: Galatians 1:14 is the one place in the English Bible where a man names the traditions of his fathers, and he names them as the thing he was zealous for before he was called out of it. Benjamin uses the phrase of the Lamanites, who cannot believe the record 'because of the traditions of their fathers, which are not correct' — the same diagnosis, made from outside instead of from inside. The Book of Mormon's standing explanation for Lamanite unbelief, repeated from here to Alma, is worded out of Paul's account of his own former self.

links.note: 'Because of the traditions of their fathers, which are not correct.' The plural phrase is a KJV singleton and it belongs to Galatians 1:14, where Paul is explaining what he had to be converted away from. The Book of Mormon makes it a hereditary and corporate condition rather than a personal zeal, which is a real change of sense; but it is Paul's noun phrase, and the Book of Mormon has no other.

pericopes.text: O my sons, I would that ye should remember that these sayings are true; and also, that these records are true. And behold, also the plates of Nephi, which contain the records and the sayings of our fathers, from the time they left Jerusalem, until now; and they are true; and we can know of their surety, because we have them before our eyes.

And now, my sons, I would that ye should remember to search them diligently, that ye may profit thereby; and I would that ye should keep the commandments of God, that ye may prosper in the land, according to the promises which the Lord made unto our fathers.

links.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

provenance.route: 1 Kings 2:3 → KJV → 1 Nephi 2:20 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “that ye may prosper” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 29:9, which supplies the plural; 1 Kings 2:3 has the singular 'that thou mayest prosper'. Neither has 'prosper in the land', which is the Book of Mormon's own compound and occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Mediation is the point of this row. The formula is not being taken from the Bible here — it is being taken from Lehi, who took it from 1 Kings 2:3 and Joshua 1:7 at 1 Nephi 2:20 and repeated it in his own deathbed charge at 2 Nephi 1:20. What makes the route worth arguing rather than assuming is that Benjamin is at the same point in the same script: a dying king charging the son who will succeed him, four verses before he says he must go the way of all the earth in 1 Kings 2:2's words. The chapter reaches David's charge to Solomon twice, once through Lehi and once directly, and the two arrivals are two verses apart.

links.note: 'Keep the commandments of God, that ye may prosper in the land, according to the promises which the Lord made unto our fathers.' By Mosiah the conditional is the Book of Mormon's own covenant refrain, established at 1 Nephi 2:20 and already inherited once at 2 Nephi 1:20, so the proximate model is Lehi rather than the KJV; 'according to the promises which the Lord made unto our fathers' says as much on the page. The biblical root is still visible in the plural 'that ye may prosper', which is Deuteronomy 29:9's form and not 1 Kings 2:3's.

pericopes.text: And many more things did king Benjamin teach his sons, which are not written in this book.

links.text: And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book:

provenance.other: “which are not written in this book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The formula recurs in the Book of Mormon and was catalogued at 1 Nephi 6:3 and Words of Mormon 1:5 as a colophon convention with no reproduced wording; this is the first place the wording itself is reproduced.
provenance.significance: The two sentences are the same sentence with two nouns changed: 'And many other signs truly did Jesus … which are not written in this book' / 'And many more things did king Benjamin teach his sons, which are not written in this book.' John's colophon is the KJV's one formal statement that a record has been deliberately cut short, and its function there is to convert an abridgement into a claim about the reader — 'these are written, that ye might believe' (20:31). The Book of Mormon has used the gesture since 1 Nephi 6; here it takes the words, and it takes them at the point where a king's private teaching is withheld from the public record just before a public sermon begins.

links.note: Seven words reproduced exactly from the KJV's only verse that contains them, inside a clause that also matches John's word order ('And many other … did Jesus' / 'And many more things did king Benjamin'). Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his 36; catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because a complete clause is reproduced from an identifiable verse. Note the difference from the earlier occurrences of this convention: at 1 Nephi 6:3 and Words of Mormon 1:5 the Book of Mormon makes John's move without John's words, and here it makes it with them.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after king Benjamin had made an end of teaching his sons, that he waxed old; and he saw that he must very soon go the way of all the earth; therefore, he thought it expedient that he should confer the kingdom upon one of his sons.

links.text: I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man;

provenance.other: “go the way of all the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the fuller phrase 'the way of all the earth' occurs in exactly two, Joshua 23:14 and 1 Kings 2:2, and both are a leader's farewell. Joshua's is 'this day I am going', a participle, so the Book of Mormon's infinitive here follows David. 'Waxed old' is Joshua's word (Joshua 23:1), which is why the composite names both.
provenance.significance: The phrase entered this corpus at 2 Nephi 1:14, in Lehi's mouth and in David's tense; here it re-enters in a different hand and in the third person, as narration rather than speech. What comes with it is the whole of 1 Kings 2:1-3 rather than the tag: David dies, confers the kingdom on a named son, charges him to keep the commandments that he may prosper — and Mosiah 1:7, 1:9, 1:10 and 1:15 supply the prospering, the going, the conferral and the charge, in the source's order. The Book of Mormon has read 1 Kings 2 as a template for royal succession and used it twice, once for a prophet's death and once for a king's.

links.note: 'He waxed old; and he saw that he must very soon go the way of all the earth; therefore, he thought it expedient that he should confer the kingdom upon one of his sons.' Two KJV farewells are fused: Joshua 23:1's 'waxed old' and 1 Kings 2:2's 'go the way of all the earth', the latter a singleton in this exact form. The argument for 1 Kings 2 as the governing source rather than a tag is structural — the conferral of the kingdom on a son, the charge 'concerning all the affairs of the kingdom' at 1:15, and the prosperity conditional at 1:7 are 1 Kings 2:1-3's three moves, and Benjamin makes all three inside seven verses. Across a book boundary from 2 Nephi 1:14, so written as a link rather than left to the register (ADJUDICATING §4).

pericopes.text: Therefore, he had Mosiah brought before him; and these are the words which he spake unto him, saying: My son, I would that ye should make a proclamation throughout all this land, among all this people, or the people of Zarahemla, and the people of Mosiah, which dwell in the land, that thereby they may be gathered together: for on the morrow, I shall proclaim unto this my people, out of mine own mouth, that thou art a king, and a ruler over this people, which the Lord our God hath given us.

links.text: Since the day that I brought forth my people out of the land of Egypt I chose no city among all the tribes of Israel to build an house in, that my name might be there; neither chose I any man to be a ruler over my people Israel:

provenance.other: “a ruler over” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Ruler over my people' occurs in four (2 Samuel 7:8, 1 Chronicles 11:2, 1 Chronicles 17:7, 2 Chronicles 6:5), all of David; only 2 Chronicles 6:5 takes the indefinite article the Book of Mormon uses.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 6:5-6 is the opening of Solomon's temple dedication, and it pairs the two things Benjamin pairs in these two verses: a place where God will put his NAME, and a man appointed a RULER over his people. Mosiah 1:10-11 announces a ruler and then announces a name — 'I shall give this people a name, that thereby they may be distinguished' — and 1:18 gathers the people to the temple to hear it. The Book of Mormon has taken the temple speech's two elements, transferred the name from the sanctuary to the congregation, and set the transfer at the sanctuary. That inversion is the reading; neither text states it.

links.note: 'That thou art a king, and a ruler over this people, which the Lord our God hath given us.' The four-word run is a KJV singleton, and its verse is the one place in the KJV where God's choice of a ruler stands in the same sentence as the house built for his name. The case is not the run alone — it is that the next verse of Mosiah takes up the naming and verse 18 takes the people to the temple, so the two halves of 2 Chronicles 6:5-6 arrive together and in order. Moderate rather than high because 'a ruler over this people' is ordinary English and could have reached the page without a source.

pericopes.text: And moreover, I shall give this people a name, that thereby they may be distinguished above all the people which the Lord God hath brought out of the land of Jerusalem; and this I do, because they have been a diligent people in keeping the commandments of the Lord.—
And I give unto them a name, that never shall be blotted out, except it be through transgression.

links.text: He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.

provenance.route: Revelation 3:5 (with John 10:28) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “blot out his name” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 29:20 and Revelation 3:5 — a curse and a promise, and the Book of Mormon has the promise's negative form. The giving-formula is a second singleton: “and I give unto them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:28, where what is given is eternal life and the guarantee is 'they shall never perish'.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's sentence is built out of the KJV's two verses about a name that cannot be lost, and it takes something from each. From John 10:28 it takes the frame and the adverb — 'And I give unto them … they shall never perish' becomes 'And I give unto them a name, that never shall be blotted out'. From Revelation 3:5 it takes the substance, a name kept in a book against erasure. What neither source has is Benjamin's exception, 'except it be through transgression': John's giver says no man shall pluck them out of his hand, and Revelation's promises the overcomer outright. The Book of Mormon has fused two unconditional promises and then made the result conditional — which is what Mosiah 5:11-12 will spend a chapter defending.

links.note: 'And I give unto them a name, that never shall be blotted out, except it be through transgression.' Two KJV singletons meet in eleven words: John 10:28's 'And I give unto them', and Revelation 3:5's name that is not blotted out. The link is filed under Revelation because the sense — a name preserved in a register, forfeitable by conduct — is Revelation's and not John 10's, and because Deuteronomy 29:20, the KJV's only other blotting of a name, blots it as a curse on the man who blesses himself in his own heart. Benjamin is promising the Johannine security and immediately withdrawing its unconditionality.

pericopes.text: Yea, and moreover I say unto you, That if this highly favored people of the Lord should fall into transgression, and become a wicked and an adulterous people, that the Lord will deliver them up, that thereby they become weak, like unto their brethren; and he will no more preserve them, by his matchless and marvellous power, as he hath hitherto preserved our fathers.

links.text: A wicked and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given unto it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas. And he left them, and departed.

provenance.other: “wicked and adulterous” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthew 12:39 has 'An evil and adulterous generation' and Mark 8:38 'this adulterous and sinful generation'; the Book of Mormon has Matthew 16:4's adjective and Matthew 16:4's order.
provenance.significance: Matthew 16:4 is spoken to a people who have been given every sign and ask for another, and the sentence ends with Jesus leaving them — 'And he left them, and departed'. Benjamin's threat is that same withdrawal in Old Testament terms: the Lord 'will no more preserve them, by his matchless and marvellous power'. The gospel verse supplies both halves of what Benjamin says will happen to a highly favoured people that turns, and it is the only KJV verse that supplies the phrase.

links.note: 'Become a wicked and an adulterous people.' The adjective pair is a KJV singleton and belongs to Matthew's second sign-refusal. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'people' for 'generation' — a real change, since Matthew's noun is temporal and the Book of Mormon's is national — and inserts the article that the 1830 text carries ('a wicked and an adulterous people'). What the borrowed phrase brings with it is the outcome: in Matthew the speaker leaves, and here the Lord will no more preserve.

links.text: And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.

provenance.other: “highly favoured” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Note that the 1830 text spells it 'highly favored', without the KJV's -our-, so this is a case where the first edition does NOT preserve the King James orthography (contrast CONVENTIONS §8's 'shew' and 'marvellous', the latter of which stands two clauses later in this same verse).
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's standing epithet for a chosen people or person — 'highly favored of the Lord', from Nephi's first sentence onward — exists in the English Bible only as the angel's greeting to Mary, where it is said to one woman and is immediately explained as meaning that she will bear a son. Benjamin turns the singular annunciation formula into a national status that can be forfeited: 'if this highly favored people of the Lord should fall into transgression'. Recorded as an echo because a single adverb-participle pair is thin evidence, but the pair is a KJV singleton and the Book of Mormon uses it constantly.

links.note: 'If this highly favored people of the Lord should fall into transgression.' The two-word phrase is a KJV singleton, and its one occurrence is Gabriel's. The Book of Mormon has used it since 1 Nephi 1:1 as a formula for divine election, which is a stable usage rather than a fresh allusion here — but it enters this book in a new hand and in the conditional, which is what makes it worth stating: what the KJV says once, unconditionally, to Mary, Benjamin says of a nation and makes revocable.

links.text: That he told her all his heart, and said unto her, There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother’s womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.

provenance.other: “become weak” occurs in exactly two KJV verses. The other is Isaiah 14:10, where the shades taunt the fallen king of Babylon — 'Art thou also become weak as we?' — which has the comparison but not the conditional and not the covenant; the Book of Mormon's clause has both. “be like any other man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Judges 16:17 is the KJV's one statement of the conditional Benjamin is making: a person set apart to God from birth, whose distinction rests on a kept condition, who says in so many words that breaking it will make him weak and like everyone else. Verse 20 completes it — 'he wist not that the LORD was departed from him' — which is Benjamin's 'he will no more preserve them'. Benjamin's people are Samson at national scale: highly favoured, strong only by a covenant, and one transgression away from being indistinguishable from their brethren.

links.note: 'That thereby they become weak, like unto their brethren; and he will no more preserve them, by his matchless and marvellous power.' The elements are Samson's and they arrive in Samson's order: the condition, the becoming weak, the being like other men, the withdrawal of the preserving power. The verbal contact is two short phrases and the wording is adapted, so this is filed as an allusion at moderate rather than as a close-verbal link — but 'become weak' plus 'like unto' plus a lost covenant condition has one home in the KJV, and 'brethren' is doing exactly the work Judges 16:17's 'any other man' does. Note that the 1830 'marvellous' preserves the KJV spelling the later editions dropped (CONVENTIONS §8).

pericopes.text: For I say unto you, that if he had not extended his arm in the preservation of our fathers, they must have fallen into the hands of the Lamanites, and become victims to their hatred.
And it came to pass that after king Benjamin had made an end of these sayings to his son, that he gave him charge concerning all the affairs of the kingdom.

And moreover, he also gave him charge concerning the records which were engraven on the plates of brass; and also, the plates of Nephi; and also, the sword of Laban, and the ball or director, which led our fathers through the wilderness, which was prepared by the hand of the Lord, that thereby they might be led, every one according to the heed and diligence which they gave unto him.

Therefore, as they were unfaithful, they did not prosper nor progress in their journey, but were driven back, and incurred the displeasure of God upon them; and therefore, they were smitten with famine and sore afflictions, to stir them up in remembrance of their duty.

links.text: Yea, I think it meet, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by putting you in remembrance;

provenance.other: “stir you up by putting you in remembrance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “stir you up” in exactly one. 2 Peter 3:1 has the same idea in different words ('stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance'), so the collocation of stirring with remembrance belongs to 2 Peter and to no other KJV writer.
provenance.significance: The context is worth recovering because it is the same context. 2 Peter 1:13-15 is a man who knows he must shortly put off his tabernacle, saying that while he remains he will keep stirring his readers up in remembrance, and providing that they may have these things in remembrance after his decease. Mosiah 1 is a king who has just said he must go the way of all the earth, explaining why the record exists and handing it on. Benjamin gives the phrase to God — famine and affliction are what stir the fathers up — but the sentence sits inside Peter's situation exactly: an imminent death, a record left behind, and remembrance as the thing the record is for.

links.note: 'They were smitten with famine and sore afflictions, to stir them up in remembrance of their duty.' The collocation of stirring up with putting in remembrance is 2 Peter's and the KJV has it nowhere else. The Book of Mormon changes the agent — a writer stirs his readers in 2 Peter, chastisement stirs the fathers here — and the phrase becomes one of the book's standard idioms for affliction as pedagogy. Moderate because the borrowed material is a verb-plus-prepositional-phrase rather than a clause, and because the changed agent means the sense is adapted rather than carried.

pericopes.text: And now, it came to pass that Mosiah went and did as his father had commanded him, and proclaimed unto all the people which were in the land of Zarahemla, that thereby they might gather themselves together, to go up to the temple, to hear the words which his father should speak unto them.

links.text: And they made proclamation throughout Judah and Jerusalem unto all the children of the captivity, that they should gather themselves together unto Jerusalem;

provenance.other: “made proclamation throughout” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; 'made a proclamation' occurs in five, of which 1 Kings 15:22 ('made a proclamation throughout all Judah') is the closest rival and gathers nobody. The borrowing is split across two verses of Mosiah: 1:10 has 'make a proclamation throughout all this land … that thereby they may be gathered together', and 1:18 has 'proclaimed unto all the people … that thereby they might gather themselves together'.
provenance.significance: Ezra 10:7-9 is the KJV's one sequence of proclamation, national gathering, and assembly at the house of God, and it is a covenant-renewal assembly: the people sit in the street of the house of God, trembling, and put away what has separated them. Mosiah 1:18 through chapter 6 is the same sequence at greater length — proclamation, gathering, the temple, a covenant, and a new name. That the Book of Mormon's great covenant assembly is announced in the words of the post-exilic one is worth recording whether or not the writer intended it.

links.note: 'Proclaimed unto all the people which were in the land of Zarahemla, that thereby they might gather themselves together, to go up to the temple.' Three elements of Ezra 10:7-9 in the source's order, with the singleton 'made proclamation throughout' standing eight verses earlier at 1:10. 'Gather themselves together' is a common KJV phrase on its own (eight verses) and carries no weight by itself; what carries the link is the sequence — proclamation to a whole people, gathering, and the house of God as the destination — which the KJV runs only here.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after Mosiah had done as his father had commanded him, and had made a proclamation throughout all the land, that the people gathered themselves together throughout all the land, that they might go up to the temple to hear the words which king Benjamin should speak unto them.
And there were a great number, even so many that they did not number them; for they had multiplied exceedingly, and waxed great in the land.

links.text: And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen; and they had possessions therein, and grew, and multiplied exceedingly.

provenance.other: “multiplied exceedingly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Exodus 1:7, the verse usually remembered for this, reads 'increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty' — a different phrase. 'Waxed great' occurs in five verses and carries no weight on its own.
provenance.significance: Genesis 47:27 is the last verse of the settlement in Goshen and the hinge of the Exodus story: a family becomes a nation in a land it was given rather than born to, and the multiplication is what makes the next book's oppression possible. Mosiah 2:2 uses the phrase of a people who have likewise been brought into a land not their own, in the paragraph that gathers them for the covenant sermon. The Book of Mormon runs Exodus typology continuously from 1 Nephi 2 onward, and this is the Goshen verse.

links.note: 'For they had multiplied exceedingly, and waxed great in the land.' A KJV singleton doing the same narrative work as its source — the census-defeating growth of a transplanted people. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because a two-word formula is thin, and because the second clause ('waxed great in the land') is not from Genesis 47:27 and matches no KJV verse.

pericopes.text: And they also took of the firstlings of their flocks, that they might offer sacrifice and burnt offerings, according to the law of Moses;

and also, that they might give thanks to the Lord their God, who had brought them out of the land of Jerusalem, and who had delivered them out of the hands of their enemies, and had appointed just men to be their teachers; and also, a just man to be their king, who had established peace in the land of Zarahemla, and who had taught them to keep the commandments of God, that they might rejoice, and be filled with love towards God, and all men.

links.text: And the children of Israel remembered not the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side:

provenance.other: “delivered them out of the hands of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV's much commoner idiom is 'delivered them INTO the hands of' their enemies (Judges 2:14 and many others), which is the opposite transaction; the deliverance direction with this exact string is Judges 8:34's alone.
provenance.significance: This is the register's best kind of finding and it turns on a single word of the source: 'remembered NOT'. Judges 8:34 is the KJV's one sentence about being delivered out of enemy hands, and it is a sentence about ingratitude — Israel forgot the God who did it, as soon as Gideon was dead. Mosiah 2:4 is a people assembled specifically to 'give thanks to the Lord their God, who … had delivered them out of the hands of their enemies', immediately before their own leader dies. The Book of Mormon has taken the words of the KJV's classic failure of gratitude and used them for an act of gratitude, at the moment Judges says gratitude fails.

links.note: Nine words in sequence, including the whole clause 'the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of', from a KJV verse the machine ranked first in the chapter and ranked correctly. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; filed as an allusion rather than a quotation because the Book of Mormon breaks the clause with 'who had brought them out of the land of Jerusalem' before completing it. The reversal of Judges's sense is the argument.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when they came up to the temple, they pitched their tents round about, every man according to his family, consisting of his wife, and his sons, and his daughters, and their sons, and their daughters, from the eldest down to the youngest, every family being separate, one from another;

links.text: And when the cloud was taken up from the tabernacle, then after that the children of Israel journeyed: and in the place where the cloud abode, there the children of Israel pitched their tents.

provenance.route: Numbers 9:17 with Numbers 2:2 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “pitched their tents” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse pitches them at the tabernacle where the cloud rested. The arrangement — by household, each family separate, facing the sanctuary — is Numbers 2:2's: 'Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house: far off about the tabernacle of the congregation shall they pitch.'
provenance.significance: Two verses of Numbers supply the phrase and the floor plan of Israel's wilderness camp, and Mosiah 2:5-6 rebuilds that camp around a temple instead of a tabernacle, with the tent doors turned toward it. What the Book of Mormon adds is the doors, which Numbers does not specify — and that detail turns a camp into a congregation, since a door facing the sanctuary is a position for hearing rather than for marching. The scene is the wilderness camp reassembled for a sermon.

links.note: 'They pitched their tents round about, every man according to his family … every family being separate, one from another' — and in the next verse, 'every man having his tent with the door thereof towards the temple'. The phrase is a KJV singleton and the arrangement is Numbers 2:2's, household by household about the sanctuary. Note that the Feast of Tabernacles reading (Leviticus 23:42) is the usual one offered for this scene and is not what the wording supports: Leviticus has booths, not tents, and no orientation.

pericopes.text: and they pitched their tents round about the temple, every man having his tent with the door thereof towards the temple, that thereby they might remain in their tents, and hear the words which king Benjamin should speak unto them;

for the multitude being so great, that king Benjamin could not teach them all within the walls of the temple; therefore, he caused a tower to be erected, that thereby his people might hear the words which he should speak unto them.

links.text: And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, and Shema, and Anaiah, and Urijah, and Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, and Mishael, and Malchiah, and Hashum, and Hashbadana, Zechariah, and Meshullam.

provenance.other: “pulpit of wood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “made for the purpose” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse. The English Bible has one purpose-built raised platform from which a leader addresses an assembled nation, and it is Ezra's.
provenance.significance: Nehemiah 8 is the KJV's only account of the scene Mosiah 2 stages: a whole people gathered in one place at the sanctuary, a leader raised on a structure erected specially so that he can be seen and heard, a reading of the law before men, women and everyone who could understand, and a covenant renewal that runs on for chapters. Benjamin's tower is Ezra's pulpit, his 'those that were not under the sound of his voice' answers Nehemiah 8:2's 'all that could hear with understanding', and the multi-day festal assembly that follows in Mosiah 3-6 answers Nehemiah 8-10. 1 Nephi 1:19 already reached this chapter of Nehemiah for a different detail, so it is not a first contact — but this is where the whole scene is taken.

links.note: 'The multitude being so great, that king Benjamin could not teach them all within the walls of the temple; therefore, he caused a tower to be erected.' No wording is reproduced — the Book of Mormon says 'tower' where the KJV says 'pulpit of wood' — so this is filed as conceptual, and the case rests on the fact that the KJV builds such a structure exactly once, for exactly this purpose, in a chapter whose other elements Mosiah 2 also has. Nehemiah 8:5 supplies the corollary the Book of Mormon keeps: Ezra was 'above all the people', and that is why he opened the book where they could see.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he began to speak to his people from the tower; and they could not all hear his words, because of the greatness of the multitude; therefore, he caused that the words which he spake, should be written and sent forth among those that were not under the sound of his voice, that they might also receive his words.

And these are the words which he spake and caused to be written, saying: My brethren, all ye that have assembled yourselves together, you that can hear my words which I shall speak unto you this day: for I have not commanded you to come up hither, to trifle with the words which I shall speak, but that you should hearken unto me, and open your ears that ye may hear, and your hearts that ye may understand, and your minds that the mysteries of God may be unfolded to your view.

links.text: And he read therein before the street that was before the water gate from the morning until midday, before the men and the women, and those that could understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law.

provenance.other: “hear with understanding” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “were attentive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Nehemiah 8:2 and 8:3, consecutive verses of the same assembly. Both of the Book of Mormon's audience-qualifications in this chapter answer them: 'you that can hear my words' here, and 'you little children, which can understand my words' at 2:40.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 6:10's ear-and-heart pairing ('hear with their ears, and understand with their heart') stands behind any English sentence of this shape, and Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27 quote it. But the mediation test is indecisive here — see the exclusion register at this verse — and Isaiah's clause is a judgment on people who will NOT hear, where Benjamin's is an invitation to people who will.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's opening does what Ezra's assembly does and states it as a condition of attendance: the audience is defined as those who can hear and understand, and the ears are the organ the text keeps naming. What the Book of Mormon adds is the third term — 'your minds that the mysteries of God may be unfolded to your view' — which converts a public reading of the law into an initiation. Nehemiah's people hear the law; Benjamin's are promised the mysteries.

links.note: 'Open your ears that ye may hear, and your hearts that ye may understand, and your minds that the mysteries of God may be unfolded to your view.' The ear-and-understanding pair, and the qualification of the audience by capacity to understand, are Nehemiah 8:2-3's, where both phrases are KJV singletons. 'Mysteries of God' is 1 Corinthians 4:1's singleton, already catalogued at Mosiah 1:3, so the sentence joins the Ezra assembly to the Pauline stewardship in one breath.

pericopes.text: I have not commanded you to come up hither, that ye should fear me, or that ye should think that I, of myself, am more than a mortal man;

links.text: And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:

provenance.route: Acts 14:11-15 (with Acts 10:26) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “of like passions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; James 5:17 has 'subject to like passions', which is the form the Book of Mormon's 'subject to all manner of infirmities' is closer to in construction. Acts 10:26's 'I myself also am a man' is the other KJV refusal of divine honour and has no shared wording.
provenance.significance: There are two scenes in the KJV where a crowd is about to treat a man as more than a man and he stops them: Cornelius falling at Peter's feet, and Lystra bringing oxen to Barnabas and Paul because 'the gods are come down to us in the likeness of men'. Both refusals take the same form Benjamin's does — do not fear me, I am what you are — and Acts 14:15 supplies the vocabulary of shared human nature. Benjamin then does what Paul does next in the same sentence: turns from himself to the God 'which made heaven, and earth', which is where Mosiah 2:20-25 goes.

links.note: 'I have not commanded you to come up hither, that ye should fear me, or that ye should think that I, of myself, am more than a mortal man; but I am like as yourselves, subject to all manner of infirmities in body and mind.' Little is reproduced verbally, but the move is one the KJV makes twice and only twice, and Acts 14:15's 'men of like passions with you' is its one fixed phrase. The link is filed here rather than at 2:11 because 2:10's refusal of fear is the half that matches Lystra; 2:26's 'I, even I, whom ye call your king, am no better than ye yourselves are' repeats it at the end of the speech.

pericopes.text: but I am like as yourselves, subject to all manner of infirmities in body and mind; yet, as I have been chosen by this people, and was consecrated by my father, and was suffered by the hand of the Lord that I should be a ruler, and a king over this people; and have been kept and preserved by his matchless power, to serve thee with all the might, mind, and strength which the Lord hath granted unto me;

links.text: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 6:5 via Mark 12:30 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The mediation is the finding and it needs stating carefully. tools/mediation-check.py reports one decisive point for Deuteronomy 6:5 — the Book of Mormon has 'might', which is Deuteronomy's word and not Mark's. That report is an artifact of how the diff aligns the two verses, because the Book of Mormon ALSO has 'mind' and 'strength', and neither is available from Deuteronomy 6:5 at all: the Hebrew shema in the KJV runs heart, soul, might, and 'mind' enters the English scriptures only in the Synoptic quotations. “with all thy mind” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, and all three are Synoptic quotations of the shema; Mark 12:30 is the one that has mind before strength, which is the Book of Mormon's order, since Luke 10:27 reverses them and Matthew 22:37 omits strength altogether.
provenance.significance: 'Might, mind, and strength' is not a biblical triad. It is the Deuteronomic term plus the two the New Testament added, with the Deuteronomic 'heart' and 'soul' dropped — a conflation that could only be made by someone holding both forms of the shema at once. Benjamin is not quoting the love-command either: he applies its measure to service rather than to love, 'to serve thee with all the might, mind, and strength which the Lord hath granted unto me', which is the move the whole speech makes from 2:17 onward — service of others as service of God.

links.note: 'To serve thee with all the might, mind, and strength which the Lord hath granted unto me.' Three of the shema's four measures, taken from two different KJV forms of it. Moderate rather than high because a triad of near-synonyms is easy to produce independently and because Benjamin's application is his own; but the presence of 'mind' rules out Deuteronomy 6:5 as the sole source, which is what makes this an OT-via-NT row rather than a Deuteronomic one. Note also 'kept and preserved by his matchless power', which repeats Mosiah 1:13's 'matchless and marvellous power' from the previous chapter.

pericopes.text: I say unto you, that as I have been suffered to spend my days in your service, even up to this time, and have not sought gold nor silver, nor no manner of riches of you;

links.text: I have coveted no man’s silver, or gold, or apparel.

provenance.other: “coveted no man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “with all humility of mind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both in this speech. Nehemiah 5:14-18, the other biblical apologia by a ruler who did not live off the people, is a real rival for the taxes at 2:14 and is catalogued there; it has nothing corresponding to the blood at 2:27.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 2:12-29 is Paul's Miletus farewell, kept in Paul's order. Acts 20:18 'ye know, from the first day that I came into Asia, after what manner I have been with you at all seasons' → 2:12 'I have been suffered to spend my days in your service, even up to this time'. Acts 20:33 'I have coveted no man's silver, or gold' → 2:12 'have not sought gold nor silver'. Acts 20:34 'these hands have ministered unto my necessities' → 2:14 'I, myself, have labored with mine own hands'. Acts 20:26 'I am pure from the blood of all men' → 2:27 'that your blood should not come upon me'. Acts 20:25 'ye all … shall see my face no more' → 2:29 'I can no longer be your teacher, nor your king'. Five elements, one source-passage, and the same genre: a departing leader's self-defence before the people he has served, delivered because he is about to be taken from them.

links.note: 'I have not sought gold nor silver, nor no manner of riches of you.' The disclaimer is Paul's at Miletus, where 'coveted no man's silver, or gold' is a KJV singleton, and it is the first of five contacts with the same speech across the next eighteen verses. The rest are catalogued at 2:14, 2:27 and 2:28. What makes the passage rather than the phrase the source is that the Book of Mormon reproduces the sequence: service from the first day, no money taken, hands that laboured, innocence of blood, and a farewell.

pericopes.text: neither have I suffered that ye should be confined in dungeons, nor that ye should make slaves one of another, or that ye should murder, or plunder, or steal, or commit adultery, or even I have not suffered that ye should commit any manner of wickedness, and have taught you that ye should keep the commandments of the Lord, in all things which he hath commanded you;

links.text: Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery, and swear falsely, and burn incense unto Baal, and walk after other gods whom ye know not;

provenance.other: “murder and commit adultery” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “steal murder” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Jeremiah 7:9, the only place in the KJV where the decalogue's prohibitions are strung as a rhetorical question. Hosea 4:2's list is 'swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery', with different verb forms; the Ten Commandments themselves are in the second person singular and negative.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 7 is the Temple Sermon: Jeremiah stands in the gate of the LORD's house and asks a people who have come to worship whether they mean to steal, murder and commit adultery and then stand in this house and say they are delivered. Benjamin is standing at his temple, addressing a people camped around it, and lists the same crimes — as things he has NOT suffered among them. The Book of Mormon has taken the temple-gate indictment and inverted it into a temple-gate acquittal.

links.note: 'Or that ye should murder, or plunder, or steal, or commit adultery.' The KJV strings these three verbs together once, at Jeremiah 7:9, and the Book of Mormon reorders them and adds 'plunder', which is in no KJV verse. Moderate rather than high because a list of capital crimes is the most predictable content such a sentence could have; what raises it above coincidence is the setting, since both lists are spoken at a temple to a congregation assembled for worship.

pericopes.text: and even I, myself, have labored with mine own hands, that I might serve you, and that ye should not be laden with taxes, and that there should nothing come upon you which was grievous to be borne; and of all these things which I have spoken, ye yourselves are witnesses this day.

links.text: Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.

provenance.other: “these hands have ministered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “ye yourselves know” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse. The Book of Mormon has both halves: the labouring hands, and the appeal to the hearers as witnesses of it.
provenance.significance: Acts 20:34-35 gives the reason Paul worked: 'so labouring ye ought to support the weak'. Benjamin gives a different reason — that the people should not be laden with taxes — and the difference is the whole distance between an apostle and a king. But the sentence is built the same way and ends the same way, on the hearers' own testimony: 'ye yourselves know' becomes 'ye yourselves are witnesses this day', which also carries Acts 20:26's 'I take you to record this day'.

links.note: 'Even I, myself, have labored with mine own hands, that I might serve you … and of all these things which I have spoken, ye yourselves are witnesses this day.' Two KJV singletons from one verse of the Miletus speech, in the same relation to each other: the manual labour, and the audience called to confirm it. This is the second of the five contacts with Acts 20 catalogued in this chapter; see the argument at 2:12.

links.text: And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.

provenance.other: “grievous to be borne” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:4 and Luke 11:46, the same woe in two gospels. tools/mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence between them at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces, so the choice has to be made by eye — and it is Luke's, on one word: Luke's lawyers 'lade men with burdens grievous to be borne', and the Book of Mormon has 'laden'. Matthew's Pharisees 'bind heavy burdens', a verb the Book of Mormon does not use.
provenance.alternative: Nehemiah 5:14-18, catalogued at this verse, accounts for the office and the taxes; Luke accounts for the wording. Neither displaces the other.
provenance.significance: The woe is against religious leaders who load a people with what they will not carry themselves, and its sting is in the second clause: 'ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.' Benjamin's answer to that clause is the whole of 2:14 — not only did he not lade them, he laboured with his own hands. He is stating, of a king, the exact opposite of what Jesus says of the lawyers, phrase for phrase, and the borrowed phrase is what makes the contrast legible.

links.note: 'That ye should not be laden with taxes, and that there should nothing come upon you which was grievous to be borne.' Both of the KJV verses containing this phrase are the same woe against leaders, and the Book of Mormon's 'laden' is Luke's verb rather than Matthew's. What Benjamin denies having done to his people is precisely what Luke 11:46 accuses the lawyers of doing to theirs, and the denial sits in the same sentence as the labouring hands of Acts 20:34 — so the verse is built out of two New Testament passages about leaders and their hands.

links.text: Now that which was prepared for me daily was one ox and six choice sheep; also fowls were prepared for me, and once in ten days store of all sorts of wine: yet for all this required not I the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy upon this people.

provenance.other: “the bread of the governor” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Nehemiah 5:14 and 5:18. No wording is reproduced by the Book of Mormon; the case is entirely one of matching content, which is why kjvSpecific is 'uncertain' here and 'yes' on the Acts 20 rows.
provenance.alternative: Acts 20:33-34, catalogued at 2:12 and 2:14, accounts for the not-taking and the labouring on its own and does so with reproduced wording. Nehemiah is proposed for what Acts does not have: the taxes.

links.note: 'That ye should not be laden with taxes, and that there should nothing come upon you which was grievous to be borne.' Paul at Miletus refused money and worked with his hands; he did not levy anything, because he governed nothing. The one biblical ruler who defends himself in these terms is Nehemiah, who for twelve years 'required not I the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy upon this people', and whose predecessors 'were chargeable unto the people'. Benjamin's sentence needs both sources, and this half is Nehemiah's — the same book, and within seven chapters, of the assembly that gave the chapter its staging at 2:7 and 2:9.

pericopes.text: Yet, my brethren, I have not done these things that I might boast, neither do I tell these things that thereby I might accuse you; but I tell you these things, that ye may know that I can answer a clear conscience before God this day.

links.text: The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:

provenance.other: “the answer of a good conscience” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV's other conscience formulas are different: Acts 24:16's 'a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men', 2 Timothy 1:3's 'pure conscience', Hebrews 13:18's 'a good conscience'. Only 1 Peter 3:21 puts 'answer' and 'conscience' and 'toward God' in one phrase, which is the phrase Benjamin has.
provenance.significance: In 1 Peter the answer of a good conscience toward God is what baptism IS — the thing the water enacts, in a passage about a covenant made in the presence of God. Benjamin uses the phrase twice in the chapter, at 2:15 and again at 2:27 ('walking with a clear conscience before God'), and the second time it is the ground on which he convenes the assembly that will end, four chapters later, in a covenant and a new name. The Book of Mormon has borrowed a baptismal formula for a covenant-renewal scene, which is what Mosiah 5-6 turns out to be.

links.note: 'That I can answer a clear conscience before God this day.' 'Answer' as a verb governing 'conscience' is not ordinary English and not ordinary KJV; the noun phrase behind it is 1 Peter 3:21's, a singleton. Moderate rather than high because the Book of Mormon converts the noun to a verb and substitutes 'clear' for 'good', so what is shared is a construction rather than a string. The clause is also the point where the Acts 20 farewell and this borrowing coincide: Paul is 'pure from the blood', Benjamin is clear in conscience, and both say 'this day'.

pericopes.text: Behold, I say unto you, that because I said unto you that I had spent my days in your service, I do not desire to boast, for I have only been in the service of God.
And behold, I tell you these things, that ye may learn wisdom; that ye may learn that when ye are in the service of your fellow beings, ye are only in the service of your God.

links.text: And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.

provenance.alternative: Ephesians 6:7 ('with good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men') and Colossians 3:23-24 say something adjacent in words closer to Benjamin's 'service', and neither has Matthew's identification of the served person with the judge.
provenance.significance: The identity Benjamin states — service of your fellow beings IS service of your God — is stated once in the KJV, by a king on a throne separating sheep from goats, and it is stated there as the criterion of judgement. Benjamin is a king, speaking about the service a king owes and is owed, and the sentence he arrives at is the sentence Matthew's King speaks. Note also what Matthew 25:46 supplies two verses later and this chapter takes at 2:33: 'everlasting punishment', a KJV singleton. The judgement scene is being drawn on at both ends of the sermon.

links.note: 'When ye are in the service of your fellow beings, ye are only in the service of your God.' Nothing verbal is reproduced, which is why this is filed as figural; the argument is that the KJV makes this equation exactly once and makes it in a king's mouth. What Benjamin does with it is characteristic — Matthew's King identifies himself with the served, and Benjamin instead makes the service transitive, so that the debt he has just refused to claim (2:15-16) is redirected to God at 2:19-24.

pericopes.text: Behold, ye have called me your king; and if I, whom ye call your king, do labor to serve you, then had not ye ought to labor to serve one another?

And behold, also, if I, who ye call your king, who has spent his days in your service, and yet hath been in the service of God, doth merit any thanks from you, O how had you ought to thank your heavenly King!

I say unto you, my brethren, that if you should render all the thanks and praise which your whole souls hath power to possess, to that God who hath created you, and hath kept and preserved you, and hath caused that ye should rejoice, and hath granted that ye should live in peace one with another;

I say unto you, that if ye should serve him who hath created you from the beginning, and art preserving you from day to day, by lending you breath, that ye may live and move, and do according to your own will, and even supporting you from one moment to another; I say, if ye should serve him with all your whole soul, and yet ye would be unprofitable servants.

links.text: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.

provenance.other: “live and move” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Acts 17:25 supplies the other half of Benjamin's clause: God 'giveth to all life, and breath, and all things' — the breath, the life, and the not-needing-anything that Mosiah 2:21 turns into 'lending you breath, that ye may live and move'.
provenance.significance: Paul at Athens is arguing that God needs nothing from his worshippers, which is precisely Benjamin's argument in 2:20-25: you cannot put God in your debt, because the breath you would thank him with is on loan. Two verses of the Areopagus speech supply both terms, and a third supplies this chapter's 2:37 ('dwelleth not in temples made with hands'). The Book of Mormon has read Acts 17:24-28 as a unit and distributed it across a sermon about indebtedness — including the sting Paul's Greek audience would have felt and Benjamin's does too: the giver of breath is not housed in the building you are camped around.

links.note: 'Him who hath created you from the beginning, and art preserving you from day to day, by lending you breath, that ye may live and move.' The KJV says 'live, and move' once. Benjamin's addition is the metaphor of a loan, which converts Paul's ontological claim into an accounting one and sets up the ledger of 2:23-24 — created, granted, blessed, paid, and still indebted. The 1830 'art preserving' (for 'is preserving') is one of the first edition's ungrammatical readings that later editions smoothed; it does not bear on the source.

links.text: So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.

provenance.other: “unprofitable servants” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthew 25:30 has the singular 'unprofitable servant', of a man who buried his talent — a different case, since Luke's servants have done everything they were told.
provenance.significance: Luke 17:7-10 is a small parable with two moves, and Benjamin makes both. First, Luke 17:9: 'Doth he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded him? I trow not' — which is Mosiah 2:19-24's question about thanks and merit. Second, Luke 17:10: even after doing all that is commanded, the servant is unprofitable. Benjamin's version is harder than Luke's, because he inserts an infinite regress the parable does not have — God pays immediately, so obedience never closes the account and the debt grows: 'ye are still indebted unto him; and are, and will be, forever and ever'. The borrowed phrase is Luke's; the arithmetic is the Book of Mormon's.

links.note: 'If ye should serve him with all your whole soul, and yet ye would be unprofitable servants.' A KJV singleton reproduced with its logic intact — the conditional 'if ye should serve … and yet' is Luke 17:10's 'when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you' turned into a hypothetical. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because the clause and its argument are reproduced from an identifiable verse. Verse 24's 'of what have ye to boast?' completes Luke 17:9's question about thanks.

pericopes.text: And behold, all that he requires of you, is to keep his commandments; and he hath promised you that if ye would keep his commandments, ye should prosper in the land; and he never doth vary from that which he hath said; therefore, if ye do keep his commandments, he doth bless you, and prosper you.
And now, in the first place, he hath created you, and granted unto you your lives, for which ye are indebted unto him.

And secondly: He doth require that ye should do as he hath commanded you, for which if ye do, he doth immediately bless you; and therefore, he hath paid you. And ye are still indebted unto him; and are, and will be, forever and ever; therefore, of what have ye to boast?

And now I ask, Can ye say aught of yourselves? I answer you, Nay. Ye cannot say that thou art even as much as the dust of the earth; yet thou wast created of the dust of the earth: but behold, it belongeth to him who created you.

links.text: In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.

provenance.route: Genesis 2:7 and 3:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'The dust of the earth' occurs in nine KJV verses and cannot identify a source on its own; Genesis 2:7's formation is 'of the dust of the ground'. The reason for naming Genesis 3:19 rather than any of the nine is the return — Benjamin is 'about to yield up this mortal frame to its mother earth', which is 'unto dust shalt thou return' and nothing else.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's argument is a strange one and the strangeness is the point: you cannot say you are even as much as the dust, though you were made of it, because the dust belongs to its maker and you do not have even that standing. Genesis gives him both ends of the sentence — made of dust, returning to dust — and Abraham at Genesis 18:27 gives him its posture, 'I who am but dust and ashes', spoken while bargaining with God. Benjamin removes the bargaining position: Abraham's dust could still plead, and Benjamin's cannot claim.

links.note: 'Ye cannot say that thou art even as much as the dust of the earth; yet thou wast created of the dust of the earth: but behold, it belongeth to him who created you.' Filed as conceptual with kjvSpecific 'no' because every phrase here is common to all English Bibles; what makes it a link rather than an ambient biblicism is the pairing with 2:26, where the same speaker says 'I am also of the dust' and names his death as a yielding up to the earth, which completes Genesis 3:19's sentence in the order Genesis has it.

pericopes.text: And I, even I, whom ye call your king, am no better than ye yourselves are; for I am also of the dust. And thou beholdest that I am old, and am about to yield up this mortal frame to its mother earth;

therefore, as I said unto you that I had served you, walking with a clear conscience before God, even so I at this time have caused that ye should assemble yourselves together, that I might be found blameless, and that your blood should not come upon me, when I shall stand to be judged of God of the things whereof he hath commanded me concerning you.

links.text: Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.

provenance.route: Acts 20:26 (with Ezekiel 33:6) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “pure from the blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The idea is Ezekiel's watchman — if the watchman does not blow the trumpet, the blood of the slain 'will I require at the watchman's hand' (Ezekiel 33:6) — and Paul is applying Ezekiel to himself at Miletus. The Book of Mormon has Paul's application rather than Ezekiel's oracle: the leader declares himself clear, which Ezekiel never does.
provenance.significance: Benjamin gives two reasons for convening the assembly, and both are the reasons a departing teacher gives: 'that I might be found blameless, and that your blood should not come upon me, when I shall stand to be judged of God'. The clause 'this day' at 2:14, the innocence of blood here, and the farewell at 2:29 are Acts 20:26, 20:34 and 20:25 in the source's own order. What Benjamin adds to Paul is the judgement scene — the reckoning is not merely declared, it is dated to a future court.

links.note: 'That I might be found blameless, and that your blood should not come upon me, when I shall stand to be judged of God.' The formula is Paul's at Miletus, where it is a KJV singleton, and behind Paul stands Ezekiel's watchman. This is the fourth of the five Acts 20 contacts in this chapter; the fifth is the farewell at 2:29, and 2:28's 'rid my garments of your blood' takes the same idea to a different verse of Acts, catalogued there.

pericopes.text: I say unto you, that I have caused that ye should assemble yourselves together, that I might rid my garments of your blood, at this period of time when I am about to go down to my grave, that I might go down in peace, and my immortal spirit may join the choirs above in singing the praises of a just God.

links.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

provenance.other: “shook his raiment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Nehemiah 5:13 shakes a lap and Acts 13:51 shakes dust from feet; only Acts 18:6 shakes a garment and pairs the gesture with blood on the hearers' heads and the speaker's own cleanness.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's phrase is unintelligible without Acts 18:6 and immediately clear with it. 'Rid my garments of your blood' is not a figure the Old Testament uses — blood is on heads, or required at hands — and the only place in the KJV where a garment is shaken to disclaim responsibility for a people's blood is Paul at Corinth. That the Book of Mormon has both halves of the Pauline blood-idiom in consecutive verses (Acts 20:26's purity at 2:27, Acts 18:6's shaken garment at 2:28) is the kind of double contact that makes a single one credible.

links.note: 'That I might rid my garments of your blood, at this period of time when I am about to go down to my grave, that I might go down in peace.' The garment-and-blood gesture is Acts 18:6's, a KJV singleton, and it arrives one verse after Acts 20:26's 'pure from the blood'. The Book of Mormon has made a gesture of rejection into a gesture of discharge — Paul shakes his raiment at people who have refused him, Benjamin at people who have obeyed him.

links.text: Do therefore according to thy wisdom, and let not his hoar head go down to the grave in peace.

provenance.other: “to the grave in peace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 2 Kings 22:20 has 'thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace', of Josiah, with 'gathered into' rather than 'go down to'; Genesis 42:38 and 44:29 bring gray hairs 'with sorrow to the grave' and lack the peace.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's quiet return to 1 Kings 2. Mosiah 1:9 took David's 'I go the way of all the earth' from 1 Kings 2:2; four verses later in the same charge, David tells Solomon not to let Joab's hoar head go down to the grave in peace, and it is that phrase — negated in the source, affirmed here — that Benjamin uses of his own death. Read together, Benjamin has taken David's deathbed speech and kept for himself the peace David denied his enemy. The Book of Mormon has quarried one chapter of 1 Kings twice in two chapters of Mosiah.

links.note: 'At this period of time when I am about to go down to my grave, that I might go down in peace.' A KJV singleton, and its one occurrence is in David's charge to Solomon — the passage Mosiah 1:9 already used. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because the phrase is idiomatic enough to have been written without a source and because its sense in 1 Kings 2:6 is inverted; the argument for it is proximity in the source to a borrowing already established one chapter earlier.

pericopes.text: And moreover, I say unto you, that I have caused that ye should assemble yourselves together, that I might declare unto you that I can no longer be your teacher, nor your king;

for even at this time, my whole frame doth tremble exceedingly, while attempting to speak unto you; but the Lord God doth support me, and hath suffered me that I should speak unto you, and hath commanded me that I should declare unto you this day, that my son Mosiah, is a king and a ruler over you.

And now, my brethren, I would that ye should do as ye hath hitherto done. As ye have kept my commandments, and also the commandments of my father, and have prospered, and have been kept from falling into the hands of your enemies, even so if ye shall keep the commandments of my son, or the commandments of God, which shall be delivered unto you by him, ye shall prosper in the land, and your enemies shall have no power over you.
But O my people, beware lest there shall arise contentions among you, and ye list to obey the evil spirit, which was spoken of by my father Mosiah.

For behold, there is a wo pronounced upon him who listeth to obey that spirit; for if he listeth to obey him, and remaineth and dieth in his sins, the same drinketh damnation to his own soul; for he receiveth for his wages an everlasting punishment, having transgressed the law of God, contrary to his own knowledge.

links.text: For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

provenance.other: “drinketh damnation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's 'to his own soul' replaces Paul's 'to himself'; the verb and its object are otherwise Paul's exactly, and the metaphor of drinking a judgement has no other KJV home.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is about the Lord's Supper — a covenant meal taken unworthily, by a congregation that has assembled and not discerned what it is assembled for. Benjamin is presiding over an assembly that is about to become a covenant (Mosiah 5), his people are camped around the temple with their sacrifices already offered (2:3), and the warning he issues to anyone who listeth to obey the evil spirit is the warning Paul issues to the unworthy communicant. The metalepsis is exact: the danger of an assembly is that some of those present will drink their own damnation at it.

links.note: 'The same drinketh damnation to his own soul.' A KJV singleton lifted whole, with the possessive changed. The verse then continues into two further borrowings — 'he receiveth for his wages an everlasting punishment', where 'wages' is Romans 6:23's figure and 'everlasting punishment' is Matthew 25:46's singleton, catalogued separately at this verse — so 2:33 carries three New Testament judgement formulas in one sentence.

links.text: And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.

provenance.route: Matthew 25:46 (with Romans 6:23) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “everlasting punishment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'The wages of' occurs in three, of which Romans 6:23 ('the wages of sin is death') is the only one that makes a punishment a wage. 'Die in your sins' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 8:24 twice over, which is the source of 'remaineth and dieth in his sins'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 25 is being used at both ends of this sermon: verse 40's identification of service with service of the King stands behind Mosiah 2:17, and verse 46's sentence stands here. The Book of Mormon fuses it with Romans 6:23, and the fusion changes the theology — Matthew's punishment is a destination one is sent to, Paul's death is a wage one has earned, and Benjamin's is both: 'he receiveth for his wages an everlasting punishment'. That is the same accounting metaphor the chapter has run since 2:23, now applied to the debtor who defaults.

links.note: 'For he receiveth for his wages an everlasting punishment, having transgressed the law of God, contrary to his own knowledge.' Three New Testament formulas meet in the verse — Paul's wage, Matthew's everlasting punishment, John 8:24's dying in one's sins — and each is a KJV singleton or near it. What the Book of Mormon supplies is the aggravation, 'contrary to his own knowledge', which none of the three has and which the whole chapter has been establishing since 2:34's claim that everyone present has been taught.

pericopes.text: I say unto you, that there are not one among you, except it be your little children, that have not been taught concerning these things; but what knoweth that ye are eternally indebted to your Heavenly Father, to render to him all that you have, and are, and also have been taught, concerning the records which contain the prophecies which hath been spoken by the Holy Prophets, even down to the time our father Lehi left Jerusalem;
and also, all that hath been spoken by our fathers, until now. And behold, also, they spake that which was commanded them of the Lord; therefore, they are just and true.

And now, I say unto you, my brethren, that after ye have known and have been taught all these things, if ye should transgress, and go contrary to that which hath been spoken, that ye do withdraw yourselves from the Spirit of the Lord, that it may have no place in you to guide you in wisdom’s paths, that ye may be blessed, prospered, and preserved.

I say unto you, that the man that doeth this, the same cometh out in open rebellion against God; therefore, he listeth to obey the evil spirit, and becometh an enemy to all righteousness; therefore, the Lord hath no place in him, for he dwelleth not in unholy temples.

links.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

provenance.other: “enemy of all righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reads 'an enemy to all righteousness', with 'to' for 'of'; no other KJV verse contains the phrase in either preposition.
