provenance.significance: Acts 13:10 is Paul's denunciation of Elymas the sorcerer, and the two charges it makes are the two Benjamin makes here: the man is a child of the devil, and he is the enemy of all righteousness. Benjamin's version supplies the mechanism Acts leaves implicit — 'he listeth to obey the evil spirit' — so that becoming the enemy of all righteousness is presented as a chosen allegiance rather than a character. That is the doctrine of the whole passage, from 2:32's warning about listing to obey to 2:33's 'contrary to his own knowledge'.

links.note: 'The same cometh out in open rebellion against God; therefore, he listeth to obey the evil spirit, and becometh an enemy to all righteousness.' A KJV singleton with one preposition changed, taken from the KJV's fiercest denunciation of a man in league with the devil. 'Open rebellion' is in no KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own; the borrowed phrase is what gives the sentence its scriptural force.

links.text: Howbeit the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands; as saith the prophet,

provenance.route: Acts 7:48 / Acts 17:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 7:48 and Acts 17:24, and in both it is a New Testament speaker's gloss on Isaiah 66:1-2. The Old Testament itself never puts it this way; Isaiah asks 'where is the house that ye build unto me?', whose mediation was decided at 1 Nephi 17:39. Which of the two Acts verses is in view cannot be settled from the wording, since they are identical at every point the Book of Mormon reproduces.
provenance.significance: The sentence is doing something audacious in its setting. Benjamin is speaking from a tower at a temple, to a people camped in a ring around that temple with the doors of their tents turned toward it, and the doctrine he states is that the Lord does not dwell in unholy temples — with 'temple' meaning the man. Acts supplies the formula in both of its occurrences, and 1 Corinthians 3:16-17 supplies the transfer to the person ('ye are the temple of God'; 'if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy'), which is the sense Benjamin has. The Areopagus verse is also the one that gave 2:21 its breath and motion, so the chapter takes both halves of Acts 17:24-28.

links.note: 'Therefore, the Lord hath no place in him, for he dwelleth not in unholy temples.' The KJV's phrase appears twice, both times in Acts, and the Book of Mormon compresses it — 'unholy temples' for 'temples made with hands' — which shifts the object from a building to a person and requires 1 Corinthians 3:16-17 to complete the thought. Moderate because the compression leaves only three words in common; the case is that the sentence cannot be assembled from the Old Testament, where this doctrine exists as a rhetorical question and not as a proposition.

pericopes.text: Therefore, if that man repenteth not, and remaineth and dieth an enemy to God, the demands of Divine Justice doth awaken his immortal soul to a lively sense of his own guilt, which doth cause him to shrink from the presence of the Lord, and doth fill his breast with guilt, and pain, and anguish, which is like an unquenchable fire, whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever.

links.text: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

provenance.other: “ascendeth up for ever and ever” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Revelation 19:3 has 'her smoke rose up for ever and ever', in the past tense and of Babylon; only 14:11 has the present participle-form the Book of Mormon uses, and only 14:11 attaches it to torment rather than to a burning city.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:11-12 is used as a unit across four verses of this chapter, in the source's order. Verse 11's ascending torment is Mosiah 2:38's 'flames ascendeth up forever and ever'; verse 12's 'here are they that keep the commandments of God' is Mosiah 2:41's 'those that keep the commandments of God'. Revelation places the endurance of the saints immediately after the smoke of the damned as a deliberate contrast, and Benjamin's peroration does the same thing at the same interval: the awful situation of the fallen at 2:40, the blessed and happy state of the obedient at 2:41.

links.note: 'Which is like an unquenchable fire, whose flames ascendeth up forever and ever.' A KJV singleton, with the 1830's uninflected 'ascendeth' after a plural subject preserving the source's verb form more exactly than the corrected text does. Note that the same verse of Revelation is cross-referenced by Hardy at Mosiah 3:27, one chapter later; the borrowing catalogued here is a separate and earlier occurrence of it.

links.text: Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

provenance.other: “unquenchable fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; Luke 3:17 renders the same saying of John the Baptist as 'fire unquenchable', in the other word order, and Mark 9:43-48 has 'the fire that never shall be quenched'. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's order.
provenance.significance: John the Baptist's fire is a threshing image — the chaff separated from the wheat and burned — and it is about a judgement that is coming, not one already in progress. Benjamin uses the phrase for something internal and present: guilt and pain and anguish in the breast of a man who has not repented, 'which is like an unquenchable fire'. The simile is the Book of Mormon's own move; what it borrows is the adjective, and the adjective in the KJV belongs to one verse.

links.note: 'Doth fill his breast with guilt, and pain, and anguish, which is like an unquenchable fire.' Moderate rather than high: a single compound adjective is thin evidence, and Mark and Luke both say something close in different words. It is filed as a link rather than passed over because the Book of Mormon has Matthew's exact form, and because the second half of the same clause takes another judgement singleton from Revelation 14:11.

pericopes.text: And now I say unto you, that mercy hath no claim on that man; therefore, his final doom is to endure a never ending torment.

O all ye old men, and also ye young men, and you little children, which can understand my words, (for I have spoken plain unto you, that ye might understand,) I pray that ye should awake to a remembrance of the awful situation of those that have fallen into transgression;

and moreover, I would desire that ye should consider on the blessed and happy state of those that keep the commandments of God. For behold, they are blessed in all things, both temporal and spiritual; and if they hold out faithful to the end, they are received into Heaven, that thereby they may dwell with God, in a state of never ending happiness. O remember, remember that these things are true; for the Lord God hath spoken it.

links.text: Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.

provenance.other: “keep the commandments of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 12:17 and Revelation 14:12 — the phrase the Book of Mormon uses constantly belongs, in this exact form, to the Apocalypse. Revelation 14:12 is the one that stands next to a description of endless torment.
provenance.significance: The pairing is the argument. Mosiah 2:38-41 sets the never-ending torment of the unrepentant against the never-ending happiness of those who keep the commandments and 'hold out faithful to the end', and it does so in four verses; Revelation 14:11-12 sets the smoke that ascends for ever against the patience of the saints who keep the commandments of God, and it does so in two. Both make endurance the answer to endlessness, and both use the same two phrases to do it. Benjamin's 'hold out faithful to the end' is what Revelation calls the patience of the saints.

links.note: 'Those that keep the commandments of God … and if they hold out faithful to the end, they are received into Heaven, that thereby they may dwell with God, in a state of never ending happiness.' The phrase is one of two KJV occurrences, and the other, Revelation 12:17, is in a war passage with nothing else in common. The case for 14:12 is its position: the Book of Mormon reproduces Revelation's own sequence, torment then endurance, across the same short span. Moderate because 'keep the commandments of God' had by Mosiah long since become the Book of Mormon's own idiom.

pericopes.text: And again my brethren, I would call your attention, for I have somewhat more to speak unto you: for behold, I have things to tell you, concerning that which is to come;
and the things which I shall tell you, are made known unto me, by an Angel from God. And he said unto me, Awake; and I awoke, and behold, he stood before me.
And he said unto me, Awake, and hear the words which I shall tell thee: for behold, I am come to declare unto you the glad tidings of great joy.

links.text: And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.

provenance.route: Luke 2:10 with Luke 1:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “tidings of great joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Luke 2:10, the angel over Bethlehem — where the adjective is 'good'. “glad tidings” occurs in exactly four KJV verses; the one that matters is Luke 1:19, where Gabriel says he is sent 'to shew thee these glad tidings'. The Book of Mormon's 'glad tidings of great joy' is the two phrases welded together, and it exists in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Both halves of the conflation come from angels announcing the same birth, forty verses apart in the same gospel, and Mosiah 3:2-4 is doing what both Lucan annunciations do. Gabriel stands before Zacharias, says his prayer is heard, and brings glad tidings; the angel of Luke 2 says fear not and brings tidings of great joy to be declared to all people. Benjamin's angel stands before him (3:2), tells him the Lord has heard his prayers (3:4), brings glad tidings of great joy, and tells him to declare them to his people so they may be filled with joy. The Book of Mormon has taken Luke's two annunciation scenes and made one out of them, in the chapter that will name Mary four verses later.

links.note: 'I am come to declare unto you the glad tidings of great joy.' A KJV singleton with one adjective replaced from a second angelic speech in the same gospel. The tell that this is a fusion rather than an approximation is that Luke 2:10's 'good tidings' and Luke 1:19's 'glad tidings' are both fixed KJV phrases, and the Book of Mormon has the one whose noun-phrase belongs to the other. The next verse then supplies Luke 1:13's 'thy prayer is heard' as 'the Lord hath heard thy prayers'.

pericopes.text: For the Lord hath heard thy prayers, and hath judged of thy righteousness, and hath sent me to declare unto thee that thou mayest rejoice; and that thou mayest declare unto thy people, that they may also be filled with joy.

For behold, the time cometh, and is not far distant, that with power, the Lord Omnipotent who reigneth, which was, and is from all eternity to all eternity, shall come down from Heaven, among the children of men, and shall dwell in a tabernacle of clay, and shall go forth amongst men, working mighty miracles, such as healing the sick, raising the dead, causing the lame to walk, the blind to receive their sight, and the deaf to hear, and curing all manner of diseases;

links.text: And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.

provenance.other: “omnipotent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, in the whole Bible, and the Book of Mormon's clause reproduces its two neighbouring words as well: 'the Lord God omnipotent reigneth' → 'the Lord Omnipotent who reigneth'. Every one of the title's five occurrences in Benjamin's sermon descends from this one verse.
provenance.significance: The title Benjamin's angel gives Christ — used five times in this sermon and almost nowhere else in the Book of Mormon — is a hapax of the King James Bible. It occurs at Revelation 19:6, in the hallelujah of the great multitude at the marriage of the Lamb, which is a shout of acclamation rather than a name. The Book of Mormon has converted a liturgical cry into a christological title, and then built a covenant liturgy around it: at Mosiah 5:2 the assembled people answer 'with one voice', which is what Revelation 19:6 describes. The sermon takes the multitude's shout and gives it to the multitude.

links.note: 'The Lord Omnipotent who reigneth, which was, and is from all eternity to all eternity.' An English word that appears in the KJV once, taken with the participle attached to it there. That an angel in 124 BC should name Christ with a word the English Bible uses only in the Apocalypse is precisely the kind of anachronism this catalogue exists to record; the 1830 text capitalizes it as a title, which the later editions retain.

links.text: The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.

provenance.other: “receive their sight” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The mediation test is decisive and turns on two words. Matthew 11:5 and Luke 7:22 are the same answer to John's disciples in two gospels, and they differ at the first item: Matthew has 'the blind receive their sight', Luke has 'the blind see'. tools/mediation-check.py on Mosiah 3:5 reports one decisive point, for Matthew — the Book of Mormon reads 'the blind to receive their sight'. Isaiah 35:5-6 is the Old Testament root of the list ('the eyes of the blind shall be opened … then shall the lame man leap as an hart') and shares none of this wording.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's angel is describing miracles a century and a quarter before they happen, in the words Jesus used to describe them after they had happened — and specifically in the words of the answer to John the Baptist, which is itself a claim that Isaiah 35 has been fulfilled. Recover Matthew 11's context and the borrowing acquires an argument: the list exists in the gospel as evidence offered to a doubter about whether this is 'he that should come'. Mosiah 3 offers the same list, to the same purpose, before the fact.

links.note: 'Working mighty miracles, such as healing the sick, raising the dead, causing the lame to walk, the blind to receive their sight, and the deaf to hear.' Four items of Matthew's list, reordered and turned into infinitives, with the KJV's distinctive 'receive their sight' preserved. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because the content of an identifiable verse is reproduced item by item. Hardy's apparatus cross-references both gospels here; the wording decides for Matthew.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Mosiah 3.5 (cross-references Matthew 11:5 and Luke 7:22)

links.text: How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, which are crushed before the moth?

provenance.route: Job 4:19 with 2 Corinthians 5:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “houses of clay” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the KJV's only figure for the body as a clay dwelling. The body as a tabernacle is Paul's and Peter's — 2 Corinthians 5:1's 'our earthly house of this tabernacle', 2 Peter 1:13's 'as long as I am in this tabernacle', already drawn on at Mosiah 2:17. 'Tabernacle of clay' fuses the two and is in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The compound is a small but exact instance of what this chapter does throughout: an Old Testament figure and a New Testament figure welded into one phrase that neither testament contains. Job's houses of clay are an argument about human frailty made by Eliphaz to prove that no man is pure before God; Paul's tabernacle is an argument that the frailty is temporary. Applied to the incarnation — God 'shall dwell in a tabernacle of clay' — the fused phrase makes the Lord Omnipotent of the previous clause take on Eliphaz's crushable house.

links.note: 'Shall come down from Heaven, among the children of men, and shall dwell in a tabernacle of clay.' Recorded as an echo because neither source phrase is reproduced intact; what is reproduced is the KJV's two metaphors for the body, joined. Job 4:19's is a singleton, which is what makes 'clay' traceable at all — the KJV's other clay is a potter's.

pericopes.text: and he shall cast out Devils, or the evil spirits which dwelleth in the hearts of the children of men.

And lo, he shall suffer temptations, and pain of body, hunger, thirst, and fatigue, even more than man can suffer, except it be unto death: for behold, blood cometh from every pore, so great shall be his anguish for the wickedness and the abominations of his people.

links.text: And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.

provenance.other: “great drops of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Luke 22:44 is the only place in the Bible where blood and sweat are joined at all. 'Pore' occurs in no KJV verse, and 'anguish' is not Luke's word — Luke has 'agony', another KJV rarity.
provenance.significance: Luke's sentence is a simile and hedged twice over — his sweat was AS IT WERE great drops of blood — and the Book of Mormon removes both hedges: 'blood cometh from every pore'. That is an interpretation of Luke, not a repetition of him, and it is the interpretation that became standard in nineteenth-century English devotional writing. What the Book of Mormon adds beyond the physical detail is the cause: Luke gives the agony no object, and Mosiah 3:7 supplies one — 'so great shall be his anguish for the wickedness and the abominations of his people' — which makes Gethsemane rather than Golgotha the place where the suffering for sin is done.

links.note: 'For behold, blood cometh from every pore, so great shall be his anguish.' No wording is reproduced, which is why this is filed as conceptual; the case is that the KJV contains exactly one verse in which a man bleeds under mental suffering, and the Book of Mormon is describing that verse without quoting it. The surrounding list — temptations, pain of body, hunger, thirst, fatigue — is the Book of Mormon's own and matches no passion narrative.

pericopes.text: And he shall be called Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Father of Heaven and Earth, the creator of all things, from the beginning; and his mother shall be called Mary.

links.text: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God;

provenance.route: Mark 1:1 / Acts 8:37 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Jesus Christ the Son of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 1:1; Acts 8:37's confession inserts a verb ('Jesus Christ IS the Son of God') and is therefore a different string. 'Jesus Christ, the Son of God' is the title formula of Mark 1:1 and the baptismal confession of Acts 8:37; the KJV has it in that exact form at those two places. Our index of Frederick (data/frederick-refs.json, built by tools/parse-frederick.py) records that Mosiah 3:8 is discussed within his book near both of them — but that index measures CO-OCCURRENCE, which is to say that these passages appear close together in his argument, and it is not a claim that Frederick derives this verse from either. His subject is the Gospel of John. No citation is made from it here for that reason.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 3:8 is the first place in the Book of Mormon where the full name 'Jesus Christ' is given as a prophecy of what the Messiah 'shall be called', and it comes with the two titles the KJV attaches to that name at the opening of a gospel and at the moment of a convert's baptism. What follows in the same verse — Father of Heaven and Earth, creator of all things from the beginning — is not Mark's or Luke's but Colossians 1:16 and John 1:3, so the sentence assembles a full christological title out of scattered New Testament formulas and then adds the human detail, 'his mother shall be called Mary', which no title formula has.

links.note: 'And he shall be called Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Father of Heaven and Earth, the creator of all things, from the beginning; and his mother shall be called Mary.' The title as the Book of Mormon gives it is a KJV singleton — Mark 1:1's, exactly, without the copula that Acts 8:37 inserts — which is stronger evidence than the formula's familiarity in New Testament English would suggest. The rest of the sentence is a compilation rather than a borrowing. It is catalogued rather than passed over because the verse is one of the four Frederick rows for this book (PLAN §7.3 as restated) and because the naming of Mary makes it the chapter's most conspicuous anachronism.

pericopes.text: And lo, he cometh unto his own, that salvation might come unto the children of men, even through faith on his name; and even after all this, they shall consider him a man, and say that he hath a Devil, and shall scourge him, and shall crucify him.

links.text: He came unto his own, and his own received him not.

provenance.other: “he came unto his own” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has the present tense, 'he cometh unto his own', because the angel is speaking of what has not yet happened; every other word of the clause is John's.
provenance.significance: John 1:11 is a two-part sentence and the Book of Mormon uses both parts, split across the verse. 'He cometh unto his own' is the first half; 'they shall consider him a man, and say that he hath a Devil, and shall scourge him, and shall crucify him' is what the Fourth Gospel's 'his own received him not' turns out to mean, spelled out in the gospels' own vocabulary — 'he hath a devil' is John 10:20's charge. The angel is narrating the Johannine prologue forward into the passion.

links.note: 'And lo, he cometh unto his own, that salvation might come unto the children of men … and even after all this, they shall consider him a man, and say that he hath a Devil.' Five words of a KJV singleton with only the tense changed, and the rejection that John states abstractly is given in the terms of the gospel narratives. The passion verbs in the same verse come from a different gospel and are catalogued separately at this verse.

links.text: And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him: and the third day he shall rise again.

provenance.route: Mark 10:33-34 with Matthew 20:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: A conflation, and the mediation tool should not be trusted alone on it. Running Mosiah 3:9 against Matthew 20:19 and Mark 10:34 returns one 'decisive' point for Mark, on the word 'scourge' — but Matthew has 'scourge' too, and the tool has simply aligned Mark's 'scourge' against Matthew's 'deliver'. Read by eye the division is clean: the SYNTAX is Mark's, whose third passion prediction runs 'and shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him' in finite verbs with the auxiliary repeated, which is exactly the Book of Mormon's 'and shall scourge him, and shall crucify him'; the VERB is Matthew's, since Mark's fourth item is 'kill' and only Matthew 20:19 has 'crucify'. “to scourge and to crucify” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:19, and the Book of Mormon does not have that infinitive form.
provenance.significance: Two versions of the same prediction, one supplying the shape of the sentence and the other the manner of the death. What is worth noticing is which detail the Book of Mormon drops: both gospels have the mocking and the spitting, and Mosiah 3:9 keeps only the two acts that are judicial — scourging and crucifixion — because its interest is in a verdict rather than in humiliation. The verse's whole argument is that the world will judge him ('they shall consider him a man') so that at 3:10 'he standeth to judge the world'.

links.note: 'And shall scourge him, and shall crucify him.' Mark's construction with Matthew's verb, from the two synoptic passion predictions that stand at the same point in each gospel. The link is filed under Mark because the repeated 'and shall' auxiliary is his and is the more distinctive feature; Matthew supplies 'crucify', which Mark does not have anywhere in the prediction. Flagged as a conflation rather than a choice, so the mediation is not being represented as decided when it is not.

pericopes.text: And he shall rise the third day from the dead; and behold, he standeth to judge the world. And behold, all these things are done, that a righteous judgment might come upon the children of men.

links.text: For he taught his disciples, and said unto them, The Son of man is delivered into the hands of men, and they shall kill him; and after that he is killed, he shall rise the third day.

provenance.route: Mark 9:31 with Luke 24:46 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “he shall rise the third day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Matthew 20:19 and Mark 10:34 both read 'the third day he shall rise again', in the other order and with 'again'; Luke 24:46 reads 'to rise from the dead the third day', which supplies the Book of Mormon's 'from the dead' but not its word order. Running the mediation tool on Mosiah 3:10 against Mark 9:31 and Luke 24:46 returns a 'decisive' point for Luke on the word 'dead' — that is an artifact of the alignment, since the Book of Mormon has Mark's clause AND Luke's phrase, and the tool has nowhere to put the surplus.
provenance.significance: Four KJV verses predict the resurrection on the third day and the Book of Mormon has taken the one clause that is unique to Mark and then appended Luke's prepositional phrase, producing 'he shall rise the third day from the dead' — a sentence that exists in no gospel. This is the third conflation in two verses, after the Mark-and-Matthew passion at 3:9 and the two Lucan annunciations at 3:3, which is worth stating as a pattern: the angel's speech does not quote a gospel, it composes from all four.

links.note: 'And he shall rise the third day from the dead; and behold, he standeth to judge the world.' The clause is Mark 9:31's, a KJV singleton, with Luke 24:46's 'from the dead' added after it rather than before. The judgement that follows in the same verse is not from any resurrection prediction; it is the chapter's own turn, and it sets up the judgement-seat material of 3:24-27.

pericopes.text: For behold, and also his blood atoneth for the sins of those who have fallen by the transgression of Adam, who hath died, not knowing the will of God concerning them, or who have ignorantly sinned.
But wo, wo unto him who knoweth that he rebelleth against God: for salvation cometh to none such, except it be through repentance and faith on the Lord Jesus Christ.

And the Lord God hath sent his Holy Prophets among all the children of men, to declare these things to every kindred, nation, and tongue, that thereby whosoever should believe that Christ should come, the same might receive remission of their sins, and rejoice with exceeding great joy, even as though he had already come among them.
Yet the Lord God saw that his people were a stiffnecked people, and he appointed unto them a law, even the law of Moses.

And many signs, and wonders, and types, and shadows shewed he unto them, concerning his coming; and also Holy Prophets spake unto them concerning his coming; and yet they hardened their hearts, and understood not that the law of Moses availeth nothing, except it were through the atonement of his blood;

links.text: For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.

provenance.route: Hebrews 10:1 with Colossians 2:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “a shadow of good things to come” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Shadow' used of the law of Moses occurs in three KJV verses — Colossians 2:17 ('a shadow of things to come'), Hebrews 8:5 ('the example and shadow of heavenly things'), Hebrews 10:1 ('a shadow of good things to come'). 'Types' is in no KJV verse in this sense; 'availeth nothing' is not a KJV phrase either, though Galatians 5:6 and 6:15 have 'availeth any thing' of circumcision.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 3:14-15 states the New Testament's argument about the law of Moses in the New Testament's own figures and gives it a Book of Mormon chronology. Galatians 3:19 supplies the reason the law was given — 'it was added because of transgressions' — which becomes 'the Lord God saw that his people were a stiffnecked people, and he appointed unto them a law'. Hebrews and Colossians supply the shadow. What the Book of Mormon adds is the claim that the shadow was legible at the time: the prophets 'spake unto them concerning his coming', and the failure at 3:15 is not that the types were obscure but that the hearers 'hardened their hearts'.

links.note: 'And many signs, and wonders, and types, and shadows shewed he unto them, concerning his coming … and understood not that the law of Moses availeth nothing, except it were through the atonement of his blood.' No clause is reproduced, so this is conceptual and moderate; the pairing 'types and shadows' has become so standard in later usage that it is easy to forget the KJV never uses it. The catalogued source is the passage that makes the argument, not a phrase — the law as shadow, insufficient of itself, pointing at a coming reality.

pericopes.text: and even if it were possible that little children could sin, they could not be saved; but I say unto you, they are blessed: for behold, as in Adam, or by nature they fall, even so the blood of Christ atoneth for their sins.

And moreover, I say unto you, that there shall be no other name given, nor no other way nor means whereby salvation can come unto the children of men, only in and through the name of Christ, the Lord Omnipotent.

links.text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.

provenance.other: “none other name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “whereby we must be saved” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Acts 4:12, both of them. The Book of Mormon reproduces the structure of the whole sentence: the exclusive negative, the name, and the relative clause of salvation.
provenance.significance: Acts 4:12 is Peter's answer before the Sanhedrin to the question 'by what name have ye done this?', and its force there is forensic — a defendant naming the only authority he will plead. Mosiah 3:17 is the hinge of Benjamin's sermon and does the same work in advance: it is the verse the covenant of Mosiah 5 will be made under, where the people take upon them the name of Christ because 'there is no other name given whereby salvation cometh' (5:8). The Book of Mormon has taken the New Testament's most exclusive claim about the name of Jesus and made it the ground of a covenant taken a century before the name was given.

links.note: 'There shall be no other name given, nor no other way nor means whereby salvation can come unto the children of men, only in and through the name of Christ.' Two KJV singletons from one verse, in their source order, with 'given' and the salvation clause intact; the 1830 double negative 'nor no other way' is the first edition's own. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because the sentence's whole structure is reproduced from an identifiable verse.

pericopes.text: For behold, he judgeth, and his judgment is just, and the infant perisheth not, that dieth in his infancy; but men drinketh damnation to their own souls, except they humble themselves, and become as little children, and believeth that salvation was, and is, and is to come, in and through the atoning blood of Christ, the Lord Omnipotent:

links.text: And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.

provenance.other: “become as little children” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Mark 10:15 and Luke 18:17 have 'receive the kingdom of God as a little child', which is a different construction, and Matthew 19:14's 'suffer little children' is a different saying.
provenance.significance: Matthew 18:3-4 has two parts and Mosiah 3 uses both: become as little children, and 'whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child' is the greatest. Benjamin's 'except they humble themselves, and become as little children' fuses the two verses into one clause. The chapter then does something Matthew does not — it makes the child a doctrine as well as a model, ruling at 3:16 and 3:18 and 3:21 that little children are saved without repentance because they cannot sin, and at 3:19 that the natural man's conversion is precisely becoming 'as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient'. Matthew's simile is turned into an anthropology.

links.note: 'Except they humble themselves, and become as little children.' A KJV singleton with Matthew 18:4's humbling folded into it. Note that the same sentence contains 'drinketh damnation to their own souls', which is 1 Corinthians 11:29's singleton phrase already catalogued at Mosiah 2:33 and repeated again at 3:25 — so the phrase is by now the sermon's own idiom rather than a fresh borrowing.

links.text: And the four beasts had each of them six wings about him; and they were full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, LORD God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come.

provenance.other: “which was and is and is to come” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Revelation 1:4 and 1:8 have the same three tenses in a different order and with the relative repeated — 'which is, and which was, and which is to come' — and the Book of Mormon has Revelation 4:8's order, was before is, which is the odd one.
provenance.significance: The eternity formula and the omnipotence title come from the same book and are used in the same sermon: Revelation 19:6 at 3:5 and Revelation 4:8 here, both of them acclamations sung by the worshippers around the throne rather than statements about God. The Book of Mormon has taken two liturgical shouts of the Apocalypse and made them the vocabulary of an angel's christology. And it has moved the formula's object: in Revelation the three tenses describe the Lord God Almighty, and at Mosiah 3:18 they describe salvation — 'that salvation was, and is, and is to come' — so an attribute of God has been predicated of what God does.

links.note: 'Believeth that salvation was, and is, and is to come, in and through the atoning blood of Christ.' Seven words of a KJV singleton in its exact and unusual order, which is what identifies the verse: the two commoner forms at Revelation 1:4 and 1:8 put 'is' first. The same formula stands in shortened form at 3:5, 'which was, and is from all eternity to all eternity', where the Book of Mormon supplies its own second half.

pericopes.text: for the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been, from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever; but if he yieldeth to the enticings of the Holy Spirit, and putteth off the natural man, and becometh a saint, through the atonement of Christ, the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love, willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon him, even as a child doth submit to his father.

links.text: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 2:14 with Romans 8:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “natural man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The predicate is supplied from elsewhere in Paul: Romans 8:7's 'the carnal mind is enmity against God', and James 4:4's 'the enemy of God'. The KJV never calls the natural man an enemy to God; the Book of Mormon's most quoted sentence is a fusion of a Corinthian noun with a Roman predicate.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 2:14 is an epistemological claim — the natural man cannot RECEIVE the things of the Spirit, because they are spiritually discerned — and Romans 8:7 is a moral one, that the carnal mind is hostile and cannot submit. Mosiah 3:19 keeps Romans's hostility and Corinthians's noun, and then answers Romans 8:7's 'not subject to the law of God' with its own remedy: the man who is put off becomes 'submissive … willing to submit to all things'. The sentence is built so that the cure is the exact negation of the diagnosis, and both halves are Pauline.

links.note: 'For the natural man is an enemy to God, and has been, from the fall of Adam, and will be, forever and ever.' A KJV singleton given a predicate the KJV attaches to a different subject. What the Book of Mormon adds is the temporal frame — from the fall, and forever — which converts Paul's description of an unconverted person into a statement about the human condition since Adam, and which the second half of the verse then undoes.

links.text: Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds;

provenance.other: “put off the old man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; Ephesians 4:22 has 'put off concerning the former conversation the old man', with the object separated from the verb. Colossians 3:12's list is 'bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering', which is Mosiah 3:19's 'meek, humble, patient, full of love' item for item in the same order — meekness, humbleness, longsuffering, charity — with only the nouns turned into adjectives.
provenance.significance: The whole sequence of Colossians 3:9-12 is reproduced in one sentence and in the source's order: put off the old man (3:9), put on the new (3:10), as the elect of God, holy (3:12) → 'becometh a saint', and then the five virtues. The Book of Mormon's one substitution is the one that matters — 'the natural man' for 'the old man' — which imports 1 Corinthians 2:14's noun into a Colossian sentence and produces the phrase the book is best known for. Colossians 3:11's 'Christ is all, and in all' also stands between the putting off and the virtues, which is where Mosiah 3:19 puts 'through the atonement of Christ, the Lord'.

links.note: 'And putteth off the natural man, and becometh a saint, through the atonement of Christ, the Lord, and becometh as a child, submissive, meek, humble, patient, full of love.' A KJV singleton with one noun replaced, followed by the virtue list of the same paragraph in the same order. The child at the end is Matthew 18:3's, catalogued at 3:18, so the verse joins Paul's baptismal ethic to Matthew's saying about children — which is why the Book of Mormon's convert must both put on the new man and become as a little child.

pericopes.text: And moreover, I say unto you, that the time shall come, when the knowledge of a Saviour shall spread throughout every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.

links.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

provenance.other: “nation and kindred and tongue and people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Apocalypse has the fourfold formula seven times and permutes the order every time; Revelation 5:9's is 'kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation', which also occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Mosiah 3:20 has Revelation 14:6's order exactly, and the shorter list at 3:13 has neither.
provenance.significance: This is the finding that ties the two chapters together. Revelation 14:6-12 is used across Benjamin's sermon in the source's own order and at both ends of it: 14:6's angel preaching the everlasting gospel to every nation is Mosiah 3:20's knowledge of a Saviour spreading through every nation; 14:10's cup of the wrath of God is Mosiah 3:26; 14:11's smoke ascending for ever is Mosiah 2:38 and again 3:27; 14:12's saints who keep the commandments of God is Mosiah 2:41. Five contacts with seven consecutive verses of one chapter, and the announcing angel of Revelation 14:6 is the same figure as the announcing angel of Mosiah 3:2. The sermon is built on the Apocalypse's angel-of-the-gospel passage.

links.note: 'When the knowledge of a Saviour shall spread throughout every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.' The four terms in Revelation 14:6's order, which is a KJV singleton — the order is the evidence, since the Apocalypse itself never repeats a permutation. The shorter 'every kindred, nation, and tongue' at 3:13 is the same formula loosely recalled, and is recorded there in recurrenceRefs rather than as a second link.

pericopes.text: And behold, when that time cometh, none shall be found blameless before God, except it be little children, only through repentance and faith on the name of the Lord God Omnipotent;

and even at this time, when thou shalt have taught thy people the things which the Lord thy God hath commanded thee, even then are they found no more blameless in the sight of God, only according to the words which I have spoken unto thee.
And now, I have spoken the words which the Lord God hath commanded me.

And thus saith the Lord: They shall stand as a bright testimony against this people, at the judgment day; whereof, they shall be judged, every man, according to his works, whether they be good, or whether they be evil;

links.text: And the sea gave up the dead which were in it; and death and hell delivered up the dead which were in them: and they were judged every man according to their works.

provenance.other: “according to their works” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which Revelation 20:12 and 20:13 are two and are the only ones in a judgement scene; the third, 2 Corinthians 11:15, is about false apostles. The Book of Mormon's 'judged, every man, according to his works' has Revelation's word order with the pronoun made singular.
provenance.significance: Revelation 20:12 opens the books and 20:13 gives up the dead, and the Book of Mormon's 'they shall stand as a bright testimony against this people, at the judgment day' is the books' function stated as a purpose: Benjamin's words themselves become the record by which his hearers are judged. That is the sermon's own claim about itself, made twice — here, and at 2:27, where the assembly exists so the speaker will be found blameless. The Apocalypse supplies the courtroom; Benjamin supplies the exhibit.

links.note: 'Whereof, they shall be judged, every man, according to his works.' The KJV's judgement-seat formula, from the one scene where it belongs. What follows in the same verse is a second and closer borrowing from Ecclesiastes, catalogued separately here — so the sentence takes its court from Revelation and its verdict-categories from the Preacher.

links.text: For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.

provenance.other: “whether it be good or whether it be evil” occurs in exactly two KJV verses. The other is Jeremiah 42:6, where the remnant promise to obey the LORD's answer whatever it turns out to be — a statement about willingness, not about judgement. Only Ecclesiastes 12:14 attaches the phrase to a divine assize, and it is the last verse of the book.
provenance.significance: Ecclesiastes ends on this sentence, and it is the KJV's most compact statement that everything will be assessed and sorted. Benjamin's peroration ends on it too, and then does what Ecclesiastes never does: it takes the 'evil' branch and follows it to the lake of fire (3:25-27). Wisdom literature's flat assurance that God will judge is being used as the premise of an apocalypse — which is exactly the join this chapter has been making all along, between an Old Testament frame and a New Testament content.

links.note: 'Every man, according to his works, whether they be good, or whether they be evil.' Nine words reproduced from one of the KJV's two verses containing them, with the singular 'it' made plural to agree with 'works'. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because a complete clause is reproduced from an identifiable verse. Note that the 1830 text reads 'whether they be good, or whether they be evil', preserving the KJV's full doubled construction, which is what makes the source visible.

pericopes.text: and if they be evil, they are consigned to an awful view of their own guilt and abominations, which doth cause them to shrink from the presence of the Lord, into a state of misery and endless torment, from whence they can no more return; therefore, they have drunk damnation to their own souls.—

Therefore, they have drunk out of the cup of the wrath of God, which justice could no more deny unto them, than it could deny that Adam should fall, because of his partaking of the forbidden fruit; therefore, mercy could have claim on them no more forever.

links.text: The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb:

provenance.other: “the wine of the wrath of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “cup of his indignation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse. 'The cup of' occurs in ten KJV verses and 'the wrath of God' in several, but the two are joined in one sentence only at Revelation 14:10 — 'the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out … into the cup of his indignation'. The Book of Mormon compresses the two vessels into one, 'the cup of the wrath of God', which is in no KJV verse. Isaiah 51:17's 'cup of his fury' and Jeremiah 25:15's 'wine cup of this fury' are the Old Testament figures and neither has 'wrath of God'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:10 and 14:11 are consecutive and Mosiah 3:26 and 3:27 are consecutive, and they run in the same order: first the drinking of the cup, then the torment with fire and brimstone whose smoke ascends for ever. The Book of Mormon then adds its own clause between them — that justice 'could no more deny' this than it could deny that Adam should fall — which converts Revelation's vision into an argument about the necessity of the atonement, the argument the whole chapter has been making since 3:11.

links.note: 'Therefore, they have drunk out of the cup of the wrath of God, which justice could no more deny unto them.' The compression of Revelation 14:10's two vessels into one cup, followed in the next verse by 14:11's fire and smoke. This is the fourth of the five contacts with Revelation 14:6-12 in Benjamin's sermon; the argument for reading them as one borrowing rather than five is set out at 3:20.

pericopes.text: And their torment is as a lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames are unquenchable, and whose smoke ascendeth up forever and ever. Thus hath the Lord commanded me. Amen.

links.text: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.

provenance.route: Revelation 14:10-11 with Revelation 20:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “ascendeth up for ever and ever” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the Book of Mormon reproduces its subject as well: 'their torment' → 'whose smoke'. “lake of fire and brimstone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:10; Revelation 14:10 has the fire and brimstone without the lake, and 21:8 has 'the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone'. “unquenchable fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:12.
provenance.significance: Three KJV singletons in one sentence, from three different judgement passages, and the sentence they make is the one the whole sermon has been driving at since Mosiah 2:38 — which used two of the same three. Read together, 2:38 and 3:27 are the same borrowing made twice, once in the king's voice and once in the angel's, and the repetition is the sermon's structure rather than a redundancy: what Benjamin argued from experience, the angel's message confirms from revelation. Revelation 14:10-11 supplies the fire and the smoke, Revelation 20:10 supplies the lake, and John the Baptist supplies the adjective.

links.note: 'And their torment is as a lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames are unquenchable, and whose smoke ascendeth up forever and ever.' The verse Hardy's apparatus cross-references here is Revelation 14:11, and the wording bears him out — but the sentence needs two further verses to be accounted for, since 'lake' comes from Revelation 20:10 and 'unquenchable' from Matthew 3:12. Note the 1830's 'ascendeth' after a singular subject, which matches the KJV's own inflection exactly; the same phrase at Mosiah 2:38 has the 1830 verb after a plural subject, where the KJV form is preserved against the grammar (CONVENTIONS §8).

pericopes.text: And now, it came to pass that when king Benjamin had made an end of speaking the words which had been delivered unto him by the Angel of the Lord, that he cast his eyes round about on the multitude, and behold, they had fell to the earth, for the fear of the Lord had come upon them;

and they had viewed themselves in their own carnal state, even less than the dust of the earth. And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying, O have mercy, and apply the atoning blood of Christ, that we may receive forgiveness of our sins, and our hearts may be purified: for we believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who created Heaven and earth, and all things, who shall come down among the children of men.

provenance.other: “with one voice” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 24:3 and Acts 19:34. Acts 19:34 is the Ephesian mob shouting for Diana; Exodus 24:3 is the people of Israel ratifying the covenant at Sinai.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's assembly is a covenant-ratification scene, and it borrows the sentence that ratifies the Sinai covenant. The metalepsis is exact: at Exodus 24:3 the one voice says 'All the words which the LORD hath said will we do', and two chapters later, at Mosiah 5:2, the one voice will say 'we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us'. The KJV's only covenantal use of the phrase is the one the Book of Mormon has taken, and it has taken it twice, at the two ends of the same assembly.

links.note: 'And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying, O have mercy…'. The phrase is a KJV rarity with two homes, and only one of them is a covenant scene. Everything around it presses the same way: a people gathered before their leader, prostrate, answering as one, and about to bind themselves by oath — which is Exodus 24. The 1830 wording adds 'aloud', which is in neither KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own.
links.text: And Moses came and told the people all the words of the LORD, and all the judgments: and all the people answered with one voice, and said, All the words which the LORD hath said will we do.

provenance.other: “purifying their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 15:9, where the purifying agent is faith.
provenance.significance: Acts 15:9 is Peter's argument at the Jerusalem council that God made no difference between Jew and Gentile because he purified Gentile hearts by faith. Benjamin's multitude is a single covenant people, not a disputed one — but the sentence they use to ask for a clean heart is the sentence the New Testament uses to abolish the distinction between insiders and outsiders, and Mosiah 3:20 has just promised that the knowledge of the Saviour will 'spread throughout every nation, kindred, tongue and people'.

links.note: 'That we may receive forgiveness of our sins, and our hearts may be purified: for we believe in Jesus Christ.' Two clauses, and each is a New Testament rarity. The purification of the heart by belief is Acts 15:9's exact formula — purified hearts, and faith as the instrument — and the KJV has no other verse that puts those two together in those words. The Old Testament asks for a clean heart (Psalm 51:10) but never purifies one by faith.
links.text: And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith.

provenance.other: “receive forgiveness of sins” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:18. The KJV's usual idiom is 'remission of sins' (Matthew 26:28, Acts 2:38, Acts 10:43), which Mosiah 4:3 uses in the very next verse.
provenance.significance: The pairing matters more than either half. Mosiah 4 reaches Acts 26 twice: 'receive forgiveness of … sins' here, and 'truth and soberness' — also a KJV singleton — at 4:15, seven verses further on in Paul's defence before Agrippa. A chapter that touches one page of the New Testament twice is using that page, not remembering a phrase.

links.note: 'That we may receive forgiveness of our sins.' The KJV normally says 'remission', and Mosiah 4:3 duly says 'remission' one sentence later; the switch to 'forgiveness' here lands on the one verse where the KJV says it that way. Acts 26:18 is Paul reciting his commission — eyes opened, darkness to light, the power of Satan — which is the movement Benjamin's multitude has just undergone in 4:1-2.
links.text: To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after they had spoken these words, the spirit of the Lord came upon them, and they were filled with joy, having received a remission of their sins, and having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had in Jesus Christ which should come, according to the words which king Benjamin had spoken unto them.

And king Benjamin again opened his mouth, and began to speak unto them, saying, My friends and my brethren, my kindred and my people, I would again call your attention, that ye may hear and understand the remainder of my words which I shall speak unto you:
for behold, that if the knowledge of the goodness of God at this time, hath awakened you to a sense of your nothingness, and your worthless and fallen state;

provenance.other: “the goodness of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 52:1 and Romans 2:4. Only Romans 2:4 attaches it to longsuffering and to repentance; “goodness and forbearance and longsuffering” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 2:4.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a reproach — 'despisest thou the riches of his goodness … not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?' — put to people who presume on mercy. Benjamin turns the reproach into a diagnosis of what has just happened in front of him: the knowledge of the goodness of God has led these people to repentance, on the ground, in one verse. Recover Romans 2 and the passage reads as Paul's rhetorical question answered in the affirmative by a whole city.

links.note: 'If the knowledge of the goodness of God at this time, hath awakened you to a sense of your nothingness.' The phrase recurs at 4:6 and 4:11 and each time it drags Romans 2:4's other terms with it: 4:6 lists 'his patience, and his long suffering', which is Paul's 'forbearance and longsuffering', and the whole sequence is the goodness of God producing repentance. Two KJV verses have the phrase and only one has the argument.
links.text: Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?

pericopes.text: I say unto you, that if ye have come to a knowledge of the goodness of God, and his matchless power, and his wisdom, and his patience, and his long suffering towards the children of men, and also, the atonement which hath been prepared from the foundation of the world, that thereby salvation might come to him that should put his trust in the Lord, and should be diligent in keeping his commandments, and continue in the faith even unto the end of his life; I mean the life of the mortal body;

provenance.other: “prepared for you from the foundation of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:34. The KJV never writes 'prepared from the foundation of the world' without the intervening 'for you'; the nearest other verse to join preparation to that phrase is Revelation 13:8's 'the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world'.
provenance.significance: This is the first of three visits Benjamin's sermon pays to Matthew 25:31-46. Here the atonement is what was prepared from the foundation of the world; at 4:26 the works of mercy are Matthew's own list, hungry, naked, sick; at 5:9-10 the saved are found at the right hand of God and the rest on the left. Matthew 25 supplies this discourse with its eschatology, its ethics and its stage directions, and the borrowing at 4:6 is the one that sets the frame — Benjamin has substituted 'the atonement' for Matthew's 'kingdom' in the King's own sentence.

links.note: 'The atonement which hath been prepared from the foundation of the world, that thereby salvation might come.' Six of the seven words are Matthew 25:34's and in Matthew's order; what changes is the thing prepared. The KJV has 'foundation of the world' in six verses but only one where something is prepared from it, and that one is the judgment scene this chapter goes on to quote twice more. Revelation 13:8 stands behind the substitution — it is where the KJV puts an atoning act at the foundation of the world.
links.text: Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:

pericopes.text: I say, that this is the man that receiveth salvation, through the atonement which was prepared from the foundation of the world, for all mankind, which ever was ever since the fall of Adam, or which is or which ever shall be, even unto the end of the world;

and this is the means whereby salvation cometh. And there is none other salvation, save this which hath been spoken of; neither is there any conditions whereby man can be saved, except the conditions which I have told you.

Believe in God; believe that he is, and that he created all things, both in Heaven and in Earth; believe that he hath all wisdom, and all power, both in Heaven and in Earth; believe that man doth not comprehend all the things which the Lord can comprehend.

provenance.other: “believe that he is” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:6. The construction is peculiar English — an absolute 'is' with no predicate — and it exists in the KJV only here.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:6 is the hinge of the chapter on faith: it defines the minimum content of belief and then says God rewards those who seek him. Benjamin takes the minimum and expands it into a creed — he is, he created all things, he has all wisdom and all power — and then, at 4:10, adds the thing Hebrews leaves implicit: 'if you believe all these things, see that ye do them.' The suppressed half of Hebrews 11:6, that God 'is a rewarder', is what Benjamin's next twenty verses argue about beggars and substance.

links.note: 'Believe in God; believe that he is, and that he created all things.' Four words, but they are the four rarest possible: the KJV's only bare predicative 'believe that he is', taken with its following 'and that he', which the dossier's n-gram stream caught as a seven-word run. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and not one of his quotations; the case rests on absolute rarity, not on length. Note that the 1830 'hath all wisdom' was smoothed to 'has' in 1920, moving the sentence away from the KJV's register.
links.text: But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.

pericopes.text: And again: Believe that ye must repent of your sins and forsake them, and humble yourselves before God, and ask in sincerity of heart that he would forgive you: and now, if you believe all these things, see that ye do them.

And again I say unto you, as I have said before, that as ye have come to the knowledge of the glory of God, or if ye have known of his goodness, and have tasted of his love, and have received a remission of your sins, which causeth such exceeding great joy in your souls, even so I would that ye should remember, and always retain in remembrance, the greatness of God, and your own nothingness, and his goodness and long suffering towards you unworthy creatures, and humble yourselves even in the depths of humility, calling on the name of the Lord daily, and standing steadfastly in the faith of that which is to come, which was spoken by the mouth of the Angel;

provenance.other: “calling on the name of the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 22:16. The KJV's other forms are all finite — 'call on the name of the LORD' (Genesis 4:26, Psalm 116:17, Joel 2:32, Acts 2:21) — and the participial phrase is Ananias's alone.
provenance.significance: Ananias's words are spoken to a man who has just been struck down, blinded, and told to arise; Benjamin's are spoken to a multitude that has just fallen to the earth and been raised by a remission of sins. The suppressed half of Acts 22:16 is 'arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins' — which is the sequence Mosiah 6:1-2 will complete when Benjamin takes the names of everyone who has entered the covenant.

links.note: 'Calling on the name of the Lord daily, and standing steadfastly in the faith of that which is to come.' The participle is the tell. Every other KJV occurrence conjugates the verb; only Acts 22:16 leaves it hanging as a description of a posture, which is exactly how Benjamin uses it — not an act to perform once but a daily condition. 'Standing steadfastly in the faith' anticipates 5:15's 'steadfast and immovable', where the source is 1 Corinthians 15:58.
links.text: And now why tarriest thou? arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord.

pericopes.text: and behold, I say unto you, that if ye do this, ye shall always rejoice, and be filled with the love of God, and always retain a remission of your sins; and ye shall grow in the knowledge of the glory of Him that created you, or in the knowledge of that which is just and true.

provenance.other: “grow in the knowledge” occurs in no KJV verse; 2 Peter 3:18 reads 'grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour'. “the knowledge of the glory” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Habakkuk 2:14 and 2 Corinthians 4:6.
provenance.significance: The verse fuses the only two KJV idioms available to it — Peter's imperative to grow in knowledge and Paul's 'light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ' — and the fusion is what makes it a Book of Mormon sentence rather than a quotation. Where Paul locates the glory in Christ's face, Benjamin locates it in creation: 'the knowledge of the glory of Him that created you'.

links.note: 'Ye shall grow in the knowledge of the glory of Him that created you.' Neither source supplies the whole clause and neither is deniable in it: the verb and its object are 2 Peter 3:18's, the genitive chain is 2 Corinthians 4:6's. Recorded at moderate because a composite of two common idioms is a weaker thing than a singleton, and because 'grow in the knowledge' as such is in no KJV verse.
links.text: But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.

pericopes.text: And ye will not have a mind to injure one another, but to live peaceably, and to render to every man according to that which is his due.

provenance.other: “live peaceably” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 12:18. “dues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 13:7. “render to every man according to” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Proverbs 24:12 and Romans 2:6.
provenance.significance: The verse is built out of a continuous stretch of Romans, in Paul's own order: recompense no man evil for evil (12:17), live peaceably with all men (12:18), render to all their dues (13:7). The Book of Mormon has not taken a phrase from Romans; it has taken a paragraph's argument and compressed it into one sentence, and the compression preserves the sequence. That is the strongest kind of evidence the sequence subscore can carry.

links.note: 'Ye will not have a mind to injure one another, but to live peaceably, and to render to every man according to that which is his due.' Three clauses and each is Paul's. The mediation test is decisive and it is decisive twice over: 'render to every man according to' is shared by Proverbs 24:12 and Romans 2:6, so on its own the verse cannot choose between Testaments — but Mosiah's object is neither Proverbs' 'works' nor Romans 2:6's 'deeds'. It is 'his due', which is Romans 13:7's word and appears nowhere else in the KJV. The Book of Mormon has read Romans 2:6 with Romans 13:7 and taken the noun from the second.
links.text: Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.

pericopes.text: And ye will not suffer your children, that they go hungry, or naked; neither will ye suffer that they transgress the laws of God, and fight and quarrel one with another, and serve the Devil, which is the master of sin, or which is the evil spirit which hath been spoken of by our fathers; he being an enemy to all righteousness;

provenance.other: “enemy of all righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10. The Book of Mormon has 'enemy to all righteousness', which occurs in no KJV verse — the preposition is its only departure.
provenance.significance: Acts 13:10 is Paul blinding Elymas the sorcerer, and the epithet comes in a series: 'O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness.' Benjamin has taken the second and third members of that series and kept them together — his warning is about children who 'serve the Devil' and about the devil as 'an enemy to all righteousness'. The 'child of the devil' that Paul spat at a magician has become, in Benjamin's mouth, a thing parents can let their own children become by neglect.

links.note: 'He being an enemy to all righteousness.' A KJV singleton with one preposition changed, and the change is the kind that a memory makes and a transcription does not. What secures the link is not the phrase alone but its company: Acts 13:10's 'child of the devil' sits four words away from it, and Mosiah 4:14's clause about children who 'serve the Devil' sits eleven words away from the borrowing. Two halves of one verse, in one sentence, with the same subject.
links.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

pericopes.text: but ye will teach them to walk in the ways of truth and soberness; ye will teach them to love one another, and to serve one another;

provenance.other: “truth and soberness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:25. 'Soberness' itself occurs only there; the KJV's usual noun is 'sobriety' (1 Timothy 2:9, 2:15).
provenance.significance: Paul says it to Festus, who has just shouted that he is mad: 'I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.' The words are a defence of a man accused of raving in front of a king. Benjamin, speaking in front of his own people from a tower, tells them to teach their children to walk in that same speech. Read with 4:2's borrowing from Acts 26:18, the chapter has been in Paul's Agrippa speech twice, and it takes both times from Paul's own words rather than from the narrative around them.

links.note: 'Ye will teach them to walk in the ways of truth and soberness.' The pairing is a KJV singleton and the second noun is a KJV hapax, which is as much rarity evidence as a four-word phrase can carry. The n-gram stream found this one and ranked it low; it is one of the chapter's cleaner borrowings.
links.text: But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.

pericopes.text: and also, ye yourselves will succor those that stand in need of your succor; ye will adminster of your substance unto him that standeth in need; and ye will not suffer that the beggar putteth up his petition to you in vain, and turn him out to perish.

Perhaps thou shalt say, The man hath brought upon himself his misery, therefore I will stay my hand, and will not give unto him of my food, nor impart unto him of my substance, that he may not suffer, for his punishments are just.

But I say unto you, O man, whosoever doeth this, the same hath great cause to repent; and except he repenteth of that which he hath done, he perisheth forever, and hath no interest in the kingdom of God.

For behold, are we not all beggars? Do we not all depend upon the same being, even God, for all the substance which we have; for both food, and raiment, and for gold, and for silver, and for all the riches which we have of every kind?

provenance.other: “lifteth up the beggar” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 2:8. 'Beggar' is a rare KJV word — 1 Samuel 2:8 and Luke 16:20, 16:22 — and Mosiah 4 uses it five times in eight verses.
provenance.significance: Hannah's song is the KJV's one place where a beggar is raised from the dunghill and set among princes, and it is sung at the founding of Israel's monarchy by the mother of the prophet who will anoint its kings. Benjamin is a king, on a tower, at the moment of handing the kingdom to his son, telling the assembled kingdom that they are all beggars. The reversal Hannah sings about — princes and beggars changing places — is what Benjamin performs on himself in 2:14 and asserts of everyone here.

links.note: 'For behold, are we not all beggars?' The word is the evidence. The KJV has three verses with a beggar in them and only one where the beggar is the subject of a theology rather than a parable, and it is the song Benjamin's whole sermon on kingship and dependence is shaped like. Volume is thin — no clause is reproduced — but the vocabulary is rare and the thematic coherence is total, which is the shape Hays's criteria give a genuine echo as against a quotation.
links.text: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD’s, and he hath set the world upon them.

pericopes.text: And behold, even at this time, ye have been calling on his name, and begging for a remission of your sins. And hath he suffered that ye have begged in vain? Nay; he hath poured out his spirit upon you, and hath caused that your hearts should be filled with joy, and hath caused that your mouths should be stopped, that ye could not find utterance, so exceeding great was your joy.

links.text: And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.

provenance.other: 'Utterance' occurs in five KJV verses, and Acts 2:4 is the only one where the Spirit is its giver. “poured out my spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 39:29; Acts 2:17-18, quoting Joel, has 'I will pour out of my Spirit'.
provenance.significance: The scene is Pentecost run backwards. In Acts 2 the Spirit is poured out, the mouths are opened, and utterance is given; in Mosiah 4:20 the Spirit is poured out, the mouths are stopped, and utterance cannot be found. Both crowds are prostrate and both are overwhelmed, and the Book of Mormon has kept every element of the Pentecost sequence while inverting its one distinctive effect. A speechless Pentecost is a considered thing to write, not an accident of vocabulary.

links.note: 'He hath poured out his spirit upon you … and hath caused that your mouths should be stopped, that ye could not find utterance.' The two rare terms of Acts 2 are both here, in Acts's order, and the second is negated. 'Utterance' is not common KJV English — five verses in the whole Bible — and only Acts 2:4 makes the Spirit its source, which is the connection the negation depends on. Filed at moderate because the shared wording is two words and the argument rests on the inversion.

pericopes.text: And now, if God, who hath created you, on whom you are dependant for your lives, and for all that ye have and are, doth grant unto you whatsoever ye ask that is right, in faith, believing that ye shall receive, O then, how had ye ought to impart of the substance that ye have, one to another?

provenance.other: “believing ye shall receive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:22 (the KJV punctuates 'believing, ye shall receive'). “ask in faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 1:6. Mark 11:24's parallel reads differently — 'believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them'.
provenance.significance: The mediation is decidable inside the New Testament. Matthew and Mark carry the same saying and word it differently, and Mosiah 4:21 has Matthew's participle and Matthew's future — not Mark's 'believe that ye receive'. Then James 1:6 supplies the qualifier Matthew lacks, 'ask in faith', which is what lets Benjamin add his own 'whatsoever ye ask that is right'. A promise given without limit in Matthew is being fenced by James before it is used.

links.note: 'Doth grant unto you whatsoever ye ask that is right, in faith, believing that ye shall receive.' Matthew's clause arrives whole, with 'that' inserted; the surrounding conditions are James's and Benjamin's own. The argument the borrowing serves is not about prayer at all — it is the premise of an a fortiori about almsgiving: if God gives you whatever you ask, how ought you to give to one another. The New Testament's most unqualified promise has been made into an obligation to the poor.
links.text: And all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.

pericopes.text: And if ye judge the man who putteth up his petition to you for your substance, that he perish not, and condemn him, how much more just will be your condemnation, for withholding your substance, which doth not belong to you, but to God, to whom also, your life belongeth; and yet ye put up no petition, or repenteth not of the thing which thou hast done.—
I say unto you, Wo be unto that man, for his substance shall perish with him; and now, I say these things unto those which are rich, as pertaining to the things of this world.

links.text: But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.

provenance.other: “perish with thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:20. The KJV has no other sentence in which a man's money or goods are consigned to perish along with the man.
provenance.significance: Peter says it to Simon the sorcerer, who offered money for the gift of God. Benjamin says it of a rich man who refused money to a beggar. The two errors are opposite — one buys what cannot be bought, the other withholds what was never his — and the Book of Mormon has answered both with the same sentence, which is exactly the kind of unstated correspondence Hays calls metalepsis. The verse just before Benjamin's, 4:22, has already said that the substance 'doth not belong to you, but to God': Simon's mistake was to think the things of God purchasable, and Benjamin's rich man's is to think the things of God his own.

links.note: 'Wo be unto that man, for his substance shall perish with him.' Not a verbatim run — 'substance' for 'money', 'him' for 'thee' — but the construction is a KJV singleton and there is nothing else in the Bible it could be. Acts 13:10's 'enemy to all righteousness' at 4:14 and Acts 8:20 here put the chapter in Acts's apostolic-rebuke scenes twice; the register of Benjamin's denunciations is Lukan.

pericopes.text: And again, I say unto the poor, ye that have not and yet hath sufficient, that ye remain from day to day; I mean all you that deny the beggar, because ye have not; I would that ye say in your hearts, that I give not because I have not; but if I had, I would give.
And now, if ye say this in your hearts, ye remain guiltless, otherwise ye are condemned, and your condemnation is just: for ye covet that which ye have not received.

And now, for the sake of these things which I have spoken unto you; that is, for the sake of retaining a remission of your sins from day to day, that ye may walk guiltless before God, I would that ye should impart of your substance to the poor, every man according to that which he hath, such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and administering to their relief, both spiritually and temporally, according to their wants,

provenance.other: “I was sick and ye visited me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:36. Isaiah 58:7 is the standing Old Testament candidate for a list of this kind and it will not do the work: it has bread for the hungry and a covering for the naked, but no sick and no visiting, and its verb for the naked is 'cover', not 'clothe'.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's list is Matthew's list, minus the stranger and the prisoner and plus 'administering to their relief, both spiritually and temporally' — an addition that turns a judgment scene into a welfare instruction. Recover the context and the borrowing is doing what Matthew 25 does: the works are the criterion of the judgment, which is why the chapter has already taken 'prepared from the foundation of the world' from Matthew 25:34 at 4:6 and will take the right hand and the left from Matthew 25:33 at 5:9-10. Three separate borrowings from one pericope, spread across two chapters of one sermon.

links.note: 'Such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick.' The mediation test decides it: run Mosiah 4:26 against Isaiah 58:7 and Matthew 25:35-36 and the Old Testament candidate fails on two words the Book of Mormon has and Isaiah does not — 'sick' and 'visiting' — while the verb applied to the naked is Matthew's 'clothe' and not Isaiah's 'cover'. Nominalizing Matthew's first-person narrative into a list of gerunds is the reason this is catalogued as a paraphrastic quotation rather than a verbatim one; below Skousen's threshold, and none of his thirty-six.
links.text: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.

pericopes.text: and see that all these things are done in wisdom and order: for it is not requisite that a man should run faster than what he hath strength. And again: It is expedient that he should be diligent, that thereby he might win the prize; therefore, all things must be done in order.

provenance.other: “receiveth the prize” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 9:24. “the prize” occurs in exactly two, 1 Corinthians 9:24 and Philippians 3:14. The KJV never uses 'win' of the prize; that verb is the Book of Mormon's.
