provenance.significance: Paul's footrace is a warning that only one runner receives the prize, so run to obtain. Benjamin inverts the pace and keeps the image: 'it is not requisite that a man should run faster than what he hath strength', and then, in the same breath, 'that thereby he might win the prize'. The suppressed context is 1 Corinthians 9:27, where Paul keeps his body under lest he himself be a castaway — the same anxiety about running past one's own strength, reached by the opposite counsel.

links.note: 'It is not requisite that a man should run faster than what he hath strength … that thereby he might win the prize.' Running and the prize in one sentence is Pauline and, in the KJV, nearly unique to this verse. The 1830 reading 'faster than what he hath strength' was tidied in 1920 by deleting 'what', which removes the awkward relative that makes the sentence sound like the KJV in the first place.
links.text: Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.

provenance.other: “decently and in order” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 14:40, which is the KJV's only instruction that things be 'done in order' at all.
provenance.significance: Both of this verse's borrowings come from one letter, and the chapter's argument is the same as Paul's in 1 Corinthians 12-14: gifts and works are to be distributed and exercised in proportion and in order, not in excess. Benjamin's 'all things must be done in order' closes a paragraph about giving in the way Paul's closes a chapter about speaking.

links.note: 'See that all these things are done in wisdom and order … therefore, all things must be done in order.' The formula is stated twice in one verse, and the KJV states it once in the whole Bible. The n-gram stream proposed Mark 4:11 for the same run ('all these things are done in'), which is the trap the pilot named: the longest match is not the source. Mark's next word is 'parables'.
links.text: Let all things be done decently and in order.

pericopes.text: And I would that ye should remember, that whosoever among you that borroweth of his neighbor, should return the thing that he borroweth, according as he doth agree, or else thou shalt commit sin, and perhaps thou shalt cause thy neighbor to commit sin also.

provenance.other: “borrow ought of his neighbour” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 22:14 — the Covenant Code's law of bailment.
provenance.significance: Benjamin has been legislating like Moses for twenty verses, and here he legislates in Moses' own words, from the code that immediately precedes the covenant-ratification scene his people re-enacted at 4:2. Exodus 22 is the law; Exodus 24 is the assembly that swears to keep it. Mosiah 4 has now used both, in that order. But the sanction has changed: Exodus 22:14 says the borrower 'shall surely make it good', a restitution; Benjamin says 'thou shalt commit sin', and adds that the defaulter may make his neighbour sin too. A civil liability has become a spiritual one.

links.note: 'Whosoever among you that borroweth of his neighbor, should return the thing that he borroweth.' The subject, verb and indirect object are Exodus 22:14's, which is the KJV's only sentence about borrowing from a neighbour. The transformation is the finding: the Covenant Code assesses damages, Benjamin assesses guilt, and he extends the guilt to the lender's own sin — which is not in Exodus at all.
links.text: And if a man borrow ought of his neighbour, and it be hurt, or die, the owner thereof being not with it, he shall surely make it good.

pericopes.text: And finally, I cannot tell you all the things whereby ye may commit sin: for there are divers ways and means, even so many, that I cannot number them.

But this much I can tell you, that if ye do not watch yourselves, and your thoughts, and your words, and your deeds, and observe to keep the commandments of God, and continue in the faith of what ye have heard concerning the coming of our Lord, even unto the end of your lives, ye must perish. And now, O man, remember, and perish not.

provenance.other: “continue in the faith” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 14:22 and Colossians 1:23. Only Colossians 1:23 goes on to 'which ye have heard', which occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Colossians 1:23, 1 John 2:7, 1 John 2:24).
provenance.significance: Colossians 1:23 makes continuance conditional — 'if ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away' — and it is that conditional, not the exhortation, that Benjamin ends his sermon on: continue, or 'ye must perish'. The suppressed half of Paul's verse, 'grounded and settled … be not moved away', surfaces one chapter later as 'steadfast and immovable' at 5:15, where the wording is 1 Corinthians 15:58's. Benjamin's peroration and his benediction are built from the same Pauline idea reached through two different verses.

links.note: 'Continue in the faith of what ye have heard concerning the coming of our Lord, even unto the end of your lives, ye must perish.' Two of Colossians 1:23's clauses stand in one Book of Mormon clause, in Paul's order, and Acts 14:22 — the other verse with 'continue in the faith' — has neither the hearing nor the condition. The phrase has already been used once in the chapter, at 4:6; this is the occurrence that carries the source, because it is the one that brings 'which ye have heard' with it.
links.text: If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which ye have heard, and which was preached to every creature which is under heaven; whereof I Paul am made a minister;

pericopes.text: And now, it came to pass that when king Benjamin had thus spoken to his people, he sent among them, desiring to know of his people, If they believed the words which he had spoken unto them.

And they all cried with one voice, saying, Yea, we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us; and also, we know of their surety and truth, because of the Spirit of the Lord Omnipotent, which hath wrought a mighty change in us, or in our hearts, that we have no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually.

provenance.other: “to do evil but to do good” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 4:22. “evil continually” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:5 — the verdict before the flood, that every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was only evil continually.
provenance.significance: Both sources are diagnoses of a corrupt heart and the Book of Mormon has reversed both. Jeremiah's people 'are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge'; Benjamin's people have 'no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually'. Genesis 6:5's 'only evil continually' becomes 'good continually'. The metalepsis is what the reversal recovers: Jeremiah 4:22's first clause is 'my people is foolish, they have not known me', and eleven verses later, at Mosiah 5:13, Benjamin asks 'how knoweth a man the master which he hath not served'. The chapter has taken Jeremiah's charge of not knowing God and answered it with a people who now do.

links.note: 'That we have no more disposition to do evil, but to do good continually.' The clause is Jeremiah 4:22's, turned inside out: the KJV has that sequence of words once, and there the two verbs are a reproach rather than a testimony. The adverb comes from the other direction — 'continually' with a moral object is Genesis 6:5's word for the antediluvian heart. What the people report is precisely the undoing of both verses, which is why the borrowing is more interesting than a quotation would be.
links.text: For my people is foolish, they have not known me; they are sottish children, and they have none understanding: they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.

pericopes.text: And we, ourselves, also, through the infinite goodness of God, and the manifestations of his Spirit, have great views of that which is to come; and were it expedient, we could prophesy of all things.
And it is the faith which we have had on the things which our king hath spoken unto us, and hath brought us to this great knowledge, whereby we do rejoice with such exceeding great joy;

and we are willing to enter into a covenant with our God, to do his will, and to be obedient to his commandments in all things that he shall command us, all the remainder of our days, that we may not bring upon ourselves a never ending torment, as has been spoken by the Angel, that we may not drink out of the cup of the wrath of God.

provenance.other: 'The wrath of God' occurs in ten KJV verses, but only Revelation 14:10 puts it in a cup and gives it to somebody to drink: 'shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out … into the cup of his indignation'. “torment ascendeth up” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:11, which supplies the torment that has no end.
provenance.significance: The two elements of the covenant's negative sanction — a torment without end, and a cup of the wrath of God — stand in consecutive verses of one Revelation passage and nowhere else together in the KJV. This is not the first time Benjamin's sermon has been in Revelation 14: Hardy's apparatus cross-references Revelation 14:11 at Mosiah 3:27, two chapters earlier, and Revelation 14:1 stands behind Mosiah 5:12's name written in the heart. One page of Revelation is supplying this discourse with its picture of judgment, and the covenant at 5:5 is being sworn against it.

links.note: 'That we may not bring upon ourselves a never ending torment … that we may not drink out of the cup of the wrath of God.' Two images, consecutive in the source and consecutive here. The Book of Mormon compresses Revelation's 'wine of the wrath of God … into the cup of his indignation' into a single 'cup of the wrath of God', which is a phrase in no KJV verse — a fusion of the two halves of Revelation 14:10 rather than a copy of either. The 1830 'never ending torment' was hyphenated in 1920; the unhyphenated form is the KJV's own habit.
links.text: The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb:

pericopes.text: And now, these are the words which king Benjamin desired of them; and therefore he said unto them, Ye have spoken the words that I desired; and the covenant which ye have made, is a righteous covenant.

And now, because of the covenant which ye have made, ye shall be called the children of Christ, his sons, and his daughters: for behold, this day he hath spiritually begotten you; for ye say that your hearts are changed, through faith on his name; therefore, ye are born of him, and have become his sons, and his daughters.

provenance.other: “shall be called the children of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:9. Romans 9:26 has 'they be called the children of the living God' without the modal.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Matthew's beatitude promises that the peacemakers 'shall be called the children of God'; Mosiah 5:7 promises that the covenanters 'shall be called the children of Christ'. Changing the genitive from God to Christ inside a beatitude is a christological claim made by a single word, and it is made in the KJV's own sentence — which is what makes it visible at all. Read with the metalepsis, the promise Jesus attaches to peacemaking Benjamin attaches to covenanting.

links.note: 'Ye shall be called the children of Christ, his sons, and his daughters.' Six consecutive words of the Sermon on the Mount with the seventh replaced. The machine stream found this one; it is worth recording that it also proposed Romans 9:26, which has the same clause without 'shall' and in a Hosea quotation about a people who were not a people — a background this verse can carry, since Benjamin's people are being given a name they did not have.
links.text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.

provenance.other: “sons and daughters saith the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 6:18, where Paul fuses 2 Samuel 7:14 with Isaiah 43:6. The mediation tool returns no decisive divergence, because Mosiah reproduces neither source's full clause; the decision is made by eye and it is not close. 2 Samuel 7:14 has a son and no daughter.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 43:6, 'bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth', is the Old Testament source of Paul's second half and could be reached directly.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 6:18 is the promise God made to David's heir, opened out by Paul to a whole congregation — a dynastic sonship made general. Mosiah 5:7 is a king in the act of handing over a dynasty telling his people that they, not only his son, are the sons and daughters begotten this day. The verse that democratizes the Davidic promise is being used at precisely the moment the Book of Mormon's own succession is taking place, one chapter before Mosiah is consecrated.

links.note: 'His sons, and his daughters … therefore, ye are born of him, and have become his sons, and his daughters.' The pair is repeated twice in one verse, which is Paul's pair and not the Old Testament's: 2 Samuel 7:14, the verse Paul is quoting, has only 'he shall be my son'. Filed at moderate because 'sons and daughters' is not by itself rare English; what carries it is the pairing with 'Father' and the covenant frame, both of which are 2 Corinthians 6:18's.
links.text: And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty.

provenance.other: “born of him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 2:29. The KJV's other new-birth formulas are 'born of God' (1 John 3:9, 4:7, 5:1, 5:4, 5:18), 'born again' (John 3:3, 1 Peter 1:23) and 'born of the Spirit' (John 3:6).
provenance.significance: 1 John 2:29 makes the new birth inferable from conduct — 'every one that doeth righteousness is born of him' — which is the move Benjamin makes at 5:2, where the people know their own change by their disposition to do good. The pronoun is what carries the link: 'born of him' rather than 'born of God' puts Christ, not the Father, in the genitive, and that is exactly the substitution Mosiah 5:7 has already made in the beatitude.

links.note: 'Therefore, ye are born of him.' Three words, but the KJV says it this way once. Everywhere else the new birth is 'of God', and the Johannine letters' one exception is the verse where the antecedent is ambiguous between Father and Son — the ambiguity Mosiah 5:7 resolves toward Christ and then states outright. Filed as an echo at moderate because three words cannot carry more, and recorded because its rarity is absolute.
links.text: If ye know that he is righteous, ye know that every one that doeth righteousness is born of him.

pericopes.text: And under this head, ye are made free; and there is no other head whereby ye can be made free. There is no other name given, whereby salvation cometh; therefore, I would that ye should take upon you the name of Christ, all you that have entered into the covenant with God, that ye should be obedient unto the end of your lives.

provenance.other: “there is none other name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 4:12, and “neither is there salvation in any other” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is the same one. The two halves of Benjamin's claim answer to the two halves of Peter's.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's sermon has taken Acts 4:12 apart and used it twice, a chapter apart. Mosiah 4:8 has the first half — 'there is none other salvation, save this which hath been spoken of' — and Mosiah 5:8 has the second — 'There is no other name given, whereby salvation cometh.' Neither verse quotes the whole; between them they reproduce it. Recover the context and the borrowing is Peter's, spoken before the rulers and elders of Israel in defence of a healing done in a name; Benjamin's is spoken by a ruler of Israel who is giving that name away.

links.note: 'There is no other name given, whereby salvation cometh.' Every content word is Acts 4:12's and the syntax is Acts 4:12's in miniature: none other name — given — whereby — salvation. It is catalogued as a paraphrastic quotation rather than a verbatim one because the KJV's 'under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved' is condensed rather than copied; well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six. The doubling across 4:8 and 5:8 is stronger evidence than either occurrence alone, because a writer working from memory of one verse does not usually split it across two sermons and get both halves.
links.text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass that whosoever doeth this, shall be found at the right hand of God, for he shall know the name by which he is called: for he shall be called by the name of Christ.

provenance.other: 'On the left hand' occurs in seven KJV verses, all but one of them geographical — Damascus, Cyprus, the borders of Zebulun. Only Matthew 25 makes it a verdict: “on his right hand but the goats on the left” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:33.
provenance.significance: This completes the chapter-length borrowing from Matthew 25 that began at Mosiah 4:6 with 'prepared from the foundation of the world' and continued at 4:26 with the hungry, the naked and the sick. Benjamin has now used the parable's opening (the separation), its blessing formula, and its list of works, in Matthew's own order across two chapters. The one thing he changes is the criterion: Matthew sorts by what was done to the least of these, Benjamin by whether a man knows the name he is called by — and since 4:26 has already made Matthew's works the content of the covenant, the two criteria are the same criterion said twice.

links.note: 'Shall be found at the right hand of God … he findeth himself on the left hand of God' (5:9-10). No clause is reproduced, which is why this is catalogued as conceptual rather than close-verbal, and the case rests on the pair. The KJV's right hand of God is a place of enthronement (Mark 16:19, Acts 7:55); its left hand is almost always a compass point. Only Matthew 25 makes the two a forensic pair, and this sermon has been quoting Matthew 25 since 4:6.
links.text: And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.

pericopes.text: And now, it shall come to pass that whosoever shall not take upon them the name of Christ, must be called by some other name; therefore, he findeth himself on the left hand of God.

And I would that ye should remember also, that this is the name that I said I should give unto you, that never should be blotted out, except it be through transgression; therefore, take heed that ye do not transgress, that the name be not blotted out of your hearts.

provenance.other: “blot out his name” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 29:20 and Revelation 3:5. Deuteronomy blots the name of a covenant-breaker from under heaven as a curse; Revelation promises the overcomer that his name will not be blotted out of the book of life.
provenance.significance: Both candidates are covenant sanctions and the Book of Mormon has the shape of the second. Revelation 3:5 is a promise stated as a negative — 'I will NOT blot out his name' — and Mosiah 5:11 is the same promise in the same negative form: the name 'never should be blotted out, except it be through transgression'. Deuteronomy 29:20 states it as a threat with no exception clause. The suppressed context is Revelation 3:5's second half, 'I will confess his name before my Father', which is what Mosiah 5:9 has just described as being found at the right hand of God and known by name.

links.note: 'This is the name that I said I should give unto you, that never should be blotted out, except it be through transgression.' The KJV's two blottings-out are a curse and a promise, and Benjamin's is a promise with a condition — Revelation's form with Deuteronomy's escape clause reattached. Where Revelation keeps the name in a book, Benjamin keeps it in the heart, which is the change 5:12 then makes explicit.
links.text: He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.

pericopes.text: I say unto you, I would that ye should remember to retain the name written always in your hearts, that ye are not found on the left hand of God, but that ye hear and know the voice by which ye shall be called, and also, the name by which he shall call you:

provenance.other: “written in their foreheads” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:1. “fleshy tables of the heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 3:3, which is the KJV's only writing done on a heart by the Spirit rather than by God's finger on stone.
provenance.alternative: Jeremiah 31:33 and its quotation at Hebrews 8:10 write in the heart, but what they write is the law, not a name; the mediation check between them returns no divergence Mosiah reproduces.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's covenanters carry a name; Revelation's hundred and forty-four thousand carry a name; the difference is where. Revelation writes it on the forehead, where anyone can read it, and Mosiah writes it in the heart, where 5:13 says a stranger cannot. That relocation is the argument of the whole passage — the name is not a badge but a knowledge, and a man who does not know the voice does not have it. Revelation 14 has already supplied 5:5's cup of wrath, so the chapter is working through one page of Revelation as it works through one page of Matthew.

links.note: 'Retain the name written always in your hearts.' The nearest KJV language for a name written on a person is Revelation 14:1's foreheads; the nearest for writing on a heart is 2 Corinthians 3:3's fleshy tables. The Book of Mormon has neither phrase intact, which is why this is moderate and conceptual rather than verbal — but each half is a KJV singleton, and the sentence needs both.
links.text: And I looked, and, lo, a Lamb stood on the mount Sion, and with him an hundred forty and four thousand, having his Father’s name written in their foreheads.

provenance.other: “know his voice” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:4. John 10:3 is the KJV's only verse in which a shepherd 'calleth his own sheep by name'; the conjunction of a voice that is known and a name by which one is called exists nowhere else in the Bible.
provenance.significance: The whole of Mosiah 5:12-14 is John 10:3-5 in order. The sheep hear his voice and he calls them by name (10:3) → Mosiah 5:12, hear and know the voice, and the name by which he shall call you. They know his voice (10:4) → 5:13, how knoweth a man the master. A stranger will they not follow (10:5) → 5:13, 'is a stranger unto him'. Then 5:14 supplies an animal illustration in which the beast that does not belong is driven off — which is the good-shepherd discourse's own logic, run from the flock's side rather than the shepherd's.

links.note: 'That ye hear and know the voice by which ye shall be called, and also, the name by which he shall call you.' Two of John 10:3-4's three distinctive elements, in John's order, one verse before the third arrives. The reason to catalogue this at 5:12 rather than 5:13 is that the naming and the voice are here, together, and they are together in the KJV only in the good shepherd discourse.
links.text: To him the porter openeth; and the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out.

pericopes.text: for, how knoweth a man the master which he hath not served, and which is a stranger unto him, and is far from the thoughts and intents of his heart?

provenance.other: “thoughts and intents of the heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 4:12. Jeremiah 30:24's 'intents of his heart' is the only other place the KJV uses 'intents' of a heart at all, and it has no 'thoughts'.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 4:12 is about a word that discerns what is inside a man; Mosiah 5:13 is about a master who is 'far from the thoughts and intents of his heart' — the same interior, described by its distance from God rather than by God's access to it. Hebrews' next verse is the one that matters for the borrowing: 'neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight'. Benjamin's question is how a man can know a master he has not served, and Hebrews' answer is that the master already knows him.

links.note: 'And is far from the thoughts and intents of his heart.' Five words of a KJV singleton, reproduced exactly. The machine stream found it and ranked it 2.00, which for once is right. The inversion is the argument: what Hebrews says God's word penetrates, Benjamin says an unserved master is remote from.
links.text: For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

provenance.other: “a stranger will they not follow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:5, which continues 'for they know not the voice of strangers'.
provenance.significance: John 10:5 is the negative half of the good shepherd's argument, and Mosiah 5:13 is its negative half too: a master who is a stranger is a master nobody can know. The link is filed separately from 5:12's because the source verses are consecutive and the Book of Mormon's clauses are consecutive, and the sequence is worth showing as a sequence.

links.note: 'The master which he hath not served, and which is a stranger unto him.' The shared word is one — 'stranger' — which on its own would be nothing; what carries it is position. Mosiah 5:12 has just used John 10:3-4's voice and name, and John 10:5 is the next verse in the source. Filed at moderate for that reason and not higher, since a one-word contact is only as strong as the sequence around it.
links.text: And a stranger will they not follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers.

pericopes.text: And again: Doth a man take an ass which belongeth to his neighbor, and keep him? I say unto you, Nay; he will not even suffer that he shall feed among his flocks, but will drive him away, and cast him out. I say unto you, that even so shall it be among you, if ye know not the name by which ye are called.

provenance.other: “take him away and cast him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 22:13. “many are called but few are chosen” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 22:14, the next verse.
provenance.significance: Matthew 22:11-14 is the KJV's one story about a man expelled from an assembly because he lacked the mark that showed he belonged, and it ends on the word Benjamin's verse ends on: called. 'Even so shall it be among you, if ye know not the name by which ye are called' sits four words from a borrowing whose source is followed immediately by 'many are called, but few are chosen'. Recovering the parable turns Benjamin's stray ass into the guest without a wedding garment, and the covenant name into the garment.

links.note: 'He will not even suffer that he shall feed among his flocks, but will drive him away, and cast him out.' The KJV's only 'take him away, and cast him' is the king's sentence on the man without a wedding garment. The Book of Mormon substitutes 'drive' for 'take' and 'out' for 'into outer darkness', which is why this is moderate rather than high — but the five-word frame is a singleton, the expulsion is the same expulsion, and the parable's punchline is the sentence Benjamin is writing toward.
links.text: Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness, there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

provenance.other: “which ye are called” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 2:7 — 'that worthy name by the which ye are called'. The KJV has no other verse in which a person is called BY a name in this construction.
provenance.significance: The context is the reason to record this rather than pass it over. James 2:1-7 is an argument against despising the poor in the assembly: the rich oppress you and blaspheme the worthy name by which you are called, so do not have the faith of Christ with respect of persons. Mosiah 4 has just spent twenty verses on beggars, on substance withheld, and on the rich whose substance shall perish with them; Mosiah 5 ends on the name by which they are called. Benjamin has used James 2's two subjects in James 2's order, one chapter apart.

links.note: 'If ye know not the name by which ye are called.' The construction is a KJV singleton and it is one Benjamin uses three times in four verses (5:11, 5:12, 5:14). Taken alone it would be a shared idiom; taken with the sermon's preceding chapter on the poor and the rich, which is James 2's own argument, it is a borrowing from a passage the discourse has been drawing on already.
links.text: Do not they blaspheme that worthy name by the which ye are called?

pericopes.text: Therefore, I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works, that Christ, the Lord God Omnipotent, may seal you his, that you may be brought to Heaven, that ye may have everlasting salvation and eternal life, through the wisdom, and power, and justice, and mercy of Him, who created all things, in Heaven and in Earth, who is God above all. Amen.

provenance.other: “always abounding” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:58, and so does the run 'stedfast unmoveable always abounding'. The Book of Mormon modernizes both spellings — 'steadfast and immovable' for 'stedfast, unmoveable' — and adds the conjunction.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is the last verse of the resurrection chapter, and its ground is stated in its own second half: 'forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord'. Benjamin's benediction ends on 'everlasting salvation and eternal life', which is what makes the labour not vain, and 4:20 has already asked whether this people has 'begged in vain' and answered no. The phrase the Book of Mormon will use for the rest of the record — steadfast and immovable — enters it here, out of the KJV's only sentence that says it.

links.note: 'I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works.' Three consecutive terms of 1 Corinthians 15:58 in Paul's order, with one substitution: 'good works' for 'the work of the Lord'. The substitution is doing the chapter's work, since Benjamin has spent 4:16-26 defining what the good works are. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six; the rarity is what carries it, since 'always abounding' exists in one KJV verse and nowhere else in English scripture.
links.text: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

provenance.other: 'Sealed' is common KJV English — 26 verses — but almost all of them seal a document. Only Ephesians 1:13 and 4:30, 2 Corinthians 1:22, and Revelation 7:3 seal people, and only Revelation 7:3 seals them with a name. “who created all things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 3:9, two chapters on from the sealing.
provenance.significance: The verse holds both halves of the Ephesian idea: God seals those who believe, and God created all things by Jesus Christ. Revelation 7:3 supplies the missing middle, sealing servants in their foreheads — which is where Revelation 14:1 wrote the name that Mosiah 5:12 has just moved into the heart. Sealing and naming are one act in Revelation and Benjamin has kept them one act here: Christ seals them his, and what makes them his is the name they retain.

links.note: 'May seal you his … through the wisdom, and power, and justice, and mercy of Him, who created all things, in Heaven and in Earth.' Two contacts, neither decisive alone. The KJV seals people in four verses and Ephesians 1:13 is the one that seals believers on believing, which is Benjamin's condition; 'who created all things' is a KJV singleton at Ephesians 3:9. Filed at moderate as an echo because the sealing language is diffuse and the creation formula is a doxological commonplace the Book of Mormon uses on its own account at 4:9.
links.text: In whom ye also trusted, after that ye heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation: in whom also after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise,

pericopes.text: And now, king Benjamin thought it was expedient, after having finished speaking to the people, that he should take the names of all those who had entered into a covenant with God, to keep his commandments.

provenance.other: “make a sure covenant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 9:38, and it is the KJV's only covenant that is ratified by writing down the names of the people who enter it: 'we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it', followed in Nehemiah 10:1-27 by the list of names.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 6:1-6 runs the Nehemiah 9-10 sequence in Nehemiah's order and this is its first term. A public reading of the law to an assembled people (Nehemiah 8) → a covenant sealed by name (9:38-10:27) → an oath binding them to walk in God's law and observe his commandments, judgments and statutes (10:29) → Mosiah 6:1, names taken; 6:3, 'the oath which they had made'; 6:6, walking, observing, keeping. The Book of Mormon's one narrative of a written covenant roll is built on the Bible's one narrative of a written covenant roll, and the borrowing is structural rather than verbal, which is why it is filed at moderate and conceptual.

links.note: 'That he should take the names of all those who had entered into a covenant with God, to keep his commandments.' No clause is reproduced. What is reproduced is a procedure the KJV describes once — a covenant made sure by recording who is in it — and the three following verses go on reproducing it. The machine stream proposed Ezekiel 16:8 and Jeremiah 34:10 for 'entered into a covenant', which is the KJV's ordinary phrase; the distinctive act here is the taking of names, and only Nehemiah has it.
links.text: And because of all this we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there was not one soul, except it were little children, but what had entered into the covenant, and had taken upon them the name of Christ.

provenance.other: “nameth the name of Christ” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 2:19, and so does “them that are his”. 'The name of Christ' as such occurs in two verses, 2 Timothy 2:19 and 1 Peter 4:14, but 1 Peter's is about being reproached for it, not taking it upon oneself.
provenance.significance: This is the strongest single piece of evidence in the three chapters and it is not at the verse where the words are. 2 Timothy 2:19 holds three things in twenty-eight words: a seal, the sentence 'The Lord knoweth them that are his', and naming the name of Christ. Mosiah 5:13-15 and 6:2 hold the same three, in the same order and across four verses — 5:13 asks how a man can know a master he has not served, 5:15 asks that Christ 'may seal you his', and 6:2 says every soul 'had taken upon them the name of Christ'. 'Seal', 'his', and 'the name of Christ' are all in one KJV verse and all in one stretch of Benjamin's conclusion. The suppressed half is Paul's condition, 'depart from iniquity', which Mosiah 5:11 has already supplied as the exception under which the name is blotted out.

links.note: 'There was not one soul, except it were little children, but what had entered into the covenant, and had taken upon them the name of Christ.' Taken alone the phrase is shared with two KJV verses and the link would be moderate at best. Taken with 5:15's 'seal you his' — where 'them that are his' is a KJV singleton at the same verse that names the name of Christ — the coincidence stops being a coincidence. Recorded at 6:2 because that is where the borrowed words stand; the argument is made across 5:13-6:2 and the recurrence field carries it.
links.text: Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.

pericopes.text: And again: It came to pass that when king Benjamin had made an end of all these things, and had consecrated his son Mosiah, to be a ruler and a king over his people, and had given him all the charges concerning the kingdom, and also had appointed priests to teach the people, that thereby they might hear and know the commandments of God, and to stir them up in remembrance of the oath which they had made, he dismissed the multitude, and they returned, every one according to their families, to their own houses.

provenance.other: “appointed him to be ruler” and “king in my stead” both occur in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse, 1 Kings 1:35 — David installing Solomon. “king over his people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 15:1, Samuel anointing Saul. “charged Solomon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 2:1.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's succession is Solomon's. 1 Kings 1:35 makes the heir both ruler and king in one sentence, which is the pairing Mosiah 6:3 keeps — 'a ruler and a king over his people' — and 1 Kings 2:1-3 has the dying father charging his son, which is Mosiah 6:3's 'given him all the charges concerning the kingdom' and 6:5's death two verses later. The Book of Mormon has taken the Davidic transfer whole: appointment, double title, charge, death, and then at 6:6 the son walking in the ways of the Lord, which is 1 Kings 2:3's own next clause.

links.note: 'Had consecrated his son Mosiah, to be a ruler and a king over his people, and had given him all the charges concerning the kingdom.' The double title is the tell. The KJV appoints a man ruler and calls him king in one breath exactly once, and that once is the verse where a king hands his throne to his son before dying. 'Over his people' comes from the other royal installation, Saul's. The machine stream's best proposal here was Acts 7:35's 'to be a ruler and a', six words — and Acts's next word is 'deliverer', Moses and not a king. Read the whole candidate verse.
links.text: Then ye shall come up after him, that he may come and sit upon my throne; for he shall be king in my stead: and I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and over Judah.

provenance.other: “departed every one to his house” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 6:19, the dismissal of the assembly after David brings up the ark. 1 Kings 8:66 is the same act at the end of Solomon's temple dedication — 'he sent the people away … and they went unto their tents'.
provenance.significance: The KJV has two great royal assemblies that end with the king sending the people home, and they are David's and Solomon's — the same two reigns this chapter has been quoting since 6:3. Mosiah 6:3's dismissal formula falls exactly where 1 Kings 8:66's does, at the close of a multi-day gathering built around a king, a sacrifice and a covenant, and the phrase it uses is 2 Samuel 6:19's.

links.note: 'He dismissed the multitude, and they returned, every one according to their families, to their own houses.' The Book of Mormon inserts 'according to their families', which is neither source's, and keeps the rest. Filed at moderate as an echo because dismissing an assembly is a thing narratives have to say and the KJV's ways of saying it are few; what raises it above nothing is that the two KJV verses which say it this way are the two royal assemblies this chapter is already imitating.
links.text: And he dealt among all the people, even among the whole multitude of Israel, as well to the women as men, to every one a cake of bread, and a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine. So all the people departed every one to his house.

pericopes.text: And Mosiah began to reign in his father’s stead. And he began to reign in the thirtieth year of his age, making in the whole, about four hundred and seventy-six years from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “thirty years old when he began to reign” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 5:4 — David. “to reign in his stead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 1:8, and it is Solomon's own account of his accession: 'thou hast shewed great mercy unto David my father, and hast made me to reign in his stead.' The KJV's ordinary regnal formula is the past 'reigned in his stead' (1 Kings 11:43 and dozens more); the infinitive is Solomon's alone.
provenance.significance: Two verses, two kings, one succession. Mosiah begins to reign at the age at which David began to reign, in the words in which Solomon described succeeding David. Neither datum is required by the narrative — the Book of Mormon supplies a regnal age here and nowhere else in the chapter — and the chronological note that follows ('four hundred and seventy-six years from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem') is itself a Kings-style synchronism. This verse is where the Davidic frame of 6:3-6 becomes arithmetic.

links.note: 'And Mosiah began to reign in his father's stead. And he began to reign in the thirtieth year of his age.' The two clauses are the two KJV singletons, in reverse order to their sources. The n-gram stream proposed 2 Kings 15:13 for the first and Ezekiel 1:1 for the second, both of which share the frame and neither of which has the age and the accession together; the verse that has both is David's.
links.text: David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years.

pericopes.text: And king Benjamin lived three years, and he died.
And it came to pass that king Mosiah did walk in the ways of the Lord, and did observe his judgments, and his statutes, and did keep his commandments in all things whatsoever he commanded him.

provenance.other: “his judgments and his statutes” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 8:11 and Nehemiah 10:29. Deuteronomy has 'his commandments, and his judgments, and his statutes' inside a warning against forgetting; Nehemiah has walking, observing, commandments, judgments and statutes, in that order, inside an oath.
provenance.significance: The mediation is between two Old Testament verses rather than between Testaments, and the deciding evidence is the verb and the frame. Both candidates list judgments and statutes in that order, and only Nehemiah supplies 'walk' and 'observe', which are Mosiah 6:6's two other verbs. Nehemiah also supplies the setting: 10:29 is the oath sworn by the people whose names were sealed in 10:1-27, which is Mosiah 6:1's list, and it is 'the oath which they had made' that Mosiah 6:3 says the priests are appointed to stir the people up in remembrance of. The chapter's evaluation of Mosiah's reign is written in the vocabulary of the covenant his people had just signed.

links.note: 'Did walk in the ways of the Lord, and did observe his judgments, and his statutes, and did keep his commandments.' Five of Nehemiah 10:29's terms in Nehemiah's sequence. The machine stream ranked Deuteronomy 8:11 and Nehemiah 10:29 within a hundredth of each other, which is a fair reading of the shared string and a poor reading of the evidence: Deuteronomy's verse is a prohibition ('Beware that thou forget not'), and it has no 'walk' and no 'observe'.
links.text: They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God’s law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes;

provenance.other: “walk in his ways to keep his statutes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 2:3, which is David's dying charge to Solomon: 'keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments'.
provenance.significance: This is the other half of a link the chapter makes twice. Nehemiah 10:29 supplies the covenant-oath vocabulary; 1 Kings 2:3 supplies the same four nouns in a father's charge to a son who is about to reign — which is what Mosiah 6:3 has just narrated in 1 Kings 1:35's words. Read with 6:3 and 6:4, the sequence is David's exactly: appoint him ruler and king, charge him, die, and let the son walk in the ways of the Lord. The Book of Mormon has not chosen between its two sources and neither should the catalogue; both are registered, with Nehemiah carrying the verbs and Kings carrying the situation.

links.note: 'Did walk in the ways of the Lord, and did observe his judgments, and his statutes, and did keep his commandments in all things whatsoever he commanded him.' 1 Kings 2:3 is the KJV's only sentence pairing walking in his ways with keeping his statutes, and it stands two verses after 'he charged Solomon his son' — the charge Mosiah 6:3 says Benjamin gave. Filed at moderate rather than high because Nehemiah 10:29 accounts for the wording better and because a double attribution weakens each; the reason to keep it is that no reading of 6:3-6 as a whole works without it.
links.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

pericopes.text: And king Mosiah did cause his people that they should till the earth. And he also, himself did till the earth, that thereby he might not become burthensome to his people, that he might do according to that which his father had done, in all things. And there was no contention among all his people, for the space of three years.

provenance.other: 'Burdensome' occurs in five KJV verses. One is Zechariah's burdensome stone; the other four are Paul refusing to be a charge on a congregation (2 Corinthians 11:9, 12:13, 12:14, 1 Thessalonians 2:6). “not be burdensome to you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:14. 2 Thessalonians 3:8 gives the practice behind the principle — “chargeable to any of you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is that one: 'wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you'. The 1830 reads 'burthensome', an archaic spelling that is not the KJV's; 1920 corrected it to the KJV's 'burdensome'.
provenance.significance: Mosiah's tilling is a Pauline argument in a king's mouth. The one thing the King James Bible says about not being burdensome is said by an apostle who supported himself with his hands so that his ministry would cost nothing, and Mosiah works the earth himself for exactly that reason. Note the direction of the 1830-to-1920 change: the first edition's 'burthensome' obscures the borrowing and the later correction restores it, so the modern text shows the KJV more plainly than the earliest one does — the reverse of the usual pattern in this catalogue.

links.note: 'That thereby he might not become burthensome to his people.' The word carries the link and it is a word the KJV reserves almost entirely to one Pauline argument. What secures it is the rationale, which is Paul's and not a king's: 2 Corinthians 12:14 refuses support on the ground that 'the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children', and 2 Thessalonians 3:8 refuses it by working night and day. Mosiah's fields are the same refusal. Filed at moderate because the shared vocabulary is one word and the argument does the rest.
links.text: Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours but you: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children.

pericopes.text: And now, it came to pass that after king Mosiah had had continual peace, for the space of three years, he was desirous to know concerning the people which went up to dwell in the land of Lehi-Nephi, or in the city of Lehi-Nephi: for his people had heard nothing from them, from the time they left the land of Zarahemla; therefore, they wearied him with their teasings.

provenance.other: 'Wearied' occurs in twelve KJV verses, but only Malachi 2:17 has the construction the Book of Mormon uses — a transitive 'wearied X with Y', where Y is the speech of a discontented people. Isaiah 43:24's 'thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities' is the nearest rival and puts sins, not words, in the instrumental slot.
provenance.alternative: Judges 16:16, where Delilah 'pressed him daily with her words, and urged him', is the closer match for 'teasings' as a behaviour and shares no vocabulary at all.
provenance.significance: Recover Malachi 2:17 and the wearying is a demand for an absent God: 'Ye have wearied the LORD with your words … Where is the God of judgment?' Mosiah 7:1 opens the Limhi narrative with a people wearying their king for news of a colony nobody has heard from — the demand for an absent party, put to the one person who cannot produce him. The chapter answers it by producing not the colony but a sermon about the God who brought the fathers out (7:19-20), which is Malachi's answer as well.

links.note: 'His people had heard nothing from them … therefore, they wearied him with their teasings.' The verbal contact is one word plus a construction, and that is all it is: 'wearied him with their teasings' against Malachi's 'wearied the LORD with your words'. What recommends it is that the Book of Mormon's idiom for this is otherwise absent — nobody else in the corpus is wearied with anything — and that the KJV supplies exactly one model for the phrase.
links.whyNot: 'Wearied' is ordinary English and 'teasings' is not a KJV word at all; the shared material is a single verb in a common frame. A reader who wants a source will find the frame in Isaiah 43:24 as easily as in Malachi, and a reader who does not want one has lost nothing.
links.text: Ye have wearied the LORD with your words. Yet ye say, Wherein have we wearied him? When ye say, Every one that doeth evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delighteth in them; or, Where is the God of judgment?

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that king Mosiah granted that sixteen of their strong men might go up to the land of Lehi-Nephi, to inquire concerning their brethren.
And it came to pass that on the morrow, they started to go up, having with them one Ammon, he being a strong and mighty man, and a descendant of Zarahemla; and he was also their leader.
And now, they knew not the course they should travel in the wilderness, to go up to the land of Lehi-Nephi; therefore, they wandered many days in the wilderness, even forty days did they wander.
And when they had wandered forty days, they came to a hill, which is north of the land of Shilom, and there they pitched their tents.
And Ammon took three of his brethren, and their names were Amaleki, Helem, and Hem, and they went down into the land of Nephi;

and behold, they met the king of the people, which was in the land of Nephi, and in the land of Shilom; and they were surrounded by the king’s guard, and was taken, and was bound, and was committed to prison.

And it came to pass when they had been in prison two days, they were again brought before the king, and their bands were loosed; and they stood before the king, and was permitted, or rather commanded that they should answer the questions which he should ask them.

provenance.other: “bands were loosed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 16:26. The KJV's other prison-release formulas use different nouns: Peter's 'chains fell off from his hands' (Acts 12:7), Joseph's 'the keeper of the prison looked not to any thing' (Genesis 39:23), Paul's 'my bonds in Christ' (Philippians 1:13).
provenance.significance: Acts 16 is the Philippian jail: Paul and Silas are beaten, put in the inner prison, and at midnight the earthquake looses everyone's bands — after which the jailer, who had meant to kill himself, brings them out and asks what he must do to be saved. Mosiah 7 runs the same sequence inverted. Ammon and his brethren are imprisoned two days, their bands are loosed by the king's order rather than by an earthquake, and the man who had intended to put them to death (7:11) is the one who then convenes his people to hear a sermon about deliverance. The KJV's one released-bands verse is the one where the jailer is converted, and Limhi is Mosiah's jailer.

links.note: 'When they had been in prison two days, they were again brought before the king, and their bands were loosed.' Four words, but they are the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, and they arrive in the setting that produced them — a prison, a release, and a captor about to become a hearer. The rest of the verse is court-narrative boilerplate ('brought before the king' is Esther 9:11's phrase and four others'); the loosed bands are not.
links.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one’s bands were loosed.

pericopes.text: And he saith unto them, Behold, I am Limhi, the son of Noah, which was the son of Zeniff, which came up out of the land of Zarahemla to inherit this land, which was the land of their fathers, which was made a king by the voice of the people.

provenance.other: “voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7. The chapter's other refusals read 'hearken unto their voice' (8:9, 8:22), so the full phrase is not even a Samuel formula; it is a single verse.
provenance.significance: The one KJV verse that contains 'the voice of the people' is the verse in which God tells Samuel to give Israel a king, and glosses the request as apostasy: 'they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.' Limhi introduces his own dynasty with that phrase — Zeniff 'was made a king by the voice of the people' — and the sentence he is speaking is a confession that the dynasty produced bondage, a slain prophet and a tax. The book then ends by dismantling kingship in favour of judges chosen, in Mosiah 29's repeated formula, by the voice of the people. The phrase enters the book carrying 1 Samuel 8's verdict on monarchy and leaves it as the name of the alternative.

links.note: 'Zeniff, which came up out of the land of Zarahemla to inherit this land … which was made a king by the voice of the people.' The phrase that will govern the political argument of the whole book of Mosiah appears here at its first use in this narrative, in a genealogy of failed kings, and it is a KJV singleton belonging to the Bible's own account of why Israel should not have had a king. 2 Nephi 10:11 has the phrase earlier in the corpus in a different sense (a land with no kings); this is the first place it does the work 1 Samuel 8 does.
links.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

pericopes.text: And now, I desire to know the cause whereby ye were so bold as to come near the walls of the city, when I, myself, was with my guards, without the gate?
And now, for this cause have I suffered that ye should be preserved, that I might inquire of you, or else I should have caused that my guards should have put you to death.— Ye are permitted to speak.

And now, when Ammon saw that he was permitted to speak, he went forth and bowed himself before the king; and rising again, he said, O king, I am very thankful before God this day, that I am yet alive, and am permitted to speak; and I will endeavor to speak with boldness:

for I am assured that if ye had known me, ye would not have suffered that I should have wore these bands. For I am Ammon, and am a descendant of Zarahemla, and have come up out of the land of Zarahemla, to inquire concerning our brethren, which Zeniff brought up out of that land.

And now, it came to pass that after Limhi had heard the words of Ammon, he was exceeding glad, and said, Now, I know of a surety that my brethren which was in the land of Zarahemla, are yet alive. And now, I will rejoice; and on the morrow, I will cause that my people shall rejoice also.

provenance.other: “know of a surety” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 15:13 and Acts 12:11. Only Acts 12:11 has the full sequence the Book of Mormon reproduces — 'he said, Now I know of a surety, that' — because Genesis 15:13 is an imperative addressed to Abram, not a first-person realisation.
provenance.significance: Acts 12:11 is Peter outside the prison, having just walked past two wards and an iron gate, saying that he now knows the Lord has delivered him out of the hand of Herod. Mosiah 7 puts the sentence in the mouth of a king who has himself just held four men in a prison for two days and loosed their bands (7:8, and see Acts 16:26 there). Limhi's 'surety' is that his brethren are alive; Peter's is that he is. Read together with 7:8 the chapter has borrowed both of Acts's prison-deliverance verses within seven verses of each other, and it is about to spend the rest of the chapter arguing that God delivers people out of bondage.

links.note: 'Now, I know of a surety that my brethren which was in the land of Zarahemla, are yet alive.' Eight consecutive words of Acts 12:11 in the 1830 text ('said, Now I know of a surety, that'), from one of only two KJV verses with the idiom, and the one whose grammar matches. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six; catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the run plus the singular fit of the frame. Note also that the machine's top-scoring rival here is Luke 23:8's 'he was exceeding glad' at the head of the same verse, which is Herod's gladness at seeing Jesus and is covered by the standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 3:8.
links.text: And when Peter was come to himself, he said, Now I know of a surety, that the LORD hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews.

pericopes.text: For behold, we are in bondage to the Lamanites, and are taxed with a tax which is grievous to be borne. And now, behold, our brethren will deliver us out of our bondage, or out of the hands of the Lamanites, and we will be their slaves: for it is better that we be slaves to the Nephites, than to pay tribute to the king of the Lamanites.

provenance.other: “grievous to be borne” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 23:4 and Luke 11:46, which are the same woe in two Gospels. Luke reads 'burdens grievous to be borne'; Matthew reads 'heavy burdens and grievous to be borne'. The Book of Mormon's 'a tax which is grievous to be borne' has no conjunction and so follows Luke's attributive construction rather than Matthew's coordinated one — a thin discriminator, and the reason both are recorded.
provenance.significance: The phrase belongs, in both Gospels, to a woe against religious authorities who lay burdens on other men and will not lift a finger to move them. Limhi applies it to a tribute of half of everything the colony grows and owns, exacted by a foreign king — a burden laid by a power that bears none of it. The metalepsis is that the KJV's only idiom for an unbearable burden is an idiom of clerical hypocrisy, and Limhi's next move is to concede that his own people's iniquity is what put the burden there (7:20).

links.note: 'We are in bondage to the Lamanites, and are taxed with a tax which is grievous to be borne.' Five words from a two-verse KJV idiom, and the phrase does real work in the chapter: it returns at 7:23 as the rhetorical question that opens Limhi's lament ('is not this grievous to be borne?'), so the borrowing is not incidental but the frame of the complaint. Adjudicated here at first use; 7:23 is Limhi repeating himself.
links.text: And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.

pericopes.text: And now, king Limhi commanded his guards that they should no more bind Ammon, nor his brethren, but caused that they should go to the hill which was north of Shilom, and bring their brethren into the city, that thereby they might eat, and drink, and rest themselves from the labors of their journey; for they had suffered many things: they had suffered hunger, thirst, and fatigue.

And now, it came to pass on the morrow, that king Limhi sent a proclamation among all his people, that thereby they might gather themselves together to the temple, to hear the words which he should speak unto them.

And it came to pass that when they had gathered themselves together, that he spake unto them in this wise, saying, O ye, my people, lift up your heads and be comforted: for behold, the time is at hand, or is not far distant, when we shall no longer be in subjection to our enemies, notwithstanding our many strugglings, which have been in vain; yet I trust there remaineth an effectual struggle to be made.

provenance.other: “lift up your heads” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Psalm 24:7, Psalm 24:9 and Luke 21:28. The two Psalm verses address gates, not people ('Lift up your heads, O ye gates'), which leaves Luke 21:28 as the only KJV verse in which the imperative is spoken to a congregation. “the time is at hand” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 1:3 and Revelation 22:10.
provenance.significance: Luke 21:28 sits inside the Olivet discourse, immediately after distress of nations and men's hearts failing them for fear, and the reason given for lifting the head is that 'your redemption draweth nigh'. Limhi keeps the imperative and replaces the eschatological reason with a political one: the time is at hand when 'we shall no longer be in subjection to our enemies'. The suppressed correspondence is that Luke's redemption is deliverance from the world and Limhi's is deliverance from a tax — and the chapter will refuse that reduction at 7:33, where the deliverance turns out to be conditional on turning to the Lord.

links.note: 'O ye, my people, lift up your heads and be comforted: for behold, the time is at hand.' Both halves are KJV rarities and they arrive in Luke's own order: the imperative to lift the head, then 'for' plus a clause announcing that the deliverance is near. Luke has 'for your redemption draweth nigh'; the Book of Mormon has 'for behold, the time is at hand', which is Revelation's phrase doing Luke's job. The imperative is then repeated at the head of 7:19, where it introduces the historical creed — so the Olivet sentence is being used as a sermon exordium.
links.text: And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh.

pericopes.text: Therefore, lift up your heads, and rejoice, and put your trust in God, in that God who was the God of Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob; and also, that God who brought the Children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, and caused that they should walk through the Red Sea on dry ground, and fed them with manna, that they might not perish in the wilderness; and many more things did he do for them.

provenance.route: Exodus 14:16, 14:22 → Hebrews 11:29 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “through the Red sea” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:29. Exodus never puts those words together: at 14:22 the children of Israel 'went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground', at 15:4 Pharaoh's captains are 'drowned in the Red sea', at 13:18 God leads the people 'through the way of the wilderness of the Red sea'. “on dry ground through” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 14:16.
provenance.significance: This is the mediation case the chapter turns on, and rarity settles it where the diff cannot. The Book of Mormon's clause 'walk through the Red Sea on dry ground' is a fusion of two KJV singletons: the crossing is named in the New Testament's words and the surface is named in the Old Testament's. Hebrews 11:29 supplies 'through the Red sea' and nothing in the Hebrew Bible does; Exodus 14:16 supplies 'on dry ground through' and Hebrews reads 'as by dry land'. So the sentence is not Exodus with a New Testament gloss or Hebrews with an Exodus correction — it is a writer who has both phrases available and takes the more vivid noun from each.

links.note: 'That God who brought the Children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, and caused that they should walk through the Red Sea on dry ground.' tools/mediation-check.py declines this pair — Exodus 14:22 and Hebrews 11:29 do not differ at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces word for word — but the rarity counts decide it in the tool's place. 'Through the Red sea' is Hebrews' alone and 'on dry ground' is Exodus'. Hebrews 11:29 has already been the source at 1 Nephi 4:2, where the same verse governs a Red Sea recital used as a warrant for courage; here it governs a Red Sea recital used as a warrant for hope, which is Hebrews 11's own rhetorical use of it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Mosiah 7.19 (cross-references Exodus 14:21-22 for the Red Sea crossing)
links.text: By faith they passed through the Red sea as by dry land: which the Egyptians assaying to do were drowned.

provenance.other: “fed thee with manna” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 8:3; the only other verse joining the verb to the noun is Deuteronomy 8:16, 'who fed thee in the wilderness with manna'. Exodus 16, which narrates the manna at length, never says God fed anyone with it — at 16:35 'the children of Israel did eat manna forty years', with Israel as the subject.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 8 is the chapter that explains why the wilderness was allowed to be hard: God 'humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna … that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only'. Limhi is preaching to a colony under a tax of half its grain, and the verse he reaches for is the one in which hunger is pedagogy and the ration is a lesson. Four verses later he will say the bondage came 'because of our iniquities' (7:20), which is Deuteronomy 8's argument arriving at its point.

links.note: 'And fed them with manna, that they might not perish in the wilderness.' The KJV's only construction in which God is the subject of feeding and manna the instrument is Deuteronomy 8:3, twice repeated in that chapter and nowhere else. The purpose clause is the Book of Mormon's own; Deuteronomy's is 'that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only'. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Exodus 16:35 at this verse, which is where the manna narrative is, but the wording is Deuteronomy's — see the exclusion register at this verse.
links.text: And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live.

provenance.route: Exodus 3:6, or its New Testament citations → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV's formula is always distributive — 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' (Exodus 3:6, 3:15, 3:16, 4:5; Matthew 22:32; Mark 12:26; Luke 20:37; Acts 3:13; 7:32). The undistributed list “Abraham and Isaac and Jacob” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 8:11 and Luke 13:28, and in neither is it governed by 'God of'. The Book of Mormon's 'that God who was the God of Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob' has the Old Testament's governing noun over the New Testament's compressed list, which is why the mediation is recorded as uncertain rather than decided.
provenance.significance: Whoever wrote this sentence had the burning-bush formula and did not reproduce it. That is worth recording precisely because it is a negative result: the one place in the chapter where a famous KJV phrase was available and was not copied is the place where a copyist would have been most likely to copy.

links.note: 'In that God who was the God of Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob.' The patriarchal triad is unmistakably the Exodus 3 formula in function — it opens a historical creed that runs on through Egypt, the Red Sea and the manna — but it is not the Exodus 3 formula in form, because the KJV always repeats 'the God of' before each name and here it is said once. The compressed list as such is a Gospel construction (Matthew 8:11, Luke 13:28), so the sentence is either Exodus loosely remembered or Exodus filtered through the Gospels' way of listing the three. The mediation-check cannot separate them and neither can I.
links.whyNot: Three patriarchal names in canonical order are the most quotable sequence in the Hebrew Bible and require no source at all; a preacher could produce this line without a text in front of him. What keeps the row is the company it sits in — Egypt, the Red Sea and the manna follow in Exodus order in the same sentence.
links.text: Moreover he said, I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. And Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon God.

pericopes.text: And again: That same God hath brought our fathers out of the land of Jerusalem, and hath kept and preserved his people, even until now. And behold, it is because of our iniquities and abominations, that has brought us into bondage.—

provenance.other: “our fathers out of the land of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 24:17, which also supplies 'preserved us in all the way wherein we went' and 'the house of bondage' — three of the four things Mosiah 7:20 says.
provenance.significance: Joshua 24 is the covenant renewal at Shechem, and 24:17 is the people's answer to 'choose you this day whom ye will serve': the LORD brought our fathers out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, and preserved us. Limhi is standing at a temple (7:17) addressing a gathered people and reciting the same creed with one substitution — Jerusalem for Egypt — and then adds the clause Joshua's people did not say: 'it is because of our iniquities and abominations, that has brought us into bondage.' The house of bondage they came out of in Joshua is the bondage they have gone back into here, and the sermon's whole argument is that they walked into it themselves.

links.note: 'That same God hath brought our fathers out of the land of Jerusalem, and hath kept and preserved his people, even until now.' The exodus formula is everywhere in the KJV — 'out of the land of Egypt' occurs in eighty-one verses — but the specific possessive, 'our fathers out of the land of', is Joshua 24:17's alone, and Joshua 24:17 is also the only verse in that family that pairs the bringing-out with preserving. Substituting Jerusalem for Egypt is the Book of Mormon's standing move in exodus recitals; what is new here is that the bondage in the verse is the present one.
links.text: For the LORD our God, he it is that brought us up and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, and which did those great signs in our sight, and preserved us in all the way wherein we went, and among all the people through whom we passed:

pericopes.text: And ye all are witnesses this day, that Zeniff, who was made king over this people, he being over zealous to inherit the land of his fathers, therefore being deceived by the cunning and craftiness of king Laman, who having entered into a treaty with king Zeniff, and having yielded up into his hands the possessions of a part of the land, or even the city of Lehi-Nephi, and the city of Shilom, and the land round about;

provenance.other: “cunning craftiness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:14. 'Craftiness' alone occurs in five (Job 5:13, Luke 20:23, 1 Corinthians 3:19, 2 Corinthians 4:2, Ephesians 4:14), and only Ephesians pairs it with 'cunning'.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 4:14 is about children 'tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive'. Limhi applies it not to false teaching but to a treaty: king Laman yielded up two cities in order to get a people inside his borders where he could tax them. The suppressed correspondence is the last clause of Ephesians 4:14 — 'whereby they lie in wait to deceive' — which is precisely what Mosiah 9:10 says Laman was doing, and which no reader who does not recover the verse will see.

links.note: 'Being deceived by the cunning and craftiness of king Laman, who having entered into a treaty with king Zeniff.' The KJV joins these two nouns in one verse only, and the Book of Mormon joins them here and again at Mosiah 9:10, where Zeniff's own record calls it 'the cunning and the craftiness of king Laman' in almost the same words. This is the first use in the book and the argument is made here; 9:10 is Zeniff's account of the same event and is registered as a recurrence.
links.text: That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;

pericopes.text: and all this he done, for the sole purpose of bringing this people into subjection, or into bondage. And behold, we at this time do pay tribute to the king of the Lamanites, to the amount of one half of our corn, and our barley, and even all our grain of every kind, and one half of the increase of our flocks, and our herds; and even one half of all we have or possess, the king of the Lamanites doth exact of us, or our lives.
And now, is not this grievous to be borne? And is not this, our afflictions, great? Now behold, how great reason have we to mourn.
Yea; I say unto you, great are the reasons which we have to mourn: for behold, how many of our brethren have been slain, and their blood hath been spilt in vain, and all because of iniquity.

For if this people had not fallen into transgression, the Lord would not have suffered that this great evil should come upon them. But behold, they would not hearken unto his words; but there arose contentions among them, even so much that they did shed blood among themselves.

And a Prophet of the Lord have they slain; yea, a chosen man of God, who told them of their wickedness and abominations, and prophesied of many things which is to come, yea, even the coming of Christ.

provenance.other: “slain them which shewed before” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:52, and so does “coming of the Just One”. The KJV's other prophet-killing verses — 1 Kings 19:10 ('slain thy prophets with the sword'), Nehemiah 9:26 ('slew thy prophets'), Matthew 23:37 ('thou that killest the prophets') — none of them says the prophets were killed for foretelling the Messiah. Acts 7:52 is the only verse in the Bible that makes that the charge.
provenance.significance: Acts 7 is Stephen's speech, and Mosiah 7:19-26 is built on its shape: the God of Abraham and the patriarchs, the bringing out of Egypt, the wilderness, then the accusation that the fathers killed the prophet who foretold the coming of the Just One. Stephen is stoned for saying it. Limhi says it about Abinadi, who was burned for saying that Christ was God and would take upon him flesh (7:27) — and the man Limhi's own father killed for it was killed by the king Limhi succeeded. The metalepsis is that the borrowed sentence is the last thing its original speaker ever said, and the reason he was killed was that he said it.

links.note: 'And a Prophet of the Lord have they slain; yea, a chosen man of God, who told them of their wickedness and abominations, and prophesied of many things which is to come, yea, even the coming of Christ.' Two KJV singletons from one verse, and the whole logical structure of that verse: prophets slain, and slain specifically for having shown beforehand the coming of the Messiah. This is the chapter's headline. Limhi's sermon from 7:19 has been running the historical creed of Acts 7 — patriarchs, Egypt, wilderness — and it lands where Stephen's lands, on the charge that the fathers murdered the prophet who announced the Just One. The 1830 'which is to come' was corrected to 'are' in 1920; the KJV's own idiom here is Acts 7:52's participial 'shewed before of the coming', which the Book of Mormon expands into a finite clause.
links.text: Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? and they have slain them which shewed before of the coming of the Just One; of whom ye have been now the betrayers and murderers:

pericopes.text: And because he saith unto them, That Christ was the God, the Father of all things, and saith that he should take upon him the image of man, and it should be the image after which man was created in the beginning; or in other words, he said that man was created after the image of God, and that God should come down among the children of men, and take upon him flesh and blood, and go forth upon the face of the earth;

provenance.other: “partakers of flesh and blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 2:14, and so does “took part of the same”. 'Flesh and blood' by itself occurs in five KJV verses, but Hebrews 2:14 is the only one in which the phrase names what the Son took on rather than what human beings are limited by (Matthew 16:17, 1 Corinthians 15:50, Galatians 1:16, Ephesians 6:12). “took upon him” belongs to Philippians 2:7's 'took upon him the form of a servant'.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 2:14 gives the reason for the incarnation as the destruction of him that had the power of death. Abinadi's doctrine as Limhi reports it — God comes down among the children of men, takes upon him flesh and blood, and goes forth upon the earth — is Hebrews 2:14's clause with Philippians 2:7's verb, and the sentence that follows in Mosiah 7:28 is that they put him to death for saying it. The suppressed correspondence is that Hebrews 2:14's whole point is that the one who takes flesh takes it in order to die.

links.note: 'And that God should come down among the children of men, and take upon him flesh and blood, and go forth upon the face of the earth.' The KJV has exactly one verse in which a divine subject takes on flesh and blood, and this is its wording; the verb 'take upon him' is Philippians 2:7's, from the other great KJV incarnation sentence. What the Book of Mormon adds is 'come down' and 'go forth upon the face of the earth', neither of which is in either source. The doctrinal content of the verse — that Christ is 'the God, the Father of all things' — is the reading the 1837 edition began smoothing elsewhere in the corpus and left untouched here.
links.text: Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;

provenance.other: “the image of God” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Genesis 1:27, Genesis 9:6 and 2 Corinthians 4:4. Only Genesis 1:27 has it as the pattern of the human creature's making; 2 Corinthians 4:4 applies it to Christ, and Genesis 9:6 uses it as the ground of the law against homicide.
