provenance.significance: Limhi's report of Abinadi runs the identification in both directions in one sentence: Christ takes the image of man, and that image is the one after which man was made, because man was created after the image of God. Genesis 9:6's use of the phrase is the sanction against shedding man's blood — which is what verse 28 says they then did to the man who preached it.

links.note: 'It should be the image after which man was created in the beginning; or in other words, he said that man was created after the image of God.' The self-correcting doubling ('or in other words') is the Book of Mormon's own habit, but the two halves it bridges are Genesis 1:27's phrase used twice with the terms reversed. 'In the beginning' is Genesis 1:1's, and the sentence is doing what Genesis 1 does: establishing the image before anything is said about what happens to it.
links.text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

pericopes.text: and now, because he said this, they did put him to death; and many more things did they do, which brought down the wrath of God upon them. Therefore, who wondereth that they are in bondage, and that they are smitten with sore afflictions?

For behold, the Lord hath said, I will not succor my people in the day of their transgression; but I will hedge up their ways, that they prosper not; and their doings shall be as a stumbling block before them.

provenance.other: “my people in the day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Obadiah 1:13, where it appears inside 'my people in the day of their calamity' and the phrase 'in the day of their calamity' is then repeated three times in the one verse. “in the day of their” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Jeremiah 18:17, Obadiah 1:12 and Obadiah 1:13.
provenance.significance: Obadiah 1:13 is the indictment of Edom for what Edom did not do: a brother nation stood at the gate of God's people in the day of their calamity and did not help. Mosiah 7:29 takes the sentence and puts God in Edom's position — 'I will not succor my people in the day of their transgression' — with one substitution, transgression for calamity, that supplies the whole justification. The suppressed point of correspondence is that the KJV's model for refusing to succour a people in their day is a text about a crime; the Book of Mormon's oracle answers the charge before it is made by changing what the day is a day of.

links.note: 'For behold, the Lord hath said, I will not succor my people in the day of their transgression.' Seven of the Book of Mormon's words track a KJV singleton, and the one word changed is the one that changes the moral sense of the sentence. This is the opening of a three-verse pastiche of prophetic oracle (7:29-31) which has no single biblical source and is assembled out of at least four — Obadiah here, Hosea 2:6 and Jeremiah 18:15 in the rest of this verse, Hosea 8:7 at 7:30 and Hosea 12:1 at 7:31.
links.text: Thou shouldest not have entered into the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; yea, thou shouldest not have looked on their affliction in the day of their calamity, nor have laid hands on their substance in the day of their calamity;

provenance.other: “hedge up thy way” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hosea 2:6, and the verb phrase 'hedge up' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Job 3:23's 'whom God hath hedged in' and Job 1:10's 'hast not thou made an hedge about him' are the only other hedging verses and both are protective.
provenance.significance: Hosea 2:6 hedges up the way of an unfaithful wife with thorns so that she cannot find her paths — and the reason given three verses later is 'then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now.' The hedge in Hosea is not punishment but obstruction with an object: it exists to make return the only remaining road. That is exactly the argument Limhi's sermon makes, and the reason the oracle at 7:29-31 is followed at 7:33 by 'if ye will turn to the Lord'. The borrowed image already contains the sermon's conclusion.

links.note: 'But I will hedge up their ways, that they prosper not.' The KJV uses 'hedge up' once, and the Book of Mormon uses it here, changing Hosea's singular way to a plural and his adulterous wife to a nation. Hosea's purpose clause is 'that she shall not find her paths'; the Book of Mormon's is 'that they prosper not', which is the standard promise of the Book of Mormon's own land covenant inverted. Both halves of the verse's second clause are prophetic borrowings: the hedge is Hosea's and the stumbling is Jeremiah 18:15's.
links.text: Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths.

provenance.other: “stumble in their ways” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 18:15. Jeremiah 18:17, two verses later, supplies both 'as with an east wind' and 'in the day of their calamity' — so a single short passage of Jeremiah holds three of the four distinctive elements of Mosiah 7:29-31: stumbling in their ways, the day of their calamity, and the east wind that arrives at 7:31.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 18 is the potter's-house chapter, whose argument is that a nation God has framed evil against may still turn and be spared. Verses 15-17 are its indictment: my people have forgotten me, they have been made to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, and I will scatter them as with an east wind. Mosiah 7:29-31 reproduces the indictment and then, at 7:33, reproduces the potter's-house offer — turn, and the sentence is lifted. Reading the borrowed oracle back into Jeremiah 18 makes Limhi's sermon a small Jeremiah 18 rather than a collage of doom sayings.

links.note: 'And their doings shall be as a stumbling block before them.' Taken alone this clause points at Ezekiel — 'I lay a stumbling-block before him' at Ezekiel 3:20, 'the stumblingblock of their iniquity' at Ezekiel 14:3 — and the machine proposed Ezekiel 3:20. Jeremiah 18:15 is preferred because it holds the two nouns the Book of Mormon actually pairs, stumbling and ways, in the same clause, and because Jeremiah 18:17 then accounts for both the day-of formula in the first half of this verse and the east wind two verses later. The verse's material is composite and the case for any single source is correspondingly moderate; what is not moderate is that Jeremiah 18:15-17 explains more of the passage than any other candidate.
links.text: Because my people hath forgotten me, they have burned incense to vanity, and they have caused them to stumble in their ways from the ancient paths, to walk in paths, in a way not cast up;

provenance.route: Isaiah 49:8 → 2 Corinthians 6:2 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “succoured” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Samuel 21:17 and 2 Corinthians 6:2; the whole verb family, 'succour' and its inflections, occurs in six. Of those six only 2 Corinthians 6:2 and Hebrews 2:18 have God or Christ as the one who succours.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 6:2 quotes Isaiah 49:8, and the KJV translates the same Hebrew verb 'helped' in Isaiah and 'succoured' in Paul. Where a text has 'succour' in a divine-help clause it is following the New Testament's English, not the Old Testament's. Mosiah 7:29 has the word and inverts the clause: Paul's 'in the day of salvation have I succoured thee' becomes 'I will not succor my people in the day of their transgression', with the day of salvation turned into a day of transgression and the succour withdrawn. Read back, Paul's verse continues 'behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation' — and Limhi's sermon ends four verses later by offering exactly that now.

links.note: 'I will not succor my people in the day of their transgression.' The verbal frame of the clause is Obadiah 1:13's and is catalogued there; what this row records is the single word, and the mediation it settles. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence for Isaiah 49:8 against 2 Corinthians 6:2, because the 1830 text spells the word 'succor' and the tool matches whole tokens, so the one place where the two candidates genuinely differ — Isaiah's 'helped' against Paul's 'succoured' — is reported as 'neither'. That is a limitation of the token match, not an absence of evidence: the word is in the KJV's New Testament only, in this sense, and the Book of Mormon has it.
links.whyNot: One word, and a word whose 1830 spelling differs from the KJV's. If the writer simply knew 'succour' as ordinary English — it was not archaic in 1830 — then no verse is being echoed and the day-of formula at Obadiah 1:13 carries the whole link. The row is kept because the mediation finding is worth stating even at moderate confidence, and because the inversion of Paul's day of salvation into a day of transgression is too neat to leave unrecorded.
links.text: (For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)

pericopes.text: And again: He saith, If my people shall sow filthiness, they shall reap the chaff thereof, in the whirlwind; and the effects thereof, is poison.

provenance.other: “reap the whirlwind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hosea 8:7. The chaff-and-whirlwind pairing that the Book of Mormon adds is Hosea 13:3's, 'as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor'; 'whirlwind' alone occurs in twelve KJV verses and 'chaff' in fourteen, so neither noun identifies a source on its own and their combination in one prophet does.
provenance.significance: Hosea 8:7's sowing and reaping is an agricultural futility oracle: what is sown produces nothing that can be eaten, and what little it yields strangers swallow up. Mosiah 7 is spoken to a people paying half of their corn, barley and grain to a foreign king — strangers swallowing the yield is not a metaphor in this chapter, it is the tax described at 7:22. The borrowed proverb has become literal.

links.note: 'If my people shall sow filthiness, they shall reap the chaff thereof, in the whirlwind.' The KJV's one 'reap the whirlwind' with its sowing clause intact, and with a second Hosea image spliced in: the chaff driven with the whirlwind at Hosea 13:3. The substitution is 'filthiness' for 'the wind', which turns Hosea's tautology — sow wind, reap wind — into a moral proposition, and the 1830 reading of the following clause ('the effects thereof, is poison', corrected to 'effect' in 1920) keeps the plural the first edition printed.
links.text: For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk; the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up.

pericopes.text: And again: He saith, If my people shall sow filthiness, they shall reap the east wind, which bringeth immediate destruction.

provenance.route: Hosea 12:1, Hosea 13:15 and Jeremiah 18:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'East wind' occurs in nineteen KJV verses and identifies no source by itself. “followeth after the east wind” occurs in exactly one, Hosea 12:1, and it is the only KJV verse in which a people pursues the east wind as an object rather than being struck by one. Hosea 13:15 supplies the destructive sense — 'an east wind shall come, the wind of the LORD … and his spring shall become dry' — and Jeremiah 18:17 the scattering, 'I will scatter them as with an east wind before the enemy'.
provenance.significance: Verse 31 is verse 30 said again with a different wind, and the substitution is the argument: the whirlwind of Hosea 8:7 destroys the harvest, the east wind of Hosea 13:15 dries up the spring at the source. 'Immediate destruction' is the Book of Mormon's gloss on the difference, and it is a correct reading of Hosea — the whirlwind scatters what has grown, the east wind kills the thing that grows.

links.note: 'If my people shall sow filthiness, they shall reap the east wind, which bringeth immediate destruction.' The sowing-and-reaping frame is Hosea 8:7's, repeated from 7:30; only the object changes. Where the east wind comes from is less certain than that it comes from Hosea, who uses it three times: Ephraim following after it at 12:1, the LORD's east wind drying the spring at 13:15. Jeremiah 18:17's scattering east wind is a live third possibility and matters because Jeremiah 18:15 is already the source of the stumbling clause at 7:29 — on which reading the whole oracle at 7:29-31 is Jeremiah 18:15-17 with Hosea's images laid over it. Recorded as moderate because the three candidates cannot be separated by wording.
links.text: Ephraim feedeth on wind, and followeth after the east wind: he daily increaseth lies and desolation; and they do make a covenant with the Assyrians, and oil is carried into Egypt.

pericopes.text: And now, behold, the promise of the Lord is fulfilled; and ye are smitten, and afflicted.

But if ye will turn to the Lord with full purpose of heart, and put your trust in him, and serve him with all diligence of mind; and if ye do this, he will, according to his own will and pleasure, deliver you out of bondage.

provenance.other: “purpose of heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 11:23. 'Turn to the Lord' occurs in five KJV verses and 'turn unto the Lord' in nine, so the turning is generic and the qualifier is not.
provenance.significance: Acts 11:23 is Barnabas arriving at Antioch, seeing the grace of God, and exhorting a mixed congregation that with purpose of heart they should cleave unto the Lord — the first sermon preached to a church of people who were not supposed to be there. Limhi's congregation is a colony that went where it should not have gone, and his closing exhortation is Barnabas's. The suppressed correspondence is the clause before the one borrowed: Barnabas exhorts them because he has 'seen the grace of God', which is the warrant Limhi's sermon has spent thirty verses trying to establish out of the exodus.

links.note: 'But if ye will turn to the Lord with full purpose of heart, and put your trust in him, and serve him with all diligence of mind.' The KJV has one 'purpose of heart' and it is attached, as here, to an exhortation to cleave or turn to the Lord. The Book of Mormon adds 'full', which no KJV verse has. The same source was adjudicated at Jacob 6:5, in a different hand and a different book; per the standing ruling on cross-book recurrence the link is written again here rather than filed as a repeat, because a reader of Mosiah shown nothing at 7:33 has been told there is no borrowing in the chapter's last sentence.
links.text: Who, when he came, and had seen the grace of God, was glad, and exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord.

provenance.other: 'Serve him with' occurs in five KJV verses; only 1 Chronicles 28:9 completes the phrase with a doubled organ of intention, 'with a perfect heart and with a willing mind'. “with all diligence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 4:23, 'Keep thy heart with all diligence'.
provenance.significance: 1 Chronicles 28 is David's charge to Solomon at the handing over of the temple plans, and 28:9's conditional is the one Limhi's verse reproduces: seek him and he will be found of thee, forsake him and he will cast thee off. Limhi is speaking in a temple (7:17) to a people he is about to lead out of bondage, and he closes with a king's charge rather than a prophet's oracle. The oracle of 7:29-31 threatens; this sentence, borrowed from the succession charge of a king to his heir, offers.

links.note: 'Turn to the Lord with full purpose of heart, and put your trust in him, and serve him with all diligence of mind.' The distinctive structure is the doubling — a heart-phrase and then a mind-phrase governed by 'serve him with' — which in the KJV is 1 Chronicles 28:9's alone: 'serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind'. 'With all diligence' comes from the other half of the same idea in Proverbs 4:23, where diligence is what the heart is kept with. The conditional that follows in the Book of Mormon ('and if ye do this, he will … deliver you out of bondage') is 1 Chronicles 28:9's conditional with deliverance in the place of being found.
links.text: And thou, Solomon my son, know thou the God of thy father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind: for the LORD searcheth all hearts, and understandeth all the imaginations of the thoughts: if thou seek him, he will be found of thee; but if thou forsake him, he will cast thee off for ever.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after king Limhi had made an end of speaking to his people, for he spake many things unto them, and only a few of them have I written in this book, he told his people all the things concerning their brethren which were in the land of Zarahemla;

and he caused that Ammon should stand up before the multitude, and rehearse unto them all that had happened unto their brethren, from the time that Zeniff went up out of the land, even until the time that he, himself came up out of the land.
And he also rehearsed unto them the last words which king Benjamin had taught them, and explained them to the people of king Limhi, so that they might understand all the words which he spake.

provenance.other: “that they might understand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:45. Nehemiah 8:8's expounding scene, the closest Old Testament analogue, reads 'gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading'.
provenance.significance: Luke 24:45 is the risen Christ on the road and at table, opening the understanding of disciples so that they can understand the scriptures — the KJV's one verse about a hearer's capacity being enlarged so that an existing text becomes intelligible. Ammon is doing the same office for Benjamin's last words, which the people of Limhi have never heard, and the chapter he is in will go on to define a seer as the person through whom things otherwise unknowable are made known (8:17). The verse quietly establishes that the chapter's subject is not translation but comprehension.

links.note: 'He also rehearsed unto them the last words which king Benjamin had taught them, and explained them to the people of king Limhi, so that they might understand all the words which he spake.' Four words from the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, in the KJV's own expounding scene. The contact is short and the construction ordinary, which is why this is an echo rather than an allusion; what recommends it is that Mosiah 8 is a chapter about the machinery of understanding an inaccessible text, and it opens with the Gospel's sentence about exactly that.
links.text: Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after he had done all this, that king Limhi dismissed the multitude, and caused that they should return, every one unto his own house.

And it came to pass that he caused that the plates which contained the record of his people, from the time that they left the land of Zarahemla, should be brought before Ammon, that he might read them.
Now, as soon as Ammon had read the record, the king inquired of him to know if he could interpret languages. And Ammon told him that he could not.

And the king saith unto him, I being grieved for the afflictions of my people, I caused that forty and three of my people should take a journey into the wilderness, that thereby they might find the land of Zarahemla; that we might appeal unto our brethren to deliver us out of bondage;

and they were lost in the wilderness, for the space of many days, yet they were diligent, and found not the land of Zarahemla, but returned to this land, having travelled in a land among many waters; having discovered a land which was covered with bones of men, and of beasts, &c., and was also covered with ruins of buildings of every kind; having discovered a land which had been peopled with a people, which were as numerous as the hosts of Israel.

provenance.other: “full of bones” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 37:1 — Matthew 23:27's whited sepulchres are 'full of dead men's bones', a different phrase. The Book of Mormon's wording ('covered with bones of men, and of beasts') shares no run with either, which is why this is recorded as figural.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 37 is the one chapter of the Bible that holds both halves of what Limhi's expedition brought back. Verses 1-2 are a plain full of the bones of a destroyed people; verses 16-19 are the two written sticks that are joined in the prophet's hand and become one. Mosiah 8:8-9 reports, in two consecutive sentences, a land covered with the bones of a destroyed people and twenty-four engraved plates brought back from it — and the whole point of the plates, stated at 8:12, is to learn the cause of that destruction. Ezekiel's bones live when the word comes to them; the Jaredite record will speak when a seer is found for it.

links.note: 'Having discovered a land which was covered with bones of men, and of beasts … having discovered a land which had been peopled with a people, which were as numerous as the hosts of Israel.' There is almost no shared wording here and the link is proposed on the shape of the scene: explorers set down in a plain of bones belonging to a numerous people, who then return with a written record of them. Recorded because the figure is doing work — the chapter's argument from 8:12 onward is that the bones cannot say what killed them and the plates can, which is Ezekiel 37's own move from bones to word.
links.whyNot: Purely figural, with the two halves of the figure drawn from opposite ends of Ezekiel 37 and neither half verbally present. Bones on a battlefield need no literary source; an army destroyed leaves bones. A reader who declines this row loses nothing but the reading, and the reading is the only thing on offer.
links.text: The hand of the LORD was upon me, and carried me out in the spirit of the LORD, and set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones,

pericopes.text: And for a testimony that the things that they have said is true, they have brought twenty-four plates, which are filled with engravings; and they are of pure gold.
And behold, also, they have brought breast-plates, which are large; and they are of brass, and of copper, and are perfectly sound.

And again: They have brought swords, the hilts thereof hath perished, and the blades thereof were cankered with rust; and there is no one in the land that is able to interpret the language or the engravings that are on the plates. Therefore, I said unto thee, Canst thou translate?

provenance.other: “cankered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 5:3, where it is joined in a single sentence to gold, to rust, and to bearing witness. The KJV's other corrosion verse, Matthew 6:19-20, has 'moth and rust doth corrupt' and neither the metal nor the testimony.
provenance.significance: James 5:3 is a woe against rich men who have heaped up treasure for the last days: their gold and silver is cankered, and the rust of it 'shall be a witness against you'. Mosiah 8:9-11 has every element and reverses the verdict. The relics are gold (8:9), they are cankered with rust (8:11), and they are produced explicitly 'for a testimony that the things that they have said is true' (8:9) — a witness for the men who carry them rather than against the men who hoarded them. The suppressed correspondence is that the one KJV verse in which corroded metal testifies is a verse in which corroded metal testifies to a judgment, and the people whose gold this was are all dead.

links.note: 'They have brought swords, the hilts thereof hath perished, and the blades thereof were cankered with rust.' The KJV uses 'cankered' once, and the Book of Mormon uses it of the same substance in the same collocation — metal, rust, and a testimony. The argument does not rest on 'rust', which is ordinary English; it rests on the fact that the archaic participle James used is the one word of the description that is not ordinary, and that the two other terms of James's sentence, the gold and the witness, are both in Mosiah 8:9, two verses earlier. Adjudicated here because this is where the rare word is.
links.text: Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days.

provenance.other: “there is not a man” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 19:31 and Daniel 2:10; only Daniel's is about a man who can decipher something for a king. “art thou able” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 2:26 — Nebuchadnezzar's question to Daniel, which is Limhi's question to Ammon.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 8:6-19 is Daniel 2 rebuilt. A king asks a foreigner brought before him whether he can interpret (8:6, Daniel 2:26); the answer is that he cannot; the king says there is no one in his realm able to do it (8:11, Daniel 2:10-11); a man is then named who can, and the ability is said to be a gift from God and not from the man (8:13, Daniel 2:27-30); and when the king hears it he blesses God (8:19, Daniel 2:19, 2:47). Daniel 2's own thesis — 'there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets' — is the thesis of Ammon's speech on seership at 8:16-18. What the Book of Mormon changes is the object: a dream in Daniel, a written record here, so that the gift required is translation rather than interpretation of a vision.

links.note: 'And there is no one in the land that is able to interpret the language or the engravings that are on the plates. Therefore, I said unto thee, Canst thou translate?' This row records the type-scene rather than a phrase, and it is filed at the verse where the scene's governing sentence sits. The verbal contacts are individually short — 'there is not a man upon the earth that can shew the king's matter' against 'there is no one in the land that is able to interpret'; 'Art thou able to make known unto me' against 'Canst thou translate?' — but there are five of them in fourteen verses and they arrive in Daniel's order. The strongest single one is at 8:13 and is catalogued there.
links.text: The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said, There is not a man upon the earth that can shew the king’s matter: therefore there is no king, lord, nor ruler, that asked such things at any magician, or astrologer, or Chaldean.

pericopes.text: And I say unto thee again, Knowest thou of any one that can translate? for I am desirous that these records should be translated into our language. For, perhaps they will give us a knowledge of a remnant of the people which have been destroyed, from whence these records came; or, perhaps they will give us a knowledge of this very people which hath been destroyed; and I am desirous to know the cause of their destruction.

Now Ammon saith unto him, I can assuredly tell thee, O king, of a man that can translate the records: for he hath wherewith that he can look, and translate all records that are of ancient date; and it is a gift from God. And the things are called interpreters; and no man can look in them, except he be commanded, lest he should look for that he had not ought, and he should perish. And whosoever is commanded to look in them, the same is called seer.

provenance.other: “I have found a man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 2:25, and so does “make known unto the king the interpretation”. Both are in Arioch's single sentence to Nebuchadnezzar.
provenance.significance: Arioch's sentence is the hinge of Daniel 2: the man who cannot interpret tells the king that he knows a man who can. Ammon's is the hinge of Mosiah 8, and it is the same sentence with 'translate' for 'make known the interpretation'. Daniel then insists at 2:30 that the secret 'is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have more than any living' — and Ammon's next clause is 'it is a gift from God', followed at 8:16 by the flat statement that no man can possess the power of God. Both texts take care that the interpreter should not be credited with the interpretation.

links.note: 'Now Ammon saith unto him, I can assuredly tell thee, O king, of a man that can translate the records: for he hath wherewith that he can look, and translate all records that are of ancient date; and it is a gift from God.' Two KJV singletons stand behind this, both from Arioch's report to Nebuchadnezzar, and the speech act is identical: a courtier who cannot do the thing tells a king where the man who can is to be found. 'Of ancient date' and 'interpreters' are the Book of Mormon's own vocabulary and have no KJV background at all, which is worth saying — the borrowing is the frame of the scene, not its furniture.
links.text: Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste, and said thus unto him, I have found a man of the captives of Judah, that will make known unto the king the interpretation.

pericopes.text: And behold, the king of the people which is in the land of Zarahemla, is the man that is commanded to do these things, and which hath this high gift from God.
And the king saith, That a seer is greater than a prophet.

provenance.other: “called a Seer” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 9:9, which is the Bible's only definition of the word and is itself an editorial gloss inserted into the narrative to explain an obsolete title. 'Seer' occurs elsewhere as a title (1 Samuel 9:11, 2 Samuel 24:11, 1 Chronicles 29:29 and others) but nowhere else is it defined against 'prophet'.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 9:9 says that the office now called prophet used to be called seer — the two words name one thing at different dates. Limhi asks whether a seer is greater than a prophet and Ammon answers that a seer is a revelator and a prophet also, which is a ruling against 1 Samuel 9:9's equation and in the same terms. And the chapter around it is 1 Samuel 9's chapter: a man goes to a seer because something is lost and cannot be found. Saul is looking for his father's asses; Limhi has sent out forty-three men who were lost in the wilderness and found not the land of Zarahemla (8:7-8), and asks about a seer in the next breath. The KJV's one verse defining a seer sits inside its one story about consulting a seer over something lost.

links.note: 'And the king saith, That a seer is greater than a prophet.' The whole of Mosiah 8:15-17 is an argument about the relation between two titles, and the KJV contains exactly one verse that relates them — a parenthetical antiquarian note explaining that they are the same office under two names. The Book of Mormon takes the pair as a hierarchy instead, and Ammon's answer (8:16-17) is a definition of what the greater term adds: revelation, and the making known of what is past and to come. 'Revelator' is not a KJV word at all; the nearest thing to it is Daniel 2:47's 'revealer of secrets'.
links.text: (Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.)

pericopes.text: And Ammon saith, That a seer is a revelator, and a prophet also; and a gift which is greater, can no man have, except he should possess the power of God, which no man can; yet a man may have great power given him from God.

But a seer can know of things which has past, and also of things which is to come; and by them shall all things be revealed, or rather, shall secret things be made manifest, and hidden things shall come to light, and things which is not known, shall be made known by them; and also, things shall be made known by them, which otherwise could not be known.

provenance.other: The saying exists in the KJV in four forms. Luke 8:17: 'nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known'. Mark 4:22: 'nothing hid, which shall not be manifested; neither was any thing kept secret'. Matthew 10:26 and Luke 12:2: 'nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; and hid, that shall not be known'. Mosiah 8:17 has 'made manifest', 'hidden', 'made known' and 'revealed' — and the two words that separate the candidates fall to Luke. “nothing is secret” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 8:17; “shall not be made manifest” likewise belongs to Luke 8:17 alone among the four forms, since Mark reads 'shall not be manifested'.
provenance.significance: tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Luke 8:17 against Mark 4:22: the Book of Mormon has 'made manifest' and not Mark's 'manifested', and it has the root of Luke's 'hid' where Mark reads 'kept secret'. Matthew 10:26 and Luke 12:2 are excluded by 'covered' and 'revealed' standing where Mosiah has manifesting and knowing. So of the four KJV forms of one saying the Book of Mormon has the Lukan one, and specifically the Luke 8 one rather than the Luke 12 one. Recover Luke 8:17's context and the saying is the conclusion of the parable of the lamp — a light is not lit to be put under a bed — which is what Mosiah 8:13-18 is about: an instrument by which what is hidden is looked at.

links.note: 'And by them shall all things be revealed, or rather, shall secret things be made manifest, and hidden things shall come to light, and things which is not known, shall be made known by them.' The verse is a fourfold expansion of a single Gospel saying, and it self-corrects mid-sentence in the Book of Mormon's characteristic way — 'or rather' — from the strong claim to the Gospel's own terms. The mediation is settled by the tool rather than by eye, which is what the tool is for: two decisive divergences, both for Luke.
links.text: For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest; neither any thing hid, that shall not be known and come abroad.

provenance.other: “deep and secret” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 2:22. “secret things” occurs in exactly two, Deuteronomy 29:29 and Daniel 2:22 — and Deuteronomy's verse says the opposite of Mosiah 8:17, that the secret things belong to God and are not ours.
provenance.significance: Daniel 2:22 is the doxology at the centre of the chapter Mosiah 8 has been rebuilding since verse 6: 'He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him.' Mosiah 8:17 has the secret things revealed and hidden things coming to light in one clause. The point of Daniel 2:22 in Daniel is that the interpreter is not the source — the light dwells with God — and that is why Ammon's speech insists at 8:16 that no man can possess the power of God and at 8:18 that the means is provided rather than owned.

links.note: 'Shall secret things be made manifest, and hidden things shall come to light.' Two KJV words for concealment and one for light, arranged as Daniel 2:22 arranges them. The Gospel saying behind the verse (Luke 8:17, catalogued above) accounts for the manifesting and the knowing but has no light in it and does not use 'secret things' as a substantive; Daniel does both. The verse is composite and both rows are needed to describe it.
links.text: He revealeth the deep and secret things: he knoweth what is in the darkness, and the light dwelleth with him.

pericopes.text: Thus God hath provided a means that man, through faith, might work mighty miracles; therefore, he becometh a great benefit to his fellow beings.

provenance.other: “having provided” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:40. God is the subject of 'provide' in only a handful of KJV verses — Genesis 22:8's 'God will provide himself a lamb' is the other memorable one — and Hebrews 11:40 is the only one where what is provided is a means to an end for other people.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:40 closes the catalogue of faith: God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect — an economy in which one generation's instrument serves another's. Mosiah 8:18 says the same of the interpreters: God has provided a means by which a man, through faith, works miracles and so 'becometh a great benefit to his fellow beings'. Both sentences make the provision corporate rather than personal, and both attach it to faith. The chapter that this verse ends is about a record left by a destroyed people being read by a later one.

links.note: 'Thus God hath provided a means that man, through faith, might work mighty miracles; therefore, he becometh a great benefit to his fellow beings.' The contact is a two-word collocation with God as subject, in a sentence whose logic — provision, faith, benefit accruing to others — is Hebrews 11:40's. It is an echo and not more: 'provided a means' is not in the KJV, and 'work mighty miracles' is a fusion of the KJV's 'mighty works' and its 'miracles' that belongs to no single verse.
links.text: God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect.

pericopes.text: And now, when Ammon had made an end of speaking these words, the king rejoiced exceedingly, and gave thanks to God, saying, Doubtless, a great mystery is contained within these plates; and these interpreters was doubtless prepared for the purpose of unfolding all such mysteries to the children of men.

provenance.other: “blessed the God of heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 2:19. “revealer of secrets” occurs in exactly one, Daniel 2:47, which is the king's response when the secret is disclosed — the structural counterpart of Limhi's response here.
provenance.significance: Daniel 2 is punctuated twice by a doxology on hearing that the secret can be told: Daniel blesses the God of heaven at 2:19 and Nebuchadnezzar blesses Daniel's God at 2:47. Mosiah 8:19 puts the king in Daniel's position rather than Nebuchadnezzar's — Limhi gives thanks before the translation has happened, on the strength of a promise — and the content of his praise is the Danielic one: that a mystery is contained in the record and that the instrument was 'prepared for the purpose of unfolding all such mysteries'.

links.note: 'When Ammon had made an end of speaking these words, the king rejoiced exceedingly, and gave thanks to God.' This is the closing beat of the Daniel 2 type-scene catalogued at 8:11 and 8:13 — the doxology on hearing that the untranslatable thing can be translated — and it is recorded at moderate confidence because it is the beat with the least verbal contact of the five. 'Gave thanks to God' is Acts 27:35's phrase, in a wholly unrelated setting (Paul breaking bread on a foundering ship); the argument here is positional rather than lexical.
links.text: Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a night vision. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.

provenance.route: Ephesians 5:32, Colossians 1:26 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “a great mystery” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:32. 'Mystery' in the KJV is almost entirely a Pauline word and almost always means something once hidden and now disclosed; Colossians 1:26's 'the mystery which hath been hid from ages and from generations, but now is made manifest' is the formula Mosiah 8:19 puts to work.
provenance.significance: The Pauline mystery is not a puzzle but a disclosure — a thing kept from previous ages and now unfolded. Limhi uses the word in precisely that sense and applies it to a physical record kept from previous ages: 'a great mystery is contained within these plates; and these interpreters was doubtless prepared for the purpose of unfolding all such mysteries to the children of men.' The KJV's abstract theological term has been given a literal object, which is what the whole chapter does to Daniel 2's vocabulary of revelation.

links.note: 'Doubtless, a great mystery is contained within these plates.' Three words matching a KJV singleton, in a sentence whose sense of 'mystery' is unmistakably the Pauline one and not the modern one. Recorded as an echo because the phrase is short and Ephesians 5:32's own subject — Christ and the church — has nothing to do with this verse; the borrowing is the term and its Pauline logic, which Colossians 1:26 states more fully than Ephesians does.
links.text: This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.

pericopes.text: O how marvellous are the works of the Lord, and how long doth he suffer with his people; yea, and how blind and impenetrable are the understandings of the children of men: for they will not seek wisdom, neither do they desire that she should rule over them.

provenance.other: “come to devour” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 56:9 and Jeremiah 12:9; Isaiah 56:9 is the one that puts the devourers in a forest ('all ye beasts in the forest'). Isaiah 56:10 supplies blindness and 56:11 shepherds 'that cannot understand'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 56:9-11 runs in the order Mosiah 8:20-21 runs. Beasts of the field and of the forest are summoned to devour; the watchmen are blind; the shepherds cannot understand. The Book of Mormon takes the same three elements and redistributes them — blindness and failure of understanding go to the people in 8:20, the devouring beasts of the forest and the fled shepherd to the flock in 8:21 — so that the reproach Isaiah aims at negligent leaders is aimed instead at a people who will not seek wisdom. Limhi's own leadership is exactly what is at issue in this book, and the reassignment is not innocent.

links.note: 'How blind and impenetrable are the understandings of the children of men.' Blindness paired with a failure of understanding, immediately followed at 8:21 by a shepherdless flock devoured by beasts of the forest, is the sequence of Isaiah 56:9-11 and of no other passage in the KJV. No single phrase is reproduced — 'impenetrable' is not a KJV word — so the case rests on the sequence rather than on wording, and is recorded as moderate accordingly. Ezekiel 34, the other great shepherd oracle, has the flock and the beasts but no blindness.
links.text: His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber.

provenance.route: Revelation 15:3 or Psalm 139:14 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “marvellous are thy works” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 139:14 and Revelation 15:3. Mosiah 8:20 has 'marvellous are the works of the Lord', which substitutes the name for the pronoun and so matches neither exactly; 'the works of the LORD' on its own occurs in seven verses.
provenance.significance: Revelation 15:3 is the verse 1 Nephi 1:14 borrows six words from at the head of the book, where it turns out to be the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Its reappearance here, in the mouth of a king praising God for a set of interpreters, is a small piece of continuity: the corpus's standard formula for exclaiming at God's works is the one Revelation labels the song of Moses. Whether Mosiah 8:20 is reaching for Revelation or for the Psalm cannot be decided from the wording.

links.note: 'O how marvellous are the works of the Lord, and how long doth he suffer with his people.' The 1830 edition prints 'marvellous' with the KJV's double l, which later editions modernized to 'marvelous' — one of the places where the first edition shows the borrowing and the current text hides it (CONVENTIONS §8). The phrase itself is the KJV's standard exclamation and belongs to two verses, one of which the corpus has already used at 1 Nephi 1:14; recorded as an echo because the substitution of 'the works of the Lord' for 'thy works' breaks the run at exactly the point where a source could be identified.
links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: The Book of Mormon's exact phrases are not in the KJV: 'seek wisdom' occurs in no KJV verse (Proverbs 14:6 has 'seeketh wisdom'), and no KJV verse has wisdom ruling over anyone. What is borrowed is the grammar — the feminine pronoun for wisdom, which in the KJV belongs to Proverbs 1-9 and to nothing else in the Protestant canon.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 1:20-33 is Wisdom crying in the streets and being refused, and 1:28 is what follows: they shall seek me, and shall not find me. Limhi inverts the sequence — they will not seek her in the first place — and adds a political verb that Proverbs never uses of her, that she should rule over them. Read against Proverbs 8:15, where Wisdom says 'By me kings reign', the addition is not arbitrary: Limhi is a king saying that his people will not be governed by the thing that ought to govern kings, in a chapter whose whole subject is a king seeking knowledge he cannot supply himself.

links.note: 'For they will not seek wisdom, neither do they desire that she should rule over them.' The feminine pronoun is the whole of the verbal evidence and it is decisive as to which book is in view: outside Proverbs 1-9 the KJV does not personify wisdom as a woman. Which verse of Proverbs, if any, cannot be settled — Proverbs 1:28's refused Wisdom is the closest scene and Proverbs 8:15's reigning kings the closest to the ruling. Filed as figural for that reason. The machine's proposal here was Joel 2:17's 'that the heathen should rule over them', which is the wrong 'they'.
links.text: Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me:

pericopes.text: Yea, they are as a wild flock, which fleeth from the shepherd, and scattereth, and are driven, and are devoured by the beasts of the forest.

provenance.other: 'No shepherd' occurs in six KJV verses, of which Ezekiel 34:5 is the only one that follows the shepherdlessness with scattering and with beasts devouring the flock — the exact three-beat sequence of Mosiah 8:21. Ezekiel 34:8 repeats it. “beasts of the forest” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 104:20 and Micah 5:8, neither of which involves a flock; the forest comes from Isaiah 56:9's 'all ye beasts in the forest', where the beasts are summoned to devour.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 34's flock is scattered because there is no shepherd, and the chapter's charge is against the shepherds who abandoned it. Mosiah 8:21 reverses the blame: the flock is wild and flees from the shepherd, so the scattering is the sheep's doing. That inversion is the point of Limhi's whole simile — his people will not seek wisdom (8:20), so the shepherd is not missing, he is being run from. Ezekiel 34 goes on to promise that God will himself seek out the scattered sheep; Mosiah 8 has just spent nineteen verses on a king trying to find a seer.

links.note: 'Yea, they are as a wild flock, which fleeth from the shepherd, and scattereth, and are driven, and are devoured by the beasts of the forest.' Four elements in Ezekiel 34:5's order — flock, shepherd, scattering, devouring beasts — with one word imported from Isaiah 56:9's summons to the beasts in the forest. The Book of Mormon adds 'wild' and 'fleeth', which no shepherd oracle in the KJV has and which are what turn Ezekiel's indictment of leaders into an indictment of the led. Matthew 9:36's 'scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd' is the New Testament form of the same figure and is close, but it has no beasts and no flight.
links.text: And they were scattered, because there is no shepherd: and they became meat to all the beasts of the field, when they were scattered.

pericopes.text: I, Zeniff, having been taught in all the language of the Nephites, and having had a knowledge of the land of Nephi or of the land of our fathers’ first inheritance, and I having been sent as a spy among the Lamanites, that I might spy out their forces, that our army might come upon them and destroy them; but when I saw that which was good among them, I was desirous that they should not be destroyed;

provenance.other: “exceeding good land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 14:7 — Joshua and Caleb's minority report. 'Spy out' occurs in ten KJV verses, of which six belong to Numbers 13 and Judges 18, so the verb alone identifies no source; what identifies one is the sequence in which it stands here.
provenance.significance: Numbers 13-14 is the Bible's one story of a spy who comes back with a good report and is nearly killed for it. Twelve men are sent to spy out the land; ten bring an evil report; two say it is an exceeding good land; and the congregation bids stone them (14:10). Mosiah 9:1-2 is that story with one man: Zeniff is sent to spy out the Lamanites' forces, sees 'that which was good among them', contends with his brethren for a treaty, and is condemned to death and rescued. The metalepsis cuts against Zeniff. In Numbers the favourable report is the true one and the men who give it are the only two of their generation to enter the land; here the favourable report begins a chapter that ends in slaughter and a book that ends in bondage — and Limhi has already told the reader at 7:21 that Zeniff was deceived.

links.note: 'I having been sent as a spy among the Lamanites, that I might spy out their forces … but when I saw that which was good among them, I was desirous that they should not be destroyed.' The verbal contact is thin and deliberate — 'spy out' and 'good' — and the case is made by the scene, which the KJV tells once. Zeniff's own account is at pains to make him Caleb: the lone dissenter who saw good where his brethren saw a target. What follows in the next verse is the stoning that Numbers 14:10 threatens and does not carry out.
links.text: And they spake unto all the company of the children of Israel, saying, The land, which we passed through to search it, is an exceeding good land.

pericopes.text: therefore, I contended with my brethren in the wilderness: for I would that our ruler should make a treaty with them. But he being an austere and a blood-thirsty man, commanded that I should be slain; but I was rescued, by the shedding of much blood: for father fought against father, and brother against brother, until the greatest number of our army was destroyed in the wilderness; and we returned, those of us that were spared, to the land of Zarahemla, to relate that tale to their wives, and their children.

provenance.other: 'Austere' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 19:21 and Luke 19:22, which are the servant's charge in the parable of the pounds and the nobleman's acceptance of it. The word occurs nowhere else in the Bible in English.
provenance.significance: Recover the parable and the borrowing pays. The austere man of Luke 19 is a nobleman who went into a far country to receive a kingdom, whose citizens sent a message after him saying 'We will not have this man to reign over us' — and whose last words in the parable are 'those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me' (19:27). Mosiah 9:2's austere man does exactly that: 'commanded that I should be slain'. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's only adjective for such a master and put it on a ruler who then performs the parable's closing act. The 1830 running text hyphenates the second adjective, 'blood-thirsty', and that word is a KJV rarity too — see the Proverbs 29:10 row on this verse.

links.note: 'But he being an austere and a blood-thirsty man, commanded that I should be slain.' Two words describe the ruler and both are KJV rarities: 'austere' belongs to Luke 19 alone and 'bloodthirsty' to Proverbs 29:10 alone. That a single clause should reach for both is the argument. Nothing else in the verse touches Luke, and the parable's subject — stewardship of money — has nothing to do with a war council in a wilderness; what has been taken is the character and the sentence he passes.
links.text: And he saith unto him, Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant. Thou knewest that I was an austere man, taking up that I laid not down, and reaping that I did not sow:

provenance.other: “bloodthirsty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 29:10. The KJV's usual idiom is periphrastic — 'bloody men' (Psalm 26:9, 59:2), 'the man of blood' — so the compound adjective is a single verse's property.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 29:10 reads in full: 'The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul.' Both halves of the proverb are in Mosiah 9:2. The bloodthirsty ruler hates the man who has just argued for sparing an enemy, and orders him killed; and someone — the verse does not say who — rescues him at the cost of much blood. A reader who recovers the proverb finds that the KJV's one bloodthirsty verse also contains the rescuer.

links.note: 'An austere and a blood-thirsty man.' The 1830 hyphenation preserves the word as a compound; the KJV prints it solid, once. Recorded at moderate rather than high because a single adjective is a slender thing to build on, and because 'bloodthirsty' was ordinary English in 1830 and needed no source — the reason for keeping the row is that the other adjective in the same phrase is also a KJV rarity, and that Proverbs 29:10's second clause describes what happens next in the verse.
links.text: The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul.

provenance.other: 'Against his brother' occurs in five KJV verses, of which only Isaiah 19:2 and Ezekiel 38:21 describe a civil war. Isaiah 19:2 is the only one built as a chain of identical nouns on either side of 'against' — 'every one against his brother, and every one against his neighbour; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom' — which is the construction Mosiah 9:2 uses. Within that verse, “every one against his brother” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and so does “city against city” — the construction is Isaiah 19:2's property even though the particular nouns Mosiah 9:2 puts either side of 'against' are not Isaiah's.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 19:2 is the oracle against Egypt, and what God does to Egypt in it is set it against itself. Mosiah 9:2 has a Nephite army destroying the greater part of itself in a wilderness over a question of policy toward the Lamanites — an internal war in a people who have just refused to be a nation of one mind. The chapter then spends itself on a colony founded by the survivors of that self-slaughter.

links.note: 'For father fought against father, and brother against brother, until the greatest number of our army was destroyed in the wilderness.' No phrase is reproduced; the borrowing, if it is one, is the KJV's formula for civil war — a noun repeated on both sides of 'against' — which Isaiah 19:2 establishes and Matthew 10:21 and Luke 12:53 vary with different nouns on each side ('the brother shall deliver up the brother', 'the father shall be divided against the son'). Isaiah's identical-noun form is what the Book of Mormon has.
links.whyNot: 'Brother against brother' is an English idiom for civil war independent of any verse, and the Book of Mormon's pairing is father/father and brother/brother where Isaiah's is brother/neighbour and city/city. The construction is shared; no words are.
links.text: And I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians: and they shall fight every one against his brother, and every one against his neighbour; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.

pericopes.text: And yet, I being over zealous to inherit the land of our fathers, collected as many as were desirous to go up to possess the land, and started again on our journey into the wilderness, to go up to the land; but we were smitten with famine and sore afflictions: for we were slow to remember the Lord our God.

provenance.other: “let us go up at once” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 13:30, Caleb's answer to the evil report. “go up and possess” occurs in exactly two, Deuteronomy 1:21 and Deuteronomy 9:23, both of them Moses recalling the same episode. 'Possess it' on its own occurs in forty-six verses and identifies nothing.
provenance.significance: Caleb's 'Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it' is the sentence that gets Israel into the land a generation late, and Deuteronomy 9:23 is the sentence that judges the generation that would not act on it. Zeniff collects 'as many as were desirous to go up to possess the land' and is immediately smitten with famine 'for we were slow to remember the Lord our God' — which is Deuteronomy's verdict on the failed attempt at Numbers 14:40-45, where the people went up anyway, without the LORD among them, and were smitten. The type-scene begun at 9:1 completes here in its unfavourable half.

links.note: 'And yet, I being over zealous to inherit the land of our fathers, collected as many as were desirous to go up to possess the land … but we were smitten with famine and sore afflictions: for we were slow to remember the Lord our God.' The going-up-to-possess formula is Deuteronomic and Zeniff uses it with Caleb's confidence and Numbers 14:44's outcome. Confidence is moderate because the formula is common enough in Deuteronomy that no one verse can be isolated; what is not moderate is that the whole of 9:1-3 walks through Numbers 13-14 in order — spy, good report, dissent, near-death, and then a presumptuous ascent that is smitten.
links.text: And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless, after many days’ wandering in the wilderness, we pitched our tents in the place where our brethren were slain, which was near to the land of our fathers.

And it came to pass that I went again with four of my men, into the city, in unto the king, that I might know of the disposition of the king, and that I might know if I might go in with my people, and possess the land in peace.
And I went in unto the king, and he covenanted with me, that I might possess the land of Lehi-Nephi, and the land of Shilom.
And he also commanded that his people should depart out of the land, and I and my people went into the land, that we might possess it.
And we began to build buildings, and to repair the walls of the city, yea, even the walls of the city of Lehi-Nephi, and the city of Shilom.

And we began to till the ground, yea, even with all manner of seeds, with seeds of corn, and of wheat, and of barley, and with neas, and with sheum, and with seeds of all manner of fruits: and we did begin to multiply and prosper in the land.
Now, it was the cunning and the craftiness of king Laman, to bring my people into bondage, that he yielded up the land, that we might possess it.

provenance.other: “cunning craftiness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:14. The argument is made in full at Mosiah 7:21, where the phrase enters the book.
provenance.significance: The interest of the second occurrence is that it is in a different hand. Mosiah 7:21 is Limhi speaking to his people two generations later; Mosiah 9:10 is Zeniff's own record, which the book has just begun quoting verbatim. The two men use the same Pauline phrase for the same king's treaty, which within the fiction means Limhi got it from the record he has been reading and which for this catalogue means the borrowing is doing structural work rather than decorating a sentence.

links.note: 'Now, it was the cunning and the craftiness of king Laman, to bring my people into bondage, that he yielded up the land, that we might possess it.' The KJV's one 'cunning craftiness', used a second time of the same event by a different narrator. Under the standing rule a repeat within a book is registered rather than re-argued, and the argument is at 7:21; this row exists because Zeniff's account and Limhi's agree word for word about the deceit and because Ephesians 4:14's closing clause, 'whereby they lie in wait to deceive', is what this verse spells out.
links.text: That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;

pericopes.text: Therefore, it came to pass that after we had dwelt in the land for the space of twelve years, that king Laman began to grow uneasy, lest by any means my people should wax strong in the land, and that they could not overpower them and bring them into bondage.

provenance.route: Genesis 15:13 → Acts 7:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “bring them into bondage” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:6. Acts 7:6 is Stephen paraphrasing Genesis 15:13, and Genesis 15:13 does not contain the phrase: it reads 'they shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years'. The whole 'into bondage' family is four verses — Nehemiah 5:5, Acts 7:6, 2 Corinthians 11:20, Galatians 2:4 — and three of the four are New Testament.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's mediation finding, and the tool could not make it. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence for Genesis 15:13 against Acts 7:6, because its alignment sets 'they should bring them into bondage' opposite Genesis's 'is not theirs' and so reports the Book of Mormon as reading neither. The rarity count decides what the alignment could not: the Old Testament's promise of Egyptian bondage says 'serve', and only the New Testament's retelling of it says 'bring them into bondage'. Mosiah 9:11 has Stephen's phrase, not Abraham's. And the substance follows: what Laman fears is that his immigrant population will 'wax strong in the land' and become unmanageable, which is Exodus 1:9-10's fear in Acts 7:17-19's words.

links.note: 'King Laman began to grow uneasy, lest by any means my people should wax strong in the land, and that they could not overpower them and bring them into bondage.' The KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, and it belongs to Stephen's speech — the same speech Mosiah 7:26 borrowed at its climax. Note also what the mediation does to the chapter's politics: Zeniff's colony is cast in the position of Israel in Egypt, growing too numerous for a king who then enslaves it, and the language used for the enslavement is the language of the Bible's own great retelling of that story rather than of the story itself.
links.text: And God spake on this wise, That his seed should sojourn in a strange land; and that they should bring them into bondage, and entreat them evil four hundred years.

provenance.other: “deal wisely” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 1:10, where it is Pharaoh's euphemism for what he is about to do. 'Subtilly' occurs in three (1 Samuel 23:22, Psalm 105:25, Acts 7:19), of which Acts 7:19 and Psalm 105:25 both describe the same Egyptian policy — so the KJV has three separate words for it and the Book of Mormon uses none of them, choosing Ephesians 4:14's 'cunning craftiness' instead.
provenance.significance: Exodus 1:8-14 is the template for Mosiah 9:9-12 point by point and in order: the immigrants multiply and prosper (9:9, Exodus 1:7); a king fears they will grow too strong (9:11, Exodus 1:9-10); he deals craftily rather than openly (9:10, Exodus 1:10); and the object is forced labour, so that the host nation may live off the work of their hands (9:12, Exodus 1:11-14). The one element the Book of Mormon adds is the treaty — Laman gives the land away in order to get the people into it — which makes the deceit contractual rather than merely administrative, and which is why the borrowed word for it comes from Ephesians rather than from Exodus.

links.note: 'Lest by any means my people should wax strong in the land, and that they could not overpower them and bring them into bondage.' Pharaoh's calculation, in the Book of Mormon's words: Exodus 1:10 reads 'let us deal wisely with them; lest they multiply … and so get them up out of the land.' The 'lest' clause with a demographic fear inside it is the shared structure, and the sequence around it is Exodus 1's. No phrase of Exodus is reproduced, which is why the row is conceptual; the reproduced phrase in this verse is Acts 7:6's and is catalogued separately.
links.text: Come on, let us deal wisely with them; lest they multiply, and it come to pass, that, when there falleth out any war, they join also unto our enemies, and fight against us, and so get them up out of the land.

pericopes.text: Now, they were a lazy, and an idolatrous people; therefore, they were desirous to bring us into bondage, that they might glut themselves with the labors of our hands; yea, that they might feast themselves upon the flocks of our fields.

provenance.other: “bring us into bondage” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 2:4 — the first person plural, as against Acts 7:6's 'bring them into bondage' at Mosiah 9:11. The Book of Mormon uses each pronoun in its correct grammatical setting: Laman's intention toward a third party at 9:11, and the colony's own account of what was intended toward them at 9:12.
provenance.significance: Galatians 2:4 is the sentence that names Paul's opponents 'false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage'. Set it beside Mosiah 9 and the whole chapter is in it. Zeniff opens the chapter as a man sent to spy (9:1); Laman brings his people in under a treaty rather than openly (9:6-7, 9:10); and the object throughout is to bring them into bondage. One Pauline verse holds the spying, the false dealing and the enslavement that the chapter takes nineteen verses to narrate — and the reader who recovers it finds that in Galatians the bondage is a religious one and the liberty is Christ's.

links.note: 'They were desirous to bring us into bondage, that they might glut themselves with the labors of our hands.' A KJV singleton, and the pronoun is right: 'us' here where 9:11 had Acts 7:6's 'them', which is the discrimination ADJUDICATING §4 warns is the adjudicator's to catch and not the tool's. 'Glut' is not a KJV word in any form — the KJV has 'glutton' and 'gluttonous' — so the vivid half of the sentence is the Book of Mormon's own.
links.text: And that because of false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage:

provenance.other: “feed themselves” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ezekiel 34:2 and Ezekiel 34:10, both in the shepherd oracle and both meaning that those who should feed a flock are eating it instead.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 34 is already the source at Mosiah 8:21, five verses earlier in the same reading, where Limhi's people are a wild flock devoured by beasts. Mosiah 9:12 turns the same chapter's other half on the Lamanites: they mean to 'feast themselves upon the flocks of our fields', which is Ezekiel's charge against shepherds who feed themselves and not the flocks. Two consecutive chapters of Mosiah reach into the same oracle for opposite ends of the figure — the flock at 8:21 and the eaters at 9:12.

links.note: 'Yea, that they might feast themselves upon the flocks of our fields.' 'Feast' is not Ezekiel's verb and the flocks here are literal livestock rather than a people, so the contact is a reflexive construction and a noun; that is an echo and no more. It is recorded because Ezekiel 34 is demonstrably in view in this stretch of the book — Mosiah 8:21 takes its shepherdless scattered flock from Ezekiel 34:5 — and because the Lamanites' offence in this verse is exactly the one Ezekiel 34 exists to condemn.
links.whyNot: Two words, one of them a common reflexive, and the sense is different: Ezekiel's shepherds eat the flock they were given to keep, while the Lamanites eat a flock that was never theirs. Without the Ezekiel 34:5 borrowing one chapter earlier there would be nothing here to record.
links.text: Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?

pericopes.text: Therefore, it came to pass that king Laman began to stir up his people, that they should contend with my people; therefore, there began to be wars and contentions in the land.

For, in the thirteenth year of my reign in the land of Nephi, away on the south of the land of Shilom, when my people were watering and feeding their flocks, and tilling their lands, a numerous host of Lamanites came upon them, and began to slay them, and to take of their flocks, and the corn of their fields.
Yea, and it came to pass that they fled, all that were not overtaken, even into the city of Nephi, and did call upon me for protection.

And it came to pass that I did arm them with bows, and with arrows, with swords, and with cimeters, and with clubs, and with slings, and with all manner of weapons which we could invent, and I and my people did go forth against the Lamanites, to battle;

yea, in the strength of the Lord did we go forth to battle against the Lamanites: for I and my people did cry mightily to the Lord, that he would deliver us out of the hands of our enemies, for we were awakened to a remembrance of the deliverance of our fathers.

provenance.other: “in the strength of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 71:16 and Micah 5:4. Micah's is 'he shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD'; Psalm 71:16's is 'I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD'. The Book of Mormon's verb is 'go' — 'in the strength of the Lord did we go forth to battle' — which is the Psalm's and not Micah's.
provenance.significance: Psalm 71 is an old man's prayer not to be forsaken when his strength fails, and 71:16 is his resolution to go in a strength that is not his own and to make mention of God's righteousness 'even of thine only'. Zeniff's army is outnumbered and armed with whatever it could invent (9:16); the psalm it is quoting is about having nothing left to go in. The next verse says God heard, which is what Psalm 71 is asking for.

links.note: 'Yea, in the strength of the Lord did we go forth to battle against the Lamanites.' Of the KJV's two occurrences of the phrase, one has the Book of Mormon's verb and one does not, and the discrimination is worth making because the phrase becomes a formula in the corpus after this. The rest of the verse is the chapter's own: 'cry mightily to the Lord' is Jonah 3:8's and is catalogued separately, and 'deliver us out of the hands of our enemies' is close to Luke 1:74's 'delivered out of the hand of our enemies' but has the plural where Luke has the singular and Judges 8:34 has the plural, so no source is isolable there.
links.text: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.

provenance.other: “cry mightily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8, the king of Nineveh's decree. The KJV's other intensifiers for prayer are 'cried with a loud voice' and 'cried unto the LORD', neither of which is this adverb.
provenance.significance: Jonah 3:8 is a king's proclamation to a doomed city: let man and beast be covered with sackcloth and cry mightily unto God, and let them turn from their evil way — and in the next verse the question is whether God will turn and repent so that they perish not. Mosiah 9:17-18 is a king's account of his own people crying mightily and being heard. The suppressed correspondence is that Jonah 3's criers are the enemy nation, spared against the prophet's wishes; Zeniff opens this chapter by arguing that the enemy nation should be spared.

links.note: 'For I and my people did cry mightily to the Lord, that he would deliver us out of the hands of our enemies.' The KJV's one 'cry mightily', in a verse that is itself a king's edict about how a people in danger should pray. Zeniff is a king reporting that his people did it. The phrase is short and the setting is different — sackcloth and repentance in Jonah, a battle line here — but the adverb has one home in the KJV and the Book of Mormon has borrowed it into another king's mouth.
links.text: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.

pericopes.text: And God did hear our cries, and did answer our prayers; and we did go forth in his might. Yea, we did go forth against the Lamanites; and in one day and a night, we did slay three thousand and forty-three; we did slay them, even until we had driven them out of our land.

provenance.other: “forth in his might” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 5:31 — 'let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might'. The antecedent of 'his' there is the sun, not God, which is the reason for the moderate confidence.
provenance.significance: Judges 5:31 is the last line of the Song of Deborah, a victory song after an outnumbered Israelite force destroyed a superior army: 'So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD.' Mosiah 9:18 is the same sentence in prose — God heard, we went forth in his might, we slew them until we had driven them out of our land — and the chapter ends, as Judges 5:31 does, with a count and a rest. The suppressed correspondence is that Judges 5's victory is won by a woman with a tent peg and celebrated in a poem; Zeniff's is won with cimeters and clubs and counted to the man.

links.note: 'And God did hear our cries, and did answer our prayers; and we did go forth in his might.' Four words from the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, at the end of the Bible's other outnumbered-army battle report. The Book of Mormon shifts the possessive from the sun to God, which is a real change of sense and keeps this at moderate; what recommends the row is that the phrase has exactly one home and that Judges 5:31 is the closing formula of exactly this kind of narrative.
links.text: So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might. And the land had rest forty years.

pericopes.text: And I, myself, with mine own hands, did help to bury their dead. And behold, to our great sorrow and lamentation, two hundred and seventy-nine of our brethren were slain.

provenance.other: “great lamentation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:2 — 'And devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him.' Genesis 50:10's mourning for Jacob is 'a great and very sore lamentation', and Zechariah 12:11 has 'a great mourning'; neither is this phrase.
provenance.significance: Acts 8:2 is the burial of Stephen, and it stands eight verses after Acts 7:52 — the verse Limhi borrows at Mosiah 7:26 to say that his fathers slew the prophet who foretold the coming of Christ. Within this three-chapter stretch the Book of Mormon has taken the climax of Stephen's speech and the sentence about his burial, in that order: the prophet killed for announcing the Just One at 7:26, and the men burying their dead with great lamentation at 9:19. The pairing is not visible from either verse alone. Note too what Acts 8:2 supplies that this verse needs: it is the KJV's one place where the burying and the lamenting are done by the same hands, which is Zeniff's whole point — 'I, myself, with mine own hands, did help to bury their dead.'

links.note: 'And I, myself, with mine own hands, did help to bury their dead. And behold, to our great sorrow and lamentation, two hundred and seventy-nine of our brethren were slain.' The KJV's one 'great lamentation' is a burial verse, and this is a burial verse. 'With mine own hands' is in no KJV verse — the nearest is Philemon 1:19's 'with mine own hand', of writing — so the borrowing is the lamentation and not the hands. The chapter closes on a count of the dead, and the source it closes on is the burial of the man whose speech opened Limhi's sermon two chapters earlier.
links.text: And devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that we again began to establish the kingdom; and we again began to possess the land in peace. And I caused that there should be weapons of war made, of every kind, that thereby I might have weapons for my people, against the time the Lamanites should come up again to war against my people.

And I set guards round about the land, that the Lamanites might not come upon us again unawares, and destroy us; and thus I did guard my people, and my flocks, and keep them from falling into the hands of our enemies.
And it came to pass that we did inherit the land of our fathers, for many years; yea, for the space of twenty and two years.
And I did cause that the men should till the ground, and raise all manner of grain, and all manner of fruit, of every kind.

And I did cause that the women should spin, and toil, and work, and work all manner of fine linen; yea, and cloth of every kind, that we might clothe our nakedness; and thus we did prosper in the land; thus we did have continual peace in the land, for the space of twenty and two years.

And it came to pass that king Laman died, and his son began to reign in his stead. And he began to stir his people up in rebellion against my people; therefore, they began to prepare for war, and to come up to battle against my people.—
But I having sent my spies out round about the land of Shemlon, that I might discover their preparations, that I might guard against them, that they might not come upon my people and destroy them.

And it came to pass that they came up upon the north of the land of Shilom, with their numerous hosts, men armed with bows, and with arrows, and with swords, and with cimeters, and with stones, and with slings; and they had their heads shaved, that they were naked; and they were girded about with a leathern girdle about their loins.

links.text: And the same John had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.

provenance.route: 2 Kings 1:8 → Matthew 3:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “leathern” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:4; “leathern girdle about” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Mark 1:6 dresses the Baptist in “a girdle of a skin about his loins” and 2 Kings 1:8 dresses Elijah in “a girdle of leather about his loins” — neither uses the adjective.
provenance.alternative: 2 Kings 1:8, Elijah's description, which is the Old Testament original the Baptist's costume is written to recall.
provenance.significance: The garment the King James Bible gives to exactly one man is here given to an army. In the KJV the leathern girdle is prophetic dress: it identifies Elijah to Ahaziah's messengers and it identifies John in the wilderness of Judaea as Elijah come again. Zeniff hangs it on naked, shaven, sword-carrying Lamanites descending on Shilom, and the sign of the prophet becomes the uniform of the enemy. The inversion is worth having in a book whose next two chapters are about a prophet nobody recognises: Abinadi will come to Noah's court in disguise (12:1), unmarked, while the men who look like prophets are the ones coming to kill.

links.note: 'They were girded about with a leathern girdle about their loins.' `mediation-check.py` returns two decisive points for Matthew 3:4 over 2 Kings 1:8: the Book of Mormon has 'leathern', which is Matthew's word and occurs nowhere else in the KJV, and it does not have 2 Kings' 'of leather'. The 1830 reading is the fuller and more redundant one — 'girded about with a leathern girdle about their loins' — and 1920 deleted the first 'about', pulling the sentence closer to the Matthean phrase it is built on.
