Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six; the case here is rarity, not length.

links.text: They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin.

provenance.other: “armed with bows” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Chronicles 12:2. The armoury it names — bows, hurled stones, shot arrows — is the same short list, in the same order, that the Lamanite muster carries.
provenance.significance: 1 Chronicles 12 is the roll of the men who came to David at Ziklag while he was still a fugitive from Saul: the verse's whole point is that these are the warriors who chose the right king. Zeniff's sentence takes the equipment and leaves the loyalty behind.

links.note: The verse's inventory is 'bows, and with arrows, and with swords, and with cimeters, and with stones, and with slings'. Only the first element has a KJV fingerprint — 'armed with bows' is a singleton — and the two following nouns, stones and slings, are the other two weapons of 1 Chronicles 12:2. The rest of the list ('cimeters') is the Book of Mormon's own. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because a four-word run inside a weapons list is exactly the kind of match the n-gram stream produces by accident; the singleton is what keeps it above the floor.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I caused that the women and children of my people should be hid in the wilderness; and I also caused that all my old men that could bear arms, and also all my young men that were able to bear arms, should gather themselves together, to go to battle against the Lamanites; and I did place them in their ranks, every man according to his age.

And it came to pass that we did go up to battle against the Lamanites. And I, even I, in my old age, did go up to battle against the Lamanites. And it came to pass that we did go up in the strength of the Lord, to battle.

links.text: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.

provenance.other: “in the strength of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 71:16 and Micah 5:4. Micah's is about the messianic shepherd who 'shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD'; Psalm 71:16's is a man saying he will go.
provenance.alternative: Micah 5:4, which has the identical string but no first-person verb of motion.
provenance.significance: Psalm 71 is the psalm of an old man — 'cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth' (71:9), 'now also when I am old and grayheaded, O God, forsake me not' (71:18). Zeniff says in the same breath 'I, even I, in my old age, did go up to battle' and 'we did go up in the strength of the Lord, to battle'. The one KJV verse in which a speaker says he will *go* in the strength of the Lord sits eight verses from the KJV's clearest prayer of an aged man going out with his own strength gone. Recovering that context turns Zeniff's aside about his age from a narrative detail into the psalm's argument.

links.note: 'And it came to pass that we did go up in the strength of the Lord, to battle.' The next verse supplies the antithesis the psalm assumes — 'the Lamanites knew nothing concerning the Lord, nor the strength of the Lord; therefore, they depended upon their own strength' — which is the contrast Psalm 71 is built on and which no other proposed source produces. Two KJV verses hold the phrase and only one of them has a speaker going anywhere.

pericopes.text: Now, the Lamanites knew nothing concerning the Lord, nor the strength of the Lord; therefore, they depended upon their own strength. Yet they were a strong people, as to the strength of men:

they were a wild, and ferocious, and a blood-thirsty people, believing in the tradition of their fathers, which is this: Believing that they were driven out of the land of Jerusalem, because of the iniquities of their fathers, and that they were wronged in the wilderness by their brethren; and they were also wronged, while crossing the sea.

links.text: The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul.

provenance.other: “bloodthirsty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 29:10. The 1830 text hyphenates it, 'blood-thirsty', which is how a compound is set when it is being lifted rather than habitually used.
provenance.significance: The proverb is not a description but a proposition: the bloodthirsty hate the upright. Zeniff's paragraph is an argument that exactly this is what has happened — the Lamanites are bloodthirsty, and what they have taught their children is 'an eternal hatred towards the children of Nephi' (10:17), whose founding claim is that Nephi 'was more faithful in keeping the commandments of the Lord' (10:13). Proverbs supplies the hinge between the two halves of Zeniff's ethnography, and it supplies it as a moral law rather than a grievance.

links.note: 'They were a wild, and ferocious, and a blood-thirsty people.' The single word is the whole verbal case, which is why this is an echo and not an allusion — but it is a word the King James Bible uses once, in a verse about the hatred of the bloodthirsty for the righteous, and the six verses that follow it in Mosiah 10 are an anatomy of precisely that hatred. Compare Hays on volume: one word can carry an echo when the word is a KJV singleton and the context is the precursor's own subject.
links.whyNot: A single English word, and a natural coinage for any writer describing an enemy; a reader who declines this is declining a real risk rather than a real error.

pericopes.text: And again: That they were wronged while in the land of their first inheritance, after they had crossed the sea; and all this, because that Nephi was more faithful in keeping the commandments of the Lord; therefore he was favored of the Lord, for the Lord heard his prayers and answered them, and he took the lead of their journey in the wilderness.
And his brethren were wroth with him, because they understood not the dealings of the Lord; they were also wroth with him upon the waters, because they hardened their hearts against the Lord.
And again: They were wroth with him, when they had arriven to the promised land, because they said that he had taken the ruling of the people out of their hands; and they sought to kill him.

And again: They were wroth with him, because he departed into the wilderness as the Lord had commanded him, and took the records which were engraven on the plates of brass; for they said that he robbed them.

links.text: And he hewed two tables of stone like unto the first; and Moses rose up early in the morning, and went up unto mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, and took in his hand the two tables of stone.

provenance.other: “as the Lord had commanded him and took” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 34:4 — an eight-word run, the longest in this chapter and the longest the machine stream found anywhere in Mosiah 10.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the sentence changes register entirely. Exodus 34:4 is Moses going up Sinai to take the second pair of stone tables: the one place in the Bible where a man, at the Lord's command, takes into his own hands an engraved record of the law. Mosiah 10:16 is Nephi departing into the wilderness at the Lord's command and taking 'the records which were engraven on the plates of brass'. Same command, same act, same kind of object — and the sentence is being spoken by the party that calls it theft. The Lamanite tradition has preserved the Mosaic shape of the event and lost its meaning; it can still describe Nephi in Moses's own words while concluding 'that he robbed them'. That is the finding: the accusation is framed in language that acquits.

links.note: 'He departed into the wilderness as the Lord had commanded him, and took the records which were engraven on the plates of brass.' Eight continuous KJV words from Exodus 34:4, and the shared run stops exactly where the objects diverge — Moses takes 'the two tables of stone', Nephi 'the plates of brass'. The n-gram stream ranked this candidate first for the verse (rarity 1.71, longest run 8) and it is the rare case where the machine's top row is also the right one. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; it is not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And thus they have taught their children, that they should hate them, and that they should murder them, and that they should rob and plunder them, and do all they could to destroy them; therefore, they have an eternal hatred towards the children of Nephi.

links.text: Because thou hast had a perpetual hatred, and hast shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, in the time that their iniquity had an end:

provenance.other: “perpetual hatred” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 35:5. The Book of Mormon's adjective is 'eternal', not 'perpetual', so this is a conceptual echo of a KJV singleton rather than a reproduction of it.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 35 is the oracle against Mount Seir, which is Edom, which is Esau — the brother nation. Its charge is a standing, inherited hatred passed down and acted on against 'the children of Israel'. Mosiah 10:17 is the same charge in the same shape: a hatred taught to children as an inheritance, directed at 'the children of Nephi', held by the descendants of a brother. If the writer is reaching anywhere in the KJV for the idea of a permanent fraternal hatred, Ezekiel 35 is the passage, and the Lamanite-as-Edom reading is available from there without being asserted here.

links.note: 'Therefore, they have an eternal hatred towards the children of Nephi.' The concept has exactly one KJV home and the wording does not quite reach it. Recorded as an echo, at moderate, because the surrounding verse supplies the rest of Ezekiel 35's indictment — hatred taught to the next generation, blood shed against the brother nation's children — and because the King James Bible offers no other place to get the idea of a hatred that is constitutionally permanent.
links.whyNot: 'Eternal' is not 'perpetual', and the Book of Mormon uses 'eternal' constantly in its own right. A reader could reasonably hold that the resemblance is thematic and that Ezekiel supplied nothing.

pericopes.text: For this very cause hath king Laman, by his cunning and lying craftiness, and his fair promises, hath deceived me, that I have brought this, my people, up into this land, that they may destroy them; yea, and we have suffered this many years in the land.

links.text: That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;

provenance.other: “cunning craftiness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:14, where it stands in a chain with 'lie' and 'deceive' — the same three elements the Book of Mormon sentence uses, and in the same order.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 4:14 is about a danger to the immature: children tossed about, taken in by men who lie in wait to deceive. Zeniff is an old king writing his last paragraph but one, and the confession he makes with Paul's phrase is that he was the child in the figure — 'hath deceived me, that I have brought this, my people, up into this land, that they may destroy them'. The whole Zeniff record is the record of a man who was over-zealous (Mosiah 9:3) and was played for it, and the King James Bible's one name for the technique that beat him is the phrase he uses.

links.note: 'For this very cause hath king Laman, by his cunning and lying craftiness, and his fair promises, hath deceived me.' The Book of Mormon splits the KJV compound and inserts its own adjective — 'cunning AND LYING craftiness' — which is how a remembered phrase behaves rather than a copied one, and the inserted word is Ephesians' own verb 'lie' from the back half of the same clause. The 1830 text keeps the doubled auxiliary, 'hath king Laman ... hath deceived me', which 1920 tidied; the redundancy is the tell of a sentence assembled around a borrowed phrase.

pericopes.text: And now I, Zeniff, after having told all these things unto my people concerning the Lamanites, I did stimulate them to go to battle with their might, putting their trust in the Lord; therefore, we did contend with them, face to face.
And it came to pass that we did drive them again out of our land; and we slew them with a great slaughter, even so many that we did not number them.
And it came to pass that we returned again to our own land, and my people again began to tend their flocks, and to till their ground.
And now, I being old, did confer the kingdom upon one of my sons; therefore, I say no more. And may the Lord bless my people. Amen.
And now it came to pass that Zeniff conferred the kingdom upon Noah, one of his sons; therefore Noah began to reign in his stead; and he did not walk in the ways of his father.

links.text: And there came a writing to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, Thus saith the LORD God of David thy father, Because thou hast not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat thy father, nor in the ways of Asa king of Judah,

provenance.other: “walked in the ways of” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — 2 Chronicles 21:12, 22:3, 28:2 and 34:2 — and 2 Chronicles 21:12 is the only one where the ways are a father's and the statement is a negative. 'His son began to reign in his stead' at Mosiah 10:6 and 11:1 fuses two Kings formulas that the KJV never joins; see the exclusion at 10:6.
provenance.significance: The verse is not merely a regnal evaluation, it is the opening of a prophet's letter — the only piece of writing from Elijah in the Old Testament — sent to a king who abandoned his father's ways. What follows it is the oracle: the LORD will smite the king's people 'with a great plague' (21:14) and the king himself with a wasting sickness in his own body (21:15). Mosiah 11:1 opens the reign; Mosiah 12:3-7 delivers exactly that oracle to exactly that king, the people struck with 'famine and with pestilence' and Noah's own life 'valued even as a garment in a hot furnace'. The frame the chapter borrows in its first sentence is the frame the next chapter fills in.

links.note: 'Noah began to reign in his stead; and he did not walk in the ways of his father.' The Deuteronomistic succession-plus-evaluation is the King James Bible's own two-part formula for opening a bad reign, and the Book of Mormon takes both halves in order. The evaluation half is traceable: of the four KJV verses with 'walked in the ways of', only 2 Chronicles 21:12 is a negative judgment measured against the man's own father, which is precisely Mosiah 11:1's sentence. Zeniff was a flawed but praying king; his son is introduced by the formula the KJV reserves for apostates.

pericopes.text: For behold, he did not keep the commandments of God, but he did walk after the desires of his own heart. And he had many wives and concubines. And he did cause his people to commit sin, and do that which was abominable in the sight of the Lord. Yea, and they did commit whoredoms, and all manner of wickedness.

links.text: And Rehoboam loved Maachah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and his concubines: (for he took eighteen wives, and threescore concubines; and begat twenty and eight sons, and threescore daughters.)

provenance.other: “his wives and his concubines” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: 2 Chronicles 11:21, and Daniel 5:2 and 5:3, which are Belshazzar's feast. The Book of Mormon repeats the pair three times in this chapter (11:2, 11:4, 11:14), which is the pattern of a formula being used rather than a verse being quoted.
provenance.alternative: 1 Kings 11:3, Solomon's seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, which is the passage the collocation summons even though it does not carry the KJV string.
provenance.significance: Both KJV homes of the phrase belong to kings this chapter is going to resemble: Rehoboam, whose taxation split a kingdom, and Belshazzar, who drank from stolen temple vessels with his wives and his concubines while a hand wrote on the wall. Noah does both — a fifth part levied on everything (11:3) and riotous living with the same company (11:14) — and receives, two chapters later, his own writing on the wall in the person of Abinadi.

links.note: 'He did walk after the desires of his own heart. And he had many wives and concubines.' The pairing is a KJV formula rather than a citation, which is why this is an echo; it earns the entry because the chapter uses it three times in thirteen verses as the marker of Noah's court, and because the two verses that hold it in the KJV are the two Old Testament kings whose careers this chapter is running in parallel. The 1830 text's 'do that which was abominable in the sight of the Lord' shadows the Kings formula 'did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD' (forty-four KJV verses) without reproducing it — a substitution, not a quotation.

pericopes.text: And he laid a tax of one fifth part of all they possessed; a fifth part of their gold and of their silver, and a fifth part of their ziff, and of their copper, and of their brass and their iron; and a fifth part of their fatlings; and also, a fifth part of all their grain.

links.text: And it shall come to pass in the increase, that ye shall give the fifth part unto Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own, for seed of the field, and for your food, and for them of your households, and for food for your little ones.

provenance.other: “fifth part” occurs in exactly 13 KJV verses, but only three of them are a tax: Genesis 41:34, where Joseph proposes that Pharaoh 'take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt', and Genesis 47:24 and 47:26, where he makes it permanent law. The rest are Leviticus's restitution surcharge, a private penalty rather than a royal levy.
provenance.significance: A fifth part is the King James Bible's rate of royal taxation and it has one story attached. Joseph's fifth is imposed to save a people from famine and it is remembered as wisdom. Noah's fifth — 'of their gold and of their silver, and a fifth part of their ziff, and of their copper, and of their brass and their iron; and a fifth part of their fatlings; and also, a fifth part of all their grain' — is imposed to support himself, his wives, his concubines and his priests, and the chapter's own verdict two sentences later is that 'the people labor exceedingly, to support iniquity'. The rate is identical and the direction is reversed: Joseph's fifth turns grain into survival, Noah's turns labour into idleness. And the famine that Joseph's fifth averted is what Abinadi will promise Noah's people at 12:4.

links.note: The Book of Mormon does not quote Genesis here; it uses Genesis's number. What makes the borrowing arguable rather than coincidental is that the enumeration follows Joseph's own subject-matter — grain and livestock ('fatlings') — while adding the metals a Genesis famine tax would have no use for. The verse is best read as a deliberate inversion of the one biblical precedent for a twenty-percent crown levy, and it is placed immediately after the regnal evaluation of 11:1 so that the reader meets the tax as the first act of a bad reign.

pericopes.text: And all this did he take, to support himself, and his wives, and his concubines, and also, his priests, and their wives, and their concubines; thus he had changed the affairs of the kingdom.
For he put down all the priests that had been consecrated by his father, and consecrated new ones in their stead, such as were lifted up in the pride of their hearts.

Yea, and thus were they supported in their laziness, and in their idolatry, and in their whoredoms, by the taxes which king Noah had put upon his people; thus did the people labor exceedingly, to support iniquity.
Yea, and they also became idolatrous, because they were deceived by the vain and flattering words of the king and priests; for they did speak flattering things unto them.

links.text: For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness:

provenance.other: “flattering words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5. The KJV's other flattery vocabulary is 'flattering lips' (Psalm 12:2-3), 'flattering titles' (Job 32:21-22) and 'flattereth' — none of them this phrase.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one use of the phrase is a denial, and it is a denial by preachers about their own preaching: Paul is certifying to the Thessalonians that his mission was not a confidence trick. Mosiah 11:7 hands the phrase to the men Paul was distinguishing himself from — a king and a state-appointed priesthood who are supported by a tax and who speak 'flattering things' from a breastwork built so that they can rest their arms while they do it (11:11). Recover the Pauline context and the verse acquires a test: the mark of a true preacher in the King James Bible is that he does not use flattering words and does not use a cloke of covetousness, and Noah's priests fail both halves in the same paragraph.

links.note: 'They also became idolatrous, because they were deceived by the vain and flattering words of the king and priests; for they did speak flattering things unto them.' The Book of Mormon splits the phrase across the sentence and repeats the adjective, which is what a remembered phrase does. 'Vain words' is a separate and much commoner KJV string (five verses, none of them relevant); 'flattering words' is the singleton and it is doing the work. Note that 1 Thessalonians 2:5 is the negative form of exactly the charge Abinadi will bring at 12:25-26 — professional teachers who do not teach what they profess.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that king Noah built many elegant and spacious buildings; and he ornamented them with fine work of wood, and of all manner of precious things, of gold, and of silver, and of iron, and of brass, and of ziff, and of copper;

links.text: I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards:

provenance.other: “planted me vineyards” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 2:4. The Book of Mormon has 'he planted vineyards' at 11:15, which does not reproduce the string; what is reproduced is the sequence.
provenance.significance: Ecclesiastes 2:4-8 is the King James Bible's one catalogue of a king's building programme in the king's own voice: great works, houses, vineyards, gardens, pools, servants, silver and gold, singers, 'the delights of the sons of men'. Mosiah 11:8-15 runs the same list in the same order — buildings (11:8), a palace and throne (11:9), gold and silver and precious things (11:8-11), vineyards and wine (11:15), and the delights of the sons of men in the plainest possible form (11:14). What Ecclesiastes concludes about the catalogue is the thing the Book of Mormon leaves for Abinadi to say: 'all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.'

links.note: The verbal contact is thin — the shared elements are common nouns — and the case rests on sequence, which is the one Hays subscore that can carry a link on its own when the sequence is long enough and the precursor is distinctive enough. Recorded at moderate. The alternative reading, that Noah is simply Solomon in 1 Kings 10, is not exclusive of this one: Ecclesiastes 2 is the KJV's Solomon narrating his own works, which is why it, rather than 1 Kings, supplies the order.
links.whyNot: No distinctive shared wording; the argument is entirely from the order of the elements, and a reader who thinks a rich king's building list will naturally run buildings-palace-gold-vineyards is entitled to decline it.

pericopes.text: and he also built him a spacious palace, and a throne in the midst thereof, all of which was of fine wood, and was ornamented with gold, and silver, and with precious things.

links.text: But in his estate shall he honour the God of forces: and a god whom his fathers knew not shall he honour with gold, and silver, and with precious stones, and pleasant things.

provenance.other: “gold and silver and with precious” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 11:38 — a seven-word run, and the highest-scoring machine candidate anywhere in Mosiah 11 (rarity 2.42). The Book of Mormon reads 'ornamented with gold, and silver, and with precious things'; Daniel has 'precious stones, and pleasant things', so the two nouns are fused.
provenance.significance: Daniel 11:38 describes the king who will not honour the god of his fathers and who ornaments instead a god his fathers knew not. Mosiah 11 has opened, one paragraph earlier, with a king who 'did not walk in the ways of his father' and who put down all the priests his father had consecrated. Recover Daniel's context and Noah's spacious palace stops being a display of wealth and becomes a cult: the gold and silver and precious things are going where the fathers' religion used to be, which is exactly what the chapter says about the temple at 11:10-11 — Noah's workmen ornament its walls and build his priests a breastwork inside it.

links.note: 'A spacious palace, and a throne in the midst thereof, all of which was of fine wood, and was ornamented with gold, and silver, and with precious things.' The seven-word run is Daniel's, including the odd repeated preposition ('and silver, and WITH precious') that is the tell of a phrase carried over whole. Solomon's throne stands behind the sentence too — 'the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with the best gold', 1 Kings 10:18, one of only two KJV verses with 'a great throne' — but the throne supplies the furniture and Daniel supplies the words.

pericopes.text: And he also caused that his workmen should work all manner of fine work within the walls of the temple, of fine wood, and of copper, and of brass;

and the seats which was set apart for the high priests, which was above all the other seats, he did ornament with pure gold; and he caused a breastwork to be built before them, that they might rest their bodies and their arms upon, while they should speak lying and vain words to his people.

And it came to pass that he built a tower near the temple; yea, a very high tower, even so high that he could stand upon the top thereof and overlook the land of Shilom, and also the land of Shemlon, which was possessed by the Lamanites; and he could even look over all the land round about.

And it came to pass that he caused many buildings to be built in the land Shilom; and he caused a great tower to be built on the hill north of the land Shilom, which had been a resort for the children of Nephi, at the time they fled out of the land; and thus he did do with the riches which he obtained by the taxation of his people.
And it came to pass that he placed his heart upon his riches, and he spent his time in riotous living with his wives and his concubines; and so did also his priests spend their time with harlots.

links.text: And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.

provenance.other: “riotous living” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 15:13, and “wasted his substance” in exactly one, the same verse. 'With harlots' occurs in three: Proverbs 29:3, Hosea 4:14 and Luke 15:30. Mosiah 11:14 puts the singleton and one of the three in a single sentence, and the only KJV passage that holds both is the parable of the prodigal son.
provenance.alternative: Proverbs 29:3, “spendeth his substance” with harlots, also a KJV singleton, which is the wisdom saying the parable is itself built on.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible's one phrase for dissipation belongs to a story about a son who comes home. The elder brother's accusation at Luke 15:30 supplies the second half of Mosiah's sentence — 'this thy son ... which hath devoured thy living with harlots' — so the Book of Mormon has taken both the younger son's conduct and the elder son's indictment of it and given them to a king and his priests. What the parable withholds is the point: the prodigal's riotous living ends in repentance and a father running to meet him. Noah's does not. Abinadi has been sent with precisely the offer the parable makes ('except they repent', 11:20, 11:21, 11:23, 11:25), the king hardens his heart against it at 11:29, and the same vocabulary returns at 12:29 when Abinadi asks the priests why they 'spend your strength with harlots'. The far country in this version is the palace.

links.note: 'He spent his time in riotous living with his wives and his concubines; and so did also his priests spend their time with harlots.' Two Lucan phrases from one parable in one sentence, one of them a KJV singleton, and the Book of Mormon keeps Luke's verb for both halves — the prodigal 'wasted', the Book of Mormon 'spent', which is Proverbs 29:3's 'spendeth' rather than Luke's, so the sentence is drawing on the wisdom saying and the parable at once. Note that 'harlots' is reserved here for the priests and 'wives and concubines' for the king: the distinction is the Book of Mormon's, and it is what makes the priests, not Noah, the ones Abinadi charges with it at 12:29.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he planted vineyards round about in the land; and he built wine presses, and made wine in abundance; and therefore he became a wine bibber, and also his people.

links.text: And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.

provenance.route: Isaiah 5:2, or Matthew 21:33 / Mark 12:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “built a tower” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Isaiah 5:2, Matthew 21:33, Mark 12:1 — and all three are the same figure: a vineyard with a tower and a winepress in it. Outside that figure the King James Bible never builds a tower at all. “made a winepress” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 5:2.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 21:33, the parable of the wicked husbandmen, which has the same three elements and adds the servants sent and killed.
provenance.significance: Three verses in the King James Bible put a tower and a winepress in a vineyard, and every one of them is a parable about a proprietor who plants carefully and gets nothing back. Noah builds all three — a very high tower near the temple (11:12), a second great tower on the hill (11:13), vineyards and wine presses (11:15) — and the chapter's next sentence is that he became a wine bibber. He has, without knowing it, constructed the stage set of the Song of the Vineyard on his own land; and the Song's continuation is a series of woes on drunkards ('woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink', 5:11) and a promise that the vineyard will be laid waste. Abinadi arrives five verses later with a woe (11:20). If the NT form is in view instead, the vineyard is the one whose owner sends a servant the husbandmen kill, which is the plot of Mosiah 11-17 exactly.

links.note: The tower, the vineyard and the winepress are separated in the Book of Mormon by three verses, which is why the n-gram stream cannot see this and why it is filed at 11:15 with the other two in recurrenceRefs: contiguous windows are blind to a figure assembled across a paragraph (CONVENTIONS §9). No single string is reproduced; the evidence is that the King James Bible assembles these three objects in one place and nowhere else, and that Mosiah 11 assembles them too. `mediation-check.py` finds no decisive divergence between Isaiah 5:2 and Matthew 21:33 at any point the Book of Mormon reproduces — the wording is too free — so mediation is recorded as uncertain rather than guessed.
links.whyNot: Every noun involved is common, and a king with a tower and a vineyard is not by itself an allusion. The case is the co-occurrence and the KJV's total silence about towers outside this figure.

links.text: The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children.

provenance.other: 'Winebibber' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Proverbs 23:20 ('be not among winebibbers', plural), Matthew 11:19 and Luke 7:34. Only Matthew and Luke use the singular noun of a named man, and the Book of Mormon's 1830 text sets it as two words, 'wine bibber'.
provenance.alternative: Luke 7:34, which is the same saying in the same words; nothing in the verse distinguishes them.
provenance.significance: In the King James Bible the word is an accusation, and it is a false one: it is what 'they say' about the Son of man, and the saying answers it — wisdom is justified of her children. Mosiah 11:15 makes it a report rather than a slander, and it is true. What makes this more than a coincidence of vocabulary is what happens ten verses later: Abinadi's oracle at 11:25 requires the people to 'repent in sackcloth and ashes', which in the King James Bible is Matthew 11:21, two verses further down the same discourse — the woe on Chorazin and Bethsaida for not repenting. Matthew 11 is used twice in one chapter, first for the charge against the king and then for the sentence on the city.

links.note: 'He became a wine bibber, and also his people.' A single distinctive noun, but a noun the King James Bible uses of a man only twice, in one saying, and one whose whole force there is that the charge is unjust. Applied to Noah it is simply accurate, and applied to 'also his people' it becomes the civic condition Abinadi is sent to address. The link is filed as an allusion rather than an echo because the same discourse supplies 11:25 — recurrence within a single chapter is Hays's third criterion doing exactly what it is for.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lamanites began to come in upon his people, upon small numbers, and to slay them in their fields, and while they were tending their flocks.

And king Noah sent guards round about the land to keep them off; but he did not send a sufficient number, and the Lamanites came upon them and killed them, and drove many of their flocks out of the land: thus the Lamanites began to destroy them, and to exercise their hatred upon them.
And it came to pass that king Noah sent his armies against them, and they were driven back, or they drove them back for a time; therefore, they returned rejoicing in their spoil.

And now, because of this great victory, they were lifted up in the pride of their hearts; they did boast in their own strength, saying, That their fifty could stand against thousands of the Lamanites; and thus they did boast, and did delight in blood, and the shedding of the blood of their brethren, and this because of the wickedness of their king and priests.

links.text: Thou sayest, Lo, thou hast smitten the Edomites; and thine heart lifteth thee up to boast: abide now at home; why shouldest thou meddle to thine hurt, that thou shouldest fall, even thou, and Judah with thee?

provenance.route: 2 Chronicles 25:18-19 (= 2 Kings 14:9-10) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Lifted up in the pride of their hearts' is in no KJV verse; the nearest King James constructions are 'the pride of thine heart hath deceived thee' (Obadiah 1:3, Jeremiah 49:16) and “thine heart lifteth thee up to boast”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 25:19, of which only the second joins the lifting to the boasting as Mosiah 11:19 does.
provenance.significance: This is the first half of a passage the batch meets again in the next chapter. 2 Chronicles 25:18-19 (and its twin 2 Kings 14:9-10) is a single speech: a king sends another king the parable of the thistle that presumed on the cedar and was trodden down by a wild beast, and then names the fault the parable is about — 'thine heart lifteth thee up to boast'. Mosiah takes the two halves in reverse order and eleven verses apart. Here the Nephites' hearts are lifted up and they boast; at 12:12 Abinadi's accusers report his charge that the king shall be 'as the blossoms of a thistle', and at 12:11 that he shall be 'ran over by the beasts and trodden under foot'. Amaziah's fault and Amaziah's parable arrive at Noah's court in the same order they left Joash's mouth, split across the two chapters.

links.note: 'They were lifted up in the pride of their hearts; they did boast in their own strength, saying, That their fifty could stand against thousands of the Lamanites.' Two things converge on this verse. The boast is measured in the arithmetic of Leviticus 26:8 — 'five of you shall chase an hundred, and an hundred of you shall put ten thousand to flight', the covenant promise that Israel's numbers do not matter — and the boast strips it of the covenant, which is the point: the Nephites claim the ratio while 'depending upon their own strength' in Zeniff's phrase at 10:11. And the lifting-up-to-boast is the diagnosis 2 Chronicles 25:19 gives a king before the thistle takes him. Recorded at moderate because neither source is reproduced verbally; the argument is the convergence and the sequel at 12:11-12.
links.whyNot: 'Lifted up in the pride of their hearts' is a Book of Mormon formula in its own right and the chapter has already used it at 11:5. A reader may take 2 Chronicles 25:19 as a resemblance the thistle at 12:12 makes retrospectively attractive rather than a source.

links.text: And five of you shall chase an hundred, and an hundred of you shall put ten thousand to flight: and your enemies shall fall before you by the sword.

provenance.other: “shall chase an hundred” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 26:8. No word of it survives into Mosiah 11:19; what survives is the form of the claim — a small named number standing against a large unnamed one.
provenance.significance: Leviticus 26:8 is a promise, and it is conditional: it stands inside 'if ye walk in my statutes' (26:3), and the same chapter reverses it exactly for disobedience — 'ye shall flee when none pursueth' (26:17). Noah's soldiers assert the promise while the chapter is documenting the condition being broken, and the reversal arrives on schedule in the next chapter. The unit of fifty is also the Book of Mormon's own inherited arithmetic: Laman's objection at 1 Nephi 3:31 was that Laban 'can command fifty', and Nephi's answer was the Lord who is mightier than Laban and his fifty. Noah's men make Laman's calculation and call it a victory.

links.note: No verbal contact at all, which is why this is an echo at moderate and why kjvSpecific is 'no': the link is to the shape of a covenant formula, not to its English. It earns a row because Leviticus 26 is the only place in the Bible that states a battlefield ratio as a theological claim, because the boast at 11:19 states one, and because Mosiah 11-12 goes on to deliver Leviticus 26's curses in Leviticus 26's own areas — bondage (11:21, 12:2), the sword, and 'I will be slow to hear their cries' answering 'I will walk contrary unto you' (26:24).
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal survives. A reader may hold that a boast about odds needs no source.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there was a man among them, whose name was Abinadi; and he went forth among them, and began to prophesy, saying, Behold, thus saith the Lord, and thus hath he commanded me, saying, Go forth and say unto this people, thus saith the Lord: Wo be unto this people, for I have seen their abominations, and their wickedness, and their whoredoms; and except they repent, I will visit them in mine anger.

And except they repent, and turn to the Lord their God, behold, I will deliver them into the hands of their enemies; yea, and they shall be brought into bondage; and they shall be afflicted by the hand of their enemies.
And it shall come to pass that they shall know that I am the Lord their God, and am a jealous God, visiting the iniquities of my people.

links.text: Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;

provenance.other: “a jealous God, visiting the iniquity” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:5 and Deuteronomy 5:9, which are verbally identical across the whole of the borrowed clause; the verse cannot discriminate between them. The Book of Mormon's own departure is decisive of something else: it reads 'visiting the iniquities of MY PEOPLE' where both KJV verses read 'the iniquity of the fathers upon the children'.
provenance.significance: Abinadi's first oracle ends with the sanction clause of the second commandment, and his last recorded act in this chapter-pair is to recite the commandments themselves (12:34-36). The order matters: the sanction is quoted before the law it sanctions, so that when the priests are finally asked what they teach and answer 'the law of Moses' (12:28), the reader has already heard the penalty attached. And the substitution — 'the iniquities of my people' for 'the iniquity of the fathers upon the children' — cuts the generational transfer out of the commandment. Noah's people are not being punished for their fathers; they are the fathers.

links.note: 'They shall know that I am the Lord their God, and am a jealous God, visiting the iniquities of my people.' Nine continuous KJV words, and the point of interest is where the quotation stops. Exodus 20:5's clause runs on to 'the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation'; the Book of Mormon breaks off at 'the iniquities of' and substitutes its own object. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Exodus 20:5 at this verse.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass that except this people repent, and turn unto the Lord their God, they shall be brought into bondage; and none shall deliver them, except it be the Lord the Almighty God.
Yea, and it shall come to pass that when they shall cry unto me, I will be slow to hear their cries; yea, and I will suffer them that they be smitten by their enemies.

links.text: Therefore thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will bring evil upon them, which they shall not be able to escape; and though they shall cry unto me, I will not hearken unto them.

provenance.other: “they shall cry unto me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 11:11 — a seven-word run with the Book of Mormon ('they shall cry unto me, I will'), which was also the machine's top candidate for the verse. The KJV's other refusals to hear are worded differently: 'then shall they cry unto the LORD, but he will not hear them' (Micah 3:4), 'so they cried, and I would not hear' (Zechariah 7:13), 'then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer' (Proverbs 1:28).
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 11 is the covenant-lawsuit chapter: the LORD reminds Judah of the covenant made 'in the day that I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace' (11:4), finds it broken, and withdraws the hearing of prayer. Two things follow from recovering it. Abinadi's own commission is Jeremiah's — the prophet forbidden to intercede (11:14) — and the covenant formula Jeremiah invokes, deliverance from Egypt and the house of bondage, is the exact sentence Abinadi will recite at Mosiah 12:34. The oracle that suspends prayer and the commandment that grounds the covenant come from the same argument, two chapters apart.

links.note: 'When they shall cry unto me, I will be slow to hear their cries.' The seven shared words include the pronoun sequence, and the Book of Mormon then softens Jeremiah's absolute refusal into a delay — 'slow to hear' — before restoring the absolute at 11:25 ('I will not hear their prayers'). That two-stage movement is not in Jeremiah and is the Book of Mormon's own. What is Jeremiah's is the premise, that a covenant people can forfeit the hearing of its prayers, which is the doctrine the whole oracle depends on.

pericopes.text: And except they repent in sackcloth and ashes, and cry mightily to the Lord their God, I will not hear their prayers, neither will I deliver them out of their afflictions; and thus saith the Lord, and thus hath he commanded me.

links.text: Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.

provenance.route: Matthew 11:21 (or Luke 10:13) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'In sackcloth and ashes' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Esther 4:3, Matthew 11:21 and Luke 10:13. Esther's is mourning at a decree, not repentance; only the Gospel saying joins the phrase to the verb 'repent'. “repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 11:21.
provenance.alternative: Luke 10:13, which carries the same saying as 'they had a great while ago repented, sitting in sackcloth and ashes'.
provenance.significance: The Gospel saying is a counterfactual: Tyre and Sidon, the proverbially doomed pagan cities, WOULD have repented had they seen what these towns saw, and therefore it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for Chorazin and Bethsaida. Abinadi is standing in a city that has seen a prophet and demanding the sackcloth Tyre and Sidon would have put on. The threat that follows in Mosiah — bondage, unanswered prayer, no deliverer — is the Matthean 'more tolerable for them than for you' turned into an oracle. And Noah has already been given a word from two verses earlier in the same discourse (11:15, 'winebibber'), which is what makes this a use of Matthew 11 rather than a coincidence of a common idiom.

links.note: `mediation-check.py` returns no decisive divergence between Matthew 11:21 and Luke 10:13: the Book of Mormon reproduces only 'repent in sackcloth and ashes', and neither Matthew's 'long ago' nor Luke's 'sitting' appears, so this verse cannot settle which Gospel is in view. The argument for Matthew is external and contextual — Matthew 11:19 supplies 'winebibber' ten verses earlier in the same Book of Mormon chapter — and it is offered as an argument, not a demonstration. Mediation is recorded as direct-NT, which the three-verse count does establish: the OT alternative, Esther 4:3, has the mourning without the repenting.

pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that when Abinadi had spoken these words unto them, they were wroth with him, and sought to take away his life; but the Lord delivered him out of their hands.

Now when king Noah had heard of the words which Abinadi had spake unto the people, he was also wroth; and he saith, Who is Abinadi, that I and my people should be judged of him? or who is the Lord, that shall bring upon my people such great affliction?

links.text: And Pharaoh said, Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go? I know not the LORD, neither will I let Israel go.

provenance.other: “who is the Lord that I should obey his voice” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 5:2. The King James Bible asks 'Who is the LORD' in only one other place, Proverbs 30:9, and there it is a fear rather than a taunt.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon puts Pharaoh's sentence in the mouth of a king whose prophet has just demanded that he release a people from a bondage that has not started yet — and the oracle Abinadi has delivered is precisely that bondage will start (11:21, 11:23). Pharaoh's question is the KJV's definitive refusal to recognise the God who brings people out of Egypt; Noah asks it, and the answer Abinadi eventually gives, in the last words of Mosiah 12, is the first commandment: 'I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.' The question of 11:27 is answered by the quotation of 12:34, and the answer is the one Pharaoh got.

links.note: 'Who is Abinadi, that I and my people should be judged of him? or who is the Lord, that shall bring upon my people such great affliction?' The KJV sentence is reproduced through 'who is the Lord, that', and Noah's continuation replaces Pharaoh's 'I should obey his voice' with the affliction clause, which keeps the syntax and changes the object of contempt from obedience to power. The first half of the verse looks like Moses's other rejection — 'Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?' (Exodus 2:14) / 'a ruler and a judge over us' (Acts 7:27), the pair 1 Nephi 2:22 and 3:29 decided in the New Testament's favour — but `mediation-check.py` finds nothing decisive here: the Book of Mormon has neither 'prince' nor 'ruler', only 'judged of him', and the resemblance will not carry a link. See the exclusion.

pericopes.text: I command you to bring Abinadi hither, that I may slay him: for he hath said these things, that he might stir up my people to anger, one with another, and to raise contentions among my people; therefore, I will slay him.

Now the eyes of the people were blinded; therefore, they hardened their hearts against the words of Abinadi, and they sought from that time forward to take him. And king Noah hardened his heart against the word of the Lord; and he did not repent of his evil doings.

links.text: He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.

provenance.route: Isaiah 6:10 → John 12:40 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The pairing of blinded eyes with a hardened heart occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 12:40. Isaiah 6:10, which John is quoting, has neither verb: it reads 'make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes'. Fat, heavy and shut are Isaiah's three; blinded and hardened are John's two, and the Book of Mormon has John's two.
provenance.significance: John 12:40 is the verse the fourth Gospel uses to explain why people who had seen the signs did not believe, and John immediately adds that many of the chief rulers did believe but would not confess it 'lest they should be put out of the synagogue' (12:42). Mosiah 11:29 divides the blindness the same way: 'the eyes of the people were blinded' as a collective condition, and then, separately and in his own sentence, 'king Noah hardened his heart against the word of the Lord'. The people are acted upon; the king acts. That is John's distinction, not Isaiah's, and it sets up Mosiah 12's courtroom, where the priests will ask a question about Isaiah and be told they do not understand what they teach.

links.note: This is the same OT-via-NT result the pilot recorded at 1 Nephi 12:17, reached here by the same test: the two diagnostic verbs are John's and are absent from the Isaiah verse he is quoting. `mediation-check.py` returns 'neither' at every point, because the Book of Mormon restructures the sentence into two clauses rather than reproducing either version's syntax — so the case is made by vocabulary, which is decisive on its own. Isaiah 6:10's three verbs appear nowhere in Mosiah 11:29; John's two are both there.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after the space of two years, that Abinadi came among them in disguise, that they knew him not, and began again to prophesy among them, saying, Thus hath the Lord commanded me, saying: Abinadi, go and prophesy unto this my people, for they have hardened their hearts against my words; they have repented not of their evil doings; therefore, I will visit them in my anger, yea, in my fierce anger will I visit them in their iniquities and abominations;

yea, wo be unto this generation. And the Lord said unto me, Stretch forth thy hand, and prophesying, saying, Thus saith the Lord: It shall come to pass that this generation, because of their iniquities, shall be brought into bondage, and shall be smitten on the cheek; yea, and shall be driven by men, and shall be slain; and the vultures of the air, and the dogs, yea, and the wild beasts, shall devour their flesh.

links.text: And I will appoint over them four kinds, saith the LORD: the sword to slay, and the dogs to tear, and the fowls of the heaven, and the beasts of the earth, to devour and destroy.

provenance.other: “the dogs to tear and the fowls” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 15:3, and “beasts of the earth to devour” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. No other KJV verse assembles dogs, birds and wild beasts as one set of executioners: 1 Kings 14:11 and 21:24 have dogs and fowls but no beasts, Ezekiel 39:4 has birds and beasts but no dogs.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 15:3 is the LORD appointing 'four kinds' over Judah — sword, dogs, birds, beasts — and it stands two verses after the declaration that not even Moses and Samuel standing before him could turn this people. Mosiah 12:2 lists the same three scavengers and does the sword's work in its own words ('shall be slain'). The recovered context is a refusal of intercession, which is exactly the condition Abinadi's oracle reached at 11:24-25: the God who will be slow to hear their cries is the God who appoints the four kinds. Jeremiah governs this chapter beyond this verse — 26:14 stands behind 12:16 and 26:12 behind 12:29.

links.note: 'The vultures of the air, and the dogs, yea, and the wild beasts, shall devour their flesh.' Two KJV singletons out of one verse. The Book of Mormon reorders the three and substitutes 'vultures of the air' for Jeremiah's 'fowls of the heaven', which costs the link nothing, because the set of three is what has no other home in the King James Bible. 'Vulture' appears in the KJV only in the unclean-bird lists of Leviticus 11:14 and Deuteronomy 14:13 and at Job 28:7 and Isaiah 34:15, never as a scavenger of the slain — so the one substituted word is not a KJV word for this at all.

links.text: And looking round about upon them all, he said unto the man, Stretch forth thy hand. And he did so: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.route: Luke 6:10 and 6:29 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: Exodus 9:22, 'Stretch forth thine hand toward heaven, that there may be hail', which is what this oracle actually goes on to do four verses later at 12:6 — and whose pronoun the Book of Mormon does not have.
provenance.other: “stretch forth thy hand”, singular, is a KJV singleton, Luke 6:10 — John 21:18 has 'stretch forth thy handS', plural, of old age, a different verse entirely, not a second instance of this one. The commoner form, 'stretch forth THINE hand', occurs in six — Exodus 8:5, 9:22, 2 Samuel 1:14, Psalm 138:7, Matthew 12:13, Mark 3:5. The 1830 text reads 'thy'. “on the one cheek” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 6:29; every other KJV cheek is struck 'upon the cheek' (2 Chronicles 18:23, Job 16:10, Psalm 3:7, Micah 5:1).
provenance.significance: Two clauses of Mosiah 12:2 reach into one chapter of Luke, and it is the Sermon on the Plain: the man with the withered hand is told to stretch it forth at 6:10, and the disciple struck on the one cheek is told to offer the other at 6:29. Recover that and the oracle acquires an irony it does not state. The gesture Abinadi is commanded to make is the gesture of a healing the Pharisees were watching for so that they might find an accusation (6:7) — and being watched so as to be accused is what happens to Abinadi at 12:19. The blow on the cheek his oracle threatens is, in Luke, the blow a disciple is told to accept. The prophet is handed a healer's gesture and a martyr's sentence in the same verse.

links.note: 'Stretch forth thy hand, and prophesying, saying, Thus saith the Lord ... shall be smitten on the cheek.' The pronoun is the whole discriminator on the first clause, and `mediation-check.py` will not catch it, because the tool ignores single common words (ADJUDICATING §4): six KJV verses read 'thine', two read 'thy', and the Book of Mormon has 'thy'. Exodus 9:22 has the better claim on function — a prophet stretching out a hand, and hail following at 12:6 — and the worse claim on wording, so it is recorded as the alternative rather than the source. The second clause is firmer: 'on the cheek' is Luke's preposition and no other KJV verse uses it. The 1830 'and prophesying, saying' is an anacoluthon that 1920 repaired to 'and prophesy'.
links.whyNot: One pronoun carries the first clause, and 'stretch forth thy hand' is an unremarkable English sentence. If the writer had Exodus 9:22 in view and modernised the pronoun, the Lucan case evaporates and only the cheek remains.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass that the life of king Noah shall be valued even as a garment in a hot furnace; for he shall know that I am the Lord.
And it shall come to pass that I will smite this my people, with sore afflictions; yea, with famine and with pestilence; and I will cause that they shall howl all the day long.
Yea, and I will cause that they shall have burdens lashed upon their backs; and they shall be driven before, like a dumb ass.

links.text: But was rebuked for his iniquity: the dumb ass speaking with man’s voice forbad the madness of the prophet.

provenance.other: “dumb ass” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 2:16. The KJV's asses are elsewhere wild, young, saddled or laden, never dumb; and 'burdens', the other half of Mosiah 12:5's image, is the Exodus word for what taskmasters lay on a people (Exodus 1:11, 2:11, 5:4-5, 6:6-7).
provenance.significance: This catalogue has been to 2 Peter 2 before: 1 Nephi 8:23's 'mist of darkness' comes from 2 Peter 2:17, one verse further down. The chapter is a denunciation of false teachers who follow 'the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness' (2:15) and who 'promise them liberty' while being 'the servants of corruption' (2:19). That is Noah's priesthood in three clauses — men supported by a fifth part of everything (11:3-6) who tell the king 'thou hast not sinned' and 'thou shalt also prosper' (12:14-15). And the dumb ass in 2 Peter is not the figure of the oppressed: it is the animal that saw what the prophet could not and spoke to stop him. Abinadi's threat that the people will be 'driven before, like a dumb ass' hands them the beast that, in the King James Bible, is the only one in the story who is right.

links.note: 'They shall have burdens lashed upon their backs; and they shall be driven before, like a dumb ass.' Two words, and they are the KJV's only 'dumb ass'. The burdens are the Exodus vocabulary of Egyptian servitude, so the verse pairs the bondage of the first commandment's preface — quoted verbatim at 12:34 — with a Petrine phrase about Balaam. Filed at high because the collocation is a singleton and the source chapter's subject is the chapter's own subject; the whyNot is that two words is a small purchase on a long epistle.
links.whyNot: A two-word phrase, and a driven pack animal is an obvious figure for a people in bondage. What keeps the link is that the KJV supplies the adjective in exactly one place, and that place is about hireling teachers.

pericopes.text: And it shall come to pass that I will send forth hail among them, and it shall smite them; and they shall also be smitten with the east wind; and insects shall pester their land also, and devour their grain.

links.text: And the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch forth thine hand toward heaven, that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, upon man, and upon beast, and upon every herb of the field, throughout the land of Egypt.

provenance.route: Exodus 9:22-23 and 10:13-15 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'The east wind' occurs in thirteen KJV verses. Exodus 10:13 is the only one where it is an instrument of plague that brings something to eat the crops, and the only one where it follows hail. In Exodus the two plagues are consecutive; in Mosiah 12:6 the two clauses are consecutive.
provenance.significance: Abinadi's list is the Egyptian plague cycle turned against the covenant people: hail, an east wind, a devouring of the grain, then pestilence. Exodus 10:15 says the locusts 'did eat every herb of the land, and all the fruit of the trees which the hail had left' — the same two-stage destruction, hail and then insects, that Mosiah 12:6 compresses into one sentence. The reversal is the point, and it is the reversal the whole Abinadi cycle turns on: the God who identifies himself at 12:34 as the one 'which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt' is here treating his own people as Egypt. Noah has already answered Moses in Pharaoh's words at 11:27; the plagues follow the refusal, in order.

links.note: No phrase is reproduced, which is why kjvSpecific is 'no' — there is no English to test. The evidence is order, and the Book of Mormon's own departures show it is using Exodus rather than copying it: the insect plague is unnamed where Exodus names locusts, and each plague is reduced to a clause. Filed at 12:6 because that verse holds all three Exodus elements; the famine and pestilence of 12:4 and 12:7 belong to the standard prophetic triad (Jeremiah 14:12 and its kind) and are not Exodus's.
links.whyNot: Sequence alone, with no shared wording, and hail and pestilence are the common currency of prophetic threat. A reader could take this as generic plague language with no Exodus behind it.

pericopes.text: And they shall be smitten with a great pestilence; and all this will I do, because of their iniquities and abominations.

And it shall come to pass that except they repent, I will utterly destroy them from off the face of the earth; yet they shall leave a record behind them, and I will preserve them for other nations which shall possess the land; yea, even this will I do, that I may discover the abominations of this people to other nations. And many things did Abinadi prophesy against this people.

links.text: (For the LORD thy God is a jealous God among you) lest the anger of the LORD thy God be kindled against thee, and destroy thee from off the face of the earth.

provenance.other: “destroy thee from off the face of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 6:15, and “a jealous God among you” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. 'From off the face of the earth' alone occurs in five (Genesis 7:4, Deuteronomy 6:15, 1 Kings 13:34, Jeremiah 28:16, Amos 9:8); only Deuteronomy 6:15 attaches it to 'destroy' with a covenant people as the object.
provenance.significance: One KJV verse holds both halves of Abinadi's oracle. Deuteronomy 6:15 is the sanction of the Shema: because the LORD is a jealous God among you, breaking the covenant is being destroyed off the face of the earth. Mosiah 11:22 has already quoted the jealous-God clause, in Exodus 20:5's wording; Mosiah 12:8 delivers the consequence in Deuteronomy 6:15's. The two halves of one Deuteronomic sentence arrive nineteen verses apart, in the right order and attached to the right conditions — and the second half is then qualified in a way Deuteronomy does not permit: 'yet they shall leave a record behind them, and I will preserve them for other nations which shall possess the land'. The destruction is total and the record survives it, which is the Book of Mormon's doctrine of itself, inserted into the sentence that denies it.

links.note: 'Except they repent, I will utterly destroy them from off the face of the earth.' Six continuous KJV words. The one departure is the inserted 'utterly' — 'utterly destroy' is a separate and very common KJV idiom (thirty-four verses) welded onto the rarer phrase, which is how a writer who knows both is likely to produce it. The verse then turns away from its source entirely; the surviving record for 'other nations' has no Deuteronomic warrant.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they were angry with him; and they took him and carried him bound before the king, and saith unto the king, Behold, we have brought a man before thee which has prophesied evil concerning thy people, and saith that God will destroy them;

links.text: And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, There is yet one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, by whom we may enquire of the LORD: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil. And Jehoshaphat said, Let not the king say so.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 22:8 (= 2 Chronicles 18:7) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “prophesy good concerning me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 22:8, and 1 Kings 22:18 repeats it as 'prophesy no good concerning me, but evil'. “evil concerning” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 22:23. Mosiah 12:9 and 12:10 take the negative half of the formula twice in two verses: 'prophesied evil concerning thy people', 'prophesieth evil concerning thy life'.
provenance.significance: This is a scene borrowed, not only a phrase. 1 Kings 22 is the King James Bible's full-dress trial of a prophet before a king: Micaiah is hated because he prophesies evil and not good, he is fetched by a messenger, four hundred court prophets tell the king what he wants to hear, one of them strikes Micaiah on the cheek (2 Chronicles 18:23), the king orders him imprisoned, and the king dies as prophesied. Mosiah 12 runs the sequence with the roles filled: a man carried bound before the king (12:9), the charge that he prophesies evil (12:9-10), a court priesthood assuring the king 'thou hast not sinned' and 'thou shalt also prosper' (12:14-15) — which is Zedekiah's 'Go up, and prosper' at 1 Kings 22:12 doing the same work — imprisonment (12:17), and Noah's death by fire in Mosiah 19. The reader who recovers Micaiah knows how the trial ends before it begins. The blow on the cheek is already in the Book of Mormon's text too, at 12:2, though there it falls on the people.

links.note: 'We have brought a man before thee which has prophesied evil concerning thy people.' The Book of Mormon does not reproduce 1 Kings 22:8's clause whole; the shared run is short, and the case is the singleton formula used twice plus the scene it belongs to. The accusers' speech at 12:13-15 is the counterpart to the four hundred: 'we are guiltless, and thou, O king, hast not sinned; therefore, this man hast lied concerning you, and he hath prophesied in vain'.

pericopes.text: and he also prophesieth evil concerning thy life, and saith that thy life shall be as a garment in a furnace of fire.
And again: He saith that thou shalt be as a stalk, even as a dry stalk of the field, which is ran over by the beasts and trodden under foot.

links.text: And Jehoash the king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, Give thy daughter to my son to wife: and there passed by a wild beast that was in Lebanon, and trode down the thistle.

provenance.route: 2 Kings 14:9-10 (= 2 Chronicles 25:18-19) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: Job 13:25, 'wilt thou break a leaf driven to and fro? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble?' — a KJV singleton for 'dry stubble', which supplies the wind-driven plant and the dried one but has no thistle and no beast.
provenance.other: “trode down the thistle” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Kings 14:9 and its twin 2 Chronicles 25:18. 'The thistle' occurs in exactly three, the third being Hosea 10:8, where it grows on an altar and treads nothing. No other KJV passage puts a thistle, a wild beast and a treading-down together; Mosiah 12:11-12 has all three.
provenance.significance: The KJV passage is a message from one king to another and it is a parable about presumption: the thistle of Lebanon proposed marriage to the cedar and a wild beast walked over it. Joash sends it to Amaziah and then says what it means — 'thine heart lifteth thee up to boast' (2 Chronicles 25:19) — and Amaziah goes to war anyway and loses. Mosiah splits the halves across two chapters and reverses their order: Noah's soldiers are lifted up and boast at 11:19; here the king is told he will be the trodden thistle. The sting is in who repeats it. The priests quote the thistle to Noah as evidence of Abinadi's insolence, not knowing that in the King James Bible the thistle parable is what one king says to another king who is about to fall.

links.note: 'He saith that thou shalt be as a stalk, even as a dry stalk of the field, which is ran over by the beasts and trodden under foot' — and then, in the next verse, 'as the blossoms of a thistle'. Three elements across two verses, which is why no machine window can see this: contiguous n-grams are blind to a figure assembled across a verse boundary (CONVENTIONS §9). The 1830 reading is 'which is RAN over by the beasts'; 1920 repaired it to 'run over', a grammatical correction and not a move toward the KJV, whose verb is 'trode down'. 'Trodden under foot' is the Book of Mormon's own supplement from a much commoner idiom (five KJV verses).

pericopes.text: And again: He saith thou shalt be as the blossoms of a thistle, which when it is fully ripe, if the wind bloweth, it is driven forth upon the face of the land; and he pretendeth the Lord hath spoken it. And he saith all this shall come upon thee, except thou repent; and this because of thine iniquities.
And now, O king, what great evil hast thou done, or what great sins has thy people committed, that we should be condemned of God, or judged of this man?
And now, O king, behold, we are guiltless, and thou, O king, hast not sinned; therefore, this man hast lied concerning you, and he hath prophesied in vain.
And behold, we are strong, we shall not come into bondage, or be taken captive by our enemies; yea, and thou hast prospered in the land, and thou shalt also prosper.
Behold, here is the man, we deliver him into thy hands; thou mayest do with him as seemeth thee good.

links.text: As for me, behold, I am in your hand: do with me as seemeth good and meet unto you.

provenance.other: “as seemeth good” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Samuel 15:26 and Jeremiah 26:14, and only Jeremiah's is spoken by a man being handed over for trial. The Book of Mormon's 'do with him as seemeth thee good' keeps the clause and changes the person.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 26 is the other prophet's trial, and it is nearer to Mosiah 12 than Micaiah's is. A prophet prophesies against the city; the priests and the prophets seize him saying 'Thou shalt surely die' (26:8); he is brought before the authorities; he answers that the LORD sent him to prophesy against this house (26:12); he offers himself — 'do with me as seemeth good and meet unto you' — and warns that killing him will bring innocent blood on the city (26:15). Mosiah 12 supplies each element with the roles redistributed, and the telling redistribution is this one: in Jeremiah the sentence is the prophet's own, an act of self-surrender; in Mosiah 12:16 it belongs to the accusers — 'Behold, here is the man, we deliver him into thy hands; thou mayest do with him as seemeth thee good.' The words of a prophet placing himself in God's hands are given to the men handing him over to be burned. 'Behold, here is the man' does comparable work a second time; compare John 19:5.

links.note: An allusion rather than a quotation: only the four-word clause is reproduced and the grammatical person is changed. What raises it above a common idiom is the second use of Jeremiah 26 thirteen verses later — Mosiah 12:29's 'send me to prophesy against this people' takes “to prophesy against this”, a KJV singleton, from Jeremiah 26:12, the answer Jeremiah gave at his own trial. One chapter of Jeremiah supplies both the accusers' sentence and the defendant's, at the two ends of the same scene.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that king Noah caused that Abinadi should be cast into prison; and he commanded that the priests should gather themselves together, that he might hold a council with them what he should do with him.
And it came to pass that they saith unto the king, Bring him hither, that we may question him. And the king commanded that he should be brought before them.

And they began to question him, that they might cross him, that thereby they might have wherewith to accuse him; but he answered them boldly, and withstood all their questions, yea, to their astonishment: for he did withstand them in all their questions, and did confound them in all their words.

links.text: Laying wait for him, and seeking to catch something out of his mouth, that they might accuse him.

provenance.alternative: John 8:6, whose “have to accuse him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is the closer construction to the Book of Mormon's 'have wherewith to accuse him' — but whose setting is a single test question, not a cross-examination.
provenance.other: 'That they might accuse him' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 12:10, Mark 3:2 and Luke 11:54. Only Luke 11:53-54 pairs the accusation with questioning — 'began to urge him vehemently, and to provoke him to speak of many things; laying wait for him, and seeking to catch something out of his mouth' — which is what Mosiah 12:19 describes.
provenance.significance: Luke 11:53-54 is the hinge between the woes on the lawyers and Pharisees and the plot to trap Jesus in his talk. Mosiah 12 puts the two in the same order and reassigns them: the priests question Abinadi to catch him out (12:19), and Abinadi answers with a woe on professional teachers who do not know what they teach (12:25-27), which is Luke 11:52's charge — 'ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered' — in different words. The Book of Mormon has taken the Lucan sequence, questioning and then woe, and given the woe to the defendant.

links.note: 'They began to question him, that they might cross him, that thereby they might have wherewith to accuse him.' 'Cross him' is the Book of Mormon's own — the KJV never uses the verb — but the purpose clause is the Gospels' standing formula for a trap laid in questions, and Luke 11:54 is the one instance where the trap is a cross-examination rather than a sabbath healing. What follows has no KJV phrase behind it: 'confound' is a fifty-one-verse word and 'answered them' a thirty-four-verse one, so the sentence about Abinadi withstanding them is the narrator's, not the King James Bible's.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that one of them saith unto him, What meaneth the words which are written, and which have been taught by our fathers, saying:

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of Him that bringeth good tidings; that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good; that publisheth salvation; that sayeth unto Zion, Thy God reigneth;

links.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.alternative: Romans 10:15, the New Testament quotation of the same verse: 'How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!'
provenance.other: “publisheth peace” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 52:7 and Nahum 1:15, which share eleven words ('the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace'). Nahum has no mountains and no Zion; the Book of Mormon has both.
provenance.significance: The verse is quoted in the chapter as a question the priests cannot answer, which is a use of scripture no other passage in the catalogue makes: the priests produce it, verbatim, as a text 'which have been taught by our fathers', and Abinadi's reply is that quoting it is not the same as knowing it. Mosiah 15:14-18 will return and expound this same verse at length. What the immediate context supplies is the reproach: Isaiah's beautiful feet belong to the messenger who publishes peace and salvation, and the man standing in front of these priests is that messenger, in irons.

links.note: Twenty-eight continuous words with one substantive departure in the whole of it: 1830 reads 'that SAYETH unto Zion' where the KJV has 'saith', and 1920 restored the King James form (CONVENTIONS §8 — the later edition correcting back toward the source). `mediation-check.py` returns three decisive points for Isaiah 52:7 over Romans 10:15: 'bringeth good tidings that publisheth' rather than 'preach the gospel of', 'that bringeth good' rather than 'and bring glad', and no trace of Romans's 'as it is written'. This is one of the counter-examples to the pilot's OT-via-NT pattern — the Book of Mormon has the Old Testament form. At twenty-eight words it exceeds Skousen's sixteen-word operational threshold, but his itemized list of KJV quotations is unobtainable to this project (PLAN §4.1) and nothing here should be read as a claim about what is on it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Mosiah 12.24 (Isaiah 52:7-10, keyed to the last verse of the block)

pericopes.text: thy watchmen shall lift up the voice with the voice; together shall they sing, for they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord shall bring again Zion.

links.text: Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the LORD shall bring again Zion.

provenance.other: “with the voice together shall they sing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:8. The 1830 text reproduces every word of that verse in the KJV's order, with no substitution, addition or omission. The whole of the departure is punctuation.
provenance.significance: A watchman is the KJV's standing figure for a prophet — 'Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel' (Ezekiel 3:17) — and the priests read the verse to a prophet they have imprisoned. The verse promises watchmen who lift up the voice together and see eye to eye; Mosiah 12 has one watchman and a room of men who cannot answer their own question.

links.note: The one thing to record here is the pointing. The KJV reads 'shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing'; the 1830 reads 'shall lift up the voice with the voice; together shall they sing'. Not a word differs — the semicolon has moved one phrase to the left, and the sense moves with it: the KJV's watchmen sing together with one voice, the 1830's lift up the voice with the voice and then sing. Since 1830 punctuation is the compositor's as much as anyone's, this is recorded as a variant of the printed text rather than an argument about the source, but it is the kind of thing a verbatim block is for.

pericopes.text: Break forth into joy; sing together ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the Lord hath comforted his people; he hath redeemed Jerusalem.

links.text: Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the LORD hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “waste places of Jerusalem” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:9. The 1830 text reproduces the verse word for word.
provenance.significance: Jerusalem is a waste place in this verse, and the men quoting it are the descendants of a colony that left Jerusalem before it was one. The comfort and redemption Isaiah announces are addressed to ruins that Noah's court has never seen; what it is being read to is a court that is about to become one.

links.note: Word-for-word with the KJV, including the KJV singleton at its centre. Recorded verse by verse rather than as a single block so that each departure — here, none — is visible where it occurs.
