pericopes.text: yea, even so he shall be led, crucified, and slain, the flesh becoming subject even unto death, the will of the Son being swallowed up in the will of the Father;

links.text: I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.

provenance.other: “The will of the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “Swallowed up in victory” occurs in exactly one, 1 Corinthians 15:54; the KJV uses “swallowed up” fourteen times, and Paul's is the only occurrence in which what is swallowed is defeated rather than destroyed.
provenance.significance: Abinadi needs a formula for a will that is absorbed rather than overruled, because his whole Christology depends on the Son not being a second person who submits to a first. He builds it from two KJV singletons at once: John 5:30's “the will of the Father”, the one verse where Jesus states the subordination, and Paul's “swallowed up”, the one verb in the KJV for a thing that ends by being absorbed into a greater thing. Recover 1 Corinthians 15:54 and what is swallowed up there is death, three verses before Paul's “O death, where is thy sting?” — which is the doctrine Mosiah 15:8 states in the next clause. The metaphor and its object have been swapped: Paul swallows death in victory, Abinadi swallows the Son's will in the Father's, and then gets Paul's result anyway.

links.note: “The will of the Son being swallowed up in the will of the Father.” Both halves come from KJV singletons and neither is used for what its source uses it for. Recorded at moderate because the two phrases are short and the construction is the Book of Mormon's own; what argues for the borrowing is that both singletons appear in one clause, and that the verse immediately following puts Paul's actual object — death, and the victory over it — back where Paul had it.

pericopes.text: and thus God breaketh the bands of death; having gained the victory over death; giving the Son power to make intercession for the children of men;

links.text: So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

provenance.other: “Swallowed up in victory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 1 Corinthians 15:57 supplies the other half, “thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory”.
provenance.alternative: Victory over death is the commonest Christian commonplace there is and needs no verse; “the bands of death” is in no KJV verse at all and is the Book of Mormon's own phrase.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 15 is the chapter Mosiah 15:20-25 will run on at length — the resurrection, its order, those who are Christ's at his coming — and 15:8 is where it enters. Note what the Book of Mormon does not borrow. Paul's death is swallowed up in victory; Abinadi's God gains the victory over death, which puts an agent where Paul has a passive, and then makes that agent the one who breaks the bands. The phrase “the bands of death” has no KJV source and becomes this chapter's own formula, used three times in sixteen verses (15:8, 15:9, 15:23).

links.note: “Thus God breaketh the bands of death; having gained the victory over death.” The victory is Paul's, from the KJV's one “swallowed up in victory” and its sequel at 15:57; the bands are the Book of Mormon's, occurring in no KJV verse. Recorded at moderate for that reason — half the sentence has a source and half does not. What follows in the same verse, the Son given “power to make intercession”, is Isaiah 53:12's by way of Mosiah 14:12; see the second link at this verse.

links.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

provenance.other: “made intercession for the transgressors” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “Make intercession” occurs in three KJV verses: twice in Jeremiah, of praying for a people God will not hear, and once at Hebrews 7:25, of Christ who “ever liveth to make intercession for them”. Isaiah 53:12 has the participial “made intercession for the transgressors”.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15 is an exposition of Mosiah 14, and Mosiah 14 is Isaiah 53 transcribed. So the question at every re-quotation in this chapter is whether the proximate model is the KJV of Isaiah or the Book of Mormon's own copy of it made twenty verses earlier, and twice the text answers it: at 15:6 the verb is “opened”, which is Mosiah 14:7's departure from the KJV's “openeth”, and at 15:12 the sins he has borne are plural, which is Mosiah 14:12's departure from the KJV's “the sin of many”. Neither reading is available from Isaiah. That is as clean a demonstration of OT-via-earlier-BoM as the corpus offers, and it licenses reading the rest of the chapter's Isaiah 53 material the same way. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Isaiah 53:12 here, and the reference is right; what the catalogue adds is the route. Note also the change of object: Isaiah's servant makes intercession for the transgressors, Mosiah 14:12 reproduces that, and Mosiah 15:8 widens it to “the children of men”. The intercession stops being for a class and becomes for a species, which is the same universalizing move 15:28 makes with “every nation, kindred, tongue, and people”.

links.note: “Giving the Son power to make intercession for the children of men.” The verb phrase is Isaiah 53:12's, which Abinadi has recited verbatim at 14:12 twenty-four verses earlier, and the exposition is now unpacking that recitation clause by clause: 15:8 takes the intercession, 15:9 the bearing of iniquity, 15:10 the offering for sin and the seed, 15:12 the sins borne. The one addition is “power”, which turns Isaiah's completed act into a delegated capacity and makes the Son's intercession a thing the Father grants — the same subordination 15:2 and 15:7 are working out.

pericopes.text: having ascended into heaven; having the bowels of mercy; being filled with compassion toward the children of men; standing betwixt them and justice; having broken the bands of death, taken upon himself their iniquity and their transgressions; having redeemed them, and satisfied the demands of justice.

links.text: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.

provenance.other: Mosiah 14:5 reproduces Isaiah 53:5 word for word (“wounded for our transgressions … bruised for our iniquities”); Mosiah 14:11 reproduces Isaiah 53:11's “he shall bear their iniquities”. Mosiah 15:9's “taken upon himself their iniquity and their transgressions” pairs the two nouns and no KJV verse pairs them in that order.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15 is an exposition of Mosiah 14, and Mosiah 14 is Isaiah 53 transcribed. So the question at every re-quotation in this chapter is whether the proximate model is the KJV of Isaiah or the Book of Mormon's own copy of it made twenty verses earlier, and twice the text answers it: at 15:6 the verb is “opened”, which is Mosiah 14:7's departure from the KJV's “openeth”, and at 15:12 the sins he has borne are plural, which is Mosiah 14:12's departure from the KJV's “the sin of many”. Neither reading is available from Isaiah. That is as clean a demonstration of OT-via-earlier-BoM as the corpus offers, and it licenses reading the rest of the chapter's Isaiah 53 material the same way. Hardy's apparatus points to Isaiah 53:5 here. The verbal case is thin on its own — one noun pair — and it is strong in context, because 15:9 is a summary of what Abinadi has just read aloud and pairs precisely the two nouns Isaiah 53:5 pairs. What the exposition changes is voice: Isaiah's servant is wounded and bruised, passively, and bears iniquities as a burden laid on him; Abinadi's Christ takes them upon himself. The whole chapter runs that conversion, from 15:5's “suffereth himself” onward.

links.note: “Standing betwixt them and justice; having broken the bands of death, taken upon himself their iniquity and their transgressions.” No phrase of Isaiah 53:5 is reproduced, so this is catalogued on the pairing rather than on wording, and kjvSpecific is 'uncertain' accordingly. What makes it more than a commonplace is its position: it is the fourth clause of a summary that has already taken the intercession from 53:12 and will take the offering and the seed from 53:10 in the next verse, and it uses 53:5's two nouns and no others.

links.text: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;

provenance.other: “Bowels of mercies” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV's other affective uses of the word are Philippians 1:8, 2:1 and 1 John 3:17.
provenance.alternative: “Bowels of mercy” may simply be the period's ordinary devotional idiom, and Luke 1:78's “tender mercy of our God” is the nearer thing in sense.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one “bowels of mercies” is a garment: Paul tells the Colossians to put it on, along with kindness and meekness, as the elect of God. Mosiah 15:9 makes it a possession of the ascended Christ — “having the bowels of mercy” — in a list of participles describing what he has, not what anyone should wear. The borrowing moves an imperative addressed to a congregation into a description of the God it is addressed to, which is a small instance of what this whole chapter does with Isaiah 53's servant.

links.note: “Having ascended into heaven; having the bowels of mercy; being filled with compassion.” The phrase is a KJV singleton, singular where Paul is plural, and recorded as an echo because nothing else in the clause is Paul's and because the idiom was ordinary devotional English by 1829. It earns a row because the whole verse is a chain of participles and this is the only one with a KJV phrase behind it.

pericopes.text: And now I say unto you, Who shall declare his generation? Behold, I say unto you, that when his soul has been made an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. And now what say ye? And who shall be his seed?

links.text: Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand.

provenance.other: “Who shall declare his generation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 53:8 and Acts 8:33 (Philip reading it to the Ethiopian). tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive point between them: Mosiah 15:10 quotes only the four words the two verses share.
provenance.alternative: The wording cannot rule out a direct return to Isaiah 53 in the KJV, since Mosiah 14:8 and 14:10 reproduce those clauses without departure. The route is argued from 15:6 and 15:12, where the Book of Mormon's own departures do recur.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15 is an exposition of Mosiah 14, and Mosiah 14 is Isaiah 53 transcribed. So the question at every re-quotation in this chapter is whether the proximate model is the KJV of Isaiah or the Book of Mormon's own copy of it made twenty verses earlier, and twice the text answers it: at 15:6 the verb is “opened”, which is Mosiah 14:7's departure from the KJV's “openeth”, and at 15:12 the sins he has borne are plural, which is Mosiah 14:12's departure from the KJV's “the sin of many”. Neither reading is available from Isaiah. That is as clean a demonstration of OT-via-earlier-BoM as the corpus offers, and it licenses reading the rest of the chapter's Isaiah 53 material the same way. There is a further reason to notice the Acts 8:33 half of the rarity count. The KJV's only other “who shall declare his generation” is the verse an evangelist reads aloud to a stranger who asks “of whom speaketh the prophet this?” — which is, word for word, the question Abinadi puts to the priests: “And now what say ye? And who shall be his seed?” Acts 8 and Mosiah 15 are the two scenes in scripture where Isaiah 53:8 is read out and someone is asked to identify its subject, and both answer by naming a people rather than only a person.

links.note: “Who shall declare his generation? … when his soul has been made an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. And now what say ye? And who shall be his seed?” Nine words from Isaiah 53:10 continuous and four from 53:8, both of which Abinadi has read aloud as Mosiah 14:8 and 14:10. The verse is the hinge of the chapter: it takes Isaiah's promise that the servant shall see his seed, turns it into a question, and spends 15:11-13 answering it — the seed are the prophets and those who heard them. The 1830 “when his soul has been made an offering for sin” recasts Isaiah's second person (“when thou shalt make his soul an offering”) as a passive, which removes the Father as the agent of the offering at exactly the point where the chapter is arguing that the Father and the Son are one.

pericopes.text: Behold I say unto you, that whosoever hath heard the words of the prophets, yea, all the Holy Prophets which have prophesied concerning the coming of the Lord; I say unto, that all those who hath hearkened unto their words, and believed that the Lord would redeem his people, and have looked forward to that day for a remission of their sins; I say unto you, that these are his seed, or they are heirs of the Kingdom of God:
for these are they whose sins he hath borne; these are they for whom he hath died, to redeem them from their transgressions. And now, are they not his seed?

links.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

provenance.other: “he bare the sin of many” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV of Isaiah 53:12 reads “he bare the sin of many”, singular. Mosiah 14:12, transcribing it, reads “the sins of many”. Mosiah 15:12 reads “whose sins he hath borne”, plural.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15 is an exposition of Mosiah 14, and Mosiah 14 is Isaiah 53 transcribed. So the question at every re-quotation in this chapter is whether the proximate model is the KJV of Isaiah or the Book of Mormon's own copy of it made twenty verses earlier, and twice the text answers it: at 15:6 the verb is “opened”, which is Mosiah 14:7's departure from the KJV's “openeth”, and at 15:12 the sins he has borne are plural, which is Mosiah 14:12's departure from the KJV's “the sin of many”. Neither reading is available from Isaiah. That is as clean a demonstration of OT-via-earlier-BoM as the corpus offers, and it licenses reading the rest of the chapter's Isaiah 53 material the same way.

links.note: “For these are they whose sins he hath borne.” The second of the chapter's two decisive readings for the route. Isaiah's KJV has the singular “sin of many”; the Book of Mormon's own transcription pluralized it at 14:12; and the exposition here has the plural. One such agreement could be chance, since a preacher pluralizing “sin” is unremarkable — but the same pattern holds at 15:6 with “opened” for “openeth”, and two independent departures reproduced in the same exposition are what an argument from the Book of Mormon's own text rather than the Bible's looks like.

pericopes.text: Yea, and are not the prophets, every one that has opened his mouth to prophesy, that has not fallen into transgression; I mean all the Holy Prophets ever since the world began; I say unto you that they are his seed;
and these are they which hath published peace, that hath brought good tidings of good, that hath published salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

links.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.other: “that publisheth salvation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The second half of Isaiah 52:7, sixteen words, reproduced with the verbs moved into the perfect. tools/mediation-check.py at 15:18 returns two decisive points against Romans 10:15, the New Testament's quotation of this verse, and one against Nahum 1:15, its Old Testament double.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15:14-18 is not a quotation of Isaiah 52:7 but a five-fold conjugation of it, and the tenses are the argument. 15:14 gives Isaiah's predicates in the past — the prophets “hath published peace … hath published salvation”; 15:15 gives the exclamation in the past, “how beautiful … were their feet”; 15:16 in the present, “those that are still publishing peace”; 15:17 in the future, “those who shall hereafter publish peace, yea, from this time henceforth and forever”; and 15:18 collapses the plural back into Isaiah's singular “him that bringeth good tidings” and identifies him as the Lord. Isaiah's verse has one set of feet on the mountains; Abinadi runs it through every tense and then gives it a subject. The exegetical move is the same one 15:10-13 makes with “his seed”: take a singular figure out of Isaiah, distribute him across the prophets, and gather him back.

links.note: “These are they which hath published peace, that hath brought good tidings of good, that hath published salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!” Isaiah's participles — publisheth, bringeth, publisheth, saith — become perfects, and the change is the whole exegesis: Isaiah's herald is on the mountain now, and Abinadi's heralds are the prophets who have already spoken. The 1830 is worth reading here for its grammar, which 1920 corrected at six points in one verse (“which hath published” → “who have published”, three times over, and “that saith” → “and said”); the first edition's singular verbs after a plural subject preserve Isaiah's own singular participles under a plural antecedent, and the modern text's tidying erases the seam.

pericopes.text: And O how beautiful upon the mountains were their feet!

links.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.other: “Beautiful upon the mountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15:14-18 is not a quotation of Isaiah 52:7 but a five-fold conjugation of it, and the tenses are the argument. 15:14 gives Isaiah's predicates in the past — the prophets “hath published peace … hath published salvation”; 15:15 gives the exclamation in the past, “how beautiful … were their feet”; 15:16 in the present, “those that are still publishing peace”; 15:17 in the future, “those who shall hereafter publish peace, yea, from this time henceforth and forever”; and 15:18 collapses the plural back into Isaiah's singular “him that bringeth good tidings” and identifies him as the Lord. Isaiah's verse has one set of feet on the mountains; Abinadi runs it through every tense and then gives it a subject. The exegetical move is the same one 15:10-13 makes with “his seed”: take a singular figure out of Isaiah, distribute him across the prophets, and gather him back.

links.note: “And O how beautiful upon the mountains were their feet!” Isaiah's opening exclamation, five words verbatim, with two changes that are the argument: the verb goes into the past and the feet become plural and possessed. Isaiah has one messenger and a timeless present; Abinadi has the prophets of 15:11-13, dead and identified as the servant's seed, and their feet were beautiful. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Isaiah 52:7 at this verse and at 15:18, which are the first and last of the chapter's five.

pericopes.text: And again: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those that are still publishing peace!

links.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.other: “beautiful upon the mountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Nine words continuous, “how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of”, which is Isaiah 52:7's opening exactly; Nahum 1:15 begins “Behold upon the mountains the feet of” and has neither “how beautiful” nor “are”.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15:14-18 is not a quotation of Isaiah 52:7 but a five-fold conjugation of it, and the tenses are the argument. 15:14 gives Isaiah's predicates in the past — the prophets “hath published peace … hath published salvation”; 15:15 gives the exclamation in the past, “how beautiful … were their feet”; 15:16 in the present, “those that are still publishing peace”; 15:17 in the future, “those who shall hereafter publish peace, yea, from this time henceforth and forever”; and 15:18 collapses the plural back into Isaiah's singular “him that bringeth good tidings” and identifies him as the Lord. Isaiah's verse has one set of feet on the mountains; Abinadi runs it through every tense and then gives it a subject. The exegetical move is the same one 15:10-13 makes with “his seed”: take a singular figure out of Isaiah, distribute him across the prophets, and gather him back.

links.note: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those that are still publishing peace!” The third conjugation, and the only one in Isaiah's own present tense — which is why it is the one that reads most like a quotation and does the least work. Its addition is “still”, a word with no counterpart in Isaiah and no KJV parallel, doing the whole job of turning a prophetic exclamation into a claim about Abinadi's own moment: there are people publishing peace now, and he is one of them.

pericopes.text: And again: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who shall hereafter publish peace, yea, from this time henceforth and forever!

links.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.other: “beautiful upon the mountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The same nine-word opening as 15:16. “From this time forth and for evermore” is the KJV's formula (Psalm 113:2, Isaiah 9:7, Micah 4:7); Mosiah 15:17 has “from this time henceforth and forever”, which is in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15:14-18 is not a quotation of Isaiah 52:7 but a five-fold conjugation of it, and the tenses are the argument. 15:14 gives Isaiah's predicates in the past — the prophets “hath published peace … hath published salvation”; 15:15 gives the exclamation in the past, “how beautiful … were their feet”; 15:16 in the present, “those that are still publishing peace”; 15:17 in the future, “those who shall hereafter publish peace, yea, from this time henceforth and forever”; and 15:18 collapses the plural back into Isaiah's singular “him that bringeth good tidings” and identifies him as the Lord. Isaiah's verse has one set of feet on the mountains; Abinadi runs it through every tense and then gives it a subject. The exegetical move is the same one 15:10-13 makes with “his seed”: take a singular figure out of Isaiah, distribute him across the prophets, and gather him back.

links.note: “The feet of those who shall hereafter publish peace, yea, from this time henceforth and forever!” The fourth conjugation, in the future, and the one that completes the temporal sweep begun at 15:14. The closing formula is a near-miss on a KJV set phrase — the KJV says “from this time forth and for evermore” — which is the kind of variation that tells against a text being copied and for a text being composed by someone who has the King James cadence by ear. Recorded here rather than argued; the catalogue's business at this verse is the tense.

pericopes.text: And behold, I say unto you, this is not all: For O how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that is the founder of peace; yea, even the Lord, who hath redeemed his people; yea, him who hath granted salvation unto his people:

links.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.other: “beautiful upon the mountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Fifteen words continuous. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Isaiah 52:7 over Romans 10:15 — Romans opens “And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written”, which is absent, and reads “bring glad tidings of good things” where Isaiah and Mosiah read “bringeth good tidings” — and one decisive point over Nahum 1:15, whose verse begins “Behold” where Isaiah and Mosiah have “How beautiful”. Romans also drops “upon the mountains” entirely, which Mosiah 15:18 keeps.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15:14-18 is not a quotation of Isaiah 52:7 but a five-fold conjugation of it, and the tenses are the argument. 15:14 gives Isaiah's predicates in the past — the prophets “hath published peace … hath published salvation”; 15:15 gives the exclamation in the past, “how beautiful … were their feet”; 15:16 in the present, “those that are still publishing peace”; 15:17 in the future, “those who shall hereafter publish peace, yea, from this time henceforth and forever”; and 15:18 collapses the plural back into Isaiah's singular “him that bringeth good tidings” and identifies him as the Lord. Isaiah's verse has one set of feet on the mountains; Abinadi runs it through every tense and then gives it a subject. The exegetical move is the same one 15:10-13 makes with “his seed”: take a singular figure out of Isaiah, distribute him across the prophets, and gather him back. And this is the corpus's clearest case of the Book of Mormon taking an Old Testament verse in its Old Testament form when a New Testament form was available. Isaiah 52:7 is quoted at Romans 10:15 and echoed at Nahum 1:15, and the mediation test excludes both. The catalogue's usual result at a shared text is the opposite — 1 Nephi 22:20 has Acts's Deuteronomy 18, 1 Nephi 4:13 has John's Caiaphas — so a decisive direct-OT reading is worth recording as such.

links.note: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that is the founder of peace; yea, even the Lord, who hath redeemed his people.” The fifth and last conjugation returns to Isaiah's singular and answers the question the other four have been raising: whose feet? The one substitution is the point. Isaiah's herald “publisheth peace”; Abinadi's “is the founder of peace”, a phrase in no KJV verse, and the sentence then names him — the Lord. A messenger who announces peace has been replaced by the one who makes it, and the four preceding verses have distributed the office among the prophets precisely so that this verse can take it back.

pericopes.text: for were it not for the redemption which he hath made for his people, which was prepared from the foundation of the world; I say unto you, were it not for this, that all mankind must have perished.

links.text: Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:

provenance.other: “From the foundation of the world” occurs in exactly six KJV verses; “prepared for you from the foundation of the world” occurs in exactly one, and it is the only one in which something is prepared.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 13:8's Lamb “slain from the foundation of the world” is nearer in subject — a redemption fixed before time — and shares the same six-word tail.
provenance.significance: Two KJV verses put redemption before the creation, and they divide the doctrine between them: Revelation 13:8 has the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, Matthew 25:34 has the kingdom prepared from it. Mosiah 15:19 says “the redemption which he hath made for his people, which was prepared from the foundation of the world”, and takes the verb from Matthew and the object from Revelation. The result is a sentence neither verse contains, and it is the Book of Mormon's standing formula thereafter — the plan prepared, not merely the death foreseen.

links.note: “The redemption which he hath made for his people, which was prepared from the foundation of the world.” Recorded as an echo: the six-word tail is common to six KJV verses and the distinguishing word, “prepared”, is Matthew 25:34's, where what is prepared is a kingdom rather than a redemption. Kept because the combination is not available from any single verse and because Matthew 25 supplies the only KJV instance of the verb in this formula.

pericopes.text: But behold, the bands of death shall be broken, and the Son reigneth, and hath power over the dead; therefore, he bringeth to pass the resurrection of the dead.

And there cometh a resurrection, even a first resurrection; yea, even a resurrection of those that have been, and which are, and which shall be, even until the rssurrection of Christ: for so shall he be called.

And now, the resurrection of all the prophets, and all those that have believed in their words, or all those that have kept the commandments of God, these shall come forth in the first resurrection; therefore, they are the first resurrection.
They are raised to dwell with God, who hath redeemed them: thus they have eternal life through Christ, who hath broken the bands of death.

links.text: For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

provenance.other: “Eternal life through Jesus Christ” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Romans 6:23 sets eternal life against the wages of sin, which is death, and Mosiah 15:23 sets it against the bands of death which Christ has broken — the same antithesis with the same two terms, arriving in the same clause. The Book of Mormon's variation, “through Christ” for “through Jesus Christ our Lord”, is the abbreviation a text speaking six centuries before the name would need, and it is the sort of adjustment that shows the source has been handled rather than merely met.

links.note: “Thus they have eternal life through Christ, who hath broken the bands of death.” The formula is a KJV singleton in Paul's fuller form, and the verse it comes from is the KJV's one place where eternal life and death are set against each other as wage and gift. Recorded at moderate: four words, and “eternal life through Christ” is a phrase any nineteenth-century preacher had by heart. What raises it is the immediate company of death in the same sentence, which is Romans 6:23's own structure.

pericopes.text: And there are those who have part in the first resurrection; and these are they that have died before Christ came, in their ignorance, not having salvation declared unto them. And thus the Lord bringeth about the restoration of these; and they have a part in the first resurrection, or hath eternal life, being redeemed by the Lord.

links.text: Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years.

provenance.other: “Part in the first resurrection” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “The first resurrection” occurs in exactly two, Revelation 20:5 and 20:6, and nowhere else in the Bible.
provenance.significance: The doctrine of a first resurrection exists in the KJV in two verses of Revelation 20 and in no other book, so a text that organizes its eschatology around it is working from that page. Mosiah 15:21-26 uses the phrase five times in six verses and does something Revelation does not: it asks who is in it and answers by category — the prophets, those who believed their words, those who kept the commandments, those who died in ignorance, and little children — and then names who is excluded. John's first resurrection is a chronological fact about martyrs; Abinadi's is a roster, and the roster is built to answer the question 15:10 raised about the servant's seed. The phrase from Revelation is doing the work Isaiah 53:10 started.

links.note: “And there are those who have part in the first resurrection.” Five words from a KJV singleton, and the whole passage 15:21-26 turns on the two verses of Revelation 20 where “the first resurrection” exists at all. Adjudicated here rather than at 15:21 because this is where the KJV's exact phrase appears; the recurrences are recorded. The 1830 “or hath eternal life” was corrected to “have” in 1920, one of eight such number corrections in this chapter.

pericopes.text: And little children also, hath eternal life.

But behold, and fear, and tremble before God; for ye had ought to tremble: for the Lord redeemeth none such that rebelleth against him, and dieth in their sins; yea, even all those that have perished in their sins ever since the world began, that have wilfully rebelled against God, that have known the commandments of God, and would not keep them; these are they that have no part in the first resurrection.

links.text: I said therefore unto you, that ye shall die in your sins: for if ye believe not that I am he, ye shall die in your sins.

provenance.other: “Die in your sins” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 8:21 and 8:24, and the second has it twice. The third-person form Mosiah 15:26 uses — dying in their sins — occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 3:19 and 18:24, “he shall die in his iniquity”, are the Old Testament's version of the sentence and are closer in grammatical person.
provenance.significance: John 8's formula is a second-person threat delivered to hearers who are present: “ye shall seek me, and shall die in your sins: whither I go, ye cannot come.” Abinadi converts it to the third person and applies it to a class — “all those that have perished in their sins ever since the world began” — which is what he has done throughout the chapter with singular figures, at 15:10-13 with the servant's seed and at 15:14-17 with Isaiah's herald. Note that the conversion runs the opposite way from 13:32's, where a third-person KJV phrase stayed third-person because the referent was the fathers. Here a second-person phrase is made general, and the priests standing in front of him are left to place themselves in it.

links.note: “For the Lord redeemeth none such that rebelleth against him, and dieth in their sins.” The idiom is John 8's, where it occurs three times in four verses and nowhere else in the KJV, and the Book of Mormon has it in a person the KJV never uses. Recorded at moderate because the clause is short and Ezekiel offers a real alternative in the correct person; what favours John is the collocation with rebellion against a person who is standing there, which is John 8's situation exactly. The 1830's singular verbs, “rebelleth … dieth” under a plural “none such”, were regularized in 1920.

pericopes.text: Therefore, had ye not ought to tremble? For salvation cometh to none such; for the Lord hath redeemed none such; yea, neither can the Lord redeem such: for he cannot deny himself; for he cannot deny justice when it hath its claim.

links.text: If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.

provenance.other: “He cannot deny himself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Paul's clause is a promise: if we believe not, yet he abideth faithful, he cannot deny himself — the inability is God's inability to fail those who fail him. Mosiah 15:27 uses the same four words as a threat, and doubles them: “he cannot deny himself; for he cannot deny justice when it hath its claim.” The impossibility that guarantees mercy in 2 Timothy guarantees condemnation here, from the same premise, that God's nature constrains his acts. This is the metaleptic case at its cleanest — nothing in Mosiah 15:27 signals the reversal, and a reader who recovers 2 Timothy 2:13 finds the verse's comfort turned inside out.

links.note: “For he cannot deny himself; for he cannot deny justice when it hath its claim.” Four words reproduced exactly from the KJV's only occurrence, and then repeated with a new object that Paul does not have. Catalogued as a quotation on the CONVENTIONS §2 rule rather than on length — well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations — because a whole clause is reproduced from a verse that is its unmistakable source. Note that the argument the clause serves is the reverse of Paul's; see the significance field.

pericopes.text: And now I say unto you, that the time shall come that the salvation of the Lord shall be declared to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.

links.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

provenance.other: “Every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; the shorter “kindred, and tongue, and people” occurs in exactly two, Revelation 5:9 and 14:6.
provenance.significance: The four-term formula belongs to Revelation and to nothing else in the Bible, and Revelation 14:6 is the verse where it is the object of a preaching — an angel with the everlasting gospel to preach to every nation, kindred, tongue and people. That is precisely what Mosiah 15:28 predicts: “the time shall come that the salvation of the Lord shall be declared to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.” The Book of Mormon takes John's audience-formula together with John's verb, and the phrase becomes one of the corpus's own formulas thereafter.

links.note: “The salvation of the Lord shall be declared to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.” A KJV singleton reproduced with the conjunctions thinned — Revelation repeats “and” before each term, the Book of Mormon keeps only the last — which is the ordinary compression of a list said aloud rather than read. Its placement is worth noting: the universal proclamation arrives immediately after the chapter's harshest verse about those who cannot be redeemed, and immediately before the three verses of Isaiah 52:8-10 that close the chapter with the ends of the earth seeing the salvation of God. Abinadi's structure and Revelation 14's are the same, judgment then a herald to all nations.

pericopes.text: Yea, Lord, thy watchmen shall lift up their voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord shall bring again Zion.

links.text: Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice; with the voice together shall they sing: for they shall see eye to eye, when the LORD shall bring again Zion.

provenance.other: “See eye to eye” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “bring again Zion” occurs in exactly one; both are Isaiah 52:8. The one departure, “lift up their voice” for the KJV's “lift up the voice”, matches no KJV verse — the KJV's “lift up their voice” is Isaiah 24:14 and Isaiah 42:11, neither of which has watchmen.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 15:29-31 transcribes Isaiah 52:8-10 continuously, which is the second block of Isaiah in Abinadi's speech and the one nobody notices because chapter 14's is longer. Its placement is the finding. Abinadi has spent 15:14-18 on Isaiah 52:7 and now runs straight on into 52:8-10 — the verse he expounded and the verses that follow it, in order, as if he had the column in front of him. The chapter is built out of one page of Isaiah worked twice: 52:7 five times over as exegesis, then 52:8-10 as recitation.

links.note: Twenty-two words of Isaiah 52:8 with two departures. The vocative “Yea, Lord,” is prefixed, which turns Isaiah's address to Zion into an address to God and is the Book of Mormon's own; and “their voice” replaces “the voice”, a possessive that makes the watchmen's cry theirs rather than the cry. Both are small and both push the verse the same way, toward the human criers Abinadi has been identifying since 15:11 — the prophets, whose feet were beautiful, and who are the servant's seed.

pericopes.text: Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the Lord hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.

links.text: Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem: for the LORD hath comforted his people, he hath redeemed Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “Waste places of Jerusalem” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Isaiah 49:13 shares the clause “for the LORD hath comforted his people” and nothing else in this verse.
provenance.significance: The middle verse of a three-verse transcription, and the only one with no departure at all. That is worth recording for its own sake: the chapter that has just spent five verses conjugating Isaiah 52:7 through every tense reproduces 52:9 without touching a word. The distinction the catalogue is drawing throughout Abinadi's speech — between the verses he expounds and the verses he recites — is visible in the collation itself.

links.note: Isaiah 52:9 word for word, twenty-two words, the only unaltered verse in the chapter. Its subject is the redemption of Jerusalem, and it stands here between the watchmen of 52:8 and the holy arm of 52:10 exactly as it stands in Isaiah. Note what the Book of Mormon does not do with it: nothing. Where Abinadi has an argument he alters the wording (15:6, 15:14-18, 15:29); where he is reciting, he does not.

pericopes.text: The Lord hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations: and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.

links.text: The LORD hath made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.

provenance.other: “Made bare his holy arm” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “all the ends of the earth shall see” occurs in exactly one; both are Isaiah 52:10. “The salvation of our God” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 52:10 and Psalm 98:3, which reads “have seen” for “shall see”; Luke 3:6 has “all flesh shall see the salvation of God”.
provenance.significance: A twenty-nine-word run with a semicolon changed to a colon and nothing else, and it closes the chapter by answering it. Abinadi began at 15:1 with a God who would come down among the children of men; he ends with the ends of the earth seeing the salvation of our God. The verse also decides its own mediation without difficulty: Psalm 98:3 has the past tense, Luke 3:6 drops the arm and the nations and reads “all flesh”, and the Book of Mormon has Isaiah's future and Isaiah's full sentence. Isaiah 52:10 is one of this catalogue's most-used verses — it is already linked at 1 Nephi 19:17, 1 Nephi 22:11 and Enos 1:13 — and it re-enters here inside a continuous transcription rather than as a formula.

links.note: Isaiah 52:10 entire, twenty-nine words, the longest unbroken KJV run in Mosiah 15 and the third verse of the block begun at 15:29. Its two rare phrases are both KJV singletons. Neither Psalm 98:3 nor Luke 3:6, the KJV's two other approaches to the sentence, has the tense or the arm; the Book of Mormon has Isaiah's. Mosiah 16:1 will pick this same verse up again in Abinadi's own voice — “when all shall see the salvation of the Lord” — which is where the transcription stops and the preaching resumes.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that after Abinadi had spoken these words, he stretched forth his hand and said, The time shall come when all shall see the salvation of the Lord; when every nation, kindred, tongue and people, shall see eye to eye, and shall confess before God that his judgments are just;

links.text: And I heard another out of the altar say, Even so, Lord God Almighty, true and righteous are thy judgments.

provenance.route: Revelation 16:7 and Romans 14:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “righteous are thy judgments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “confess to God” occurs in exactly one; the two are Revelation 16:7 and Romans 14:11.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 19:2 has “true and righteous are his judgments” in the third person, which is Mosiah 16:1's person; and Revelation 15:4, “for thy judgments are made manifest”, is the verse that pairs the vindication of God's judgments with all nations coming to worship.
provenance.significance: Abinadi's last sentence is built out of the two KJV verses in which a creature acknowledges that God's judgments are right, and it puts the acknowledgement in the mouth of the audience formula he used at 15:28. Romans 14:11 supplies the confessing — every tongue shall confess to God, which Paul is quoting from Isaiah 45:23 as proof that all shall stand before the judgment seat — and Revelation 16:7 supplies what is confessed, that the judgments are righteous, spoken from under the altar after the third vial. Both are universal-acknowledgement verses and both concern a judgment already executed. What the Book of Mormon adds is the sight: the nations do not merely confess, they see eye to eye, which is Isaiah 52:8's phrase from the verse Abinadi transcribed twelve verses earlier.

links.note: “Every nation, kindred, tongue and people, shall see eye to eye, and shall confess before God that his judgments are just.” Three KJV strands in one clause, two of them singletons. The nation-formula is Revelation 14:6's, adjudicated at 15:28; “see eye to eye” is Isaiah 52:8's, transcribed at 15:29; and the confession is Romans 14:11's with Revelation 16:7's object. Recorded at moderate because none of the three is reproduced at length and the sentence is a compound of formulas Abinadi has already used — which is itself the finding, since 16:1 is the peroration and is assembled from the chapter he has just finished.

links.text: And Moses said unto the people, Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day: for the Egyptians whom ye have seen to day, ye shall see them again no more for ever.

provenance.other: “See the salvation of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 14:13 and 2 Chronicles 20:17, and both are a commander telling a terrified people to stand still and watch God fight. Isaiah 52:10, which Mosiah 15:31 has just transcribed, reads “the salvation of our God”.
provenance.significance: This is a small mediation finding and worth having. Mosiah 15:31 ends the previous chapter with Isaiah 52:10 verbatim — “all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God” — and one verse later Abinadi says it again in his own voice as “all shall see the salvation of the Lord”, which is not Isaiah's phrase but Exodus 14:13's. The switch is from the possessive to the divine name, and it moves the sentence from a prophecy about the nations to the formula Moses uses at the Red Sea and Jehoshaphat uses before a battle: stand still and see. Abinadi has spent two chapters as Moses (13:5) and is about to be killed; the last thing he tells his judges to expect is the sight Israel was told to expect when the sea opened.

links.note: “The time shall come when all shall see the salvation of the Lord.” Two KJV verses have the phrase and both are eve-of-deliverance speeches to a people who are about to watch rather than act. The interest is in the departure from the immediately preceding verse: Isaiah 52:10 at Mosiah 15:31 reads “the salvation of our God”, and Abinadi's own restatement one verse later takes the other KJV form. Recorded at moderate — five common words — but the substitution is real and it is visible only because the two verses are adjacent.

pericopes.text: and then shall the wicked be cast out, and they shall have cause to howl, and weep, and wail, and gnash their teeth; and this because they would not hearken unto the voice of the Lord; therefore the Lord redeemeth them not,

links.text: And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

provenance.other: “Wailing and gnashing of teeth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 13:42 and 13:50, both of the furnace of fire; the commoner “weeping and gnashing of teeth” is Matthew's elsewhere and Luke's. “Weep and howl” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joel 1:5 and James 5:1.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's list has four verbs where the KJV never has more than two, and it has taken one pair from each of the KJV's two formulas — “weep” and “gnash” from the Matthean furnace sayings, “howl” and “wail” from the prophetic and Jacobean woe-oracles. The result is a compound that exists in no verse and reads as though it existed in all of them. Note where Abinadi is standing when he says it: he has just been condemned by a king who will burn him (17:20), and the KJV's home for “wailing and gnashing of teeth” is a furnace of fire.

links.note: “They shall have cause to howl, and weep, and wail, and gnash their teeth.” A four-verb fusion of the KJV's two damnation formulas, neither reproduced whole. Recorded at moderate for that reason — no single verse is the source — and kept because every one of the four verbs is a KJV eschatological verb and the collocation of gnashing with weeping is Matthew's alone. The Book of Mormon's addition is the causal frame, “shall have cause to”, which converts a description of hell into a verdict about desert.

pericopes.text: for they are carnal and devlish, and the devil hath power over them; yea, even that old serpent that did beguile our first parents, which was the cause of their fall; which was the cause of all mankind becoming carnal, sensual, devlish, knowing evil from good, subjecting themselves to the devil.

links.text: And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.

provenance.route: Revelation 12:9 and 2 Corinthians 11:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “That old serpent” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 12:9 and 20:2, and both identify him as the Devil and Satan. “Beguiled Eve” occurs in exactly one, 2 Corinthians 11:3.
provenance.significance: Genesis never says the serpent of Eden was the devil. The identification is made in the KJV only in Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 — “that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan” — and the connection to Eden specifically is made only by Paul, who says the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty. Mosiah 16:3 asserts the whole doctrine in one clause and does it in the two sources' own words: “that old serpent that did beguile our first parents”. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 3:1-24 at this verse, which is where the story is; the wording is from the two New Testament passages that interpret it, and the catalogue puts the link where the wording is (CONVENTIONS §6a).

links.note: “Yea, even that old serpent that did beguile our first parents, which was the cause of their fall.” Two KJV phrases in eight words, from the only verses that make the identification the sentence depends on. Paul's verb is exactly reproduced with the object generalized — “beguiled Eve” becomes “beguile our first parents”, which brings Adam into a deception the New Testament pointedly assigns to Eve alone (1 Timothy 2:14 says Adam was not deceived). That generalization is not incidental: the next clause makes the fall the cause of all mankind becoming carnal, and a fall that runs through both parents is the one that can bear that weight.

links.text: This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.

provenance.other: “Earthly, sensual, devilish” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV uses “sensual” only twice, here and at Jude 19; “devilish” only here.
provenance.significance: The triad is James's and it is unique in the Bible — the one place the KJV puts those three adjectives in a row, describing a wisdom that does not descend from above. Mosiah 16:3 reproduces the sequence with the first term replaced: carnal, sensual, devilish. The substitution is the argument. James's “earthly” is a location, and the Book of Mormon's “carnal” is a nature, which is the word the verse has already used twice (“they are carnal and devilish”) and which lets the triad describe fallen humanity rather than a kind of counsel. The phrase becomes a fixed formula in the corpus, and this is where it enters.

links.note: “The cause of all mankind becoming carnal, sensual, devlish.” Two of three adjectives verbatim, in James's order, from a KJV singleton — and the 1830's spelling “devlish”, twice in this verse, is the compositor's rather than a reading, corrected in 1920. What James says of a wisdom, Abinadi says of a species. Note that the verse has already used the pair “carnal and devilish” at its opening, so the triad arrives as an expansion of Abinadi's own phrase into James's, which is why “carnal” rather than “earthly” heads it.

links.text: For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, then your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.

provenance.other: “Knowing good and evil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:5, the serpent's promise; Genesis 3:22 has “to know good and evil”. Mosiah 16:3 reads “knowing evil from good”.
provenance.significance: The serpent's promise in the KJV is that eating will make them “as gods, knowing good and evil”, and it is the one verse with that participle. Mosiah 16:3 reverses the terms and adds a preposition: “knowing evil from good”. The change turns a possession into a discrimination — not knowing both, but telling one from the other — and it turns the serpent's inducement into the fall's result, since in Mosiah's sentence the knowledge stands in a list with becoming carnal and subjecting oneself to the devil. Hardy's apparatus points to Genesis 3:1-24 for the verse as a whole, and this participle is the only phrase in it that is actually Genesis's.

links.note: “Knowing evil from good, subjecting themselves to the devil.” The participle is Genesis 3:5's, in the KJV's only occurrence, with the nouns inverted and “from” inserted. Recorded at moderate: three words, and the inversion is the kind a writer makes without a text open. It is kept because it discharges Hardy's Genesis 3 cross-reference at the point where wording actually exists, and because the rest of the verse's language is demonstrably from Revelation 12, 2 Corinthians 11 and James 3 rather than from Genesis at all — which is the finding worth having about this verse.

pericopes.text: Thus all mankind were lost; and behold, they would have been endlessly lost, were it not that God redeemed his people from their lost and fallen state.

But remember, that he that persists in his own carnal nature, and goes on in the ways of sin and rebellion against God, he remaineth in his fallen state, and the devil hath all power over him. Therefore he is as though there was no redemption made; being an enemy to God; and also is the devil an enemy to God.

links.text: Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.

provenance.other: “The carnal mind is enmity against God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The formula “the enemy of God” is James 4:4's, in the KJV's only verse making a person rather than a disposition God's enemy.
provenance.significance: Romans 8:7 is the KJV's one statement that the carnal is at enmity with God, and it gives a reason: “for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.” Mosiah 16:5 states the same doctrine and keeps the same structure — a man who persists in his carnal nature remains fallen and is an enemy to God — and then adds a sentence Paul does not have: “and also is the devil an enemy to God.” The addition puts the carnal man and the devil in one category, which is what 16:3 has just prepared by making the fall the devil's work and its result a carnal nature. Where Paul has an incapacity, Abinadi has an allegiance.

links.note: “He that persists in his own carnal nature … being an enemy to God; and also is the devil an enemy to God.” No clause is reproduced, so this is proposed on the doctrine and its vocabulary: “carnal” with “enemy/enmity” and God, which the KJV brings together in exactly one verse. James 4:4 supplies the noun in the form the Book of Mormon uses, “the enemy of God”, where Paul has the abstract “enmity”. Recorded at moderate; a reader who wants a verbal source will not find one here, and the case is that both of the KJV's two ways of saying this are present in one sentence.

pericopes.text: And now if Christ had not come into the world, speaking of things to come, as though they had already come, there could have been no redemption.
And if Christ had not risen from the dead, or have broken the bands of death, that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting, there could have been no resurrection.

links.text: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?

provenance.other: “O grave, where is thy victory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The King James text pairs the two nouns in a particular way — sting with death, victory with the grave — and Mosiah 16:7 keeps both pairings intact: “that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting”.
provenance.significance: This is a strong case for kjvSpecific because the pairing is a feature of the King James text rather than of the doctrine. Paul's rhetorical questions could be assigned either way round, and the Book of Mormon does not assign them either way round: it gives the grave the victory and death the sting, exactly as the KJV prints them, and in the KJV's own order of clauses reversed to put the grave first. A writer paraphrasing the doctrine of resurrection from memory would have no reason to keep the nouns attached to those particular predicates; a writer with the KJV's two questions in his ear would find it hard not to.

links.note: “If Christ had not risen from the dead, or have broken the bands of death, that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting, there could have been no resurrection.” Paul's two questions turned into two counterfactual clauses with the noun pairings preserved. “The bands of death” is this speech's own formula (15:8, 15:9, 15:23) and has no KJV source; everything else in the sentence is 1 Corinthians 15:55-56. Note the argumentative direction: Paul's questions are a taunt after the victory, and Abinadi's clauses are conditions before it — the same words used to say what would have failed rather than what has been overcome.

pericopes.text: But there is a resurrection, therefore the grave hath no victory, and the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ:

links.text: So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

provenance.other: “Swallowed up in victory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “the sting of death” occurs in exactly one; they are 1 Corinthians 15:54 and 15:56, two verses apart.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 16:8 splices the two. Paul says death is swallowed up in victory (15:54) and, after the taunt, that the sting of death is sin (15:56); the Book of Mormon says “the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ”, which takes 15:56's subject and 15:54's predicate and replaces Paul's abstract “victory” with a person. The substitution is the doctrine of the whole chapter in one word: what swallows death is not an outcome but Christ. It also completes a movement begun at 15:7, where the same verb was used of the Son's will being swallowed up in the Father's — the chapter borrows Paul's one distinctive verb twice and uses it once for the incarnation and once for the resurrection.

links.note: “There is a resurrection, therefore the grave hath no victory, and the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ.” Two KJV singletons two verses apart in Paul, fused into one clause with “in victory” replaced by “in Christ”. The first half of the sentence resolves 16:7's counterfactual — the grave has no victory, indicatively now — so the two verses together reproduce 1 Corinthians 15:54-56 as a hypothesis and its denial. Below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion; what carries it is that both singletons appear, in Paul's order, in eighteen words.

pericopes.text: He is the light and the life of the world; yea, a light that is endless, that can never be darkened; yea, and also a life which is endless, that there can be no more death.

links.text: In him was life; and the life was the light of men.

provenance.route: John 1:4 and John 8:12 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “In him was life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “the life of the world” occurs in exactly one, John 6:51. “The light of the world” occurs in three, of which two are John's (8:12, 9:5) and one is Jesus saying it of his disciples (Matthew 5:14).
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's title “the light and the life of the world” has no KJV verse behind it, and the reason is that it is a compound of three of them, all from one Gospel. John 1:4 puts life and light in one sentence and makes the first the source of the second; John 8:12 makes the light of the world a self-designation; John 6:51 supplies the genitive “of the world” with life rather than light attached. Mosiah 16:9 says all three at once, and then does what John's prologue does next: it treats darkness as the thing the light defeats — “a light that is endless, that can never be darkened” against John 1:5, “the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.”

links.note: “He is the light and the life of the world; yea, a light that is endless, that can never be darkened.” A Johannine title assembled from three verses, two of which contain KJV singletons. What the Book of Mormon adds is endlessness — a light that cannot be darkened, a life in which there can be no more death — which is not John's emphasis and is this speech's, since Abinadi has been arguing since 15:20 about a resurrection that ends death permanently. Frederick's monograph discusses this verse in proximity to John 1:4, 8:12 and 11:25; the index behind that (data/frederick-refs.json) records co-occurrence within his text, not a proposed source, and his argument in the book is about the Gospel of John rather than about Mosiah.
bibliography: Frederick 2016: Mosiah 16:9 co-occurs with John 1:4, 8:12 and 11:25 within a 1,500-character window (co-occurrence index, data/frederick-refs.json); he proposes no source list

links.text: And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

provenance.other: “There shall be no more death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Revelation 21:4 is the KJV's one abolition of death, and it belongs to the new heaven and new earth, after the judgment of chapter 20 that Mosiah 16:10 is about to draw on. Abinadi takes the two chapters in Revelation's order — the resurrection and the books at 16:10-11 from Revelation 20, the end of death here from Revelation 21 — but reverses them, so that the endless life comes first and the judgment after. The rearrangement matters: in Revelation the abolition of death is the reward of those who survive judgment, and in Mosiah 16:9 it is a property of the Christ who will conduct it.

links.note: “A life which is endless, that there can be no more death.” Five words from a KJV singleton, attached to the Johannine title in the first half of the verse. Recorded at moderate — the clause is short and the sentiment is unavoidable in any statement about endless life — and kept because the KJV says it once, and because 16:10-11 goes on to use Revelation 20's judgment scene, so the two chapters of Revelation are both in view within three verses.

pericopes.text: Even this mortal shall put on immortality, and this corruption shall put on incorruption, and shall be brought to stand before the bar of God, to be judged of him according to their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil.

links.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

provenance.other: “This mortal must put on immortality” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “this corruptible must put on incorruption” occurs in the same verse and is repeated at 15:54.
provenance.significance: Two things are changed and both are legible. Paul's order is corruptible then mortal; Mosiah 16:10 reverses it, mortal then corruption, which puts the resurrection of the body second and lets the sentence run on into the judgment. And Paul's “corruptible”, an adjective for the thing that is raised, becomes “corruption”, the abstract state — so the Book of Mormon has corruption putting on incorruption rather than a corruptible body doing so. This catalogue has met the verse twice before, at 2 Nephi 9:7 and Enos 1:27, and neither makes that substitution; it is peculiar to Abinadi and it fits his argument, which has been about states (fallen, carnal, redeemed) rather than about bodies since 16:4.

links.note: “Even this mortal shall put on immortality, and this corruption shall put on incorruption.” Twelve words from a KJV singleton with the two clauses transposed and one noun abstracted. Catalogued as a quotation on the CONVENTIONS §2 rule — below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations — because the whole of Paul's sentence is reproduced and no other verse in the Bible contains it. Paul's modal “must” becomes the prophetic “shall”, which converts a condition of resurrection into a prediction of it.

links.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

provenance.other: “According to their works” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, two of them Revelation 20:12 and 20:13; Revelation 20:12 is the one that also has the dead standing before God. “Whether it be good, or whether it be evil” occurs in exactly two, Ecclesiastes 12:14 and Jeremiah 42:6, and only Ecclesiastes has it of a judgment.
provenance.significance: The judgment scene is Revelation 20:12's in every part: the dead stand before God, and they are judged according to their works. Ecclesiastes 12:14 supplies the alternative that Revelation leaves implicit — God shall bring every work into judgment, whether it be good, or whether it be evil — and it is the KJV's one verse pairing that formula with judgment. The Book of Mormon's own contribution is the furniture: “the bar of God”, a phrase in no KJV verse, which imports a nineteenth-century courtroom into an apocalyptic throne scene and which becomes standard in the corpus after this. Recover Revelation 20 and 16:11's two resurrections follow, since the books of Revelation 20:12 are what sorts them.

links.note: “Shall be brought to stand before the bar of God, to be judged of him according to their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil.” Two KJV formulas end to end, Revelation's and Ecclesiastes's, joined by a phrase that is in neither. The 1830's “whether they be good or whether they be evil” follows Ecclesiastes's construction exactly while changing the pronoun from the works to the persons — Ecclesiastes judges every work, Abinadi judges the people by them — and 16:11 then divides them by John 5:29's two resurrections.

pericopes.text: If they be good, to the resurrection of endless life and happiness, and if they be evil, to the resurrection of endless damnation; being delivered up to the devil, who hath subjected them, which is damnation;

links.text: And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.

provenance.other: “The resurrection of life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the resurrection of damnation” occurs in exactly one, and it is the same verse: John 5:29.
provenance.significance: One verse of the KJV divides the resurrection in two and names both halves, and Mosiah 16:11 reproduces the division, the two names and the criterion. John: “they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.” Mosiah: “If they be good, to the resurrection of endless life and happiness, and if they be evil, to the resurrection of endless damnation.” The insertion is “endless”, twice, which is the word this chapter has been pressing since 16:4's “endlessly lost” and 16:9's endless light and life. John's two resurrections are outcomes; Abinadi's are durations, and the whole speech is an argument that what the law of Moses could not do was make anything last.

links.note: “To the resurrection of endless life and happiness … to the resurrection of endless damnation.” Both of the KJV's two names for the two resurrections come from one verse, each occurring in exactly one KJV verse, and the Book of Mormon has both with the same conditional structure and the same criterion of good and evil deeds. It is the second Johannine borrowing in three verses (see 16:9) and the second half of the judgment scene begun at 16:10 from Revelation 20:12 — the books determine the works, John's verse determines what the works are worth.

pericopes.text: having gone according to their own carnal wills and desires; having never called upon the Lord while the arms of mercy was extended towards them; for the arms of mercy was extended towards them, and they would not; they being warned of their iniquities, and yet they would not depart from them; and they were commanded to repent, and yet they would not repent.

links.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!

provenance.other: “And ye would not” occurs in exactly five KJV verses; the two that follow an offer of gathering are Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34, its Lucan double. “The arms of mercy” occurs in no KJV verse.
provenance.alternative: The refusal formula is Deuteronomic (Deuteronomy 1:43, Isaiah 30:15) and Judges 2:17's “and yet they would not hearken” is closer to Mosiah's actual words; nothing here requires the lament over Jerusalem.
provenance.significance: The lament over Jerusalem is the KJV's one scene of arms opened and refused — how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not — and Mosiah 16:12 is the same gesture with the image changed: the arms of mercy extended, twice, and twice “they would not”. The doubling is Abinadi's own and it is what makes the case, since Matthew's clause is a single refusal and the Book of Mormon's is a refrain. Note that the corpus will eventually make the borrowing explicit at 3 Nephi 10:5, where the hen and the chickens appear; here only the gesture and the refusal are present.

links.note: “Having never called upon the Lord while the arms of mercy was extended towards them; for the arms of mercy was extended towards them, and they would not.” Recorded as an echo. The words “and they would not” are common enough that they identify nothing on their own; what is proposed is the scene — an offer made repeatedly by an outstretched embrace and declined — for which the KJV has one home. The 1830's singular verb under a plural subject, “the arms of mercy was extended”, twice, was corrected to “were” in 1920.
links.whyNot: No distinctive wording whatever. “Arms of mercy” is not in the KJV, the refusal formula is in five verses and is commonest in Deuteronomy and Isaiah, and Judges 2:17 — which the n-gram stream ranks first here — is verbally nearer than Matthew. The case rests entirely on the gesture, and a reader who declines it loses a resonance and no evidence.

pericopes.text: And now had ye not ought to tremble and repent of your sins, and remember only in and through Christ ye can be saved?
Therefore, if ye teach the law of Moses, also teach that it is a shadow of those things which are to come;
teach them that redemption cometh through Christ the Lord, which is the very Eternal Father. Amen.
And now it came to pass that when Abinadi had finished these sayings, that the king commanded that the priests should take him and cause that he should be put to death.

provenance.other: “had finished these sayings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 19:1. The nearest competitors are Matthew 7:28 and 26:1, which read “ended these sayings” and “finished all these sayings”; the 1830 text has Matthew 19:1's form exactly, six words in order, and adds the KJV's own “and it came to pass, that when”.
provenance.significance: Matthew's formula is a hinge: it is how the first gospel closes a discourse and turns the narrative. Mosiah 17:1 uses it for the same office and to darker effect — Abinadi's long sermon (chapters 12–16) ends, and the sentence that closes it is the sentence that orders his execution. Recover Matthew 19:1's context and the clause is Jesus leaving Galilee for Judaea, that is, setting out for the passion; the Book of Mormon puts the identical clause at the head of its own passion narrative.

links.note: 'And now it came to pass that when Abinadi had finished these sayings, that the king commanded that the priests should take him and cause that he should be put to death.' Two KJV formulae are welded here: Matthew's discourse-closing 'when Jesus had finished these sayings' and the Chronicler's 'the king commanded that' (2 Chronicles 29:24 has 'for the king commanded that the burnt offering ... should be made', five words in the same order). The Matthean half is the one that carries the argument, because it is a singleton and because the whole chapter that follows is built out of trial and martyrdom narratives; this is the seam where the sermon becomes a passion.
links.text: And it came to pass, that when Jesus had finished these sayings, he departed from Galilee, and came into the coasts of Judaea beyond Jordan;

pericopes.text: But there was one among them, whose name was Alma, he also being a descendant of Nephi. And he was a young man, and he believed the words which Abinadi had spoken, for he knew concerning the iniquity which Abinadi had testified against them: Therefore he began to plead with the king that he would not be angry with Abinadi, but suffer that he might depart in peace.

provenance.other: No rare string is shared: 'whose name was' stands in 38 KJV verses and 'young man' in 53. The contact is structural, and the one lexical detail that matters is that both texts stop the execution narrative to give the age and the name of a bystander who has done nothing yet.
provenance.significance: The New Testament has exactly one scene in which a martyr is killed by a council and the narrator pauses, mid-execution, to introduce by name a young man standing by — and that young man becomes the movement's founding missionary. Mosiah 17 does the same thing in the same place: Alma is introduced as 'a young man' at the moment Abinadi is condemned, and the church of the Book of Mormon descends from him. The difference is the whole point of the imitation. Acts 8:1 reports that 'Saul was consenting unto his death'; Alma pleads for Abinadi's life and is driven out for it. Where Luke's young man must be knocked down on the Damascus road before he changes sides, the Book of Mormon's is already converted by the sermon he has just heard.

links.note: 'But there was one among them, whose name was Alma, he also being a descendant of Nephi. And he was a young man, and he believed the words which Abinadi had spoken.' Offered as a type-scene rather than a verbal borrowing, under CONVENTIONS §0a: the shared wording is formulaic, but the narrative position is not, and Acts 7:58 is the only place in the KJV that occupies it. Where the machine streams see Judges 17:7 and Luke 24:18 — two verses that share the formula and nothing else — the sense of the sentence is Luke's.
links.whyNot: Everything shared is KJV boilerplate. A writer producing a martyrdom narrative in King James English would introduce a bystander in these words without having Acts 7:58 in mind, and the argument rests entirely on the structural coincidence plus the later career of the man named.
links.text: And cast him out of the city, and stoned him: and the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man’s feet, whose name was Saul.

pericopes.text: But the king was more wroth, and caused that Alma should be cast out from among them, and sent his servants after him, that they might slay him.
But he fled from before them, and hid himself, that they found him not. And he, being concealed for many days, did write all the words which Abinadi had spoken.
And it came to pass that the king caused that his guards should surround Abinadi, and take him; and they bound him and cast him into prison.
And after three days, having counselled with his priests, he caused that he should again be brought before him.
And he said unto him, Abinadi, we have found an accusation against thee, and thou art worthy of death.

provenance.route: 1 Kings 2:26 + Luke 6:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Two absolute rarities in one sentence. “thou art worthy of death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 2:26; “find an accusation against” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 6:7. 'Worthy of death' without the pronoun stands in eleven verses, most of them Paul's Roman hearings, so it is the four-word form that identifies the source.
provenance.significance: Both singletons are inverted where they land. In 1 Kings a king says 'thou art worthy of death' to a priest — and then spares him, 'but I will not at this time put thee to death'. Mosiah 17:7 puts the same sentence in a king's mouth against a prophet, with the priests doing the pressing, and the clemency clause is exactly what does not follow. Luke 6:7's accusation-hunting is the scribes' and Pharisees' work against Jesus, sought before any offence has been committed; Noah's court likewise announces that it has 'found an accusation' before Abinadi has said anything in the chapter.

links.note: 'Abinadi, we have found an accusation against thee, and thou art worthy of death.' The verse is built out of two KJV singletons welded end to end, one from each Testament, and each carries its own scene with it: a king who condemns a priest and relents, and a religious court that goes looking for a charge. Neither phrase is idiomatic English outside the KJV, and the pronoun matters — 'thou art worthy of death' is 1 Kings 2:26's exact form and no one else's.
links.text: And unto Abiathar the priest said the king, Get thee to Anathoth, unto thine own fields; for thou art worthy of death: but I will not at this time put thee to death, because thou barest the ark of the LORD God before David my father, and because thou hast been afflicted in all wherein my father was afflicted.
