pericopes.text: For thou hast said that God himself should come down among the children of men; and now for this cause thou shalt be put to death, unless thou wilt recall all the words which thou hast spoken evil concerning me and my people.

Now Abinadi saith unto him: I say unto you, I will not recall the words which I have spoken unto you concerning this people, for they are true; and that ye may know of their surety, I have suffered myself that I have fallen into your hands.

Yea, and I will suffer even until death, and I will not recall my words, and they shall stand as a testimony against you. And if ye slay me, ye will shed innocent blood, and this shall also stand as a testimony against you at the last day.

provenance.other: “for a testimony against” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 10:18, Mark 6:11, Mark 13:9 and Luke 9:5 — all of them in the synoptic mission and persecution discourses, and Mark 13:9 is the one where the testimony is borne by a prisoner standing before rulers and kings. The Book of Mormon's 'shed innocent blood' is a wider idiom (seven verses); 'the innocent blood' with the article stands in four, of which Matthew 27:4 is Judas's.
provenance.significance: Mark 13:9 promises that the disciple delivered to councils and beaten in synagogues will be brought before rulers and kings, and that this will be 'for a testimony against them'. Abinadi, delivered to a council of priests and standing before a king, says that his refusal to recant 'shall stand as a testimony against you'. The borrowing turns a promise made to the persecuted into a threat spoken by one, and the phrase Mosiah adds — that the shedding of innocent blood 'shall also stand as a testimony against you at the last day' — is the eschatology Mark 13 supplies the promise with.

links.note: 'And they shall stand as a testimony against you ... ye will shed innocent blood, and this shall also stand as a testimony against you at the last day.' The exact string is Mosiah's own ('stand as a testimony' is in no KJV verse), but the four-word core and the whole situation are Mark 13:9's. Proposed at moderate confidence: the case rests on the setting doing as much work as the words, which is the right way round for an echo and not enough for an allusion.
links.whyNot: The Book of Mormon's phrase differs from all four KJV occurrences at the preposition ('as' for 'for'), and 'testimony against' is common enough legal English that the synoptic discourse need not be in view.
links.text: But take heed to yourselves: for they shall deliver you up to councils; and in the synagogues ye shall be beaten: and ye shall be brought before rulers and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them.

pericopes.text: And now king Noah was about to release him, for he feared his word; for he feared that the judgments of God would come upon him.

provenance.other: “sought to release him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 19:12. 'Released' as a verb of a ruler letting a prisoner go stands in four verses, all of them Barabbas. Mosiah's 'for he feared his word' is not John's diction but Mark 6:20's, 'For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy'.
provenance.significance: This is the clearest sequence-level borrowing in the chapter, and it runs across the verse boundary. John 19:7 has the accusers say 'by our law he ought to die'; 19:8, that Pilate 'was the more afraid'; 19:12, that he 'sought to release him: but the Jews cried out'. Mosiah 17:7–12 has the court say 'thou art worthy of death'; 17:11, that Noah feared; 17:11–12, that he 'was about to release him' but 'the priests lifted up their voices against him'. Four steps in John's order. Recovering the context supplies what Mosiah leaves unsaid: what breaks Pilate is the accusers' threat to his standing with Caesar, and what breaks Noah is the priests whose office he created.

links.note: 'And now king Noah was about to release him, for he feared his word; for he feared that the judgments of God would come upon him.' The KJV has exactly one ruler who 'sought to release' a prisoner and is overborne by the men accusing him, and the doubled motive — a ruler afraid of a prophet he is about to kill — is Mark 6:20's Herod. The Book of Mormon has fused the two reluctant executioners of the gospels into one king, and the fusion is legible because each half is rare on its own.
links.text: And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Caesar’s friend: whosoever maketh himself a king speaketh against Caesar.

pericopes.text: But the priests lifted up their voices against him, and began to accuse him, saying: He hath reviled the king. Therefore the king was stirred up in anger against him, and he delivered him up, that he might be slain.

provenance.other: “began to accuse him, saying” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 23:2 and Acts 24:2. Both are formal accusations laid before a judge with power of death — Jesus before Pilate, Paul before Felix — and in both the accusation as quoted is political rather than religious. 'Stirred up' is commoner (fifteen verses), but Acts 6:12, 'And they stirred up the people, and the elders, and the scribes', is the Stephen trial the rest of this chapter keeps returning to.
provenance.significance: The five words are the KJV's formula for the moment a lynching acquires legal form. What the priests bring is a charge of lèse-majesté — 'He hath reviled the king' — which is precisely the shape of Luke 23:2's charge, that Jesus made himself 'Christ a King' and forbade tribute to Caesar. In both, the religious grievance is translated into a political one for the ruler's ears, because the ruler will not kill for the religious one; Noah had just been about to release Abinadi over the theology.

links.note: 'But the priests lifted up their voices against him, and began to accuse him, saying: He hath reviled the king.' A five-word verbatim run from a two-verse KJV phrase, in the same office both KJV verses give it. The 1830 reading 'hath reviled' preserves the KJV's auxiliary where 1920 modernizes it to 'has', so the first edition shows the register of the borrowing more plainly than the current text does.
links.text: And they began to accuse him, saying, We found this fellow perverting the nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar, saying that he himself is Christ a King.

provenance.route: Exodus 22:28 → KJV → Book of Mormon; Acts 23:5's form of the same statute is present at Mosiah 17:8
provenance.other: “ruler of thy people” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 22:28 and Acts 23:5, which are the statute and its New Testament citation. They differ at the verb: Exodus reads 'Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people'; Acts reads 'Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people'. “speak evil of the ruler” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 23:5.
provenance.alternative: The charge may simply be the natural English for insulting a monarch, with no statute behind it.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 17 carries both forms of the one statute, four verses apart and in different mouths. The king's own demand at 17:8 is that Abinadi recall 'the words which thou hast spoken evil concerning me and my people' — Acts 23:5's idiom, and Acts 23:5's 'thy people' with it; the priests' formal charge at 17:12 is that 'He hath reviled the king' — Exodus 22:28's verb. So the Book of Mormon reproduces the Hebrew Bible's only law against insulting a ruler in the New Testament's paraphrase when the ruler speaks, and in the Old Testament's original when the lawyers do. Whether that distribution is design or accident, it is the kind of split a translation from a single source would not produce.

links.note: 'He hath reviled the king.' The charge that kills Abinadi is the one crime the Pentateuch names against a head of state, and the chapter states it twice in the KJV's two different wordings for it. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence here, because the verb is a single word and the tool ignores single common words to avoid false positives (ADJUDICATING §4); the split has to be caught by eye, and it is a real one. Recorded as direct-OT for 17:12 on the strength of 'reviled', with the Acts 23:5 half of the evidence set out above.
links.whyNot: 'Revile' stands in nine KJV verses and 'the king' in hundreds; nothing longer than one content word is shared with Exodus 22:28. The reading depends on treating 17:8 and 17:12 as one distributed borrowing rather than two independent idioms.
links.text: Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they took him, and bound him, and scourged his skin with faggots, yea, even unto death.

provenance.other: “scourged” occurs in exactly four KJV verses. One is the slave law of Leviticus 19:20; the other three — Matthew 27:26, Mark 15:15, John 19:1 — are Pilate scourging Jesus. Mark 15:15 is the only KJV verse that holds a reluctant ruler, a release granted under pressure, a scourging and a handing over to death in one sentence.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 17:11–13 does in three verses what Mark 15:15 does in one clause, and in Mark's order: the ruler would release, the crowd of accusers prevails, the prisoner is scourged, the prisoner is delivered to be killed. The Book of Mormon's variation is the instrument — faggots rather than the flagellum, so that the scourging and the execution are the same act, and the man is burned by degrees. That fusion is what makes 17:15's threat work: Abinadi's killers will suffer 'the pains that I do suffer', which requires the torture and the death to be one thing.

links.note: 'And it came to pass that they took him, and bound him, and scourged his skin with faggots, yea, even unto death.' The word is the passion narrative's word; three of its four KJV occurrences are Pilate's. Taken alone it would be common vocabulary, but it arrives at the end of the John 19:12 sequence begun at 17:11 and in Mark 15:15's exact position within it, which is what lifts it above coincidence. 'Bound him' is likewise the KJV's arrest diction (Matthew 14:3 of John the Baptist, whose executioner is the Herod already standing behind 17:11).
links.whyNot: 'Scourged' is the ordinary English for a flogging and Leviticus supplies a non-passion precedent; the case is carried by the sequence rather than by the word.
links.text: And so Pilate, willing to content the people, released Barabbas unto them, and delivered Jesus, when he had scourged him, to be crucified.

pericopes.text: And now when the flames began to scorch him, he cried unto them saying:

Behold, even as ye have done unto me, so shall it come to pass that thy seed shall cause that many shall suffer the pains that I do suffer, even the pains of death, by fire; and this because they believe in the salvation of the Lord their God.

provenance.other: “the pains of death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:24: 'Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.' The Book of Mormon uses the phrase twice in four verses, at 17:15 and again at 17:18, both times as 'the pains of death, by fire'.
provenance.significance: The one place the King James Bible speaks of 'the pains of death' is Peter's Pentecost sermon, and it speaks of them being loosed — the resurrection is defined there as God untying exactly this knot. Abinadi, burning, promises his judges the pains of death that Acts says Christ could not be held by; and he has spent chapters 15 and 16 preaching that resurrection. The borrowed phrase therefore carries its own answer with it: the pains he assigns them are the pains the sermon they refused says are loosed.

links.note: 'Thy seed shall cause that many shall suffer the pains that I do suffer, even the pains of death, by fire.' A four-word KJV singleton, and the 1830 running text has the fuller clause the later editions trim, so the doubling of 'suffer ... suffer' that makes the sentence a formula of retribution is visible in the first edition. Abinadi is not describing his sensations but pronouncing a sentence, and the phrase he pronounces it in is the resurrection's.
links.text: Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.

provenance.other: “so God hath requited me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 1:7, and it is the Bible's clearest statement of measure-for-measure retribution in a mutilated victim's own mouth: 'as I have done, so God hath requited me'. The Book of Mormon's 'even as ye have done unto me, so shall it come to pass that ...' has the same two-limbed shape with the tense reversed.
provenance.significance: Adonibezek pronounces the formula over himself, looking back at seventy kings he had maimed; Abinadi pronounces it over his judges, looking forward. Reading the two together makes Abinadi's curse a piece of Deuteronomistic jurisprudence rather than a personal grudge — the speaker is not threatening revenge but stating the rule the book of Judges says God works by, and Mosiah 19:20 and 21 will report it discharged when Noah himself is burned.

links.note: 'Behold, even as ye have done unto me, so shall it come to pass that thy seed shall cause that many shall suffer the pains that I do suffer.' The machine offers Joshua 23:8 and Ezekiel 23:38 for 'have done unto', which share the string and not the sense; Judges 1:7 shares the sense and the construction, and it is the KJV's only articulation of the principle in this exact grammatical shape. An echo, not an allusion: the wording is close in structure and not in words.
links.whyNot: Not a single distinctive word is shared — 'as ye have done ... so' is a construction, not a phrase, and the retributive formula is common enough in the prophets that no one verse need be in view.
links.text: And Adonibezek said, Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me. And they brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died.

pericopes.text: And it will come to pass that ye shall be afflicted with all manner of diseases, because of your iniquities.
Yea, and ye shall be smitten on every hand, and shall be driven and scattered to and fro, even as a wild flock is driven by wild and ferocious beasts.
And in that day ye shall be hunted, and ye shall be taken by the hand of your enemies, and then ye shall suffer, as I suffer, the pains of death, by fire.

provenance.other: “hunted” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 13:21: 'and they shall be no more in your hand to be hunted; and ye shall know that I am the LORD.' Ezekiel 13:21 and 13:23 also supply 'out of your hand', against which Mosiah sets 'by the hand of your enemies'. Jeremiah 38:23 contributes the other half of the verse — “taken by the hand of” the enemy, with the city 'burned with fire' in the same sentence — a three-word run the machine stream also found.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest piece of metalepsis. Ezekiel 13 is the oracle against false prophets and the women who prophesy out of their own hearts: God's charge against them is that they hunt souls, and his promise is to take his people out of their hand so that they shall be 'no more ... to be hunted'. Abinadi's audience is a college of false priests. He takes the KJV's only occurrence of the verb, which belongs to that oracle, and turns it round on them — the hunters will be the hunted. Ezekiel 13:22's specific accusation, strengthening 'the hands of the wicked ... by promising him life', is what Noah's priests have done for Noah, and it is the reason Abinadi will not recant the sentence of death at 17:9.

links.note: 'And in that day ye shall be hunted, and ye shall be taken by the hand of your enemies, and then ye shall suffer, as I suffer, the pains of death, by fire.' One KJV singleton, one distinctive three-word run from Jeremiah's oracle of a city burned, and Acts 2:24's 'the pains of death' returning from 17:15 to close the verse. All three sources are oracles of judgment delivered to men who would not hear them, and the Ezekiel one is addressed to precisely the class of men Abinadi is addressing.
links.text: Your kerchiefs also will I tear, and deliver my people out of your hand, and they shall be no more in your hand to be hunted; and ye shall know that I am the LORD.

pericopes.text: Thus God executeth vengeance upon those that destroy his people. O God, receive my soul.

provenance.other: “receive my spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:59, Stephen's dying prayer. 'Receive my soul' does not occur in the King James Bible at all; the Book of Mormon has substituted the one word. The second clause draws on the KJV's vengeance idiom — “execute vengeance” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 149:7 and Micah 5:15 — and “them which destroy” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 11:18, where the time of the dead is the time to 'destroy them which destroy the earth'.
provenance.significance: Abinadi dies in Stephen's words with one substitution, and the substitution is the smaller of the two changes. The larger is what he says first. Stephen's second and last sentence is 'Lord, lay not this sin to their charge'; Abinadi's is 'Thus God executeth vengeance upon those that destroy his people.' The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's model martyr's death, kept the committal and reversed the intercession — and it has to, because Mosiah 19 will narrate the vengeance and 17:15–18 has just pronounced it. Read against Acts 7, the verse is a deliberate refusal of forgiveness at the stake, which is a much stranger thing for a nineteenth-century devotional text to do than an imitation would be.

links.note: 'Thus God executeth vengeance upon those that destroy his people. O God, receive my soul.' The dying committal is Acts 7:59 with 'soul' for 'spirit' and 'O God' for 'Lord Jesus, calling upon God' — and the substitutions run in the same direction, stripping the Christological address from a prayer that in Acts is the New Testament's first prayer to Jesus. The chapter opened at 17:2 with Acts 7:58's young bystander and closes at 17:19 with Acts 7:59's prayer, in the source's order, which is the strongest reason to accept the earlier link.
links.text: And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.

pericopes.text: And now when Abinadi had said these words, he fell, having suffered death by fire; yea, having been put to death because he would not deny the commandments of God: having sealed the truth of his words by his death.

provenance.other: “put to death because” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Leviticus 19:20 and Deuteronomy 13:5, and only Deuteronomy 13:5 is about a prophet: 'And that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death; because he hath spoken to turn you away from the LORD your God.'
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 13:5 is the statute for executing a false prophet, and it is written as a formula: put to death, plus a because-clause naming the speech that earned it. Mosiah 17:20 reproduces the formula and inverts the clause — 'having been put to death because he would not deny the commandments of God'. Abinadi dies under the law against prophets who turn Israel away, for refusing to turn away himself. The chapter has been building this: Noah's court demanded a recantation (17:8), the prophet refused (17:9), and the statute that should have protected him is the one that kills him. Note the second half of Deuteronomy 13:5 as well — 'So shalt thou put the evil away from the midst of thee' — which is what Noah's priests believe they are doing and what Mosiah 19 shows them not to have done.

links.note: 'Having been put to death because he would not deny the commandments of God: having sealed the truth of his words by his death.' The Pentateuch's execution formula for false prophets, with its because-clause turned inside out. This is the chapter's closing argument and it is made grammatically rather than by assertion: nothing says Abinadi was tried under Deuteronomy 13, but his death is reported in Deuteronomy 13's sentence, and a reader who knows the statute cannot miss which side of it he is on.
links.text: And that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death; because he hath spoken to turn you away from the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to thrust thee out of the way which the LORD thy God commanded thee to walk in. So shalt thou put the evil away from the midst of thee.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that Alma, who had fled from the servants of king Noah, repented of his sins and iniquities, and went about privately among the people, and began to teach the words of Abinadi;

yea, concerning that which was to come, and also concerning the resurrection of the dead, and the redemption of the people, which was to be brought to pass through the power, and sufferings, and death of Christ, and his resurrection and ascension into Heaven.
And as many as would hear his word he did teach. And he taught them privately, that it might not come to the knowledge of the king. And many did believe his words.

And it came to pass that as many as did believe him, did go forth to a place which was called Mormon, having received its name from the king, being in the borders of the land having been infested, by times, or at seasons, by wild beasts.

Now there was in Mormon a fountain of pure water, and Alma resorted thither, there being near the water a thicket of small trees, where he did hide himself in the day-time, from the searches of the king.
And it came to pass that as many as believed him, went thither to hear his words.

And it came to pass after many days, there were a goodly number gathered together to the place of Mormon, to hear the words of Alma. Yea, all were gathered together that believed on his word, to hear him. And he did teach them, and did preach unto them repentance, and redemption, and faith on the Lord.

And it came to pass that he said unto them, Behold, here is the waters of Mormon; for thus were they called. And now, as ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light;

provenance.other: “one another's burdens” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 6:2, and “bear ye one another” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The second half of the clause is a second singleton: “burden is light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 11:30. The Book of Mormon reproduces Paul's imperative with the pronoun dropped to fit the construction — 'are willing to bear one another's burdens' — and no other word changed.
provenance.significance: Galatians 6:2 does not stop at the imperative: bearing one another's burdens is how one 'fulfil[s] the law of Christ', and that is what Alma is at this moment constituting — a covenant community defined by a law, in a book whose next hundred pages will argue about the law of Moses. The Matthew half supplies the reason the burdens become bearable: 'my yoke is easy, and my burden is light' is Christ's, and Alma's 'that they may be light' transfers the lightness from the yoke of Christ to the shared load of the congregation. Between them the two singletons make the baptismal covenant a piece of Pauline ecclesiology with a synoptic promise attached, and neither source is named.

links.note: 'As ye are desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people, and are willing to bear one another's burdens, that they may be light.' The most famous sentence in the Book of Mormon's covenant, and it is Galatians 6:2 with the second-person pronoun removed. This falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and is not one of his thirty-six; it is catalogued as a quotation here on CONVENTIONS §2's grounds — a complete clause reproduced from a verse that is identifiably and uniquely its source. Note the 1830 reading 'here is the waters of Mormon', corrected to 'are' in 1920: the first edition's grammar is the looser one throughout this chapter.
links.text: Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.

provenance.other: 'Fold' stands in 49 KJV verses, most of them the verb; “one fold” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:16. The Book of Mormon's phrase is 'the fold of God', which is in no KJV verse at all, so the contact is with the image and not with a string.
provenance.alternative: The pastoral image is common property — Psalm 100:3, Ezekiel 34, John 10 — and 'fold of God' may simply be the natural English for a flock that belongs to God.
provenance.significance: If John 10:16 is in view it is worth knowing what comes with it: the verse is Jesus promising 'other sheep I have, which are not of this fold ... and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd', which is the single New Testament sentence the Book of Mormon most insists is about itself (3 Nephi 15–16 makes it the hinge of the whole visitation). Alma inviting a hidden congregation in the wilderness to 'come into the fold of God' would then be the book's first, unannounced use of the verse it will later claim outright.

links.note: Offered under CONVENTIONS §0a rather than argued: the wording will not carry an allusion, but the phrase sits in a book that later stakes a great deal on this one verse, and a reader who knows 3 Nephi 15:21 will hear it here.
links.whyNot: No shared string longer than the word 'fold', and the sheepfold is the common stock of biblical pastoral language. If this is a borrowing it is unprovable from the wording alone.
links.text: And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.

pericopes.text: yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times, and in all things, and in all places that ye may be in, even until death, that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life:

provenance.route: Romans 12:15 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Isaiah 61:2's verb substituted
provenance.other: Three rarities converge. “weep with them that weep” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 12:15, which supplies the whole construction — a verb of grief, 'with', and the same verb again as a participle for its objects. “comfort all that mourn” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 61:2, which supplies the substituted verb; and “comfort them which” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 1:4, whose object is 'them which are in any trouble'.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Romans 12:15's construction is reproduced exactly and its verb is replaced by Isaiah 61:2's, so that 'mourn with those that mourn' says in Paul's grammar what Isaiah's servant was anointed to do. Isaiah 61 is the passage Jesus reads in the synagogue at Nazareth and claims for himself (Luke 4:18–19), and Luke's citation stops one clause short of 'to comfort all that mourn'. Alma, founding a church in hiding, writes the unread clause into the entrance requirement: what the Book of Mormon's covenant asks of every member is the office Isaiah assigns to the anointed one.

links.note: 'Yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort.' Romans 12:15's construction with Isaiah 61:2's verb, followed by a comfort clause built on the figura etymologica of 2 Corinthians 1:4 — comforting the comfortless with the comfort received. All three sources are exhortations to a congregation about its internal life, which is exactly the office the sentence is performing.
links.text: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.

provenance.other: “the first resurrection” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 20:5 and 20:6, and nowhere else in the Bible. Both are within four verses of each other in the millennium vision; there is no Old Testament source for the phrase.
provenance.significance: Revelation 20:6 says three things about those who have part in the first resurrection: the second death has no power on them, they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and they shall reign with him. Alma's covenant promises the first — 'that ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection' — and then, within nine verses, performs the second: at 18:18 he 'ordained priests, even one priest to every fifty of their number'. The apocalypse's promise of a priesthood for the first-resurrection company is realised in the chapter's own narrative as an ordination at the waters of Mormon.

links.note: 'That ye may be redeemed of God, and be numbered with those of the first resurrection, that ye may have eternal life.' A phrase with exactly one home in the KJV, and it is the Apocalypse, six hundred years and one testament away from the speaker. Also worth naming: 'stand as witnesses of God at all times, and in all things, and in all places', which has no KJV phrase behind it but occupies Acts 1:8's office ('ye shall be witnesses unto me ... unto the uttermost part of the earth') and is recorded here rather than given a link of its own.
links.text: Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years.

pericopes.text: Now I say unto you, if this be the desires of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord, as a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his spirit more abundantly upon you.—

provenance.other: “what doth hinder me to be baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:36. It is the Bible's only sentence in which the question of an impediment to baptism is put in so many words, and it is put by the candidate. Alma's 'what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord' asks the same question from the other side of the water, in modern English rather than the KJV's. Frederick's co-occurrence index (data/frederick-refs.json) records Mosiah 18:10 discussed within 1500 characters of Acts 2:38 and Acts 8:16 in Frederick 2016; that index measures adjacency on a page, not a proposed source, and his book — which argues about the Gospel of John — has no cross-reference apparatus. It is noted here as a bookmark and is not evidence for this link.
provenance.alternative: Acts 10:47, 'Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized', asks the impediment question from the officiant's side, which is Alma's side; but it shares no wording at all with Mosiah 18:10, where Acts 8:36 shares the construction.
provenance.significance: The eunuch's question is asked at a roadside water in the middle of nowhere, by a man reading a prophet he does not understand, and answered by a confession of faith; Alma's is asked at a hidden fountain by a fugitive who has just been expounding a prophet his hearers did not understand, and answered by a covenant. The Book of Mormon has kept the setting of Acts 8 — the unlikely water, the private catechesis, the immediate baptism — and replaced the eunuch's christological confession with a covenant to 'serve him and keep his commandments', which is the substitution the whole chapter is organised around.

links.note: 'Now I say unto you, if this be the desires of your hearts, what have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord.' The KJV's one impediment-to-baptism question, turned round from candidate to officiant and de-archaised. Catalogued at moderate confidence because the modernised wording is exactly what makes the case arguable rather than demonstrable: the construction is Acts 8:36's, the diction is not. The 1830 plural 'desires of your hearts', singular in 1920 and again at 18:11, is the first edition's reading in both verses.
links.text: And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?

provenance.route: Joel 2:28 or Acts 2:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the verse cannot decide between them
provenance.other: “pour out my spirit” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Proverbs 1:23 and Joel 2:28 and 2:29; Acts 2:17, quoting Joel, reads 'I will pour out of my Spirit' with the partitive 'of'. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence at this verse, and the reason is instructive: the Book of Mormon has 'pour out his spirit', third person, because Alma is speaking about God rather than as God, so the pronoun that would carry the test is not there and the partitive 'of' has nothing to attach to.
provenance.alternative: 'Pour out' with 'spirit' is also Ezekiel 39:29, Zechariah 12:10 and Proverbs 1:23; no one verse is required.
provenance.significance: The phrase governs three consecutive verses of the chapter — the promise at 18:10, Alma's prayer at 18:12 ('O Lord, pour out thy spirit upon thy servant'), and the baptismal formula at 18:13 ('may the spirit of the Lord be poured out upon you') — and it is the language of Pentecost in both Testaments. Whichever form stands behind it, Alma is describing the founding of a church in the words of the founding of the Church.

links.note: Recorded chiefly for the mediation result, which is negative and worth having: this is a case where an Old Testament verse and its New Testament quotation differ at exactly one word and the Book of Mormon's grammar removes the word. The test cannot be run here, and `mediation` is 'uncertain' as CONVENTIONS §7 requires rather than defaulted to either side.
links.whyNot: 'Pour out' plus 'spirit' is one of the commonest prophetic collocations in the KJV and the Book of Mormon uses it constantly; nothing in this verse points at Joel in particular.
links.text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

pericopes.text: And now when the people had heard these words, they clapped their hands for joy, and exclaimed, This is the desires of our hearts.

And now it came to pass that Alma took Helam, he being one of the first, and went and stood forth in the water, and cried, saying, O Lord, pour out thy spirit upon thy servant, that he may do this work with holiness of heart.

And when he had said these words, the spirit of the Lord was upon him, and he said, Helam, I baptize thee, having authority from the Almighty God, as a testimony that ye have entered into a covenant to serve him until you are dead, as to the mortal body; and may the spirit of the Lord be poured out upon you; and may he grant unto you eternal life, through the redemption of Christ, which he hath prepared from the foundation of the world.
And after Alma had said these words, both Alma and Helam was buried in the water; and they arose and came forth out of the water rejoicing, being filled with the spirit.

provenance.other: “buried with him” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 6:4 and Colossians 2:12, which are the Bible's only two statements that baptism is a burial. They differ in what follows: Romans 6:4 moves from the burial to the believer walking 'in newness of life' — “newness of life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — while Colossians 2:12 has the believer rise, 'wherein also ye are risen with him'. Mosiah 18:14 has the rising: 'both Alma and Helam was buried in the water; and they arose and came forth out of the water rejoicing'. tools/mediation-check.py finds one decisive point for Colossians, but a weak one; the argument here rests on the rising, which is a clause the tool's word-level comparison cannot see.
provenance.significance: Paul's burial metaphor is a figure of speech about what baptism means; the Book of Mormon literalises it. Alma does not say that Helam was buried with Christ, he says both men 'was buried in the water' and then 'arose and came forth out of the water' — so the burial and the resurrection are things that physically happen to two bodies in a pond, and the second man baptised in the new church is baptised by immersion because Colossians says so. Note the consequence at 18:15: Alma, having been buried alongside Helam, 'did not bury himself again in the water', which is a piece of practical reasoning about a metaphor.

links.note: 'And after Alma had said these words, both Alma and Helam was buried in the water; and they arose and came forth out of the water rejoicing, being filled with the spirit.' The 1830 reading 'was buried' — a singular verb under the compound subject, corrected to 'were' in 1920 — is the first edition's, and it matters slightly: the singular reads the two men as one act, which is what makes 18:15's exemption intelligible. The verse is the clearest place in the Book of Mormon where a Pauline figure has been turned back into a rubric.
links.text: Buried with him in baptism, wherein also ye are risen with him through the faith of the operation of God, who hath raised him from the dead.

pericopes.text: And again, Alma took another, and went forth a second time into the water, and baptized him according to the first, only he did not bury himself again in the water.

And after this manner he did baptize every one that went forth to the place of Mormon; and they were in number about two hundred and four souls; yea, and they were baptized in the waters of Mormon, and were filled with the grace of God:

provenance.other: “the same day there were added” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:41, and “they that gladly received his word” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Acts 2:41 is the only verse in the Bible that counts converts at a mass baptism with the formula 'about [number] souls'; Mosiah 18:16 counts them as 'about two hundred and four souls'.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's church is founded with Pentecost's census formula and one seventh-part of Pentecost's number, at a pond in the wilderness rather than in Jerusalem before three thousand. Recovering Acts 2:41's context makes the resemblance denser than the count: 'they that gladly received his word were baptized' matches Mosiah 18:6–7's 'as many as believed him, went thither to hear his words' almost step for step, and the sequence hearing → belief → mass baptism → counted souls is Luke's order exactly. The oddity is the number itself. 204 is not a round figure and not a biblical one; a writer imitating Acts 2:41 would have no reason to invent it, which is one of the better arguments in the chapter that the imitation is not merely decorative.

links.note: 'They were in number about two hundred and four souls; yea, and they were baptized in the waters of Mormon, and were filled with the grace of God.' The 'about ... souls' construction is Acts 2:41's and no one else's in the KJV. This link and the one at 18:17 are two halves of a single borrowing — Luke reports the founding congregation's number in verse 41 and its increase in verse 47, and Mosiah 18 reports them in verses 16 and 17.
links.text: Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.

pericopes.text: and they were called the Church of God, or the Church of Christ, from that time forward. And it came to pass that whosoever was baptized by the power and authority of God, they was added to his church.

provenance.other: “added to the church” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:47: 'And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved.' It is the New Testament's founding sentence about how a church grows, and the Book of Mormon reproduces four of its words with the possessive changed: 'whosoever was baptized by the power and authority of God, they was added to his church.'
provenance.significance: Luke's grammar makes the Lord the subject — the Lord adds, the church receives — and Alma's sentence keeps that and adds a condition Luke does not state: 'by the power and authority of God'. So the verse simultaneously borrows the New Testament's charter of church growth and inserts into it the doctrine of authority that the Book of Mormon, and the movement that published it, needed the charter to contain. That insertion is the interesting half. Acts 2:47 says nothing about who may baptise; Mosiah 18:17 makes the addition contingent on it, and 18:13's 'having authority from the Almighty God' has already supplied the formula.

links.note: 'And they were called the Church of God, or the Church of Christ, from that time forward. And it came to pass that whosoever was baptized by the power and authority of God, they was added to his church.' A four-word KJV singleton carrying Acts 2's whole ecclesiology, and the 1830 reading is the more visibly borrowed one: 'they was added to his church', where 1920 deletes the redundant pronoun. The first edition's syntax is Luke's clause with a resumptive subject bolted on, which is what a writer working from a remembered KJV sentence produces and what a careful editor removes.
links.text: Praising God, and having favour with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Alma, having authority from God, ordained priests; even one priest to every fifty of their number did he ordain to preach unto them, and to teach them concerning the things pertaining to the kingdom of God.

links.text: To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God:

provenance.other: “things pertaining to the kingdom of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 1:3, and Mosiah 18:18 reproduces all eight words in order, with 'concerning the' where Luke has 'speaking of'. The shorter “pertaining to the kingdom” is a singleton in the same verse. The organisational detail beside it — 'one priest to every fifty of their number' — has no KJV phrase behind it, though fifty as the unit under one appointed man is the Pentateuch's ('rulers of fifties', Exodus 18:21).
provenance.significance: Acts 1:3 is a summary of syllabus: it describes what the risen Christ taught the apostles during the forty days between the resurrection and the ascension, and it is the only place the KJV names that curriculum. Alma ordains priests and gives them the same syllabus verbatim. Read with 18:2 — where Alma's own preaching is summarised as 'the resurrection of the dead, and the redemption of the people ... and his resurrection and ascension into Heaven', which is Acts 1's subject matter in Acts 1's order — the chapter is founding a church on the forty days' instruction, and then, at 18:16–17, populating it with Acts 2's Pentecost census. The Book of Mormon's first church is built through the first two chapters of Acts in sequence.

links.note: 'Alma, having authority from God, ordained priests; even one priest to every fifty of their number did he ordain to preach unto them, and to teach them concerning the things pertaining to the kingdom of God.' An eight-word verbatim run from a KJV singleton, which is the longest exact borrowing in the chapter and the one the n-gram stream ranked highest (3.51). It sits below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six; it is catalogued as a quotation under CONVENTIONS §2 because the clause is complete, exact, and has one possible source.

pericopes.text: And he commanded them that they should teach nothing save it were the things which he had taught, and which had been spoken by the mouth of the holy prophets.
Yea, even he commanded them that they should preach nothing save it were repentance and faith on the Lord, who hath redeemed his people.

And he commanded them that there should be no contention one with another, but that they should look forward with one eye, having one faith and one baptism; having their hearts knit together in unity and in love, one towards another.

provenance.other: Three Pauline unity texts, each identified by a rarity. “one faith one baptism” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:5. “knit together in” is a KJV singleton, Colossians 2:2 — 'that their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love'; 2:19 reads 'knit together, increaseth', a different construction with no 'in' at all, not a second instance. “no divisions among you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 1:10, whose subject is contention in a congregation.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 4:4–6 is a seven-fold litany — one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God — and Alma takes exactly the two items that a newly baptised congregation could be said to hold in common, drops the rest, and prefixes his own: 'they should look forward with one eye'. That phrase is in no KJV verse. So the verse is a Pauline formula with a non-Pauline first term inserted at the head of it, and the inserted term is the one that turns a creed into a discipline — Ephesians lists what the church already shares, Alma commands what it must do.

links.note: 'And he commanded them that there should be no contention one with another, but that they should look forward with one eye, having one faith and one baptism; having their hearts knit together in unity and in love, one towards another.' Three of Paul's four great appeals against congregational division, fused into a single sentence in the order 1 Corinthians → Ephesians → Colossians: no divisions, one faith and one baptism, hearts knit together in love. Each is identifiable by an absolute or near-absolute rarity, and none is named.
links.text: One Lord, one faith, one baptism,

pericopes.text: And thus he commanded them to preach. And thus they became the children of God.
And he commanded them that they should observe the sabbath day, and keep it holy, and also every day they should give thanks to the Lord their God.

provenance.route: Exodus 20:8 + Exodus 31:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: A composite of two singletons. “keep it holy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 20:8, the fourth commandment in its Exodus form; “observe the sabbath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 31:16. Run against the Deuteronomic form of the commandment, tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Exodus 20:8 — the Book of Mormon has Exodus's 'keep' where Deuteronomy 5:12 has 'sanctify', and Exodus's 'holy' where Deuteronomy has 'as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee'. Its third reported point, that the Book of Mormon has Deuteronomy's 'Keep' rather than Exodus's 'Remember', is an artifact of the tool matching the 'keep' of 'keep it holy'; the Book of Mormon's actual leading verb is 'observe', which is neither, and which is Exodus 31:16's.
provenance.significance: Exodus 31:16 is not a repetition of the commandment but its covenant clause: Israel keeps the sabbath 'throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant', and it is a sign between God and Israel for ever. Mosiah 18 is a covenant chapter — the word governs 18:10 and 18:13 — and the one sabbath verse in the KJV that makes the sabbath itself a perpetual covenant is the one supplying Alma's verb. So the sabbath command given to the new church at Mormon is worded out of the two Exodus verses that between them make sabbath-keeping the sign of the covenant rather than merely a law within it.

links.note: 'And he commanded them that they should observe the sabbath day, and keep it holy, and also every day they should give thanks to the Lord their God.' Two Exodus singletons welded, and the Deuteronomic form of the commandment demonstrably not in view. The second clause quietly undoes the first — a people commanded to keep one day holy and then to give thanks 'every day' — which is the same move the New Testament makes on the sabbath and which the Book of Mormon makes here without argument.
links.text: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

pericopes.text: And he also commanded them that the priests which he had ordained should labor with their own hands for their support;

provenance.other: “with our own hands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 27:19 (jettisoning a ship's tackle) and 1 Corinthians 4:12, 'And labour, working with our own hands'. Only the second is about a minister's self-support, and it is the New Testament's programmatic statement of it. 2 Thessalonians 3:8 supplies the negative half that Mosiah 18:26 states — 'that we might not be chargeable to any of you'.
provenance.significance: Paul's tentmaking is an argument, not a biography: he works with his own hands so that the gospel shall be 'without charge' and no one may say he preached for money. Alma legislates it, which no New Testament writer does — 1 Corinthians 9 in fact defends the opposite right at length — and legislates it immediately after ordaining priests, in a chapter whose villains are the priests of Noah, a paid clergy supported by a fifth of the people's substance (Mosiah 11:3). The borrowing is therefore polemical: the anti-priestcraft rule of the new church is written in the words of the apostle who declined to be paid, and it is aimed at the priesthood the reader has just watched burn a prophet.

links.note: 'And he also commanded them that the priests which he had ordained should labor with their own hands for their support.' The phrase is Paul's and the setting supplies the argument the phrase carries; what the Book of Mormon adds is the commandment, since Paul offers his practice as a personal renunciation of a right rather than a rule for others. The 1830 'the priests which he had ordained', modernized to 'whom' in 1920, is the KJV's own relative-pronoun usage.
links.whyNot: Working with one's hands is common enough in the KJV (Ephesians 4:28, 1 Thessalonians 4:11) that no single verse is required, and 'labor for their support' is not KJV diction at all.
links.text: And labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it:

pericopes.text: and there was one day in every week that was set apart that they should gather themselves together to teach the people, and to worship the Lord their God, and also as often as it was in their power to assemble themselves together.

And the priests was not to depend upon the people for their support; but for their labor they were to receive the grace of God, that they might wax strong in the spirit, having the knowledge of God, that they might teach with power and authority from God.

And again Alma commanded that the people of the Church should impart of their substance, every one according to that which he hath; if he have more abundantly, he should impart more abundantly; and he that hath but little, but little should be required; and to him that hath not should be given.

provenance.other: “according to that a man hath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 8:12, and the whole of its construction is reproduced: Paul's 'accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not' becomes 'according to that which he hath ... and to him that hath not should be given'. The final clause inverts a second singleton: “hath not shall be taken” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:29, 'but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath'. Acts 4:35's 'distribution was made unto every man according as he had need' stands behind 18:29's 'according to their needs and their wants'.
provenance.significance: The inversion at the end of the verse is the finding. Matthew's parable of the talents states the harshest economic sentence in the gospels — to him that hath, more; from him that hath not, even what he has — and Alma's rule ends 'and to him that hath not should be given'. The Book of Mormon takes the KJV's one occurrence of that clause and reverses its verb, so that the law of the church at Mormon is the parable of the talents run backwards. Paul's collection principle supplies the first half of the sentence and the Matthean reversal supplies the last four words, and the two together are a redistribution rule assembled out of two passages neither of which is one.

links.note: 'Every one according to that which he hath; if he have more abundantly, he should impart more abundantly; and he that hath but little, but little should be required; and to him that hath not should be given.' Paul's Jerusalem-collection formula, with the graduated middle clauses of 2 Corinthians 8:13–14 compressed and the tail turned against Matthew 25:29. The verse carries five 1830 variants, all of them the first edition's looser grammar ('according to that which he hath' for 1920's 'had'), and the present-tense 'hath' is the KJV's own tense in 2 Corinthians 8:12 — the 1920 correction to 'had' moves the sentence away from its source.
links.text: For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.

pericopes.text: And thus they should impart of their substance, of their own free will and good desires towards God, and to those priests that stood in need, yea, and to every needy, naked soul.

provenance.other: 'Of their own free will' is in no KJV verse in that form; the nearest is Ezra 7:13's 'of their own freewill' (of pilgrims volunteering for Jerusalem) and the freewill offerings of Leviticus 22 and Deuteronomy 16. 2 Corinthians 9:7's contribution is the doctrine rather than the string: 'not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver'.
provenance.significance: The two verses of Mosiah 18:27–28 run the two chapters of Paul's collection appeal in order — 2 Corinthians 8 supplies the proportional rule, 2 Corinthians 9 the requirement that the giving be voluntary — and the second is the one that makes the first bearable. Alma has just imposed a graduated levy; the next sentence makes it a free will offering, which is precisely the move 2 Corinthians 9:7 makes after 8:12–14.

links.note: 'And thus they should impart of their substance, of their own free will and good desires towards God, and to those priests that stood in need, yea, and to every needy, naked soul.' Recorded as an echo because the phrase is the Old Testament's freewill-offering language rather than Paul's wording, but the sequence is 2 Corinthians 8 then 9, in Paul's order, and it follows a verse that is demonstrably 2 Corinthians 8:12. The closing 'every needy, naked soul' reaches instead for the prophetic almsgiving formula of Isaiah 58:7, 'when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him'.
links.whyNot: Not one distinctive string is shared with 2 Corinthians 9:7; the case is entirely that 18:27 is demonstrably from the previous chapter of the same appeal and this sentence does the next thing that appeal does.
links.text: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.

pericopes.text: And this he said unto them, having been commanded of God; and they did walk uprightly before God, imparting to one another, both temporally and spiritually, according to their needs and their wants.

And now it came to pass that all this was done in Mormon; yea, by the waters of Mormon, in the forest that was near the waters of Mormon; yea, the place of Mormon, the waters of Mormon, the forest of Mormon, how beautiful are they to the eyes of them who there came to the knowledge of their redeemer; yea, and how blessed are they, for they shall sing to his praise forever.

provenance.other: “how beautiful” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Song of Solomon 7:1, Isaiah 52:7 and Romans 10:15. Within the Book of Mormon the phrase has already been used five times in six chapters, all of them Abinadi's: Mosiah 12:21 quotes Isaiah 52:7 entire, and Mosiah 15:15, 15:16, 15:17 and 15:18 expound it a clause at a time. Every one of those five reads 'how beautiful upon the mountains'. Mosiah 18:30 drops the mountains and pluralises the subject — 'how beautiful are they' — and those are precisely the two ways Romans 10:15 departs from Isaiah 52:7 ('How beautiful are the feet of them'). tools/mediation-check.py, run on Isaiah 52:7 against Romans 10:15, reports one decisive point each way and calls the verse a composite.
provenance.alternative: The mountains and the feet may have gone for the plainest of reasons: Alma's subject is not a messenger but a place — the forest, the fountain, the waters — and 'how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet' cannot be said of a pond. On that reading the plural and the missing mountains are grammar, not Romans, and the verse is straightforwardly Isaiah reached through Abinadi.
provenance.significance: The route is the finding, and it is the clearest instance so far of a source arriving in the Book of Mormon by way of an earlier Book of Mormon quotation rather than the Bible. Alma heard Isaiah 52:7 from Abinadi — 17:4 says he 'did write all the words which Abinadi had spoken' — and 18:30 is the sentence in which he applies it, not to a herald on a mountain but to the place where he baptised. Recovering the source's context does the rest: Isaiah 52:7's good tidings are that the exile is over and 'Thy God reigneth', and Alma is a fugitive in a forest hiding from a king. The next verses prove the point: 18:31, 'that they might not come to the knowledge of the king'; 18:34, the flight into the wilderness. The verse that publishes peace is spoken by people who are about to run.

links.note: 'The place of Mormon, the waters of Mormon, the forest of Mormon, how beautiful are they to the eyes of them who there came to the knowledge of their redeemer.' Hardy's apparatus cross-references Isaiah 52:7 here and the link is not in doubt; what the catalogue adds is the route and the departure. Abinadi's five uses of the verse in Mosiah 12 and 15 all keep 'upon the mountains'; Alma's drops it, and drops it in the direction of the New Testament's citation of the same verse. Whether that is Romans or simply the demands of the sentence is set out in the alternative above and is not settled here.
links.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

pericopes.text: And these things were done in the borders of the land, that they might not come to the knowledge of the king.

But behold, it came to pass that the king, having discovered a movement among the people, sent his servants to watch them. Therefore on the day that they were assembling themselves together to hear the word of the Lord, they were discovered unto the king.
And now the king saith that Alma was stirring up the people to a rebellion against him; therefore he sent his army to destroy them.

provenance.other: “stirreth up the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 23:5, where it is the charge the accusers press on Pilate after his first attempt to dismiss the case. “mover of sedition” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 24:5, Tertullus's parallel charge against Paul before Felix. The Book of Mormon's 'stirring up the people to a rebellion against him' has the first verb and the second's political content.
provenance.significance: This closes a circuit begun in the previous chapter. Mosiah 17:12's 'began to accuse him, saying' is Luke 23:2, the accusation laid before Pilate; Mosiah 18:33's 'stirring up the people' is Luke 23:5, the accusation renewed three verses later when Pilate tries to let the prisoner go. The Book of Mormon has taken two consecutive charges from one hearing and distributed them across two generations of the same conflict — the first kills Abinadi, the second sends Alma into the wilderness — and it takes them in Luke's order. That is a stronger argument for the chapter-17 links than anything inside chapter 17.

links.note: 'And now the king saith that Alma was stirring up the people to a rebellion against him; therefore he sent his army to destroy them.' A KJV singleton, and the second half of a two-part borrowing from the same Lukan hearing that supplied Mosiah 17:12. The 1830 present tense 'the king saith', modernised to 'said' in 1920, is worth noting: the first edition reports the charge in the tense the KJV uses for accusations in progress.
links.text: And they were the more fierce, saying, He stirreth up the people, teaching throughout all Jewry, beginning from Galilee to this place.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Alma, and the people of the Lord were apprised of the coming of the king’s army; therefore they took their tents and their families, and departed into the wilderness.
And they were in number about four hundred and fifty souls.
And it came to pass that the army of the king returned, having searched in vain for the people of the Lord.
And now behold, the forces of the king were small, having been reduced, and there began to be a division among the remainder of the people.

provenance.other: “a division among” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 7:43 and John 9:16, and both are the same formula about the same crowd — 'there was a division among the people because of him', 'there was a division among them'. John 10:19 reads 'a division therefore again among the Jews' and so falls outside the string. Mosiah 19:2's 'there began to be a division among the remainder of the people' has John 7:43's noun, preposition and object.
provenance.significance: John's divisions are always caused by a person and always split a crowd into those who accept him and those who do not; the Book of Mormon's is caused by the same thing one chapter later, since the 'lesser part' at 19:3 is the faction that has heard Abinadi and Alma. Taking the phrase from John rather than from the KJV's political vocabulary makes the coup at Mosiah 19 a religious schism with an army attached, which is what the narrative in fact reports.

links.note: 'The forces of the king were small, having been reduced, and there began to be a division among the remainder of the people.' A four-word run whose only KJV homes are two verses of the same Johannine formula. Catalogued at moderate confidence because 'division among the people' is unremarkable English; what raises it is that the KJV reserves the phrase for exactly this situation, a population split by a preacher, and that is the situation Mosiah 18 has just produced.
links.text: So there was a division among the people because of him.

pericopes.text: And the lesser part began to breathe out threatnings against the king, and there began to be a great contention among them.

provenance.other: “breathing out threatenings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:1, and the noun itself is nearly as rare: 'threatenings' occurs in exactly two, Acts 4:29 and Acts 9:1. The 1830 first edition spells it 'threatnings', which is the KJV's own contracted orthography surviving in the running text and lost in later editions.
provenance.significance: Acts 9:1's phrase belongs to Saul of Tarsus on the road to Damascus — the persecutor a verse away from becoming the apostle. Mosiah 17:2 has already put Acts 7:58's young man at Abinadi's execution, and this catalogue reads Alma as standing in that position; two chapters later the book takes the next stage of the same man's story and gives it to the party that will overthrow king Noah. Whether the writer meant the two borrowings to be read together, the effect is that the Book of Mormon narrates its own reformation in the vocabulary of Saul's — first the young man at the stoning, then the breathing out of threatenings — and reverses the polarity, since here the threatenings are directed at the persecuting king rather than at the church.

links.note: 'And the lesser part began to breathe out threatnings against the king, and there began to be a great contention among them.' A three-word KJV singleton in its exact grammatical form, and the 1830 spelling preserves the KJV's contraction. Note the transposition: in Acts the participle describes a man moving against the disciples, in Mosiah it describes the faction that has just been made disciples moving against the state.
links.text: And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,

pericopes.text: And now there was a man among them whose name was Gideon, and he being a strong man, and an enemy to the king, therefore he drew his sword and swore in his wrath, that he would slay the king.

provenance.other: “drew his sword” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:51 — the disciple in Gethsemane who strikes the high priest's servant, and whom Jesus rebukes two verses later. The Book of Mormon's own Gideon is named for the judge of Judges 6–8, whose one sword-drawing scene is a negative: Judges 8:20's 'the youth drew not his sword: for he feared'.
provenance.alternative: 'Drew his sword' is ordinary narrative English and its absence elsewhere in the KJV may be accidental — the KJV usually writes 'drew a sword' or 'drew out his sword'.
provenance.significance: The two candidate backgrounds pull opposite ways and that is what makes the verse worth an entry. The KJV's only man who draws his sword does so in defence of a condemned prophet, against the servants of a high priest, and is told to put it up; the KJV's Gideon presides over a son who will not draw his. Mosiah's Gideon draws his against a king who has burned a prophet, and the narrative neither rebukes him nor lets him finish — 19:6 stops the blow with a Lamanite army. The Book of Mormon has taken the sword-drawing of the passion, which is forbidden, and suspended the question rather than answering it.

links.note: 'He drew his sword and swore in his wrath, that he would slay the king.' A KJV singleton, but a short one, and the sense is not transferred whole — this is why the row is an echo rather than an allusion. Recorded chiefly because Gideon's name makes the Judges background unavoidable and the Judges background says the opposite.
links.whyNot: Three ordinary words. The KJV's failure to use them elsewhere is a fact about its idiom rather than a mark of distinctiveness, and nothing else in Mosiah 19:4 touches Gethsemane.
links.text: And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest’s, and smote off his ear.

provenance.route: Psalm 95:11 or Hebrews 3:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the verse cannot decide between them
provenance.other: “sware in my wrath” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 95:11 and Hebrews 3:11, which are the psalm and the epistle's quotation of it, and they are verbally identical at the phrase; “sworn in my wrath” occurs in exactly one, Hebrews 4:3. Swearing in wrath is otherwise God's act alone in the KJV. tools/mediation-check.py, run on Psalm 95:11 against Hebrews 3:11, finds no decisive divergence, and the reason is that the two agree at every word the Book of Mormon reproduces; the Book of Mormon's own preterite is 'swore', which is neither text's 'sware' nor Hebrews 4:3's 'sworn', so the form cannot be traced. `mediation` is recorded as uncertain on that basis rather than defaulted.
provenance.significance: Every KJV oath sworn in wrath is God's, and its content is always exclusion from rest — 'they shall not enter into my rest'. Gideon's oath is a man's, and its content is regicide. Read against the psalm the sentence is blasphemous by construction: a private citizen assumes the one formula the King James Bible reserves for divine judicial anger. Read against Hebrews 3–4, whose argument is that the wilderness generation lost its rest by rebellion, it is worse, because Gideon's people are a wilderness generation in rebellion against their king.

links.note: 'And he drew his sword and swore in his wrath, that he would slay the king.' Offered under CONVENTIONS §0a: the phrase is short and the transfer from God to a man is so complete that no reader would notice it, which is an argument against the borrowing and also the reason it is interesting if it is one. The mediation result is negative and is recorded as such.
links.whyNot: Four common words, and 'swore in his wrath' is idiomatic English independent of the KJV. Nothing else in the verse points at Psalm 95 or Hebrews.
links.text: Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he fought with the king; and when the king saw that he was about to overpower him, he fled and ran and got upon the tower, which was near the temple.

provenance.other: “top of the tower” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 9:51, which is the tower of Thebez, the last of the three towers in the Abimelech narrative. Mosiah 19:5's king 'fled and ran and got upon the tower, which was near the temple' — Judges 9:46 has the men of Shechem entering 'an hold of the house of the god Berith', a tower attached to a temple, which is the only tower in the KJV so described.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's controlling source and the name gives it away. Judges 9 is the story of Gideon's son Abimelech, who makes himself king over Israel by murder, is cursed by Jotham with fire ('let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the men of Shechem ... and devour Abimelech'), burns a thousand people in a tower by a temple, and dies at a second tower when he is struck from above and, unable to face the shame of it, begs to be killed. Mosiah 19 redistributes every element and inverts the genealogy: the pursuer is called Gideon, the king who flees to the tower is the Abimelech, and the fire of Jotham's curse arrives at 19:20 on the king rather than from him. Reading the two together answers a question the Book of Mormon never asks aloud — why a man called Gideon should be the one to hunt a king up a tower. In Judges the tower-burner is Gideon's son; here Gideon is the one at the foot of the ladder.

links.note: 'He fled and ran and got upon the tower, which was near the temple. And Gideon pursued after him and was about to get upon the tower to slay the king.' The KJV has one 'top of the tower', one tower joined to a temple, and one narrative in which a usurping king, a man named Gideon and a death by fire all belong together — Judges 9. The Book of Mormon's version is that narrative with the roles reassigned, and the reassignment is legible only because the name has been kept.
links.text: But there was a strong tower within the city, and thither fled all the men and women, and all they of the city, and shut it to them, and gat them up to the top of the tower.

pericopes.text: And Gideon pursued after him and was about to get upon the tower to slay the king, and the king cast his eyes round about towards the land of Shemlon, and behold, the army of the Lamanites were within the borders of the land.
And now the king cried out in the anguish of his soul, saying, Gideon, spare me, for the Lamanites are upon us, and they will destroy them; yea, they will destroy my people.

provenance.other: “the anguish of his soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 42:21, and the shorter “the anguish of” occurs in exactly two. Genesis 42:21 is Joseph's brothers in Egypt, twenty years on: 'We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear.'
provenance.significance: The KJV's one anguish of the soul belongs to a man pleading for his life with his own kin, who hear him and refuse — and the verse is not the pleading itself but the memory of it, spoken by the men who refused, at the moment they realise they are being punished for it. Mosiah 19:7 gives that phrase to king Noah begging Gideon, and Gideon does what Joseph's brothers did not: he hears, and spares him. What follows is the point. The mercy is not the end of the story; 19:20 has Noah burned by his own people, and 19:24 has them return 'rejoicing'. The Book of Mormon has borrowed the vocabulary of a guilt that took twenty years to arrive and attached it to a reprieve that lasts thirteen verses, and it lets the reader supply the comparison. Note also 19:8's editorial line, 'the king was not so much concerned about his people, as he was about his own life' — which is exactly the accusation Genesis 42:21 has the brothers level at themselves.

links.note: 'And now the king cried out in the anguish of his soul, saying, Gideon, spare me, for the Lamanites are upon us, and they will destroy them; yea, they will destroy my people.' Five words from the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, and the 1830 reading makes the sentence worse than the modern text does: 'they will destroy them' at the first clause, corrected to 'us' in 1920, has Noah beginning the plea by speaking of his people in the third person and only afterwards claiming them. The first edition's pronoun is the evidence for 19:8's verdict on him.
links.text: And they said one to another, We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear; therefore is this distress come upon us.

pericopes.text: And now the king was not so much concerned about his people, as he was about his own life; nevertheless, Gideon did spare his life.
And the king commanded the people that they should flee before the Lamanites, and he himself did go before them, and they did flee into the wilderness with their women and their children.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites did pursue them, and did overtake them, and began to slay them.
Now it came to pass that the king commanded them that all the men should leave their wives and their children, and flee before the Lamanites.
Now there were many that would not leave them, but had rather stay and perish with them. And the rest left their wives and their children and fled.

provenance.other: “if I perish I perish” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Esther 4:16, the Bible's classic formula for choosing to share the fate of a threatened people rather than escape it. 'Perish with' is commoner — six verses — and the Book of Mormon's phrasing, 'had rather stay and perish with them', is its own.
provenance.significance: Esther's sentence is spoken by someone who could have survived by keeping quiet, and Ruth 1:17's 'where thou diest, will I die' by someone who could have gone home. Mosiah 19:12 divides a whole population by that choice in a single verse — 'there were many that would not leave them, but had rather stay and perish with them. And the rest left their wives and their children and fled' — and 19:19 shows the fugitives adopting it afterwards, swearing to return and 'also perish with them'. The chapter is testing every character against Esther's formula, and the men who fail it at 19:12 are the same men who at 19:20 burn the king who told them to run.

links.note: Recorded as an echo, not an allusion: no string is shared. What is shared is the KJV's one articulated form of the choice, and the Book of Mormon puts that choice at the exact hinge of its narrative, since the women who stay are the ones whose beauty saves the people at 19:14 and the men who run are the ones who kill the king at 19:20.
links.whyNot: A resemblance of situation with no verbal contact whatever. Solidarity with the doomed is a human commonplace and needs no source; the entry exists because Esther 4:16 is the KJV's only formulation of it and the chapter turns on the choice twice.
links.text: Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that those that tarried with their wives and their children, caused that their fair daughters should stand forth and plead with the Lamanites, that they would not slay them.

provenance.other: No phrase is shared. The KJV's own marker for the type-scene is “fair to look upon”, which occurs in exactly two verses, Genesis 24:16 and Genesis 26:7, the second of them Isaac's version of this same episode; Genesis 12:11 has 'a fair woman to look upon'. Mosiah 19:14 has 'they were charmed with the beauty of their women', which is not KJV diction at all.
provenance.significance: The patriarchal wife-sister scene has a fixed shape: a man enters a stronger people's territory, fears he will be killed, and survives because of his wife's beauty — 'they will kill me, but they will save thee alive ... that it may be well with me for thy sake; and my soul shall live because of thee'. Mosiah 19:11-15 runs the shape at national scale and moves the shame. Abraham arranges the deception himself and profits by it; Noah's men are ordered to abandon their wives outright, and it is the women who, unprompted, 'stand forth and plead' and save the people who stayed. The Genesis scene's discreditable bargain — a man's life bought with a woman's beauty — is exactly what happens here, and the Book of Mormon assigns the discredit to the men who fled rather than to the arrangement.

links.note: A figural link with no wording behind it, offered under CONVENTIONS §0a and marked kjvSpecific 'no' accordingly. It is included because the type-scene is one of the most recognisable in the Pentateuch, because Mosiah 19:11-15 reproduces its logic step for step, and because the chapter's judgment on the episode is only legible against it.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal at all; and the Lamanites sparing captive women for their beauty needs no literary source, being a commonplace of war narrative. A reader who declines this row loses nothing from the chapter's other links.
links.text: Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister: that it may be well with me for thy sake; and my soul shall live because of thee.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lamanites had compassion on them, for they were charmed with the beauty of their women;

therefore the Lamanites did spare their lives, and took them captives, and carried them back to the land of Nephi, and granted unto them that they might possess the land, under the conditions that they would deliver up the king Noah into the hands of the Lamanites, and deliver up their property, even one half of all they possessed; one half of their gold, and their silver, and all their precious things; and thus they should pay tribute to the king of the Lamanites, from year to year.
And now there was one of the sons of the king among those that was taken captive, whose name was Limhi.
And now Limhi was desirous that his father should not be destroyed; nevertheless, Limhi was not ignorant of the iniquities of his father, he himself, being a just man.

provenance.other: “being a just man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 1:19; the bare 'a just man' stands in eight. Matthew 1:19 is the only place in the Bible where the phrase is used to explain a decision not to expose someone: 'Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.'
