provenance.significance: Matthew's logic is counter-intuitive and is the whole reason the phrase is memorable: Joseph is *therefore* unwilling to shame her — justice, in that sentence, is what restrains the just man from the public punishment he is entitled to exact. Mosiah 19:17 reproduces the structure exactly, and reproduces its oddity: 'Limhi was desirous that his father should not be destroyed; nevertheless, Limhi was not ignorant of the iniquities of his father, he himself, being a just man.' The clause explains a refusal to see a guilty man exposed and killed, by a son who knows precisely what his father has done. Recover Matthew 1:19 and the sentence is not saying that Limhi was righteous despite wanting to spare his father; it is saying that sparing him is what his righteousness consists in — which is a real claim, and one the chapter then overrules, since the people burn Noah anyway.

links.note: 'Limhi was desirous that his father should not be destroyed; nevertheless, Limhi was not ignorant of the iniquities of his father, he himself, being a just man.' A four-word KJV singleton used in the one office the KJV gives it. The 1830 'those that was with him' at 19:18 and 'those that was taken captive' at 19:16, both corrected in 1920, are the first edition's grammar throughout this stretch and are noted rather than argued.
links.text: Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Gideon sent men into the wilderness secretly, to search for the king, and those that was with him. And it came to pass that they met the people in the wilderness, all save the king and his priests.

Now they had sworn in their hearts that they would return to the land of Nephi, and if their wives and their children were slain, and also those that had tarried with them, that they would seek revenge, and also perish with them.
And the king commanded them that they should not return; and they were angry with the king, and caused that he should suffer, even unto death by fire.

provenance.other: No phrase is shared; the link is the shape of the curse and its fulfilment. Judges 9:20 is Jotham's curse — 'let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the men of Shechem ... and let fire come out from the men of Shechem ... and devour Abimelech' — and Judges 9:49 reports the first half discharged, a thousand burned in the tower of Shechem, with 9:56 supplying the narrator's verdict: 'Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father.'
provenance.significance: Jotham's curse is the only reciprocal fire-curse in the Bible: fire from the king to the people, and fire from the people back to the king. Mosiah 17:15-18 has Abinadi curse Noah's seed and priests with death by fire, and Mosiah 19:20 discharges it against Noah himself — 'they were angry with the king, and caused that he should suffer, even unto death by fire' — burned by the very men he had commanded to abandon their families. The first half of Abinadi's curse is not forgotten either; Alma 25:5-11 will report the priests' descendants burned. So the Book of Mormon has built its longest-running curse on the structure of the one in Judges 9, and has laid it over the same narrative that gave chapter 19 its tower and its Gideon. Whether the writer had Judges 9 open or had merely absorbed it, the two curses do the same work: they make the king's death a judicial act of the text rather than a political accident.

links.note: 'And they were angry with the king, and caused that he should suffer, even unto death by fire.' The death Abinadi promised at 17:18 in Ezekiel's and Jeremiah's words, delivered in the form of Judges 9. Catalogued as figural because there is no wording to test — kjvSpecific is therefore 'uncertain' rather than 'yes', since the borrowing, if it is one, is of a plot and not of an English sentence. It earns high confidence from the density of the rest of the Judges 9 material in this chapter (see 19:5), not from anything in this verse alone.
links.text: But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the men of Shechem, and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem, and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech.

pericopes.text: And they were about to take the priests also and put them to death, and they fled before them.

And it came to pass that they were about to return to the land of Nephi, and they met the men of Gideon. And the men of Gideon told them of all that had happened to their wives and their children; and that the Lamanites had granted unto them that they might possess the land, by paying a tribute to the Lamanites of one half of all they possessed.
And the people told the men of Gideon that they had slain the king, and his priests had fled from them farther into the wilderness.

And it came to pass that after they had ended the ceremony, that they returned to the land of Nephi, rejoicing, because their wives and their children were not slain; and they told Gideon what they had done to the king.
And it came to pass that the king of the Lamanites made an oath unto them, that his people should not slay them.

And also Limhi, being the son of the king, having the kingdom conferred upon him by the people, made oath unto the king of the Lamanites, that his people should pay tribute unto him, even one half of all they possessed.
And it came to pass that Limhi began to establish the kingdom, and to establish peace among his people.

And the king of the Lamanites set guards round about the land, that he might keep the people of Limhi in the land, that they might not depart into the wilderness; and he did support his guards out of the tribute which he did receive from the Nephites.
And now king Limhi did have continual peace in his kingdom, for the the space of two years, that the Lamanites did not molest them nor seek to destroy them.
Now there was a place in Shemlon, where the daughters of the Lamanites did gather themselves together for to sing, and to dance, and to make themselves merry.

links.text: And see, and, behold, if the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in dances, then come ye out of the vineyards, and catch you every man his wife of the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.

provenance.other: “daughters of Shiloh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “catch you every man his wife” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them Judges 21:21. The infinitive “to dance” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 21:21 and Ecclesiastes 3:4; Mosiah 20 uses it three times in five verses. The individual words are ordinary English and no version comparison can be run on them, which is why kjvSpecific is left uncertain: what is borrowed here is a scene, not a sentence.
provenance.significance: Judges 21:19-23 is the only account in the KJV of women seized while dancing at a festival, and Mosiah 20:1-5 reproduces it almost item for item: a known place where daughters gather to dance, men lying hidden nearby, a seizure, a carrying-off into their own country, and aggrieved kinsmen who have to be pacified rather than fought. What makes the borrowing more than furniture is the motive. In Judges the Benjamites take the daughters of Shiloh because an oath has left them without wives; in Mosiah the priests of Noah take the daughters of the Lamanites because they “durst not return to their wives and their children” (20:3). Both groups are men cut off from their own households who repair the loss by theft, and in both the theft is then managed diplomatically by a third party — Judges 21:22's “Be favourable unto them for our sakes” is what Gideon proposes at Mosiah 20:19-22. Recover the source's frame and the judgment on the episode comes with it: Judges 21 is the last chapter of a book that ends “there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes”, and the men who do this in Mosiah are the priests of a king the record has already condemned.

links.note: The chapter opens by building the stage of Judges 21:19-23 and then walks the episode through it. Judges: the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in dances, the men of Benjamin lie in wait, come out of the vineyards, catch every man his wife, and go to their inheritance; when the fathers complain, they are talked round. Mosiah: the daughters of the Lamanites gather to sing and to dance, the priests of Noah tarry in the wilderness and watch them, come forth out of their secret places, carry off twenty and four of them, and when the fathers come armed they are talked round. There is no reproduced clause — this is catalogued as an allusion on the scene and the sequence, not on a run of words — but the one distinctive verbal element, the infinitive “to dance” used absolutely of a festival, occurs in only two KJV verses and one of them is Judges 21:21. The verbal case is made separately at 20:5, where the wording of the ambush is taken verbatim from the chapter next door.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there was one day a small number of them gathered together to sing and to dance.

And now the priests of king Noah, being ashamed to return to the city of Nephi, yea, and also fearing that the people would slay them, therefore they durst not return to their wives and their children.
And having tarried in the wilderness, and having discovered the daughters of the Lamanites, they laid and watched them;

and when there were but few of them gathered together to dance, they came forth out of their secret places, and took them and carried them into the wilderness; yea, twenty and four of the daughters of the Lamanites they carried into the wilderness.

links.text: And all the men of Israel rose up out of their place, and put themselves in array at Baaltamar: and the liers in wait of Israel came forth out of their places, even out of the meadows of Gibeah.

provenance.other: “came forth out of their places” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 20:33, and even the truncated “forth out of their” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Mosiah 20:5 reads “they came forth out of their secret places”, which is that singleton with one adjective inserted.
provenance.significance: The wording comes from the wrong side of the story, and that is the finding. Judges 20:33 is the ambush at Gibeah: the liers in wait of Israel come forth out of their places to destroy Benjamin for the outrage done to a woman. One chapter later the survivors of that destruction are told to lie in wait for the daughters of Shiloh, which is the scene Mosiah 20:1-5 is playing. So the chapter takes its plot from Judges 21 and its sentence from Judges 20, and in doing so gives the punishers' idiom to the men committing the offence. The priests of Noah come out of hiding in the words of the army that came out of hiding to avenge exactly this crime.

links.note: “They came forth out of their secret places, and took them and carried them into the wilderness.” The five-word frame is a KJV singleton belonging to the ambush of Judges 20:33, and the ambush there is the one that leads directly to Judges 21's seizure of the daughters of Shiloh — the scene this chapter is otherwise reproducing (see 20:1). Two verses of the same three-chapter block, used for two different things: the shape of the episode from one, the sentence from the other. “Secret places” is the addition, and it is not from Judges; it is the KJV's ordinary phrase for a hiding place, in nine verses.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when the Lamanites found that their daughters had been missing, they were angry with the people of Limhi; for they thought it was the people of Limhi.
Therefore they sent their armies forth; yea, even the king himself went before his people; and they went up to the land of Nephi, to destroy the people of Limhi.

And now Limhi had discovered them from the tower; even all their preparations for war did he discover; therefore he gathered his people together, and laid wait for them in the fields, and in the forests.
And it came to pass that when the Lamanites had come up, that the people of Limhi began to fall upon them from their waiting places, and began to slay them.
And it came to pass that the battle became exceeding sore, for they fought like lions for their prey.

And it came to pass that the people of Limhi began to drive the Lamanites before them, yet they were not half so numerous as the Lamanites. But they fought for their lives, and for their wives, and for their children; therefore they exerted themselves, and like dragons did they fight.

And it came to pass that they found the king of the Lamanites among the number of their dead; yet he was not dead, having been wounded and left upon the ground, so speedy was the flight of his people.

And they took him and bound up his wounds, and brought him before Limhi, and said, Behold, here is the king of the Lamanites; he having received a wound, hath fallen among their dead, and they have left him; and behold, we have brought him before you; and now let us slay him.

links.text: And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.

provenance.other: “bound up his wounds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 10:34. The looser “bound up” is in eleven, and none of the other ten has a wounded man in it except Isaiah 1:6, where the wounds are precisely NOT bound up.
provenance.significance: The parable of the good Samaritan is the KJV's one story about binding up the wounds of a man left lying by the way, and Mosiah 20:12-13 assembles its furniture before it uses its words: the king is “wounded and left upon the ground” by his own fleeing people, as the traveller is left half dead by the roadside and passed by; the people who stop are the enemy he came to destroy, as the one who stops is the Samaritan; and the first thing they do is bind up his wounds. Luke's question is “which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?” Mosiah answers it twice and in both directions — here, and again at 20:26, where the Lamanites see Limhi's people unarmed and “had compassion on them”, which is Luke 10:33's clause about the Samaritan. What the parable does not supply is the sentence that follows: “and now let us slay him.” The men who have just performed the Samaritan's act propose the thieves'.

links.note: “And they took him and bound up his wounds, and brought him before Limhi.” Four words verbatim from a KJV singleton, and the singleton is the good Samaritan. The situation matches the parable at every point that matters — a wounded man abandoned where he fell, help from the party with the least obligation to give it — and the chapter returns to the same twelve verses of Luke at 20:26. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as an allusion on the rarity of the phrase and the fit of the scene.

links.text: Come now therefore, and let us slay him, and cast him into some pit, and we will say, Some evil beast hath devoured him: and we shall see what will become of his dreams.

provenance.other: “let us slay him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 37:20, and the answering “let us not kill him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 37:21. Mosiah reproduces the first outright and answers it with “Ye shall not slay him” at 20:14. tools/mediation-check.py against Acts 7:9, the New Testament's retelling of the episode, returns one decisive point for Genesis: Acts has none of the words, only the fact of the sale.
provenance.significance: These are the two sentences that start the Joseph story, and they arrive here as a pair. The brothers say “let us slay him”; Reuben says “Let us not kill him”, and because he prevails Joseph goes into Egypt instead of into a pit — which is how Israel ends in bondage. Mosiah runs the same exchange: the soldiers say “now let us slay him”, the king says “Ye shall not slay him”, and because he prevails the Lamanite king lives to be pacified, his people are spared, and the people of Limhi accept servitude to them at 20:22 and are still in it two chapters later. In both texts the mercy is real and the mercy is what delivers the merciful into bondage.

links.note: “And now let us slay him” is a KJV singleton, and it belongs to Joseph's brothers at the pit; the refusal that follows it in Mosiah 20:14 answers the refusal that follows it in Genesis 37:21, itself a second singleton. The proposal and the veto are not a common pair of formulas — they are one scene in the KJV, and this chapter takes both halves of it in consecutive verses. The mediation test is worth running because Acts 7:9 retells the episode; it returns Genesis decisively, since Stephen keeps the event and none of the language.

pericopes.text: But Limhi saith unto them, Ye shall not slay him, but bring him hither, that I may see him. And they brought him. And Limhi saith unto him, What cause have ye to come up to war against my people? Behold, my people have not broken the oath that I made unto you; therefore, why should ye break the oath which ye made unto my people?
And now the king said, I have broken the oath, because thy people did carry away the daughters of my people; therefore in my anger I did cause my people to come up to war against thy people.

links.text: And Laban said to Jacob, What hast thou done, that thou hast stolen away unawares to me, and carried away my daughters, as captives taken with the sword?

provenance.other: “carried away my daughters” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 31:26, and “away my daughters” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon has “carry away the daughters of my people”, which shares the verb and the object but not the possessive, so no version comparison decides it and kjvSpecific stays uncertain.
provenance.significance: Laban overtaking Jacob is the KJV's one story of a man who musters his kinsmen and pursues a people in anger because they “carried away my daughters”, and the four beats that follow it in Genesis 31 are the four beats that follow it here. The accused party, who genuinely knows nothing of a theft, pronounces death on whoever did it — “With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live” (31:32), against “whosoever hath done this thing shall perish” (Mosiah 20:16). A search is then made through the whole company (31:33-37, “thou hast searched all my stuff”; “Therefore he caused a search to be made among his people”). The search is fruitless in the sense that matters, because the guilty party is inside the household and not where anyone is looking — Rachel sitting on the images, the priests of Noah gone into the wilderness. And the episode ends not in battle but in an oath sworn between two peoples who then separate in peace (31:44-53; Mosiah 20:24-26). Genesis 31 is the frame of the second half of this chapter, and the accusation at 20:15 is where it is set.

links.note: “Thy people did carry away the daughters of my people; therefore in my anger I did cause my people to come up to war.” The verbal contact is the verb and its object — the KJV's one “carried away my daughters” is Laban's accusation to Jacob — and on that alone this would be an echo at best. It is catalogued at moderate because the accusation is followed here by the rest of Genesis 31 in order: the innocent ruler's death-sentence on an unknown thief, the search of the whole camp, the guilty party already outside it, and a reconciling oath between two peoples. A shared phrase can be coincidence; a shared phrase that brings its own next four scenes with it is harder to call one. See 20:16 for the verse where the wording of that sentence comes from elsewhere.

pericopes.text: Now Limhi had heard nothing concerning this matter; therefore he saith, I will search among my people, and whosoever hath done this thing shall perish. Therefore he caused a search to be made among his people.

links.text: And David’s anger was greatly kindled against the man; and he said to Nathan, As the LORD liveth, the man that hath done this thing shall surely die:

provenance.other: “done this thing shall” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 12:5. The whole formula “hath done this thing” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Genesis 21:26, Judges 6:29 and 2 Samuel 12:5 — and all three are operative across Mosiah 20:16-17.
provenance.significance: Nathan's parable is the KJV's set piece of a ruler pronouncing sentence on an offender who turns out to belong to his own house, and the words Limhi uses are David's: “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” against “whosoever hath done this thing shall perish”. Limhi is not the offender, but the offenders are his father's priests, ordained by the king whose throne he sits on and whose sins have already been prophesied against this people (20:21); the sentence he swears blind lands on his own inheritance exactly as David's does. The other two KJV verses with the phrase are doing work here too. Genesis 21:26 is Abimelech answering Abraham's complaint about a well his servants had violently taken away — “I wot not who hath done this thing; neither didst thou tell me, neither yet heard I of it” — which is Mosiah 20:16's opening clause, “Now Limhi had heard nothing concerning this matter”, and that episode ends where this one ends, in an oath sworn between two rulers who part in peace. Judges 6:29 is the search after an outrage done in the night: “Who hath done this thing? And when they enquired and asked, they said, Gideon the son of Joash hath done this thing” — and the next verse of Mosiah is Gideon stepping forward, followed by a plea that the accused not be put to death, which is Joash's speech at Judges 6:31.

links.note: “Whosoever hath done this thing shall perish. Therefore he caused a search to be made among his people.” The four-word run is a KJV singleton and it is Nathan's parable: a ruler swearing death on an unknown offender who proves to be of his own house. The formula's two other KJV homes are both audible in the same breath — Abimelech's “I wot not who hath done this thing … neither yet heard I of it” behind “Limhi had heard nothing concerning this matter”, and the search of Judges 6:29 whose answer is the name Gideon, which is the next word of Mosiah 20:17. Three of the KJV's three occurrences of a phrase, converging on two consecutive verses, is not a thing a writer does by accident with one of them.
links.whyNot: The Judges 6:29 strand is the weakest of the three and should be read as resonance rather than as evidence. Gideon is not introduced here: he is already the king's captain in the narrative from Mosiah 19:4, so his name arriving after a search is asked about is at least partly the accident of a character who was going to speak anyway. The 2 Samuel 12:5 and Genesis 21:26 contacts stand on their own wording and carry the link.

pericopes.text: Now when Gideon had heard these things, he being the king’s captain, he went forth and said unto the king, I pray thee forbear, and do not search this people, and lay not this thing to their charge.

links.text: And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

provenance.other: “lay not this” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 7:60, and “to their charge” occurs in exactly three — 2 Chronicles 8:14 (of Levites and their duties), Acts 7:60, and 2 Timothy 4:16. Mosiah 20:17 reads “lay not this thing to their charge” against Acts's “lay not this sin to their charge”: a six-word frame with a single substitution, and the substituted word is the one the situation requires, since Gideon's whole point is that no sin was committed by these people.
provenance.significance: The sentence is Stephen's dying prayer for the men stoning him, and its transfer here reverses who is protected. In Acts the speaker is the victim and the people he shields are guilty; in Mosiah the speaker is an officer of the state and the people he shields are innocent — the crime was committed by the priests of the previous king, who are in the wilderness and out of reach. What survives the reversal is the posture: someone interposing himself between a punishing power and a group about to be charged. Two further things come with the source. The prayer closes a speech (Acts 7:2-53) that is a recital of Israel's history from Abraham through the exodus, and Limhi's people are about to walk that history themselves in Mosiah 22; and the other KJV verse with the phrase, 2 Timothy 4:16, joins it to a petition — “I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge” — which is the form Mosiah has, since Gideon's clause is governed by “I pray thee forbear”.

links.note: “I pray thee forbear, and do not search this people, and lay not this thing to their charge.” Six words of Acts 7:60 with “sin” changed to “thing”, and “lay not this” is a KJV singleton. The petition frame — an entreaty governing the clause — belongs to the phrase's only other New Testament home, 2 Timothy 4:16. The borrowing is a genuine reversal of function: Stephen asks that the guilty not be charged, Gideon that the innocent not be, and the same six words serve both.

links.text: He answered and said to Arioch the king’s captain, Why is the decree so hasty from the king? Then Arioch made the thing known to Daniel.

provenance.other: “the king's captain”, singular, is a KJV singleton, Daniel 2:15, where it names Arioch. 2 Chronicles 26:11 has 'the king's captainS', plural, an administrative title in a muster list, not a second instance of this exact phrase.
provenance.significance: Arioch the king's captain is carrying out a decree that a whole class of men be put to death; Daniel intercepts him, asks “Why is the decree so hasty from the king?”, and goes in to the king to have the decree stayed. Mosiah 20:16-17 has the same three elements — a hasty royal sentence on an undetermined body of people, an interception, and a petition to the king that stops it — with the roles compressed: Gideon is both the king's captain and the Daniel who intervenes. The compression is what makes this an echo rather than an allusion; if the borrowing is real, the writer has given one man both parts.

links.note: Gideon is introduced in this verse as “the king's captain”, a title the KJV uses twice, and the occurrence that is not a muster-list entry is Arioch in Daniel 2:15 — an officer standing between a king's death decree and the men it would kill, whose scene is stopped by a petition for time. That is the shape of Mosiah 20:16-17. Recorded at moderate because the fit is situational and the title is ordinary English.
links.whyNot: “The king's captain” is a plain designation, not a distinctive phrase, and its other KJV occurrence shows it is not proprietary to Daniel. Nothing else of Daniel 2 — the dream, the wise men, the request for time — appears anywhere in Mosiah 20, and the intervening speech at 20:17-22 takes its actual language from Acts 7:60 and Exodus 14:12. If the echo is declined, nothing else in the chapter changes.

pericopes.text: For do ye not remember the priests of thy father, which this people sought to destroy? And are they not in the wilderness? And is it not they which have stolen the daughters of the Lamanites?

And now behold, and tell the king of these things, that he may tell his people, that they may be pacified towards us: for behold, they are already preparing to come against us; and behold also, there are but few of us.

links.text: That thou mayest remember, and be confounded, and never open thy mouth any more because of thy shame, when I am pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done, saith the Lord GOD.

provenance.other: “pacified” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Esther 7:10 (“then was the king's wrath pacified”, intransitive, with no object of reconciliation) and Ezekiel 16:63. “Pacified toward” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 16:63. The 1830 text reads “pacified towards” in all four occurrences, and “towards” with the -s is in no KJV verse at all — a nineteenth-century spelling laid over a seventeenth-century construction, which is worth recording because it shows the borrowing being naturalised rather than copied.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 16 ends with the two ideas that are this chapter's entire diplomatic problem, four verses apart. At 16:59 Jerusalem is the party “which hast despised the oath in breaking the covenant”; at 16:63 she is told that God will nevertheless be “pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done”. Mosiah 20 turns on a broken oath — the king says at 20:15 “I have broken the oath” — and then on getting a king pacified toward a people who did not break it. Recovering the source redistributes the parts strangely and productively: in Ezekiel the offended party who must be pacified is God and the oath-breaker is his bride, while here the party who must be pacified is himself the one who admits to breaking the oath. And what pacifies him is not a covenant remembered but a people walking out to meet him with no weapons in their hands.

links.note: “That they may be pacified towards us”, and again at 20:20, 20:24 and 20:26 — four times in eight verses, of a verb the KJV uses twice in the whole Bible. Only one of the two, Ezekiel 16:63, takes a person as the object of reconciliation, and “pacified toward” is a KJV singleton there. The chapter has already used the other half of Ezekiel's ending: the oath despised in breaking the covenant at 16:59 is what Mosiah 20:14-15 is arguing about. A rare verb, its rare preposition, and its neighbouring verse's subject all landing in one episode is the kind of contact that does not need a long run of words to be real.

pericopes.text: And behold, they come with their numerous hosts; and except the king doth pacify them towards us, we must perish.
For are not the words of Abinadi fulfilled, which he prophesied against us? and all this because we would not hearken unto the word of the Lord, and turn from our iniquities?

links.text: As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil is come upon us: yet made we not our prayer before the LORD our God, that we might turn from our iniquities, and understand thy truth.

provenance.other: “turn from our iniquities” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 9:13, and so does “all this evil is come upon us”, in the same verse. “Which he spake against us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 9:12, the verse immediately before it.
provenance.significance: Daniel 9 is the KJV's model penitential confession, and its logic is precisely the logic of Mosiah 20:21: a prophet's word was spoken against this people, it has now been fulfilled, and it was fulfilled because they would not obey. Daniel 9:12-13 supplies both halves — “he hath confirmed his words, which he spake against us … all this evil is come upon us: yet made we not our prayer before the LORD our God, that we might turn from our iniquities” — and Mosiah compresses them into one rhetorical question. What the substitution does is the interesting part. Daniel's authority is Moses: “as it is written in the law of Moses.” Mosiah's is Abinadi, a prophet burned by this people's own king two chapters earlier. Putting Abinadi where Daniel puts the law of Moses is a large claim made silently, and it is made in Daniel's words.

links.note: “Are not the words of Abinadi fulfilled, which he prophesied against us? and all this because we would not hearken unto the word of the Lord, and turn from our iniquities?” Two KJV singletons from consecutive verses of Daniel 9: “which he spake against us” at 9:12, and “turn from our iniquities” at 9:13, where it is likewise governed by “all this”. The confession is Daniel's, and the substitution — Abinadi standing where Daniel has the law of Moses — is what the borrowing is for.

pericopes.text: And now let us pacify the king, and we fulfil the oath which we have made unto him: for it is better that we should be in bondage, than that we should lose our lives; therefore, let us put a stop to the shedding of so much blood.

links.text: Is not this the word that we did tell thee in Egypt, saying, Let us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians? For it had been better for us to serve the Egyptians, than that we should die in the wilderness.

provenance.other: “than that we should” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 14:12. The framing “it is better that” occurs in exactly two, Genesis 29:19 and 2 Samuel 18:3, of which only Genesis 29:19 has the comparative pair — and it compares two suitors, not two fates; the sense that decides the source is Exodus's, servitude weighed against death.
provenance.significance: This is the most consequential sentence in the chapter, and it is Israel at the Red Sea. Exodus 14:12 is the murmur — “it had been better for us to serve the Egyptians, than that we should die in the wilderness” — that Moses answers with “Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD.” In Mosiah the same calculus is offered as counsel, it is taken, and it works: the people of Limhi choose bondage over death, and it saves their lives. What the borrowing does is put a time bomb in the chapter. The murmur that scripture records in order to rebuke it becomes here a policy, and the policy holds for exactly two chapters — Mosiah 21 is the account of what that bondage costs, and Mosiah 22 is the people getting out of it by night, into the wilderness, past sleeping guards, in the shape of the very deliverance Exodus 14:12 was refusing to wait for. The Book of Mormon does not comment on this. It only quotes the murmur and then narrates the exodus.

links.note: “It is better that we should be in bondage, than that we should lose our lives.” “Than that we should” is a KJV singleton, and the verse it belongs to states the same trade in the same order: better to serve than to die. Exodus 14:12 is the murmuring of Israel at the sea, spoken by people who would rather be Egypt's slaves than risk the wilderness, and it is answered in Exodus by the parting of the water. Here it is answered by two chapters of Lamanite taskmasters and then by a night escape. The link is what makes Mosiah 20:22 legible as a decision rather than a piece of prudence.

pericopes.text: And now Limhi told the king all the things concerning his father, and the priests that had fled into the wilderness, and attributed the carrying away of their daughters to them.

And it came to pass that the king was pacified towards his people; and he said unto them, Let us go forth to meet my people, without arms; and I swear unto you with an oath, that my people shall not slay thy people.

And it came to pass that they followed the king, and went forth without arms to meet the Lamanites. And it came to pass that they did meet the Lamanites; and the king of the Lamanites did bow himself down before them, and did plead in behalf of the people of Limhi.
And when the Lamanites saw the people of Limhi, that they were without arms, they had compassion on them, and were pacified towards them, and returned with their king in peace to their own land.

links.text: But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him,

provenance.other: “had compassion on” occurs in eight KJV verses and is one of the commonest formulas of pity in the book, so the phrase identifies nothing by itself. The specific string “had compassion on them” is in two verses, 1 Kings 8:50 and Jeremiah 12:15, and neither has a wounded man or a stranger in it.
provenance.significance: The chapter's Samaritan borrowing closes here, and it closes with the roles exchanged. At 20:13 the people of Limhi bound up the wounds of the king who had come to destroy them, which is Luke 10:34; at 20:26 the Lamanites see those people standing in front of them without weapons and “had compassion on them”, which is Luke 10:33 of the Samaritan. Each side of the war has now played the parable's one good character, and each has played it toward the party that had every reason to be its victim. The parable's own question — who proved neighbour — is answered in Mosiah by both armies at once, and the answer is what ends the battle.

links.note: “They had compassion on them, and were pacified towards them, and returned with their king in peace.” On its own this clause would identify no source: “had compassion on” is in eight KJV verses. It is catalogued because the same chapter has already reproduced a Luke 10 singleton at 20:13, and this is the parable's other half, in its own words, applied to the other side. A borrowing that comes back for the neighbouring verse is a different thing from a formula that happens to recur.
links.whyNot: The verbal evidence here is thin to the point of being unusable in isolation, and a reader who declines the Luke 10:34 link at 20:13 should decline this one with it. The chain runs the wrong way — the strength of this row is entirely borrowed from another row — and “had compassion” is exactly the sort of KJV commonplace CONVENTIONS §5 keeps out of the catalogue when it stands alone.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Limhi and his people returned to the city of Nephi, and began to dwell in the land again in peace.
And it came to pass that after many days, the Lamanites began again to be stirred up in anger against the Nephites; and they began to come into the borders of the land round about.

Now they durst not slay them, because of the oath which their king had made unto Limhi; but they would smite them on their cheeks, and exercise authority over them; and began to put heavy burdens upon their backs, and drive them as they would a dumb ass:

links.text: Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?

provenance.route: Isaiah 58:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon (with Matthew 23:4 not excluded)
provenance.other: “heavy burdens” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 58:6 and Matthew 23:4, and the Book of Mormon uses the phrase once in the whole volume, here. tools/mediation-check.py was run on Isaiah 58:6 against Luke 4:18, which conflates Isaiah 58:6's freeing of the oppressed into its Isaiah 61 reading: it returns no decisive divergence, because the Book of Mormon reproduces nothing the two verses differ over. The mediation is therefore recorded as uncertain rather than guessed.
provenance.significance: Both candidates are doing something here and they are doing different things. Matthew 23:4 supplies the picture — burdens bound on men and laid upon their shoulders, which is Mosiah's “put heavy burdens upon their backs” — but Matthew's burdens are legal, imposed by teachers, and metaphorical. Isaiah 58:6 supplies the sense and the arc: it is about literal oppression, and it is the verse that undoes it, “to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke.” Every one of those four clauses becomes an event in Mosiah 21-22. The burdens are eased at 21:15; the yoke is named at 21:13; and the oppressed go free at 22:11-12, by night. Behind both stands Exodus 1:11, where taskmasters afflict Israel with their burdens, which is the narrative this whole chapter is walking through. Isaiah 58's own point is that the fast God wants is not affliction accepted but affliction ended, and Mosiah 21 is a chapter in which a people accept the affliction and are told they will not yet be delivered.

links.note: “Began to put heavy burdens upon their backs, and drive them as they would a dumb ass.” “Heavy burdens” is a two-verse KJV phrase and the Book of Mormon uses it exactly once, in the verse that opens its account of servitude. Matthew 23:4 has the image of laying them on men's shoulders; Isaiah 58:6 has the situation, real oppression, and the verb this chapter will need at 21:15, where the Lord “began to soften the hearts of the Lamanites, that they began to ease their burdens” — Isaiah's “undo the heavy burdens”. Recorded at moderate because the two candidates cannot be separated on the words, and the mediation is left uncertain for the same reason rather than settled by preference.

links.text: But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.

provenance.route: Matthew 20:25 / Mark 10:42 / Luke 22:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Exercise authority” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 20:25, Mark 10:42 and Luke 22:25 — one saying in three tellings, and the Bible's only use of the collocation. All three read “exercise authority upon them”, and “over them” belongs in each to the paired clause: “exercise dominion over them” in Matthew, “exercise lordship over them” in Mark and Luke. Mosiah 21:3's “exercise authority over them” takes the verb from one clause and the preposition from the other. tools/mediation-check.py on Matthew 20:25 against Luke 22:25 finds no decisive divergence — princes/kings, dominion/lordship, benefactors — because the Book of Mormon reproduces none of the words the three tellings differ over, so no Gospel can be named.
provenance.significance: The saying is Jesus's definition of what Gentile rule looks like from underneath, given to disciples arguing about rank: the great ones exercise authority upon those beneath them, and among you it shall not be so. Mosiah 21:3 is that sentence turned into a report of events — a people beneath a foreign power being smitten, having authority exercised over them, and being loaded like animals — and the report is of what happens to Nephites at the hands of Lamanites, i.e. of the covenant people under the Gentile pattern. If the echo is real, the chapter is quietly measuring the Lamanite occupation by the standard Christ set against.

links.note: “Exercise authority over them.” The collocation is confined in the KJV to one saying about how the rulers of the Gentiles treat their subjects, and Mosiah 21:3 is a catalogue of exactly that treatment. Registered at moderate, and as an echo rather than an allusion, because the wording is a conflation of the saying's two clauses rather than a reproduction of either, and because no Gospel form can be identified.
links.whyNot: “Exercise authority over” is unremarkable English and reads as naturally in 1830 as in 1611; a reader is entitled to say the writer needed a phrase for oppression and used the obvious one. The Gospel saying is also about honour and precedence among rulers, not about forced labour, so the context match is with one clause of it only. Nothing else in the chapter depends on this row.

pericopes.text: yea, all this was done, that the word of the Lord might be fulfilled.
And now the afflictions of the Nephites was great; and there was no way that they could deliver themselves out of their hands, for the Lamanites had surrounded them on every side.

And it came to pass that the people began to murmur with the king, because of their afflictions; and they began to be desirous to go against them to battle. And they did afflict the king sorely with their complaints; therefore he granted unto them that they should do according to their desires.
And they gathered themselves together again, and put on their armour, and went forth against the Lamanites, to drive them out of their land.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites did beat them, and drove them back, and slew many of them.

And now there was a great mourning and lamentation among the people of Limhi; the widow mourning for her husband; the son and the daughter mourning for their father; and the brothers for their brethren.

links.text: The LORD was as an enemy: he hath swallowed up Israel, he hath swallowed up all her palaces: he hath destroyed his strong holds, and hath increased in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation.

provenance.other: “Mourning and lamentation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Lamentations 2:5, and this is its first occurrence in the Book of Mormon. The itemised list that follows it — the widow for her husband, son and daughter for their father, brothers for their brethren — has its nearest KJV model in Zechariah 12:12-14, where “the land shall mourn, every family apart” is a KJV singleton and the mourning is likewise broken out household by household.
provenance.significance: The phrase belongs to the KJV's one sustained poem about a city broken by a besieging army, and Lamentations is the book this chapter keeps returning to: the mourning here at 21:9, and at 21:13 the dust, the yoke and the offered cheek of Lamentations 3:27-30. Recovering the context supplies what Mosiah does not say outright. Lamentations 2:5 begins “The LORD was as an enemy” — the disaster is God's doing, not the enemy's — and Mosiah 21 has just told the reader at 20:21 and 21:4 that all this was done that the word of Abinadi might be fulfilled. The chapter's grief is being described in the vocabulary of a book that reads national defeat as judgment, which is precisely the reading the chapter wants.

links.note: “There was a great mourning and lamentation among the people of Limhi.” A KJV singleton, from Lamentations 2:5, where it is what the LORD “increased in the daughter of Judah” after destroying her strong holds. The verse then breaks the grief down by relation, which is the shape of Zechariah 12:12-14's family-by-family mourning. Both sources read a military catastrophe as a divine visitation, and this chapter has already said, at 21:4, that this is one.

pericopes.text: Now there were a great many widows in the land; and they did cry mightily from day to day, for a great fear of the Lamanites had come upon them.

And it came to pass that their continual cries did stir up the remainder of the people of Limhi to anger, against the Lamanites. And they went again to battle; but they were driven back again, suffering much loss.

links.text: Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.

provenance.other: “Continual coming” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 18:5; “avenge me of mine adversary” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 18:3; “cry day and night” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 18:7. Mosiah reproduces none of the three verbatim, which is why this is filed at moderate — the contact is the cluster of elements, not a string.
provenance.significance: The parable of the importunate widow is the KJV's one story built out of these four things together: a widow, crying that does not stop, a hearer who does not answer at first, and vengeance on an adversary as the thing asked for. Mosiah 21:9-15 has all four in the same order — a great many widows (21:10), continual cries (21:11), an adversary they are avenged on when the cries stir the people to a third assault (21:11-12), and a hearer explicitly described as slow: “the Lord was slow to hear their cry” (21:15). Luke's parable exists to answer the question the chapter is living inside, whether God's delay means refusal: “shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them?” The Book of Mormon gives the widows the parable's part and then answers it in the negative twice over — the vengeance they get at 21:11 is three defeats, and the deliverance they get at 21:15 is not deliverance but lighter burdens.

links.note: “Their continual cries did stir up the remainder of the people of Limhi to anger, against the Lamanites.” The KJV's one continually-crying widow is the woman of Luke 18, whose “continual coming” is a singleton, whose petition is “avenge me of mine adversary”, and whose parable is expressly about elect who “cry day and night” to a God who “bear[s] long with them”. Mosiah 21 puts a whole city of widows in her place, has their crying produce exactly the vengeance she asked for, and then at 21:15 says in so many words that the Lord was slow. The verbal contact is one word, “continual”, applied to the crying of widows; the case is the co-occurrence of the parable's four distinctive elements in nine verses.
links.whyNot: A single shared adjective is not evidence, and each element on its own is common property — widows mourn, the bereaved cry, and delayed divine answer is a commonplace of the Psalms as much as of Luke. A reader who declines this will lose nothing else in the chapter, since 21:15's argument rests independently on Psalm 106:43-46.

pericopes.text: Yea, they went again, even the third time, and suffered in the like manner; and those that were not slain, returned again to the city of Nephi.

And they did humble themselves even to the dust, subjecting themselves to the yoke of bondage, submitting themselves to be smitten, and to be driven to and fro, and burdened, according to the desires of their enemies.

links.text: He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him: he is filled full with reproach.

provenance.other: “Bear the yoke” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Lamentations 3:27; “his mouth in the dust” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Lamentations 3:29; “giveth his cheek” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Lamentations 3:30. Three KJV singletons stand in four consecutive verses of one passage and all three are answered in this one verse of Mosiah, the last against 21:3's “smite them on their cheeks”. The bare phrase “in the dust” occurs in exactly fourteen KJV verses and identifies nothing by itself; what identifies Lamentations is that the dust, the yoke and the struck cheek arrive together.
provenance.significance: Lamentations 3:26-30 is the KJV's one passage recommending submission to national humiliation as a discipline — bear the yoke, sit alone and keep silence, put the mouth in the dust, give the cheek to the smiter — and it recommends it on the ground stated two verses later, that “the LORD will not cast off for ever”. Mosiah 21:13 performs that passage as narrative: humbling to the dust, taking the yoke, submitting to be smitten, in that order. What the source adds is the reason, which the Book of Mormon withholds for two more verses. Lamentations submits because mercy is coming; Mosiah's people submit and are told at 21:15 that the Lord “did not see fit to deliver them out of bondage.” The passage that promises the end of the discipline is used to describe a discipline that is not yet over — and the same phrase that closes Lamentations' argument, “according to the multitude of his mercies” (3:32), is the phrase Psalm 106:45 uses in the passage behind Mosiah 21:15. The chapter's two spinal sources quote each other.

links.note: “They did humble themselves even to the dust, subjecting themselves to the yoke of bondage, submitting themselves to be smitten.” Three KJV singletons from four consecutive verses of Lamentations 3, in the source's own order: the mouth in the dust (3:29), the yoke borne (3:27), the cheek given to him that smiteth (3:30), which the chapter has already set up at 21:3 with “they would smite them on their cheeks”. No clause is reproduced — this is catalogued on the sequence, not on a run — but the odds against three unique KJV phrases from one short passage recurring together are what carry the row. Lamentations counsels this posture because deliverance is coming; here it produces two more chapters of bondage.

links.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.

provenance.other: “Yoke of bondage” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 5:1. This is its first occurrence in the Book of Mormon; the other four are all in Alma and are that book's own reuse of the phrase.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a prohibition, and Mosiah 21:13 is its violation stated as an act of piety. “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” — and here a people, having humbled themselves to the dust, put themselves under it deliberately. The two texts are not talking about the same servitude; Paul means the law, and Mosiah means Lamanite taskmasters. But the borrowing brings Paul's terms with it, and once they are in view the chapter's arc has a second reading available: liberty lost, a yoke voluntarily accepted, and at 22:11-12 a people walking out of it by night. Whether the chapter intends that reading or merely reached for the KJV's only phrase for the thing it was describing, the phrase it reached for is Paul's warning against doing what it narrates.

links.note: “Subjecting themselves to the yoke of bondage.” A KJV singleton, reproduced entire, and the Book of Mormon's first use of it. The sense is transposed from Paul's metaphor to literal servitude, which is the direction such transpositions usually run and is not an objection: the metaphor's ground is precisely political slavery. What is worth registering is that the source forbids what the verse describes, and that the phrase's four later Book of Mormon occurrences, all in Alma, are the volume's own reuse of what it takes here.

pericopes.text: And they did humble themselves even in the depths of humility; and they did cry mightily to God; yea, even all the day long did they cry unto their God, that he would deliver them out of their afflictions.

links.text: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.

provenance.other: “Cry mightily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8, where it reads “cry mightily unto God”; Mosiah 21:14 reads “cry mightily to God”. But this is not the phrase's first appearance in the book. Abinadi has already used it at Mosiah 11:25 — “except they repent in sackcloth and ashes, and cry mightily to the Lord their God, I will not hear their prayers, neither will I deliver them out of their afflictions” — which carries Jonah's sackcloth as well as his verb, and Mosiah 21:14 reproduces Abinadi's second clause too: “that he would deliver them out of their afflictions.” The proximate model is therefore the earlier Book of Mormon prophecy, not the Bible, and the mediation is recorded accordingly.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's best-marked case of an earlier Book of Mormon text standing between the KJV and a later one, and the text does the marking itself: at 20:21, four verses earlier, Gideon has asked “are not the words of Abinadi fulfilled, which he prophesied against us?” Mosiah 21:14-15 is the fulfilment of the specific words quoted, in their own order — they do cry mightily, they do ask to be delivered out of their afflictions, and the Lord is “slow to hear their cry”, which is Abinadi's “I will not hear their prayers” softened by exactly one degree. Jonah's contribution is what makes the sentence bearable: the KJV's one “cry mightily” is Nineveh's, and Nineveh's crying works. The condition Abinadi attached — repentance, in sackcloth and ashes — is the one thing Mosiah 21:14 does not report.

links.note: “They did cry mightily to God; yea, even all the day long did they cry unto their God, that he would deliver them out of their afflictions.” The phrase is a KJV singleton belonging to the king of Nineveh's proclamation, but the Book of Mormon has already borrowed it once, in Abinadi's prophecy at Mosiah 11:25, together with the clause about deliverance out of afflictions that this verse also reproduces. So the row is filed as OT-via-earlier-BoM: what Mosiah 21:14 is quoting is Abinadi quoting Jonah, and the chapter says so itself at 20:21. The Bible contact itself is adjudicated at the phrase's first use in this book, Mosiah 9:17, where the catalogue already carries Jonah 3:8; this row records the route and the fulfilment, since what Mosiah 21:14 is following is not Jonah directly but Abinadi's use of him.

pericopes.text: And now the Lord was slow to hear their cry, because of their iniquities; nevertheless the Lord did hear their cries, and began to soften the hearts of the Lamanites, that they began to ease their burdens: yet the Lord did not see fit to deliver them out of bondage.

links.text: Nevertheless he regarded their affliction, when he heard their cry:

provenance.other: “Brought low for their iniquity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 106:43; “when he heard their cry” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 106:44, which also contains the singleton “regarded their affliction”; “that carried them captives” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, of which Psalm 106:46 is one. The Exodus source behind the psalm has “heard their cry” in exactly three KJV verses, of which Exodus 3:7 is the one about taskmasters and burdens; the psalm is the proximate model because it, and not Exodus, supplies the adverb and the order.
provenance.significance: Psalm 106:41-46 is not a parallel to Mosiah 21; it is Mosiah 21's outline, and every clause arrives in sequence. “They that hated them ruled over them” (106:41) is 21:3's exercised authority. “Their enemies also oppressed them, and they were brought into subjection under their hand” (106:42) is 21:13's subjecting themselves. “Brought low for their iniquity” (106:43) is 21:15's “because of their iniquities”. “Nevertheless he regarded their affliction, when he heard their cry” (106:44) is 21:15's “nevertheless the Lord did hear their cries” — the same adverb doing the same hinge. And “He made them also to be pitied of all those that carried them captives” (106:46) is the answer the chapter actually gets: not release, but captors who soften and ease the burdens. That last correspondence is the one that settles the row, because it explains the strangest thing in Mosiah 21. A reader asks why God would hear a prayer for deliverance and answer it with lighter chains; Psalm 106 is where that answer already exists, and the psalm reaches it because Israel is being disciplined and not abandoned. The chapter's other spine, Lamentations 3:27-33, ends on the same phrase the psalm uses one verse later — “according to the multitude of his mercies” — so the two sources this chapter runs on are already quoting each other in the KJV.

links.note: “And now the Lord was slow to hear their cry, because of their iniquities; nevertheless the Lord did hear their cries, and began to soften the hearts of the Lamanites, that they began to ease their burdens: yet the Lord did not see fit to deliver them out of bondage.” Set beside Psalm 106:43-46 the sentence is a paraphrase running clause for clause: brought low for their iniquity — nevertheless he regarded their affliction, when he heard their cry — he made them also to be pitied of all those that carried them captives. Two of those are KJV singletons and the hinge adverb is shared. This is the sort of agreement the n-gram stream is blind to by construction (CONVENTIONS §9), since it is split across clause boundaries and reordered, and it was found by reading. The theological content of the chapter — a prayer heard, and answered with an eased burden rather than a broken one — is not the writer's invention but the psalm's, and it is the strongest link in the chapter.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they began to prosper by degrees in the land, and began to raise grain more abundantly, and flocks, and herds, that they did not suffer with hunger.

Now there was a great number of women more than there was of men; therefore king Limhi commanded that every man should impart to the support of the widows and their children, that they might not perish with hunger: and this they did, because of the greatness of their number that had been slain.

links.text: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!

provenance.other: “Perish with hunger” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 15:17, and this is its first occurrence in the Book of Mormon. The KJV's other famine idioms are “die of hunger”, “consumed with hunger” and “kill this whole assembly with hunger”; “perish with hunger” is the prodigal's alone.
provenance.significance: The words are the turning point of the parable of the prodigal son — “when he came to himself”, in a far country, with his living spent and a famine on. Mosiah 21 is a chapter about a people in the position that sentence describes: they are in the land of Nephi, which their fathers left Zarahemla to possess; their substance was wasted by a king whose court Abinadi condemned for it; and 21:16-17 is the first moment they come to themselves, organising a levy so that the widows and fatherless “might not perish with hunger”. The parable's line is spoken by a man alone and about himself; the Book of Mormon puts it in the plural and makes the remedy communal — every man imparting to the support of the widows. That is the interesting alteration. The prodigal's remedy is to go home; Limhi's people cannot, and will spend two chapters trying.

links.note: “King Limhi commanded that every man should impart to the support of the widows and their children, that they might not perish with hunger.” A KJV singleton, and it belongs to the prodigal son at the point where he comes to himself in a famine. The Book of Mormon's use of it is the phrase's first in the volume, and it converts a solitary complaint into a public relief measure. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as an allusion on the rarity of the phrase.

pericopes.text: Now the people of Limhi kept together in a body as much as it was possible, and secure their grain, and their flocks;
and the king himself did not trust his person without the walls of the city, unless he took his guards with him, fearing that he might by some means fall into the hands of the Lamanites.

And he caused that his people should watch the land round about, that by some means they might take those priests that fled into the wilderness, which had stolen the daughters of the Lamanites, and that had caused such a great destruction to come upon them;

for they were desirous to take them, that they might punish them: for they had come into the land of Nephi by night, and carried off of their grain, and many of their precious things; therefore they laid wait for them.
And it came to pass that there was no more disturbance between the Lamanites and the people of Limhi, even until the time that Ammon and his brethren came into the land.

And the king having been without the gates of the city with his guard, he discovered Ammon and his brethren; and supposing them to be priests of Noah, therefore he caused that they should be taken, and bound, and cast into prison. And had they been the priests of Noah, he would have caused that they should be put to death;
but when he found that they were not, but that they were his brethren, and had come from the land of Zarahemla, he was filled with exceeding great joy.—
Now king Limhi had sent, previous to the coming of Ammon, a small number of men to search for the land of Zarahemla; but they could not find it: and they were lost in the wilderness.

Nevertheless they did find a land which had been peopled; yea, a land which was covered with dry bones; yea, a land which had been peopled, and which had been destroyed; and they having supposed it to be the land of Zarahemla, returned to the land of Nephi, having arrived in the borders of the land not many days before the coming of Ammon.

links.text: Again he said unto me, Prophesy upon these bones, and say unto them, O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD.

provenance.other: “Dry bones” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 37:4, and this is its only occurrence in the whole Book of Mormon. Ezekiel 37:1-2 supplies the setting the Book of Mormon reproduces — a valley “full of bones”, and “lo, they were very dry” — and 37:11 supplies the identification: “these bones are the whole house of Israel.”
provenance.significance: Limhi's scouts are looking for Zarahemla, which for them means kindred, rescue and the end of exile. What they find is a land covered with dry bones, and they conclude that it is Zarahemla. The mistake is the whole point of the borrowing. In Ezekiel the valley of very dry bones IS the house of Israel — “our bones are dried, and our hope is lost: we are cut off for our parts” — and the vision exists to promise that the bones will live and be brought into their own land. The scouts, that is, look for the promised reunion and find the image of it in its unrisen state, and they cannot tell the difference. What they bring home from it is a record engraven on plates, words carried out of a valley of the dead — where Ezekiel's commission is the reverse, a word carried into one: “Prophesy upon these bones, and say unto them, O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD.” Mosiah 21:28 then supplies the missing half, a king who can interpret the engravings, and the record does speak. The Jaredite plates enter the Book of Mormon through Ezekiel's valley.

links.note: “A land which was covered with dry bones; yea, a land which had been peopled, and which had been destroyed.” “Dry bones” is a KJV singleton and this is its only occurrence in the Book of Mormon; the surrounding description — a land full of bones, and the bones very dry — is Ezekiel 37:1-2. The link is not decoration: Ezekiel's bones are named at 37:11 as the whole house of Israel with its hope lost, which is exactly what the scouts take the place to be when they mistake it for Zarahemla, and the record they carry away from it will be made to speak two verses later.

pericopes.text: And they brought a record with them, even a record of the people whose bones they had found; and they were engraven on plates of ore.
And now Limhi was again filled with joy, on learning from the mouth of Ammon that king Benjamin had a gift from God, whereby he could interpret such engravings; yea, and Ammon also did rejoice.
Yet Ammon and his brethren were filled with sorrow, because so many of his brethren had been slain;

and also that king Noah and his priests had caused the people to commit so many sins and iniquities against God; and they also did mourn for the death of Abinadi; and also for the departure of Alma, and the people that went with him, who had formed a church of God through the strength and power of God, and faith on the words which had been spoken by Abinadi;

yea, they did mourn for their departure, for they knew not whither they had fled. Now they would have gladly joined with them, for they themselves had entered into a covenant with God, to serve him, and keep his commandments.
And now since the coming of Ammon, king Limhi had also entered into a covenant with God, and also many of his people, to serve him, and keep his commandments.

And it came to pass that king Limhi and many of his people was desirous to be baptized; but there was none in the land that had authority from God. And Ammon declined doing this thing, considering himself an unworthy servant;

therefore they did not at that time form themselves into a church, waiting upon the spirit of the Lord. Now they were desirous to become even as Alma and his brethren, which had fled into the wilderness.

They were desirous to be baptized, as a witness and a testimony that they were willing to serve God with all their hearts; nevertheless they did prolong the time: and an account of their baptism shall be given hereafter.
And now all the study of Ammon and his people, and king Limhi and his people, was to deliver themselves out of the hands of the Lamanites, and from bondage.

And now it came to pass that Ammon and king Limhi began to consult with the people how they should deliver themselves out of bondage; and even they did cause that all the people should gather themselves together: and this they did that they might have the voice of the people concerning the matter.

And it came to pass that they could find no way to deliver themselves out of bondage, except it were to take their women and children, and their flocks, and their herds, and their tents, and depart into the wilderness; for the Lamanites being so numerous that it was impossible for the people of Limhi to contend with them, thinking to deliver themselves out of bondage by the sword.

Now it came to pass that Gideon went forth and stood before the king, and said unto him, Now O king, thou hast hitherto hearkened unto my words many times when we have been contending with our brethren, the Lamanites.

And now O king, if thou hast not found me to be an unprofitable servant, or if thou hast hitherto listened to my words in any degree, and they have been of service to thee, even so I desire that thou wouldst listen to my words at this time, and I will be thy servant, and deliver this people out of bondage.
And the king granted unto him that he might speak. And Gideon saith unto him,

Behold the back pass through the back wall, on the back side of the city. The Lamanites, or the guards of the Lamanites, by night, are drunken; therefore let us send a proclamation among all this people, that they gather together their flocks and herds, that they may drive them into the wilderness by night.

And I will go according to thy command, and pay the last tribute of wine to the Lamanites, and they will be drunken; and we will pass through the secret pass on the left of the camp, when they are drunken and asleep:

links.text: In their heat I will make their feasts, and I will make them drunken, that they may rejoice, and sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the LORD.

provenance.other: “Make them drunken” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 51:39, and “sleep a perpetual sleep” occurs in exactly two, Jeremiah 51:39 and 51:57, which are the same oracle saying the same thing twice. Mosiah 22:7's “when they are drunken and asleep” pairs the two states, and the pairing is confined in the KJV to those two verses; drunkenness elsewhere in scripture (Nabal, Elah, Benhadad, Belshazzar) ends in a killing, not in a sleep that lets somebody slip away.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 51 is the oracle against Babylon, and the two things it promises are the two things Gideon's plan requires. God will make the garrison drunk and put it to sleep — “I will make drunk her princes, and her wise men, her captains, and her rulers, and her mighty men: and they shall sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake” — and while that is happening his people are to get out: “My people, go ye out of the midst of her, and deliver ye every man his soul.” Mosiah 22 is that oracle executed as a stratagem. What the borrowing does is assign the agency. In Jeremiah the drunkenness is the LORD's doing and the escape is a command; here the drunkenness is procured with a tribute of wine and some extra sent as a present, and the escape is a plan carried by a vote. The chapter takes a prophecy of divine judgment and stages it with a wine delivery — which is either the most secular sentence in the Limhi narrative or a claim that providence works through the tribute schedule, and the catalogue does not have to choose.

links.note: “I will go according to thy command, and pay the last tribute of wine to the Lamanites, and they will be drunken; and we will pass through the secret pass on the left of the camp, when they are drunken and asleep.” The KJV pairs drunkenness with a sleep that permits escape in exactly one place, the Babylon oracle of Jeremiah 51, where “I will make them drunken” is a singleton and the resulting “perpetual sleep” is repeated at 51:57 over the whole garrison — princes, captains, rulers, mighty men — and where the accompanying instruction to God's people is to go out of the midst of her and deliver every man his soul. That is the plan of this chapter, down to the order of its two halves. Recorded at moderate because Mosiah reproduces no clause; the case is that the combination is Jeremiah's alone.

pericopes.text: thus we will depart with our women and our children, our flocks and our herds, into the wilderness; and we will travel around the land of Shilom.

links.text: And Moses said, We will go with our young and with our old, with our sons and with our daughters, with our flocks and with our herds will we go; for we must hold a feast unto the LORD.

provenance.other: “Our flocks and with our herds” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 10:9, as does “with our young and with our old” in the same verse; “flocks and your herds” occurs in exactly two, Exodus 10:24 and Exodus 12:32, both of them Pharaoh's side of the same negotiation. Mosiah 22:8's “our flocks and our herds” drops the repeated preposition and so is not a verbatim run, which is why the row is filed at moderate rather than higher.
provenance.significance: Exodus 10:9-11 and 10:24-26 are the KJV's one negotiation over the manifest of an escape: Moses insists on taking the young, the old, the sons, the daughters, the flocks and the herds, and Pharaoh's counter-offers are to keep the little ones, then to keep the livestock. The inventory is the argument. Mosiah 22:2 and 22:8 answer the same question in the same terms — women, children, flocks, herds, tents — and answer it Moses's way, all of it goes. The difference is who is asked. In Exodus the list has to be extracted from the oppressor; here it is settled by the voice of the people at 22:1 and by a captain's plan, and the Lamanites are not consulted because they are being got drunk. Reading the two together makes 22:10's tribute of wine the substitute for the plagues: the concession Pharaoh had to be beaten into is here simply bought.

links.note: “Thus we will depart with our women and our children, our flocks and our herds, into the wilderness.” The KJV's manifest for a departure of this kind is Exodus 10:9, where “with our flocks and with our herds will we go” closes a list of exactly these categories and is the point Pharaoh spends two more exchanges trying to whittle down. Mosiah reproduces the items and the first-person future — “we will go”, “we will depart” — but not the repeated preposition, so no clause is quoted. Registered at moderate on the strength of the inventory, which is distinctive, rather than the wording, which is not.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the king hearkened unto the words of Gideon.

And it came to pass that king Limhi caused that his people should gather their flocks together; and he sent the tribute of wine to the Lamanites; and he also sent more wine, as a present unto them: and they did drink freely of the wine which king Limhi did send unto them.

And it came to pass that the people of king Limhi did depart by night into the wilderness with their flocks and their herds; and they went round about the land of Shilom in the wilderness, and bent their course towards the land of Zarahemla, being led by Ammon and his brethren.

links.text: And the city was broken up, and all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between two walls, which is by the king’s garden: (now the Chaldees were against the city round about:) and the king went the way toward the plain.

provenance.other: “Fled by night” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Kings 25:4; “out of the city by night” occurs in exactly two, Jeremiah 39:4 and 52:7, the parallel accounts of the same night; “the army of the Chaldees pursued” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Kings 25:5, which also contains the singleton “overtook him in the plains”. tools/mediation-check.py on 2 Kings 25:4 against Jeremiah 52:7 returns one decisive point, for 2 Kings: the Book of Mormon has “toward” where Jeremiah has “of”. That discrimination should be leaned on lightly — the 1830 text reads “towards”, a form in no KJV verse at all — but it is the only point at which the two accounts differ over anything Mosiah reproduces.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's largest claim and the Book of Mormon supplies its own warrant for it. 2 Kings 25:4-5 is the flight of Zedekiah: the city broken up, the men of war escaping by night through a gate in the wall, the king making for open country, and the army of the Chaldees pursuing after him and overtaking him. Mosiah 22 runs the same five beats — a passage through the back wall of the city (22:6), a departure by night (22:11), a course bent toward open country, an army sent to pursue (22:15), and then the beat that does not match: “after they had pursued them two days, they could no longer follow their tracks; therefore they were lost in the wilderness” (22:16). The pursuers are the ones who get lost. Where Zedekiah is overtaken in the plains of Jericho and his army scattered from him, Limhi's people arrive. The reason this matters more than a good parallel is chronological. 1 Nephi 1:4 sets the whole Book of Mormon in motion “in the commencement of the first year of the reign of Zedekiah”, and three chapters after this escape, at Mosiah 25:2, the land the fugitives are running to turns out to have been founded by Mulek, a son of that same Zedekiah, brought out of Jerusalem when his father's flight failed. So a people escape a walled city by night, outrun the army sent after them, and reach the refuge of the one member of Zedekiah's house who got away. The book is rewriting its own founding catastrophe with the other ending.

links.note: “The people of king Limhi did depart by night into the wilderness with their flocks and their herds … and bent their course towards the land of Zarahemla.” Set against 2 Kings 25:4-5 the sequence is Zedekiah's: a way out through the wall, a flight by night, a course toward open country, an army in pursuit. The KJV's “fled by night” is a singleton belonging to that verse and “the army of the Chaldees pursued” is a singleton belonging to the next; Mosiah reproduces neither exactly, which keeps this at moderate. What raises it above a generic escape story is the ending, which is inverted — the pursuit fails and the pursuers are the ones lost in the wilderness — and the destination, since Mosiah 25:2 will say that Zarahemla was founded by Zedekiah's surviving son. The catalogue records the shape and leaves the reader to decide whether a writer built it or found it.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is the weakest part of the row: no clause is reproduced, and every element considered separately — flight by night, a city wall, a pursuing army — is common in both scripture and life. A reader could hold that this is simply what an escape narrative looks like, and that the Zedekiah resonance is supplied by the Book of Mormon's own chronology rather than by any borrowing from 2 Kings. The row would be withdrawn if the sequence could be shown to follow some other escape account as closely; none of the KJV's others (Jacob from Laban, David from Saul, the men of Ai, Paul over the wall at Damascus) has both the night departure through the wall and the failed pursuit.

pericopes.text: And they had taken all their gold, and silver, and their precious things, which they could carry; and also their provisions with them, into the wilderness; and they pursued their journey.
And after being many days in the wilderness, they arrived in the land of Zarahemla, and joined his people, and became his subjects.
And it came to pass that Mosiah received them with joy; and he also received their records, and also the records which had been found by the people of Limhi.
And now it came to pass when the Lamanites had found that the people of Limhi had departed out of the land by night, that they sent an army into the wilderness to pursue them;
