and after they had pursued them two days, they could no longer follow their tracks; therefore they were lost in the wilderness.

Now Alma, having been warned of the Lord that the armies of king Noah would come upon them, and had made it known to his people, therefore they gathered together their flocks, and took of their grain, and departed into the wilderness before the armies of king Noah.

links.text: And being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.

provenance.other: The passive construction “warned of God” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 2:12 (the wise men), Matthew 2:22 (Joseph), and Hebrews 11:7 (Noah). All three describe a man who escapes a destruction because he was told in advance. The 1830 text reads 'warned of the Lord', which keeps the construction and changes the divine name.
provenance.significance: Matthew 2:12-14 is the KJV's compact form of the story Mosiah 23:1 is telling: a warning received, a departure by an unexpected route, and a king whose soldiers arrive too late. What the borrowing brings with it is the identity of the pursuer. In Matthew the king is Herod; here he is king Noah, and the third KJV verse in the same idiom — Hebrews 11:7 — is about Noah being warned of God and building an ark. That collision of names is an accident of the Book of Mormon's onomasticon and not an argument, but it is the kind of accident a catalogue should record rather than suppress, because a reader will meet it.

links.note: 'Now Alma, having been warned of the Lord that the armies of king Noah would come upon them ... therefore they gathered together their flocks, and took of their grain, and departed into the wilderness.' The KJV has one idiom for a divine advance warning of this kind, 'warned of God', and it appears in exactly three verses; two of them are Matthew 2:12 and 2:22, where the warning is followed immediately by a departure that evades a murderous king. The Book of Mormon has the construction, the warning, the flight and the king. It does not have the vocabulary of the flight itself, which is why this is recorded as an echo and not an allusion.
links.whyNot: 'Warned of the Lord' is not any KJV string, and the substitution of 'the Lord' for 'God' removes the one phrase that would carry the borrowing. Nothing else in the verse is Matthean: the flocks and the grain belong to the Book of Mormon's own wilderness-flight formula, established at 1 Nephi 2:4.

pericopes.text: And the Lord did strengthen them, that the people of king Noah could not overtake them, to destroy them.
And it came to pass that they fled eight days’ journey into the wilderness.
And they came to a land, yea, even a very beautiful and pleasant land; a land of pure water.
And it came to pass that they pitched their tents, and began to till the ground, and began to build buildings, &c.; yea, they were industrious, and did labor exceedingly.
And it came to pass that the people were desirous that Alma should be their king, for he was beloved by his people.

But he saith unto them, Behold, it is not expedient that we should have a king; for thus saith the Lord: Ye shall not esteem one flesh above another, or one man shall not think himself above another; therefore I say unto you, It is not expedient that ye should have a king.

links.text: One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.

provenance.other: “above another” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 14:5, where the full clause is 'One man esteemeth one day above another'. The Book of Mormon's second clause, 'or one man shall not think himself above another', carries over Paul's subject 'one man' as well. 'It is not expedient' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:1, and frames the sentence twice.
provenance.significance: Recovering the context turns the borrowing into an argument. Romans 14:5 is about the liberty of conscience: Paul refuses to let one believer's estimate of a day be imposed on another, because 'to his own master he standeth or falleth'. Alma applies the same sentence to persons rather than days, and to kingship rather than diet — 'Ye shall not esteem one flesh above another'. The chapter is about to quote Galatians 5 twice more (23:13, 23:15), and Romans 14 and Galatians 5 are the KJV's two great chapters on Christian liberty. Alma's political case against monarchy is being built, phrase by phrase, out of Paul's case for not ranking one another.

links.note: 'Ye shall not esteem one flesh above another, or one man shall not think himself above another.' Paul's 'One man esteemeth one day above another' is the KJV's only occurrence of 'above another', and Alma has the verb, the phrase, and Paul's own subject 'one man', reused across a doubled clause of the same shape Romans 14:5 uses. The frame, 'it is not expedient that we should have a king', is the KJV's one 'it is not expedient', from 2 Corinthians 12:1. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as an allusion on the strength of the two singletons.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless, if it were possible that ye could always have just men to be your kings, it would be well for you to have a king.
But remember the iniquity of king Noah and his priests: and I myself was caught in a snare, and did many things which was abominable in the sight of the Lord, which caused me sore repentance;

links.text: The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.

provenance.other: 'The fear of man' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 29:25, whose two halves are 'The fear of man bringeth a snare' and 'whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe'. 'Caught in the snare' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 9:12, of birds. The Book of Mormon's 'caught in a snare' matches neither exactly.
provenance.significance: The proposal this row makes is that Proverbs 29:25 is behind Alma's speech as a whole and not this sentence alone. Its first half supplies 23:9 — Alma, who was one of king Noah's priests and fled from him, says 'I myself was caught in a snare'; its second half supplies 23:22, 'whosoever puteth his trust in him, the same shall be lifted up at the last day'. The proverb's own logic is that the snare and the trust are alternatives, fear of a man against trust in the LORD, which is precisely the choice the chapter puts to a people being asked to appoint a king. Neither verse quotes the proverb; the speech is shaped like it.

links.note: 'I myself was caught in a snare, and did many things which was abominable in the sight of the Lord.' The snare is not glossed, and the KJV's one verse about a snare set by the fear of a man is Proverbs 29:25 — which is also the KJV's one verse pairing that snare with putting one's trust in the LORD, the figure Alma reaches for thirteen verses later. Recorded here at moderate because the verbal contact in this verse alone is a single common noun; the case is cumulative and is argued across 23:9 and 23:22 together.
links.whyNot: 'Caught in a snare' is closer as a string to Ecclesiastes 9:12's 'caught in the snare' than to anything in Proverbs 29:25, and snares are widely distributed in the KJV. If 23:22's 'putteth his trust' is judged to be independent BoM formula — and 'put your trust in God' is a Book of Mormon commonplace by Alma 38:5 — then the cumulative argument collapses and this row should be withdrawn to the exclusion register.

pericopes.text: nevertheless, after much tribulation, the Lord did hear my cries, and did answer my prayers, and hath made me an instrument in his hands, in bringing so many of you to a knowledge of his truth.

links.text: Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.

provenance.other: 'Much tribulation' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 14:22.
provenance.significance: Acts 14:22-23 is a two-verse unit — 'we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God. And when they had ordained them elders in every church' — and the Book of Mormon draws on both halves of it within this batch of chapters. Alma's 'after much tribulation' stands here; the ordaining of officers in every church stands at Mosiah 25:19, where Alma is given power 'to ordain priests and teachers over every Church'. Read together, the pair suggests the narrative of Alma's church is being told with Luke's account of Paul's church-planting in view: affliction endured, then officers appointed congregation by congregation.

links.note: 'Nevertheless, after much tribulation, the Lord did hear my cries.' The KJV says 'much tribulation' once, at Acts 14:22, where it names the condition of entry into the kingdom. The phrase carries no other Lukan vocabulary with it here, which caps this at an allusion; its interest is that Acts 14:23, the next verse, is the source proposed at Mosiah 25:19.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless, in this I do not glory, for I am unworthy to glory of myself.

And now I say unto you, As ye have been oppressed by king Noah, and have been in bondage to him and his priests, and have been brought into iniquity by them; therefore ye were bound with the bands of iniquity.

links.text: Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?

provenance.route: Isaiah 58:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Acts 8:23 supplying the noun
provenance.other: 'Bands of wickedness' and 'the oppressed go free' each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 58:6. 'Bond of iniquity' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:23. The Book of Mormon's 'bands of iniquity' is in neither: it is Isaiah's noun with Acts's genitive.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 58:6 lists four things the fast God chooses will do — loose the bands of wickedness, undo the heavy burdens, let the oppressed go free, break every yoke — and Mosiah 23:12-13 and 24:14 work through the list in order. 23:12: 'As ye have been oppressed by king Noah ... ye were bound with the bands of iniquity.' 23:13: 'ye have been delivered ... out of these bonds ... ye should stand fast in this liberty wherewith ye have been made free.' 24:14: 'I will also ease the burdens which is put upon your shoulders.' The one Isaiah item the narrative does not use is the yoke, which is also the one item Galatians 5:1 supplies at 23:13. The two chapters are running a single Isaiah verse as a programme, and taking their vocabulary for it from the New Testament.

links.note: 'Ye have been oppressed by king Noah ... therefore ye were bound with the bands of iniquity.' Isaiah 58:6 is the KJV's only 'bands of wickedness' and its only 'let the oppressed go free'; both stand in the same verse, and both stand in this sentence and the next. The substitution of 'iniquity' for 'wickedness' is not neutral — 'bond of iniquity' is a KJV singleton at Acts 8:23, spoken by Peter to Simon Magus, a man who had bought his way toward priestly office. Alma, a former priest of a corrupt king, is describing a people brought into iniquity by that king's priests. The word is borrowed from the one verse in the KJV where a false priest is told what he is in.

pericopes.text: And now as ye have been delivered, by the power of God, out of these bonds; yea, even out of the hands of king Noah and his people, and also from the bonds of iniquity, even so I desire that ye should stand fast in this liberty wherewith ye have been made free, and that ye trust no man to be a king over you;

links.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.

provenance.other: 'The liberty wherewith' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 5:1: 'Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.' The Book of Mormon reproduces 'stand fast in this liberty wherewith ye have been made free', substituting 'this' for 'the' and turning Paul's first-person plural into a second-person plural.
provenance.significance: The verse Paul is warning against being 'entangled again with the yoke of bondage' — and the Book of Mormon puts the sentence in the mouth of a man addressing people who have just come out of literal bondage and who, three chapters later, will go back into it. The suppressed half of Galatians 5:1 is the half that comes true: Alma's people are enslaved by the Lamanites at 23:37 and delivered again in chapter 24. Paul's metaphorical yoke is the plot. And the borrowing does not stop at the verse — 23:15 goes on to Galatians 5:14, and the 'no contention among them' of that verse answers Galatians 5:15's 'if ye bite and devour one another'. Mosiah 23:13-15 is Galatians 5:1-15 compressed into three sentences, in Paul's own order.

links.note: 'Even so I desire that ye should stand fast in this liberty wherewith ye have been made free.' Ten of Paul's words in Paul's order, from the one KJV verse containing the phrase 'the liberty wherewith'. The only changes are the demonstrative and the person of the verb. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six quotations; catalogued as a quotation because a complete clause of one identifiable verse is reproduced (CONVENTIONS §2). The context is the strongest part of the case: Alma is arguing against kingship, and Galatians 5:1 is the KJV's one sentence that opposes standing fast in liberty to a yoke of bondage.

pericopes.text: and also trusting no one to be your teachers nor your ministers, except he be a man of God, walking in his ways and keeping his commandments.
Thus did Alma teach his people, that every man should love his neighbor as himself; that there should be no contention among them.

links.text: For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.

provenance.route: Leviticus 19:18 → Galatians 5:14 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Love thy neighbour as thyself' stands in seven KJV verses (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 19:19; 22:39; Mark 12:31; Romans 13:9; Galatians 5:14; James 2:8), so the commandment itself cannot identify its source. The third-person form the Book of Mormon has, “love his neighbour as himself”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 12:33 — but indirect discourse ('that every man should love …') forces that conversion, so the singleton is a grammatical artifact and not evidence. tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence between Leviticus 19:18 and Galatians 5:14 for this verse, because the commandment is worded identically in both.
provenance.significance: The mediation has to be argued from sequence rather than from wording, and the sequence is decisive. Two verses earlier the chapter quotes Galatians 5:1 on the liberty wherewith ye are made free — a KJV singleton. Galatians 5:14 is where that same paragraph lands: 'For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.' And Galatians 5:15, the next verse, is 'But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another', which is the KJV's only 'bite and devour' and is answered by Alma's 'that there should be no contention among them'. Alma teaches liberty, then love of neighbour, then the avoidance of mutual consumption, in Paul's order and within three verses. That is why the row is filed OT-via-NT: the commandment is Leviticus's, but the route runs through Galatians 5.

links.note: 'Thus did Alma teach his people, that every man should love his neighbor as himself; that there should be no contention among them.' The commandment is in seven KJV verses and settles nothing on its own; what settles it is that the chapter has just quoted Galatians 5:1 and is about to gloss Galatians 5:15. Read Mosiah 23:13-15 against Galatians 5:1, 14 and 15 and the three sentences track the three verses in order, including the negative — Paul's biting and devouring becomes Alma's contention.

pericopes.text: And now Alma was their high priest, he being the founder of their Church.

And it came to pass that none received authority to preach or to teach, except it were by him from God. Therefore he consecrated all their priests, and all their teachers, and none were consecrated except it were just men.
Therefore they did watch over their people, and did nourish them with things pertaining to righteousness.

links.text: For every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins:

provenance.other: “things pertaining to” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Acts 1:3; 1 Corinthians 6:4; Hebrews 2:17; Hebrews 5:1). Two of the four are Hebrews, and in both the phrase is governed by 'high priest': 'a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God' (2:17), 'every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in things pertaining to God' (5:1).
provenance.significance: The three verses 23:16-18 run the Hebrews formula through its parts in Hebrews's own order: a high priest (23:16, 'Alma was their high priest'), taken from among men and ordained (23:17, 'he consecrated all their priests, and all their teachers'), for men in things pertaining to God (23:18, 'did nourish them with things pertaining to righteousness'). The one substitution is the last word. Hebrews 5:1's high priest deals in things pertaining to God and offers 'gifts and sacrifices for sins'; Alma's priests deal in things pertaining to righteousness and offer nothing. A book whose narrative sits under the law of Moses has taken the KJV's definition of priesthood from the epistle that argues the law of Moses is superseded, and has quietly removed the sacrifice from it.

links.note: 'They did watch over their people, and did nourish them with things pertaining to righteousness.' The KJV's four occurrences of 'things pertaining to' include two in Hebrews, both attached to a high priest and both reading 'to God'; two verses earlier this chapter has named Alma 'their high priest' and one verse earlier has him consecrating priests. Recorded at moderate: the shared string is short and the substituted noun is the Book of Mormon's own, so the case rests on the run of three verses rather than on this one.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they began to prosper exceedingly in the land; and they called the land Helam.
And it came to pass that they did multiply and prosper exceedingly in the land of Helam; and they built a city, which they called Helam.
Nevertheless the Lord seeth fit to chasten his people; yea, he trieth their patience and their faith.

links.text: He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity: he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword. Here is the patience and the faith of the saints.

provenance.other: 'The patience and the faith' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 13:10. The only other KJV verse pairing the two nouns is 2 Thessalonians 1:4, 'your patience and faith in all your persecutions', which lacks the doubled article the Book of Mormon has in 'their patience and their faith'.
provenance.significance: Read the whole of Revelation 13:10 and the borrowing predicts the next two verses of Mosiah. It runs: 'He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity: he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword. Here is the patience and the faith of the saints.' Mosiah 23:21 takes the last clause; Mosiah 23:23, two sentences later, supplies the first — 'they were brought into bondage, and none could deliver them but the Lord their God.' John's sentence exists to tell the saints that captivity is the trial in which patience and faith are shown, and the Book of Mormon has taken his summary formula and then narrated the captivity it summarises. Whether the writer saw that or not, the catalogue can show that the phrase arrives from a verse about being led into captivity, into a paragraph about being led into captivity.

links.note: 'Nevertheless the Lord seeth fit to chasten his people; yea, he trieth their patience and their faith.' The pairing with the doubled article is Revelation 13:10's and no other KJV verse's. The chastening half of the sentence is the Hebrews 12:6 doctrine the catalogue has already recorded at 1 Nephi 16:25, so the verse is a join: an Old Testament–style chastening formula finished with a phrase from the Apocalypse.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless, whosoever puteth his trust in him, the same shall be lifted up at the last day. Yea, and thus it was with this people.

links.text: And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.

provenance.other: “at the last day” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, all in John (6:39, 6:40, 6:44, 6:54; 11:24), and in four of the five the verb is 'raise … up'. The Book of Mormon reads 'lifted up at the last day', which is in no KJV verse; this is its first occurrence in the book order, and it becomes a Nephite formula thereafter (3 Nephi 27:22; Alma 13:29; 36:28; Ether 4:19).
provenance.significance: The phrase is Johannine and the sentence around it is not. John 6:40 conditions being raised up on seeing the Son and believing on him; Mosiah 23:22 conditions being lifted up on putting one's trust in him, which is the second half of Proverbs 29:25 — 'whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe'. The verse is the join between the chapter's two governing texts, the proverb whose snare Alma confessed at 23:9 and John's resurrection promise, and the join is where the Book of Mormon's own eschatological formula is minted. Later books use 'lifted up at the last day' as a fixed phrase; this is where it enters.

links.note: 'Whosoever puteth his trust in him, the same shall be lifted up at the last day.' 'At the last day' belongs to John and to nowhere else in the KJV, and John 6:40's 'every one which … believeth on him' is the same universal-conditional shape as 'whosoever … the same shall'. The verb is changed from raising to lifting, which is why this is an echo rather than an allusion. Recorded also as the second half of the Proverbs 29:25 proposal made at 23:9.

pericopes.text: For behold, I will shew unto you that they were brought into bondage, and none could deliver them but the Lord their God; yea, even the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob.

links.text: The God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob, the God of our fathers, hath glorified his Son Jesus; whom ye delivered up, and denied him in the presence of Pilate, when he was determined to let him go.

provenance.route: Exodus 3:6, 3:16 → Acts 3:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The string 'the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:13, and the Book of Mormon has it exactly. Exodus 3:6 repeats the noun — 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' — and Exodus 3:16 elides the first conjunction, 'the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob'. tools/mediation-check.py reports one decisive divergence, and it falls to Acts: the Book of Mormon has 'and of Isaac and of Jacob' where Exodus 3:6 has nothing of the kind. (The tool also scores a second 'decisive' point for Exodus on the bare word 'Isaac', which is a diff artifact — the word stands in both candidates.)
provenance.significance: The formula is the burning-bush name, and the burning bush is where God tells Moses he has seen the affliction of his people in bondage — which is exactly what Mosiah 23:23 is announcing. But the Book of Mormon does not have Exodus's wording. It has Peter's, from the sermon at the Beautiful gate, and Peter's sentence continues 'hath glorified his Son Jesus; whom ye delivered up, and denied him in the presence of Pilate'. So the divine name that guarantees deliverance is taken from the one verse where the verb 'deliver' means handing an innocent man over to be killed. Six verses later, at 23:29, Alma and his brethren 'delivered themselves up into their hands' — the same verb in the same passive posture, and the surrender that makes their bondage possible.

links.note: 'None could deliver them but the Lord their God; yea, even the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob.' Ten words reproduced from the only KJV verse that has them in that form; Exodus's two versions of the formula both differ in their connectives. The catalogue records the same source at 1 Nephi 19:10, where the Book of Mormon reads 'the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' — a hybrid. Mosiah has the pure Acts form, and is the closer of the two. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he did deliver them, and he did shew forth his mighty power unto them, and great was their rejoicings.
For behold, it came to pass that while they were in the land of Helam, yea, in the city of Helam, while tilling the land round about, behold an army of the Lamanites were in the borders of the land.

Now it came to pass that the brethren of Alma fled from their fields, and gathered themselves together into the city of Helam; and they were much frightened because of the appearance of the Lamanites.
But Alma went forth and stood among them, and exhorted them that they should not be frightened, but that they should remember the Lord their God, and he would deliver them;
therefore they hushed their fears, and began to cry unto the Lord, that he would soften the hearts of the Lamanites, that they would spare them, and their wives, and their children.

And it came to pass that the Lord did soften the hearts of the Lamanites. And Alma and his brethren went forth and delivered themselves up into their hands; and the Lamanites took possession of the land of Helam.
Now the armies of the Lamanites which had followed after the people of king Limhi, had been lost in the wilderness for many days.
And behold, they had found those priests of king Noah, in a place which they called Amulon; and they had began to possess the land of Amulon, and had began to till the ground.
Now the name of the leader of those priests was Amulon.

And it came to pass that Amulon did plead with the Lamanites; and he also sent forth their wives, which was the daughters of the Lamanites, to plead with their brethren, that they should not destroy their husbands.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites had compassion on Amulon and his brethren, and did not destroy them, because of their wives.

And Amulon and his brethren did join the Lamanites, and they were travelling in the wilderness in search of the land of Nephi, when they discovered the land of Helam, which was possessed by Alma and his brethren.

And it came to pass that the Lamanites promised unto Alma and his brethren, that if they would shew them the way which led to the land of Nephi, that they would grant unto them their lives and their liberty.

But it came to pass that after Alma had shewn them the way that led to the land of Nephi, the Lamanites would not keep their promise; but they set guards round about the land of Helam, over Alma and his brethren.

links.text: And when he shewed them the entrance into the city, they smote the city with the edge of the sword; but they let go the man and all his family.

provenance.other: 'Shewed them the entrance' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 1:25. The Book of Mormon reads 'shew them the way' (23:36) and 'had shewn them the way' (23:37); 'shew them the way' is Exodus 18:20's phrase, of teaching, not of guiding an army. The 1830 spellings 'shew' and 'shewn' are the KJV's and were modernised in 1920.
provenance.significance: Judges 1:24-25 is the KJV's one bargain-for-the-road story: spies promise a man of Bethel his life if he will show them the way into the city, he shows them, they sack the city — and they keep the promise, letting him and his family go. Mosiah 23:36-37 is the same scene with the ending reversed. The Lamanites promise Alma 'their lives and their liberty' if he will show them the way to the land of Nephi; he shows them, and 'the Lamanites would not keep their promise'. The point of cataloguing it is the inversion: in Judges the invaders are more honourable than the informer deserves, and here they are less. Note too what Alma is doing in the scene — a prophet guiding an enemy army to his own people's homeland.

links.note: 'After Alma had shewn them the way that led to the land of Nephi, the Lamanites would not keep their promise.' There is only one comparable transaction in the KJV, Judges 1:24-25, and its verb of showing survives in the Book of Mormon's 1830 spelling. Filed as figural because the wording is Exodus 18:20's and the shape is Judges's; the finding is the broken promise, which is the one element Judges does not have.
links.whyNot: The shared vocabulary is two ordinary words, 'shew' and 'way', and a captive guiding captors is a situation that needs no literary source. If the row is wrong it is wrong in the ordinary way of typological proposals — the reader supplies the resemblance.

pericopes.text: And the remainder of them went to the land of Nephi; and a part of them returned to the land of Helam, and also brought with them the wives and the children of the guards which had been left in the land.

And the king of the Lamanites had granted unto Amulon that he should be a king and a ruler over his people, which was in the land of Helam; nevertheless he should have no power to do any thing contrary to the will of the king of the Lamanites.

And it came to pass that Amulon did gain favor in the eyes of the king of the Lamanites; therefore the king of the Lamanites granted unto him and his brethren, that they should be appointed teachers over his people; yea, even over the people which was in the land of Shemlon, and in the land of Shilom, and in the land of Amulon:
for the Lamanites had taken possession of all these lands; therefore the king of the Lamanites had appointed kings over all these lands.
And now the name of the king of the Lamanites was Laman, being called after the name of his father; and therefore he was called king Laman. And he was king over a numerous people;

links.text: And it came to pass, that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child; and they called him Zacharias, after the name of his father.

provenance.other: “after the name of his father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:59. The nearest other reading is Genesis 48:6, 'called after the name of their brethren'.
provenance.significance: Luke 1:59 is not a naming, it is a naming refused: the neighbours would have called the child Zacharias after the name of his father, and Elisabeth answers 'Not so; but he shall be called John.' The Book of Mormon uses the phrase for a naming that goes through — king Laman, son of Laman — and the effect, in a chapter about a dynasty of Lamanite kings all bearing the founder's name, is the opposite of Luke's. The interest of the row is that this batch of chapters ends, at Mosiah 25:12, with the other case: the children of Amulon refusing to 'be called by the names of their fathers' and taking the name of Nephi instead. The KJV's one refused patronymic sits behind the one naming here that is not refused.

links.note: 'The name of the king of the Lamanites was Laman, being called after the name of his father.' Six words from the only KJV verse that has them. Recorded as an echo rather than an allusion because naming a son for his father needs no source and the KJV's phrasing is the natural English; what makes it worth a row is that the singleton is a naming that Luke's narrative overturns, in a chapter that is establishing a hereditary name.
links.whyNot: The collocation is close to unavoidable in English, and the Book of Mormon's onomastic notices are formulaic throughout. If the row is wrong, it is wrong because the phrase is the only way to say the thing.

pericopes.text: and he appointed teachers of the brethren of Amulon, in every land which was possessed by his people: and thus the language of Nephi began to be taught among all the people of the Lamanites.

And they were a people friendly one with another; nevertheless they knew not God; neither did the brethren of Amulon teach them any thing concerning the Lord their God, neither the law of Moses; nor did they teach them the words of Abinadi;
but they taught them that they should keep their record, and that they might write one to another.

And thus the Lamanites began to increase in riches, and began to trade one with another, and wax great, and began to be a cunning and a wise people, as to the wisdom of the world; yea, a very cunning people; delighting in all manner of wickedness and plunder, except it were among their own brethren.

links.text: For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.

provenance.other: “the wisdom of this world” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 1:20, 2:6 and 3:19 — all Paul, all in one argument. The Book of Mormon reads 'the wisdom of the world', dropping the demonstrative; that reading stands in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The phrase is a verdict, not a description, and the Book of Mormon uses it as one. 1 Corinthians 3:19 is 'the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God'; 1:20 is 'hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?'. Mosiah 24:7 says the Lamanites 'began to be a cunning and a wise people, AS TO the wisdom of the world' — the qualifier does the work of Paul's whole argument in three words, conceding the wisdom and voiding it. The next clause confirms the reading: 'yea, a very cunning people; delighting in all manner of wickedness and plunder.' Note also that the verse describes the fruit of a literacy programme, 24:4-6, in which Amulon's priests teach the Lamanites to keep records but not the words of Abinadi. What the chapter is condemning is a wisdom without revelation, which is exactly Paul's subject.

links.note: 'A cunning and a wise people, as to the wisdom of the world.' Paul's phrase, three times in 1 Corinthians and nowhere else in the KJV, used as Paul uses it — to grant a wisdom and disqualify it in the same breath. The dropped demonstrative keeps this an allusion rather than a quotation.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that Amulon began to exercise authority over Alma and his brethren, and began to persecute him, and cause that his children should persecute their children:

for Amulon knew Alma, that he had been one of the king’s priests, and that it was he that believed the words of Abinadi, and was driven out before the king; and therefore he was wroth with him, for he was subject to king Laman; yet he exercised authority over them, and put tasks upon them, and put task-masters over them.

links.text: Therefore they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens. And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses.

provenance.other: “taskmasters” occurs in exactly six KJV verses — Exodus 1:11, 3:7, 5:6, 5:10, 5:13, 5:14 — and in no book but Exodus. Exodus 1:11 is the one that pairs them with burdens: 'they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens.' The 1830 text hyphenates, 'task-masters', which stands in no KJV verse; the KJV spelling is solid.
provenance.significance: This is the word that converts a local persecution into an Exodus. Once 'task-masters' is on the page the rest of the chapter follows the Egyptian sequence without further prompting: burdens laid on shoulders (24:14), a cry that goes up to God (24:10), the cry forbidden (24:11), a covenant remembered and the burdens eased (24:13-15), an escape while the oppressors sleep (24:19), a march into the wilderness and a song of thanks (24:20-22). Exodus 3:7 — the verse in the same six that is spoken from the burning bush — is 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people … and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters', and the chapter before this one closed on the burning-bush name at Mosiah 23:23. The catalogue's claim is not that a Nephite escape resembles the Exodus in general, which any reader sees, but that it is being written with the vocabulary of Exodus 1-6 specifically.

links.note: 'He exercised authority over them, and put tasks upon them, and put task-masters over them.' Taskmasters are an Egyptian institution in the KJV and appear in no other book; Exodus 1:11 is the verse that sets them over a people to afflict them with burdens, which is the sentence Mosiah 24:9 and 24:14 divide between them. The doubled 'put tasks … put task-masters' is the Book of Mormon's own, and holds this to an allusion.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that so great was their afflictions, that they began to cry mightily to God.

links.text: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.

provenance.other: “cry mightily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8. The 1830 text reads 'cry mightily to God' against the KJV's 'cry mightily unto God'.
provenance.significance: Jonah 3:8 is a royal decree, and what it decrees is the cry: 'let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God.' The king of Nineveh commands his people to pray. Mosiah 24:10-11 takes the KJV's only phrase for that commanded cry and gives it to a people whose king commands the opposite — 'Amulon commanded them that they should stop their cries; and he put guards over them to watch them, that whosoever should be found calling upon God, should be put to death.' The two verses are a hinge: the phrase arrives from the one place in scripture where a king orders prayer, into the one place in this book where a king forbids it. Whether the inversion is designed or not, it is legible only when the source is named.

links.note: 'So great was their afflictions, that they began to cry mightily to God.' The adverb-verb pair is a KJV singleton and the Book of Mormon has it with one preposition changed. What makes the row carry is the next verse, where the cry is criminalised; Jonah 3:8 is a king's order to cry, Mosiah 24:11 a king's order to stop.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Amulon commanded them that they should stop their cries; and he put guards over them to watch them, that whosoever should be found calling upon God, should be put to death.

links.text: All the presidents of the kingdom, the governors, and the princes, the counsellors, and the captains, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree, that whosoever shall ask a petition of any God or man for thirty days, save of thee, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.

provenance.other: “ask a petition” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Daniel 6:7 and 6:12, which are the decree and its enforcement. The Book of Mormon has none of that wording; the contact is the situation and the 'whosoever … should be put to death' construction, which Daniel 6:7 shares in the form 'whosoever shall ask a petition … he shall be cast into the den of lions'.
provenance.significance: Daniel 6 is the only law in scripture that makes prayer itself a capital offence, and Mosiah 24:11 enacts the same law in a Nephite valley. What the Book of Mormon does next is the interesting part, because it is not what Daniel does. Daniel opens his windows and prays three times a day in plain view, and is thrown to the lions and delivered; Alma's people 'did not raise their voices to the Lord their God, but did pour out their hearts to him' (24:12), and are delivered by an escape. Set the two against each other and the chapter has quietly chosen the other model of faithfulness under a praying-ban — Hannah's silent prayer rather than Daniel's public one — and the choice is what the reader is meant to notice.

links.note: 'Amulon commanded them that they should stop their cries; and he put guards over them to watch them, that whosoever should be found calling upon God, should be put to death.' Daniel 6:7 is the KJV's only decree of this kind and the two sentences have the same construction: whosoever is found petitioning God incurs death. Filed as figural because the wording is not Daniel's; the row exists to put the reader beside Daniel 6 when 24:12 declines to do what Daniel did.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Alma and his people did not raise their voices to the Lord their God, but did pour out their hearts to him; and he did know the thoughts of their hearts.

links.text: Now Hannah, she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard: therefore Eli thought she had been drunken.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 1:13, 15 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Psalm 62:8 supplying the idiom
provenance.other: “her voice was not heard” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 1:13, of Hannah: 'she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard.' “poured out my soul before the LORD” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 1:15, two verses later and spoken by Hannah about the same prayer. “pour out your heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 62:8.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 24:12 is a two-clause definition of silent prayer and each clause comes from a different KJV singleton, both of them Hannah's. 'Did not raise their voices to the Lord their God' is 1 Samuel 1:13's 'her voice was not heard'; 'did pour out their hearts to him' is 1 Samuel 1:15's 'poured out my soul before the LORD' with Psalm 62:8's noun. The KJV has exactly one narrative of prayer that is deliberately inaudible, and it is Hannah at Shiloh, misread by a priest as drunkenness. Alma's people, forbidden on pain of death to be heard praying, pray the way the one silent prayer in scripture was prayed. And the third clause of the verse — 'he did know the thoughts of their hearts' — supplies what Eli could not do: the God who hears the inaudible prayer is contrasted with the priest who misjudged it.

links.note: 'Alma and his people did not raise their voices to the Lord their God, but did pour out their hearts to him; and he did know the thoughts of their hearts.' Both halves are Hannah's, from two verses two apart, and the KJV has no other silent prayer. The idiom of pouring is Psalm 62:8's 'pour out your heart before him', which supplies the organ where 1 Samuel 1:15 has the soul. Not a quotation — no clause is reproduced — but the verse has no content that is not from these three.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the voice of the Lord came to them in their afflictions, saying, Lift up your heads and be of good comfort, for I know of the covenant which ye have made unto me; and I will covenant with my people, and deliver them out of bondage.

links.text: Wherefore say unto the children of Israel, I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments:

provenance.other: “remembered my covenant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 6:5. “out of their bondage” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 6:6. “under the burdens” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 6:6 and 6:7. All three stand in one three-verse speech.
provenance.significance: Exodus 6:5-7 is God's answer to the groaning of a people under taskmasters, and it has three moves: I have remembered my covenant; I will bring you out from under the burdens; I will take you to me for a people and ye shall know that I am the LORD your God. Mosiah 24:13-14 has the same three in the same order — 'I know of the covenant which ye have made unto me; and I will covenant with my people, and deliver them out of bondage. And I will also ease the burdens which is put upon your shoulders … that ye may know of a surety that I, the Lord God, do visit my people.' The one alteration is at the first move, and it reverses the direction of the covenant: in Exodus God remembers a covenant HE made with the fathers, here he acknowledges a covenant THEY made with him at the waters of Mormon. That is a real theological substitution and it is visible only against the source.

links.note: 'I know of the covenant which ye have made unto me; and I will covenant with my people, and deliver them out of bondage.' Two KJV singletons and a doubleton, all from Exodus 6:5-7, all in this verse and the next, and in the source's order. The wording is nowhere reproduced exactly, so this is an allusion; the sequence is what makes it certain which speech is being reused.

links.text: And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh.

provenance.other: “lift up your heads” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 24:7 and 24:9, where it is addressed to the gates of the temple, and Luke 21:28, where it is addressed to people. Luke's is therefore the only KJV occurrence that can be spoken to a congregation. “be of good comfort” occurs in five KJV verses, three of them Jesus to a person he is about to heal.
provenance.significance: Luke 21:28 finishes 'for your redemption draweth nigh', and it is the one KJV verse in which raised heads are the posture of an imminent deliverance rather than of a gate opening. The voice of the Lord in Mosiah 24:13 says it to people in bondage and then names the deliverance outright — 'I will covenant with my people, and deliver them out of bondage' — and 24:16 dates it: 'on the morrow I will deliver thee out of bondage.' Luke's redemption is eschatological and this one arrives the next morning; the borrowing brings the larger sense with it, which is the ordinary work of metalepsis.

links.note: 'Lift up your heads and be of good comfort.' Of the KJV's three 'lift up your heads', two are addressed to doors; only Luke 21:28 is addressed to people, and only Luke 21:28 attaches the gesture to a coming redemption. Recorded at moderate because the phrase is short and the second half of the sentence, 'be of good comfort', points elsewhere in the Gospels.

pericopes.text: And I will also ease the burdens which is put upon your shoulders, that even you cannot feel them upon your backs, even while you are in bondage; and this will I do, that ye may stand as witnesses for me hereafter, and that ye may know of a surety that I, the Lord God, do visit my people in their afflictions.

links.text: I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots.

provenance.other: “his shoulder from the burden” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 81:6: 'I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots.' “from off thy shoulder” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 10:27, where a burden is taken off a shoulder and a yoke off a neck. These are the KJV's only two verses in which God removes a burden from a shoulder.
provenance.significance: Psalm 81 is the psalm of the Exodus told in the first person — 'I removed his shoulder from the burden … thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee' — and it is the only place in the KJV where God says he took the load off a shoulder himself. Mosiah 24:14 has God saying it again: 'I will also ease the burdens which is put upon your shoulders.' But the chapter then does something Psalm 81 does not. The burden is not removed; it is made unfeelable — 'that even you cannot feel them upon your backs, even while you are in bondage.' The bondage continues and only the weight of it is taken away, and the reason given is evidentiary: 'that ye may stand as witnesses for me hereafter.' Against the psalm, the departure is the doctrine. Isaiah 58:6, which the catalogue has already put behind Mosiah 23:12, promised to undo the heavy burdens; here the promise is kept in a form the source did not anticipate.

links.note: 'I will also ease the burdens which is put upon your shoulders, that even you cannot feel them upon your backs, even while you are in bondage.' The KJV joins burdens to shoulders in a divine first-person relief exactly twice, at Psalm 81:6 and Isaiah 10:27, and Psalm 81:6 is the Exodus one — the same deliverance this chapter has been narrating in Exodus 1 and Exodus 6 vocabulary since 24:9. The 1830 reads 'which IS put upon your shoulders'; 1920 corrected to 'are'.

links.text: And he said unto Abram, Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years;

provenance.other: “know of a surety” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Genesis 15:13, where God tells Abram his seed will be strangers and afflicted; and Acts 12:11, where Peter, just walked out of Herod's prison past sleeping guards, says 'Now I know of a surety, that the Lord hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me.' “looked upon their affliction” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 4:31, of the Lord visiting the children of Israel. The one KJV verse joining the verb 'visit' to the phrase 'in their affliction' is James 1:27.
provenance.significance: Both KJV occurrences of the idiom are load-bearing here and they are the two ends of the same story. Genesis 15:13 is where the bondage is announced — 'Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them' — and Acts 12:11 is where a man says it on the far side of a miraculous escape past sleeping guards, which is precisely what happens at Mosiah 24:19. Alma's people are told to know of a surety in the middle: still in bondage, told that the bondage is seen. The catalogue has recorded Acts 12:11 once already, at 1 Nephi 5:8, on Sariah's 'I know of a surety'; that was a woman certifying a deliverance after the fact, and this is God certifying one before it.

links.note: 'That ye may know of a surety that I, the Lord God, do visit my people in their afflictions.' Two KJV verses have 'know of a surety' and this chapter arguably uses both — Genesis 15:13's announcement of servitude and affliction, and Acts 12:11's certainty after an escape past sleeping guards. The verb 'visit' with affliction is the KJV's language for God at the Exodus (Exodus 3:16; 4:31) and, once, for the church's duty (James 1:27). Recorded at moderate: the idiom is short, and the Book of Mormon uses it elsewhere without a source.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that the burdens which was laid upon Alma and his brethren, were made light; yea, the Lord did strengthen them that they could bear up their burdens with ease, and they did submit cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord.

links.text: Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness;

provenance.other: “strengthened with all might” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “unto all patience” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are Colossians 1:11: 'Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness.' “that ye may stand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “all the will of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are Colossians 4:12: 'that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.' The Book of Mormon has 'that ye may stand as witnesses' at 24:14 and 'all the will of the Lord' here.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 24:15 puts three ideas in one sentence — God strengthens them, they endure with patience, they endure cheerfully — and Colossians 1:11 is the only KJV verse that puts the same three in one sentence, in that order, with joyfulness in the place of cheerfulness. The pairing matters because the strengthening in Mosiah is not moral but literal: the burdens are made light and the people can bear them. Paul's 'strengthened with all might … unto all patience' is an inward gift; the Book of Mormon takes the phrase and gives it a load to carry.

links.note: 'The Lord did strengthen them that they could bear up their burdens with ease, and they did submit cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord.' Strengthening, patience and cheerfulness in one clause is Colossians 1:11's collocation and nobody else's in the KJV, and the closing 'all the will of' is a singleton from Colossians 4:12, whose 'that ye may stand' the previous verse has also used. Moderate rather than high: each individual word is common, and it is the cluster, not any phrase, that identifies the source.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that so great was their faith and their patience, that the voice of the Lord came unto them again, saying, Be of good comfort, for on the morrow I will deliver thee out of bondage.

links.text: And I will deliver thee out of the hand of the wicked, and I will redeem thee out of the hand of the terrible.

provenance.other: “I will deliver thee out of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 15:21. The 1830 text reads 'on the morrow I will deliver thee out of bondage'; the 1920 edition changed 'thee' to 'you', which destroys the string — 'I will deliver you out of' stands in no KJV verse either. The borrowing is visible in the first edition and invisible in the modern text.
provenance.significance: This is the clearest case in the chapter of the running text doing work no later edition can do, and it is worth stating plainly: a reader of the current Book of Mormon cannot see this link at all. The 1830 'thee' is also grammatically odd in context — the voice is addressing a people, and 24:17 immediately reverts to the plural 'this people' — which is what one expects when a singular-address KJV phrase is carried over whole. Jeremiah 15:20-21 is God's answer to a prophet who has asked why his pain is perpetual: 'I am with thee to save thee and to deliver thee … And I will deliver thee out of the hand of the wicked.' The next verse of Mosiah takes the first half of that promise as well.

links.note: 'Be of good comfort, for on the morrow I will deliver thee out of bondage.' Six words from the KJV's only 'I will deliver thee out of', preserved by the 1830 singular and erased by the 1920 plural. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations. The companion phrase, 'I am with thee to save thee', is a singleton in the previous verse of Jeremiah and is used in the next verse of Mosiah; see the link at 24:17.

pericopes.text: And he saith unto Alma, Thou shalt go before this people, and I will go with thee, and deliver this people out of bondage.

links.text: And I will make thee unto this people a fenced brasen wall: and they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee: for I am with thee to save thee and to deliver thee, saith the LORD.

provenance.other: “I am with thee to save thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 15:20, whose full clause is 'for I am with thee to save thee and to deliver thee, saith the LORD'. The Book of Mormon reads 'I will go with thee, and deliver this people out of bondage', which converts the presence into motion.
provenance.significance: The two halves of Jeremiah 15:20-21 arrive in the two consecutive verses Mosiah 24:16-17, in the source's order and with the source's two verbs, save and deliver, reduced to one. Jeremiah 15 is a complaint chapter: the prophet has said his wound is incurable, and the answer promises accompaniment rather than relief from the fight — 'they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee'. Alma is being sent, as Jeremiah was, to go before a people rather than away from them, and the accompanying clause 'Thou shalt go before this people' is not Jeremiah but Deuteronomy 3:28, where Joshua is charged to go over before this people. The Book of Mormon has spliced the commissioning of Joshua onto the consolation of Jeremiah.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 3:28, 'he shall go over before this people', for the first clause only.

links.note: 'Thou shalt go before this people, and I will go with thee, and deliver this people out of bondage.' The second and third clauses continue the Jeremiah 15:21 borrowing of the previous verse into 15:20, whose 'I am with thee to save thee and to deliver thee' is a KJV singleton. Moderate rather than high: the accompaniment formula is common in the KJV (Exodus 33:14; Deuteronomy 31:8; Joshua 1:5), and only the pairing with 24:16 selects Jeremiah.

pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that Alma and his people, in the night time, gathered their flocks together, and also of their grain; yea, even all the night time were they gathering their flocks together.
And in the morning the Lord caused a deep sleep to come upon the Lamanites, yea, and all their task-masters were in a profound sleep.

links.text: So David took the spear and the cruse of water from Saul’s bolster; and they gat them away, and no man saw it, nor knew it, neither awaked: for they were all asleep; because a deep sleep from the LORD was fallen upon them.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 26:12 and Genesis 2:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “deep sleep from the LORD” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 26:12: 'no man saw it, nor knew it, neither awaked: for they were all asleep; because a deep sleep from the LORD was fallen upon them.' “caused a deep sleep” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 2:21, 'the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam'. Mosiah 24:19 — 'the Lord caused a deep sleep to come upon the Lamanites' — has the verb of one and the situation of the other. 'Profound sleep', the phrase used of the task-masters in the same verse, stands in no KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Of the KJV's seven deep sleeps only one is tactical, and it is 1 Samuel 26:12 — the night David walks through Saul's camp, takes the spear from the king's bolster, and walks out again without a hand raised, because the LORD has put the whole army to sleep. Mosiah 24:18-20 is the same night: an armed camp, guards who do not wake, and a people who walk out. The difference is what is taken. David takes the spear and the cruse of water in order to prove that he could have taken the king's life and did not; Alma's people take their flocks and their grain and leave. The chapter has spent eleven verses making the Lamanites into Egyptians, and at the moment of the escape it reaches instead for the one Israelite-on-Israelite night raid in scripture, where the sleeping enemy is the LORD's anointed and is deliberately spared.

links.note: 'And in the morning the Lord caused a deep sleep to come upon the Lamanites, yea, and all their task-masters were in a profound sleep.' Two KJV singletons in one sentence: Genesis 2:21's causative and 1 Samuel 26:12's divinely-sent sleep over a camp. The second supplies the scene and the first the syntax. Note that the 1830 keeps the Exodus word 'task-masters' inside the Samuel scene, which is where the chapter's two typologies meet.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Alma and his people departed into the wilderness; and when they had travelled all day, they pitched their tents in a valley, and they called the valley Alma, because he led their way in the wilderness;

links.text: Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.

provenance.other: “way in the wilderness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 43:19: 'Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.'
provenance.significance: Isaiah 43:16-19 is the new-exodus oracle — the God who made a way in the sea will make a way in the wilderness, and the deliverance to come will be a new thing that puts the old one out of mind. Mosiah 24 has been the old one, in Exodus 1 and Exodus 6 vocabulary, for eleven verses; at the moment the escape succeeds it names the valley after the man who 'led their way in the wilderness'. The KJV's only 'way in the wilderness' is the verse that says the second exodus will surpass the first. Recording the phrase is what lets a reader see that the chapter's naming of the valley of Alma is a claim and not a note.

links.note: 'They called the valley Alma, because he led their way in the wilderness.' Four words that in the KJV belong to one verse, and that verse is the new-exodus promise. Recorded as an echo, not an allusion: the Book of Mormon's syntax is possessive ('their way') where Isaiah's is a made road, and nothing else of Isaiah 43 is present.
links.whyNot: A leader making a way through a wilderness is the chapter's plain subject and needs no source; if the row is wrong, the singleton is a coincidence of a very short phrase.

pericopes.text: yea, and in the valley of Alma they poured out their thanks to God because he had been merciful unto them, and eased their burdens, and had delivered them out of bondage; for they were in bondage, and none could deliver them, except it were the Lord their God.
And they gave thanks to God, yea, all their men, and all their women, and all their children, that could speak, lifted their voices in the praises of their God.

links.text: And when he had thus spoken, he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat.

provenance.other: “gave thanks to God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 27:35. The KJV's usual constructions are 'gave thanks unto God' and 'thanked God', which is why the count is as low as it is; the singleton reflects a preposition, not a distinctive idea.
provenance.significance: Acts 27:35 is a meal on a ship that is about to break up, eaten on Paul's assurance that not a life will be lost. Mosiah 24:21-22 is a thanksgiving in a valley by a people who have just walked out of slavery. Both are the moment where a company that has been delivered but is not yet safe stops to give thanks — Alma's people are still being pursued, and the Lord tells them to run again in the next verse. The row is recorded chiefly so the catalogue can say where the phrase is, and can point at the recurrence in the next chapter.

links.note: 'And they gave thanks to God, yea, all their men, and all their women, and all their children, that could speak, lifted their voices in the praises of their God.' The exact string is a KJV singleton, but that is an accident of the preposition and the note should not pretend otherwise. The verse's own interest is not the borrowing but the qualification 'that could speak', which the KJV has no parallel for, and the fact that a people forbidden twelve verses earlier to raise their voices now raise them.
links.whyNot: 'Gave thanks to God' is unavoidable English and the singleton count is a KJV preposition preference, not evidence of distinctiveness. Nothing else of Acts 27 is present. A cautious editor would decline this row and put it in the register instead.

pericopes.text: And now the Lord said unto Alma, Haste thee and get thou and this people out of this land, for the Lamanites have awoke and doth pursue thee; therefore get thee out of this land, and I will stop the Lamanites in this valley, that they come no further in pursuit of this people.

links.text: Haste thee, escape thither; for I cannot do anything till thou be come thither. Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.

provenance.other: “haste thee” occurs in exactly three KJV verses in this imperative sense: Genesis 19:22, 1 Samuel 23:27 and Psalm 22:19. Only Genesis 19:22 is an order to a fugitive to clear the ground before God acts.
provenance.significance: Genesis 19:22 is the one verse in the KJV where God's action waits on a man's escape: 'Haste thee, escape thither; for I cannot do any thing till thou be come thither.' Mosiah 24:23 has the same logic in the same order — get out of this land, and then 'I will stop the Lamanites in this valley, that they come no further in pursuit of this people.' The intervention is held until the fugitives are out. The borrowing is worth naming because the two situations are otherwise opposite: Lot flees a city God is about to destroy, and Alma flees an army God is about to halt. What the verses share is the sequencing, and the KJV says it once.

links.note: 'Haste thee and get thou and this people out of this land … and I will stop the Lamanites in this valley.' The imperative is one of three in the KJV and the only one addressed to an escaping party whose escape is the condition of God's next move. 1 Samuel 23:27, where a messenger's 'haste thee' saves David from Saul by diverting the pursuit, is the nearest rival and is worth a reader's glance; it lacks the divine speaker.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they departed out of the valley, and took their journey into the wilderness.
And it came to pass that after they had been in the wilderness twelve days, they arrived to the land of Zarahemla; and king Mosiah did also receive them with joy.
And now king Mosiah caused that all the people should be gathered together.

Now there were not so many of the children of Nephi, or so many of those which were descendants of Nephi, as there were of the people of Zarahemla, which was a descendant of Mulok, and those which came with him into the wilderness;
and there were not so many of the people of Nephi and of the people of Zarahemla as there was of the Lamanites; yea, they were not half so numerous.
And now all the people of Nephi was assembled together, and also all the people of Zarahemla, and they were gathered together in two bodies.

And it came to pass that Mosiah did read, and caused to be read, the records of Zeniff to his people; yea, he read the records of the people of Zeniff, from the time they left the land of Zarahemla until the time they returned again.
And he also read the account of Alma and his brethren, and all their afflictions, from the time they left the land of Zarahemla, until the time they returned again.
And now when Mosiah had made an end of reading the records, his people which tarried in the land was struck with wonder and amazement,

links.text: And it shall be, when thou hast made an end of reading this book, that thou shalt bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of Euphrates:

provenance.other: “made an end of reading” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 51:63: 'And it shall be, when thou hast made an end of reading this book, that thou shalt bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of Euphrates.' The Book of Mormon's 'made an end of' is a formula it uses constantly; what is rare is the object — reading.
provenance.significance: The KJV has exactly one public reading that comes to an end, and it is Seraiah reading aloud in Babylon the book of Babylon's doom, after which the book is weighted with a stone and drowned in the river so that the city may sink and not rise. Mosiah 25:5-7 is a public reading of two records: the record of Zeniff's colony, which went up to reclaim a land and lost it, and the record of Alma, which is deliverance out of bondage. Both records are read to a people who did not live them. Jeremiah's reading is performed so a city may sink; Mosiah's is performed so a people may be joined into one, which is what the rest of the chapter does. The phrase is small and the contrast it recovers is the row's whole content.

links.note: 'And now when Mosiah had made an end of reading the records, his people which tarried in the land was struck with wonder and amazement.' 'Made an end of reading' occurs once in the KJV. The Book of Mormon's own 'made an end of speaking' formula is everywhere — including seven verses later at 25:14 — so it is the direct object that carries the borrowing, not the idiom.
links.whyNot: Only the object distinguishes this from the Book of Mormon's own stock phrase, and a narrator with a reading to end would arrive at these words without Jeremiah. The row is proposed, not pressed.

links.text: And they knew that it was he which sat for alms at the Beautiful gate of the temple: and they were filled with wonder and amazement at that which had happened unto him.

provenance.other: “wonder and amazement” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:10. The Book of Mormon changes the verb — 'struck with' for the KJV's 'filled with' — and then uses 'filled with' three times in the following four verses (25:8, 25:9, 25:11).
provenance.significance: Acts 3:10 is the crowd at the Beautiful gate seeing a man they had watched beg for years walking and leaping. Mosiah 25:7-8 is a crowd seeing people they had given up for lost — 'when they beheld those that had been delivered out of bondage'. Both are the reaction of bystanders to a deliverance they did not witness and can now see the evidence of. The catalogue has already found Acts 3:13 behind Mosiah 23:23, three verses further into the same sermon; taken together the two rows suggest that Peter's speech at the temple gate was available to this writer as a passage and not only as a phrase.

links.note: 'His people which tarried in the land was struck with wonder and amazement.' A KJV singleton with one verb changed, and the changed verb reappears in its KJV form ('filled with') in each of the next three verses. The 1830's 'was struck' where 1920 reads 'were struck' is a grammatical, not a lexical, difference and does not bear on the borrowing.

pericopes.text: for they knew not what to think; for when they beheld those that had been delivered out of bondage, they were filled with exceeding great joy.

links.text: When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy.

provenance.other: “exceeding great joy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 2:10: 'When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy.' The KJV's other superlatives of joy are 'exceeding joyful' and 'joy exceedingly'.
provenance.significance: Matthew 2:10 is the wise men's reaction at the end of a long journey, on seeing the sign that the thing they came for is real. Mosiah 25:8 is the reaction of people who have just heard a record read and then looked at the survivors standing in front of them. What both verses catch is joy at sight rather than at report — Matthew's magi rejoice when they SEE the star, and Mosiah's people rejoice 'when they beheld those that had been delivered out of bondage', after a paragraph in which hearing the record only left them not knowing what to think. Note also that the chapter opened its Matthew borrowings two chapters earlier: Mosiah 23:1's 'warned of the Lord' is Matthew 2:12's idiom, from two verses after this one.

links.note: 'For they knew not what to think; for when they beheld those that had been delivered out of bondage, they were filled with exceeding great joy.' A KJV singleton, taken whole and given a different verb of filling. Recorded at moderate rather than high because the phrase is a common intensifier in English and could be arrived at independently; what supports it is the verse before, which also runs on a KJV singleton of reaction, and Mosiah 23:1's use of the same Matthean paragraph.

pericopes.text: And again, when they thought of their brethren which had been slain by the Lamanites, they were filled with sorrow, and even shed many tears of sorrow.

And again, when they thought of the immediate goodness of God, and his power in delivering Alma and his brethren out of the hands of the Lamanites, and of bondage, they did raise their voices, and gave thanks to God.
And again, when they thought upon the Lamanites, which was their brethren, of their sinful and polluted state, they were filled with pain and anguish, for the welfare of their souls.

And it came to pass that when those which were the children of Amulon and his brethren, which had taken to wife the daughters of the Lamanites, they were displeased with the conduct of their fathers, and they would no longer be called by the names of their fathers; therefore they took upon themselves the name of Nephi, that they might be called the children of Nephi, and be numbered among those which were called Nephites.

links.text: One shall say, I am the LORD’s; and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the LORD, and surname himself by the name of Israel.

provenance.other: Isaiah 44:5 is the KJV's one description of a person taking a name that is not his by descent: 'One shall say, I am the LORD's; and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the LORD, and surname himself by the name of Israel.' “called by the name” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Deuteronomy 28:10; 2 Samuel 6:2; Isaiah 48:1), and Isaiah 48:1 is the one about being called by the name of a patriarch.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 44:5 is a conversion oracle: outsiders adopt Jacob's name and thereby join his people. Mosiah 25:12 runs it backwards and forwards at once. The children of Amulon repudiate a patronymic — 'they would no longer be called by the names of their fathers' — and take Nephi's instead, and the next verse records that all of Zarahemla was then 'numbered with the Nephites', so that a national name is being conferred by choice rather than by descent, which is exactly Isaiah's point. The counterweight sits at Mosiah 24:3, where the Lamanite king is 'called after the name of his father'. The batch has both cases: a dynasty that keeps a father's name, and children who refuse one.

links.note: 'They would no longer be called by the names of their fathers; therefore they took upon themselves the name of Nephi.' There is one passage in the KJV about surnaming oneself into another man's people, and it is Isaiah 44:5. The Book of Mormon reproduces none of its wording, which caps this at an allusion; the case rests on the singularity of the idea in the source and on the fact that this catalogue has already recorded the same verse behind 2 Nephi 28:3, in a different book and a different hand.

pericopes.text: And now all the people of Zarahemla were numbered with the Nephites, and this because the kingdom had been conferred upon none but those which were descendants of Nephi.
And now it came to pass that when Mosiah had made an end of speaking and reading to the people, he desired that Alma should also speak to the people.
And it came to pass that Alma did speak unto them, when they were assembled together in large bodies, and he went from one body to another, preaching unto the people repentance and faith on the Lord.

links.text: Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.

provenance.other: “repentance toward God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:21: 'Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.' This is the KJV's only place where repentance and faith are named together as the content of a preaching. The Book of Mormon has 'repentance and faith on the Lord' here and 'repentance and faith in God' at 25:22; neither preposition is Paul's 'toward'.
provenance.significance: Acts 20 is Paul's farewell at Miletus to the elders of Ephesus, and 20:21 is his summary of what he preached house to house. Mosiah 25:15 is a summary of what Alma preached body to body — 'he went from one body to another' — as he moves through an assembly too large for one hearing. The parallel is not only the formula but the itinerant method the formula describes; Paul's next sentences are about appointing overseers, and four verses later Alma is given power to ordain priests and teachers over every church, which is Acts 14:23. The chapter's account of how a church is organised is being told in the vocabulary of Acts.

links.note: 'Preaching unto the people repentance and faith on the Lord.' The pairing is Acts 20:21's and the KJV has it nowhere else; the Book of Mormon keeps the pair and loses Paul's preposition, twice, differently (25:15 'on the Lord', 25:22 'in God'), which is what one expects of a formula reused from memory rather than copied.

pericopes.text: And he did exhort the people of Limhi and his brethren, all those that had been delivered out of bondage, that they should remember that it was the Lord that did deliver them.

And it came to pass that after Alma had taught the people many things, and had made an end of speaking to them, that king Limhi was desirous that he might be baptized; and all his people were desirous that they might be baptized also.

Therefore Alma did go forth into the water, and did baptize them; yea, he did baptize them after the manner he did his brethren in the waters of Mormon; yea, and as many as he did baptize did belong to the Church of God; and this because of their belief on the words of Alma.

links.text: And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him.

provenance.other: “into the water” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, and Acts 8:38 is the only one where the going in is a baptism: 'they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him.' The others are Marah, the bitter-water ordeal of Numbers 5, a floating axe head, and two of the same demoniac boy.
provenance.significance: Acts 8 is the KJV's one narrated baptism outside the Jordan, performed on the road by a man who is not an apostle, at the request of a convert who asks 'what doth hinder me to be baptized?' Mosiah 25:17-18 is the same shape: king Limhi and his people ask, and Alma — who baptized in the waters of Mormon without ecclesiastical warrant, having fled the priesthood that ordained him — goes forth into the water and baptizes them. The chapter is at that moment arguing about authority: 25:19 has Mosiah granting Alma power to establish churches, and 23:17 had Alma insisting nobody preach except by his ordination from God. Philip's baptism is the New Testament's precedent for a valid ordinance performed away from the centre.

links.note: 'Therefore Alma did go forth into the water, and did baptize them.' Going down into the water to baptize is Acts 8:38's phrase and the KJV's only one; the Book of Mormon has 'go forth into' for 'go down into'. Moderate: 'into the water' is ordinary English and the practice is described repeatedly in the Book of Mormon from Mosiah 18 onward without KJV wording.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that king Mosiah granted unto Alma, that he might establish Churches throughout all the land of Zarahemla; and gave him power to ordain priests and teachers over every Church.

links.text: And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.

provenance.other: “in every church” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 14:23 and 1 Corinthians 4:17, and only Acts 14:23 pairs it with ordaining: 'when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord.' Titus 1:5 has the parallel instruction with a different unit, 'ordain elders in every city'.
provenance.significance: Acts 14:22-23 is one sentence in the KJV and this batch of chapters draws on both halves of it: 'much tribulation' at Mosiah 23:10, and the ordaining of officers church by church here. That is worth stating as a fact about the two rows rather than as a claim about a source, but the coincidence is not small — the KJV says 'much tribulation' once and 'ordained them elders in every church' once, and the two stand consecutively.
