What Mosiah 25:19-21 adds is a reason the KJV does not give: the churches are multiplied because 'there was so many people that they could not all be governed by one teacher; neither could they all hear the word of God in one assembly'. Acts leaves the plurality of churches unexplained; the Book of Mormon supplies an acoustics problem.

links.note: 'And gave him power to ordain priests and teachers over every Church.' Ordaining officers in every church is Acts 14:23's clause and the KJV's only one of its kind; the Book of Mormon substitutes its own offices for elders and 'over' for 'in'. Moderate: the substitutions are substantial and the practice is described at Mosiah 23:17 without this wording.

pericopes.text: Now this was done because there was so many people that they could not all be governed by one teacher; neither could they all hear the word of God in one assembly;

therefore they did assemble themselves together in different bodies, being called Churches; every Church having their priests and their teachers, and every priest preaching the word according as it was delivered to him by the mouth of Alma;

and thus, notwithstanding there being many Churches, they were all one Church; yea, even the Church of God: for there was nothing preached in all the Churches except it were repentance and faith in God.

links.text: But now are they many members, yet but one body.

provenance.other: “yet but one body” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:20: 'But now are they many members, yet but one body.' “are one body” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 12:5 and 1 Corinthians 12:12, both of the same figure. The Book of Mormon reads 'notwithstanding there being many Churches, they were all one Church', which has Paul's concessive structure and Paul's arithmetic with the noun changed.
provenance.significance: Paul's figure is about persons: many members, one body, so that no member may say it has no need of another. The Book of Mormon moves it up a level and applies it to congregations — many churches, one church — which is a use Paul never makes and which the KJV cannot supply. That is the finding. It also explains the chapter's odd bookkeeping, in which 25:21 has each church with its own priests and teachers and its own preaching, 25:22 insists they are nonetheless one, and 25:23 then counts them: 'there was seven Churches in the land of Zarahemla.' The Pauline sentence is doing the work of an ecclesiology, and it is doing it for a plurality of local congregations rather than for a plurality of gifts.

links.note: 'And thus, notwithstanding there being many Churches, they were all one Church; yea, even the Church of God.' The many-and-one construction is Paul's and the KJV's only 'yet but one body' is 1 Corinthians 12:20. Filed as an allusion with subtype conceptual: no clause is reproduced, but the sentence is unintelligible as English theology without the figure it is quietly transposing.
links.whyNot: 'Many … one' is a construction, not a phrase, and a writer describing several congregations of one faith might reach it unaided. The row rests on the transposition being visible, and a reader who does not see Paul behind it will see only a truism.

pericopes.text: And now there was seven Churches in the land of Zarahemla. And it came to pass that whosoever was desirous to take upon them the name of Christ, or of God, they did join the churches of God;

links.text: John to the seven churches which are in Asia: Grace be unto you, and peace, from him which is, and which was, and which is to come; and from the seven Spirits which are before his throne;

provenance.other: “seven churches” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Revelation 1:4, 1:11 and 1:20, and in no other book. There is no other numbered plurality of churches anywhere in the Bible.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon counts its churches once, and the number it arrives at is the Bible's only number of churches. Revelation 1 has seven churches in Asia, addressed as a set by a book that will judge each in turn; Mosiah 25:23 has seven churches in the land of Zarahemla, gathered from an assembly too large to hear one preacher. If the number is borrowed, what comes with it is the idea that a plurality of congregations can be addressed as a single whole — which is the claim the previous verse has just made in Paul's words. If it is not borrowed, the catalogue has still done its job by putting the reader in a position to decide.

links.note: 'And now there was seven Churches in the land of Zarahemla.' Seven churches is a Johannine number and appears in three verses of one chapter of the KJV and nowhere else. Recorded as an echo at moderate: a count is not a quotation, and this one may simply be a count.
links.whyNot: Nothing else of Revelation 1 is present — no Asia, no candlesticks, no letters, no naming of the seven — and a narrative that has just described churches multiplying had to arrive at some number. A cautious editor would decline the row. It is kept because the coincidence is exact and a reader will notice it whether or not the catalogue does.

pericopes.text: and they were called the people of God. And the Lord did pour out his spirit upon them, and they were blest, and prospered in the land.

links.text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

provenance.route: Joel 2:28 → KJV → Book of Mormon, NOT via Acts 2:17
provenance.other: “pour out my spirit upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joel 2:28. Acts 2:17 quotes the same oracle and inserts a partitive: 'I will pour out OF my Spirit upon all flesh.' “poured out my spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 39:29, 'I have poured out my spirit upon the house of Israel'. The Book of Mormon reads 'the Lord did pour out his spirit upon them', with no partitive.
provenance.significance: This is a mediation decided on one word, and the word is the one tools/mediation-check.py drops. Run against Joel 2:28 and Acts 2:17 the tool reports no decisive divergence, because it deliberately ignores single common words to avoid false positives; but the single common word IS the divergence here. Acts differs from Joel at exactly one point in the clause the Book of Mormon reproduces — Peter's Greek gives 'of my Spirit', partitively, and the KJV renders it so. Mosiah 25:24 has no 'of'. It is following the Old Testament form of the oracle and not the apostolic quotation of it, which matters because so much else in these three chapters comes through Acts (3:13 at 23:23, 3:10 at 25:7, 14:23 at 25:19, 20:21 at 25:15). Where the New Testament had the same words on offer, this verse did not take them.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 39:29, which has the pouring in the perfect and no partitive, and which is also addressed to a people just gathered and settled.

links.note: 'And the Lord did pour out his spirit upon them, and they were blest, and prospered in the land.' Joel's clause with the person of the pronoun changed. The finding is the absent 'of': Acts 2:17 quotes this very clause and adds a partitive, so the presence of Joel's form and the absence of Peter's settles the mediation as direct-OT — by eye, since mediation-check.py suppresses one-word divergences by design. The 1830 'blest' for 'blessed' is an orthographic variant of the period and carries nothing.

pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that there was many of the rising generation that could not understand the words of king Benjamin, being little children at the time he spake unto his people; and they did not believe the tradition of their fathers.

links.text: And profited in the Jews’ religion above many my equals in mine own nation, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers.

provenance.other: “traditions of my fathers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 1:14. The KJV otherwise puts the word in a hostile setting — the tradition of the elders, the tradition of men (Matthew 15, Mark 7, Colossians 2:8) — and never once approves of it.
provenance.alternative: 1 Peter 1:18, ‘vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers’, which is the other place the KJV joins tradition to ancestors; but it inverts the possessive and, like the Gospel occurrences, condemns what it names.
provenance.significance: The KJV has no positive sense of the phrase, and Mosiah 26:1 needs one: here the tradition of the fathers is the true religion and refusing it is the sin. So the narrator has taken the diction of Paul's pre-conversion zeal and reversed its polarity — Paul's ‘traditions of my fathers’ is what he had to be knocked off a horse to abandon, and Mosiah's is what the rising generation are damned for abandoning. That reversal is worth holding for one chapter: the very next chapter puts one of these unbelievers on the road with a heavenly voice and a three-day collapse, and the man who gets up is called to bear the name he had blasphemed.

links.note: ‘They did not believe the tradition of their fathers.’ The construction — tradition, possessive, fathers — is Galatians 1:14's and nowhere else's in the KJV, and the chapter's larger interest in a generation that will not receive what was handed down runs through Mosiah 26 to Alma the Younger's conversion in 27. The link is moderate rather than high because the three words are the whole of the contact and the idea of ancestral tradition needs no source; what recommends it is that English scripture supplies exactly one shape for the phrase and this is it.

pericopes.text: They did not believe what had been said concerning the resurrection of the dead; neither did they believe concerning the coming of Christ.
And now because of their unbelief, they could not understand the word of God; and their hearts were hardened.

And they would not be baptized; neither would they join the church. And they were a separate people as to their faith, and remained so ever after, even in their carnal and sinful state: for they would not call upon the Lord their God.—
And now in the reign of Mosiah, they were not half so numerous as the people of God; but because of the dissentions among the brethren, they became more numerous.

For it came to pass that they did deceive many with their flattering words, which were in the church, and did cause them to commit many sins; therefore it became expedient that those who committed sin that was in the church, should be admonished by the church.

links.text: For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness:

provenance.other: “flattering words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5. The nearest relatives are Psalm 12:2-3's ‘flattering lips’, a different noun in a different construction.
provenance.significance: 1 Thessalonians 2:5 is Paul distinguishing true preaching from false: the apostle who did not use flattering words is set against those who do, and the whole paragraph is about what a minister owes the congregation he gathered. Mosiah 26:6 borrows the phrase for exactly the people Paul is contrasting himself with — dissenters ‘which were in the church’, working from inside it — and the verse that follows sets up the church's disciplinary machinery as the answer. The catalogue's interest is that the Book of Mormon reaches for the one KJV phrase that names the offence in a specifically pastoral register, not a merely political one.

links.note: ‘They did deceive many with their flattering words, which were in the church.’ Deceit by speech is a universal idea; ‘flattering words’ is not — it is one verse of the KJV, and it is a verse about ministry corrupted from within, which is precisely Mosiah 26:6's subject. The link is high rather than certain because two words cannot be quotation, but the singleton and the coinciding setting do the work together.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they were brought before the priests, and delivered up unto the priests by the teachers; and the priests brought them before Alma, which was the high priest.
Now king Mosiah had given Alma the authority over the church.
And it came to pass that Alma did not know concerning them, for there were many witnesses against them; yea, the people stood and testified of their iniquity in abundance.
Now there had not any such thing happened before, in the church; therefore Alma was troubled in his spirit, and he caused that they should be brought before the king.

And he saith unto the king, Behold, here are many which we have brought before thee, which are accused of their brethren; yea, and they have been taken in divers iniquities. And they do not repent of their iniquities; therefore we have brought them before thee, that thou may judge them according to their crimes.

links.text: Then said Pilate unto them, Take ye him, and judge him according to your law. The Jews therefore said unto him, It is not lawful for us to put any man to death:

provenance.other: “judge him according to” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:31, and “according to your law” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The whole formula — a ruler telling accusers to take the accused and judge them by their own standard — exists once in English scripture.
provenance.significance: Read the two verses together and Mosiah 26:11-12 is John 18:29-31 with the jurisdictions exchanged. In John the religious court brings the accused to the civil ruler and the ruler hands them back: ‘Take ye him, and judge him according to your law.’ In Mosiah the high priest brings the accused to the king and the king hands them back: ‘I judge them not; therefore I deliver them into thy hands to be judged.’ The Jews' reply in John is the reason the remand fails — ‘it is not lawful for us to put any man to death’ — and it is exactly the limit Alma does not have, because Mosiah has already given him ‘the authority over the church’ (26:8). So the passage that founds Nephite church discipline is built on the passage where a civil ruler washes his hands of a religious charge, and it removes the one clause that made Pilate's remand impossible. Nothing in Mosiah says this; the borrowed formula says it.

links.note: ‘Therefore we have brought them before thee, that thou may judge them according to their crimes.’ Both halves of the KJV's one occurrence of this remand formula are here across two verses, with ‘law’ replaced by ‘crimes’ — which is the substitution the situation requires, since Alma has no written law to judge by and goes to God for one in 26:13. The 1830 ‘may judge’ (1920 ‘mayest’) leaves the second person less marked than the KJV's, but the verb, the preposition and the sequence are John's. Catalogued at 26:11, where the verbal contact sits; the remand itself is 26:12.

pericopes.text: But king Mosiah saith unto Alma, Behold, I judge them not; therefore I deliver them into thy hands to be judged.
And now the spirit of Alma was again troubled; and he went and inquired of the Lord what he should do concerning this matter, for he feared that he should do wrong in the sight of God.
And it came to pass that after he had poured out his whole soul to God, the voice of the Lord came to him, saying,

links.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

provenance.other: “poured out his soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 53:12, and “poured out my soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 1:15. Mosiah 26:14 has the third-person form, which is Isaiah's; Hannah's is first-person and past-continuous.
provenance.alternative: 1 Samuel 1:15, Hannah at Shiloh, which matches the situation — a distressed private prayer at a sanctuary answered by a priest — better than it matches the wording. Kept as a composite rather than the source because the grammar is Isaiah's.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's quietest and best-motivated borrowing. Isaiah 53:12 is transcribed whole into this same book at Mosiah 14:12, in Abinadi's mouth, and Mosiah 26:15 names Abinadi one verse later as the man whose words Alma believed. So Alma prays in the words of the chapter that converted him. Recover the rest of Isaiah 53:12 and the fit tightens: the servant ‘poured out his soul’, ‘was numbered with the transgressors’, and ‘made intercession for the transgressors’. Alma pours out his soul (26:14) over what to do about the transgressor (26:19), and the sentence he is given turns on who shall and shall not be ‘numbered among my people’ (26:32, 26:36). Three of Isaiah 53:12's four clauses are doing work in this chapter, and the one that is not — dividing the spoil — is the one with no bearing on a disciplinary case.

links.note: ‘After he had poured out his whole soul to God.’ The KJV pours out a soul twice, and Mosiah 26:14 has Isaiah's person and tense with ‘whole’ inserted. What settles the route is not the wording but the neighbourhood: this book already contains Isaiah 53 verbatim at Mosiah 14, spoken by the prophet Alma is about to be praised for believing, and the chapter goes on to use two more of that verse's clauses — intercession for the transgressor, and being numbered or not numbered among a people. Mediation is recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM on that ground; the wording alone cannot decide it, since Mosiah 14:12 and Isaiah 53:12 are identical at every word Mosiah 26:14 reproduces.

pericopes.text: Blessed art thou, Alma; and blessed are they which were baptized in the waters of Mormon. Thou art blessed because of thy exceeding faith in the words alone of my servant Abinadi.

links.text: And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.

provenance.other: “Blessed art thou” occurs in exactly five KJV verses. Three address the LORD, a land, or a woman among women; only Matthew 16:17 opens with the formula and then names a man — ‘Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona’ — which is the shape Mosiah 26:15 has: ‘Blessed art thou, Alma’.
provenance.significance: Matthew 16:17-19 is one speech in three moves: a man is blessed by name, is told a church will be built, and is handed the power to bind and loose. Mosiah 26 makes the same three moves in the same order and over eleven verses — ‘Blessed art thou, Alma’ (15), ‘thou hast established a church among this people’ (17), and then the reciprocal formula that governs the rest of the chapter, ‘him shall ye receive into the church; and him will I also receive’ (21) against ‘the same shall ye not receive into my church, for him I will not receive at the last day’ (28). That last pair is the binding-and-loosing of Matthew 16:19 with the earth-and-heaven axis rewritten as now-and-the-last-day. The Book of Mormon is not quoting the Petrine commission; it is running its structure, and it is running it over the founder of a church rather than over an apostle.

links.note: The voice from heaven blesses a named man, credits him with a church, and gives him a ratified power to admit and exclude. That is the sequence of Matthew 16:17-19 and there is no other KJV passage with it. The verbal contact at 26:15 itself is only the four-word address, one of five KJV occurrences and the only one to name a man — so the argument rests on the sequence and on the reciprocal receive/receive-not formula it produces at 26:21 and 26:28, which is Matthew 16:19's construction with a different pair of realms. High rather than certain because no clause is reproduced whole.

pericopes.text: And blessed are they, because of their exceeding faith in the words alone which thou hast spoken unto them.
And blessed art thou because thou hast established a church among this people; and they shall be established, and they shall be my people.
Yea, blessed is this people, which is willing to bear my name: for in my name shall they be called; and they are mine.

links.text: But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel:

provenance.other: “bear my name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:15. Bearing a name in the KJV is otherwise done by the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28), never by a people.
provenance.significance: Acts 9:15 is the Lord's answer to Ananias about the newly blinded Saul, and it is the KJV's only sentence about a person appointed to bear the divine name. Mosiah 26:18-20 gives that appointment to a whole people and then, two verses on, to Alma personally — ‘thou art my servant … go forth in my name’. The chapter after this one stages a persecutor struck down by a heavenly voice, laid out speechless for days, and raised up to preach the faith he had been destroying; that Mosiah 26 has already borrowed the sentence the Lord speaks about Saul between his blinding and his rising is the sort of thing this catalogue exists to notice.

links.note: ‘Blessed is this people, which is willing to bear my name.’ Two of the three words are common and the third is not: the KJV lets exactly one person bear the divine name, and he is Saul of Tarsus three days after the Damascus road. Moderate rather than high because ‘bear my name’ is short enough to be reinvented, and because Mosiah has transferred it from an individual commission to a corporate one; what keeps it worth writing is Acts 9:15's position in a narrative Mosiah 27 is about to reproduce. Note also that the 1830 ‘this people, which is willing’ preserves the singular verb that 1920 corrected to ‘are’.

pericopes.text: And because thou hast inquired of me concerning the transgressor, thou art blessed.
Thou art my servant; and I covenant with thee, that thou shalt have eternal life; and thou shalt serve me, and go forth in my name, and shall gather together my sheep.
And he that will hear my voice, shall be my sheep; and him shall ye receive into the church; and him will I also receive.

links.text: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:

provenance.other: “hear my voice” occurs in exactly 11 KJV verses and “my sheep” in exactly 10; the two meet in exactly 2 verses, John 10:16 and John 10:27, both in the good-shepherd discourse. Ezekiel 34, the other great my-sheep chapter, never joins them.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 34:11-12, which supplies ‘gather together my sheep’ at 26:20 more directly than John does; but Ezekiel's sheep are sought, not self-selected by hearing, and the conditional at 26:21 is John's move.
provenance.significance: John 10:27 states a fact about sheep — they hear. Mosiah 26:21 turns it into an entrance requirement: ‘he that will hear my voice, shall be my sheep.’ The predication runs the other way, and that reversal is the whole administrative point of the chapter, because it converts a description of the flock into a test the church can apply at the door. John 10:16's ‘other sheep I have, which are not of this fold … they shall hear my voice’ is the verse Latter-day Saint reading has long taken to point at this hemisphere, so the discourse being mined here is one the Book of Mormon has an interest in; but what 26:21 actually does with it is procedural, not prophetic.

links.note: ‘And he that will hear my voice, shall be my sheep.’ Both content phrases come from the two KJV verses that hold them together, and 26:28's negative — ‘he that will not hear my voice, the same shall ye not receive’ — completes the conversion of John's description into a rule of admission. The immediately preceding clause, ‘gather together my sheep’ (26:20), is Ezekiel 34's idiom rather than John's, so the discourse is composite; the link is filed at 26:21 because that is where the wording is decisive.

pericopes.text: For behold, this is my church; whosoever that is baptized, shall be baptized unto repentance. And whosoever ye receive, shall believe in my name; and him will I freely forgive:
for it is I that taketh upon me the sins of the world; for it is I that hath created them; and it is I that granteth unto him that believeth in the end, a place at my right hand.

links.text: The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.

provenance.other: “taketh away the sin of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:29. The KJV never elsewhere says that anyone takes sin, in either direction, with the world as its object.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 26:23 changes two words of the KJV's one formula and both changes matter: away becomes upon, and sin becomes sins. John's Lamb removes the world's sin from it; Mosiah's speaker loads it onto himself. That is the difference between an expiation described from outside and one described by the victim in the first person, which is what the whole verse is doing — ‘it is I that taketh … it is I that hath created … it is I that granteth’. The borrowed clause is being said by the Lamb rather than about him, and the preposition is what carries the change.

links.note: ‘For it is I that taketh upon me the sins of the world.’ The Baptist's formula, in the first person, with the preposition reversed. Its rarity is absolute — one KJV verse — and the substitution of ‘upon me’ for ‘away’ is too pointed to be accidental in a chapter whose subject is who bears whose sins. The same source stands behind 1 Nephi 10:10, where the Baptist's own words are given to Lehi.

links.text: And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.

provenance.other: ‘Right hand’ is far too common in the KJV to identify a source by itself — 164 verses. What is not common is the collocation this chapter builds: sheep who hear a voice, a place at a right hand, a second summons for those the judge never knew, and a sentence to everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels. Matthew 25:31-46 is the only KJV passage with all four.
provenance.significance: The verbatim hit in this chapter is at 26:27, four verses further on. Filing a moderate link here records where the discourse actually starts running Matthew 25 — at the sheep of 26:21 and the right hand of 26:23-24 — so that the quotation at 26:27 reads as the end of a sustained borrowing rather than a stray. Matthew 25:33 sets sheep at a right hand; Mosiah 26:21-24 makes one his sheep and gives him a place at that right hand, and then 26:25-27 turns to the ones on the other side.

links.note: ‘A place at my right hand’, said four verses after the sheep of 26:21 and four verses before the left-hand sentence of Matthew 25:41 is quoted outright at 26:27. Taken alone the phrase proves nothing; taken as the middle term of that sequence it shows the sheep-and-goats judgment being worked through in order. Moderate, and kjvSpecific ‘uncertain’, because no phrase here is distinctive enough to test — the evidence is the ordering, not the wording.

pericopes.text: For behold, in my name are they called; and if they know me, they shall come forth, and shall have a place eternally at my right hand.
And it shall come to pass that when the second trump shall sound, then shall they that never knew me come forth, and shall stand before me;

links.text: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

provenance.other: “last trump” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the trumpet shall sound” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both 1 Corinthians 15:52. ‘Second trump’ occurs in no KJV verse at all; the KJV numbers no trumpets outside Revelation's series of seven, and never with an ordinal attached to ‘trump’.
provenance.significance: A ‘second trump’ is only intelligible against a scheme in which trumps are counted, and the KJV's one counted trump is Paul's last one. Mosiah 26:25 assumes a first trump it never mentions — at which, on the logic of 26:24, those who know him come forth — and puts the strangers at the second. So the verse quietly makes Paul's terminal blast into a penultimate one, and the resurrection of the righteous and the resurrection of those who never knew him into two separately trumpeted events. The doctrine that follows from that ordering is developed at length later in the Book of Mormon; the vocabulary that makes it sayable is Paul's.

links.note: ‘When the second trump shall sound.’ The verb and its subject are 1 Corinthians 15:52's, which is the KJV's only sounding trumpet of the resurrection, and the ordinal is not the KJV's at all. Recorded as an echo at moderate confidence: the wording is too short to demonstrate dependence, but ‘second trump’ is a coinage that needs a numbered series to lean against and Paul's ‘last trump’ is the only one English scripture offers.

pericopes.text: and then shall they know that I am the Lord their God, that I am their Redeemer; but they would not be redeemed.
And then will I confess unto them, that I never knew them; and they shall depart into everlasting fire, prepared for the Devil and his angels.

links.text: Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

provenance.other: “everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:41. ‘Everlasting fire’ itself occurs in two, both in Matthew.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 26:27 keeps the sentence and changes the grammar of its delivery. In Matthew the Son of man says ‘Depart from me’ and the goats go; in Mosiah the ones addressed ‘shall depart into everlasting fire’ — reported rather than commanded. What is preserved exactly is the clause that gives the fire its history: it was not made for them. Matthew 25:41 is the KJV's only statement that hell was prepared for someone other than the human beings sent there, and the chapter that has spent ten verses telling Alma whom to receive ends its warning on the one verse that says the place of exclusion was built for another tenant.

links.note: A ten-word verbatim run, and the phrase is a KJV singleton. This falls below Skousen's sixteen-word operational threshold and is not one of his thirty-six extended passages; it is catalogued as a quotation because the clause is complete, unmistakable, and reproduced without variation (CONVENTIONS §2). The 1830 ‘then will I confess’ was reordered to ‘then I will confess’ in 1920, which moves the verse away from its other source, Matthew 7:23 — see the second link at this verse.

links.text: And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.

provenance.route: Matthew 7:23 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with the verb drawn from Matthew 10:32
provenance.other: “then will I profess unto them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “I never knew you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Matthew 7:23. “him will I confess” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:32.
provenance.significance: The 1830 text reads ‘And then will I confess unto them, that I never knew them’ against Matthew 7:23's ‘And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you’. Every word is the KJV's except the verb and the two pronouns, and the pronouns follow from the change of address — Matthew's judge speaks to the condemned, Mosiah's speaks about them to Alma. The verb is the interesting substitution, because the KJV's other word for this judicial act is ‘confess’, and it uses it in exactly one place: Matthew 10:32, where whoever confesses Christ before men is confessed before the Father. So Mosiah 26:27 sets the two halves of that promise against each other in one sentence: the act that is elsewhere the acknowledging of the faithful is here the formal disowning of the strangers. 1920's reordering to ‘then I will confess’ breaks the KJV's word order and makes the borrowing harder to see, which is why 1830 is the running text.

links.note: Matthew 7:23 and Matthew 25:41 are the two KJV verses of final rejection and this one sentence uses both — the first for its opening clause, the second for its close. The 1830 reading preserves Matthew's inversion, ‘then will I’, which 1920 normalized; and ‘confess’ for ‘profess’ is not a slip but the KJV's own alternative verb for the same act at Matthew 10:32, the only place it occurs in this construction. High rather than certain only because one word of the seven-word opening differs.

pericopes.text: Therefore I say unto you, That he that will not hear my voice, the same shall ye not receive into my church, for him I will not receive at the last day;

therefore I say unto you, Go; and whosoever transgresseth against me, him shall ye judge according to the sins which he hath committed; and if he confess his sins before thee and me, and repenteth in the sincerity of his heart, him shall ye forgive, and I will forgive him also;
yea, and as often as my people repent, will I forgive them their trespasses against me.

links.text: And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him.

provenance.other: “seven times in a day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 17:4, which is also the KJV's only place where a repentant offender is quoted saying ‘I repent’ as the trigger for an obligation to forgive.
provenance.significance: Luke 17:3-4 is the KJV's only forgiveness rule with all three of Mosiah 26:29-31's parts: a brother who trespasses, a rebuke, and an obligation to forgive that is renewed every time the offender says he repents. Mosiah replaces the numeral with an adverb — ‘as often as my people repent’ for ‘seven times in a day’ — which is the same generalization Matthew 18:22 performs on the same rule with ‘seventy times seven’. What Mosiah 26 adds is a second party: in Luke the forgiveness is horizontal, between brothers, and here it is doubled, ‘him shall ye forgive, and I will forgive him also’, so that the church's act and God's are made to track each other. That doubling is Matthew 16:19's, and it is what turns Luke's counsel into a procedure.

links.note: ‘As often as my people repent, will I forgive them their trespasses against me’ (26:30), and ‘when he saith that he repenteth’ (26:31), are Luke 17:3-4's two conditions in Luke's order, with the numeral generalized. ‘Trespass against thee’ is Luke's verb and Mosiah has it twice, at 26:29 and 26:30. The 1830 ‘saith that he repenteth’ keeps the KJV's present tense where 1920 has ‘says that he repents’, which is a small instance of the pattern noted at CONVENTIONS §8. Filed at 26:30 because that is where the generalization is made.

pericopes.text: And ye shall also forgive one another your trespasses: for verily I say unto you, He that forgiveth not his neighbor’s trespasses, when he saith that he repenteth, the same hath brought himself under condemnation.

links.text: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

provenance.other: “your trespasses” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 6:15, Mark 11:25 and Mark 11:26 — and all three are the same saying. ‘Forgive one another’ occurs in no KJV verse; the KJV's idiom is ‘forgiving one another’ (Ephesians 4:32, Colossians 3:13), which Mosiah has conjugated into an imperative.
provenance.significance: Matthew 6:15 makes the failure to forgive cost the unforgiving man his own pardon. Mosiah 26:31 makes it cost him something narrower and more legal — ‘the same hath brought himself under condemnation’ — which is not a KJV phrase at all, and which relocates the penalty from the Father's decision to the offender's own act. The chapter is converting sayings into statutes throughout; this is the clearest single case, because the source states a consequence and the borrowing states a liability.

links.note: ‘Ye shall also forgive one another your trespasses … He that forgiveth not his neighbor's trespasses.’ The noun is Matthew 6:15's — three KJV verses have it, all one saying — and the second clause reproduces its conditional shape. Moderate rather than high because the language of forgiving trespasses is spread across Matthew 6, Matthew 18:35 and Mark 11, and no one of them is decisively in view; what is in view is the saying they all carry.

pericopes.text: Now I say unto you, Go; and whosoever will not repent of his sins, the same shall not be numbered among my people; and this shall be observed from this time forward.
And it came to pass when Alma had heard these words, he wrote them down, that he might have them, and that he might judge the people of that church, according to the commandments of God.
And it came to pass that Alma went and judged those that had been taken in iniquity, according to the word of the Lord.
And whosoever repented of their sins and did confess them, them he did number among the people of the church;
and them that would not confess their sins and repent of their iniquity, the same were not numbered among the people of the church, and their names were blotted out.

links.text: He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.

provenance.other: “blot out his name” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 29:20 and Revelation 3:5. Deuteronomy blots the name from under heaven as a curse; Revelation 3:5 promises the overcomer that his name will not be blotted from the book of life.
provenance.significance: Revelation 3:5 is the only KJV verse that holds this chapter's two administrative acts together: not blotting a name out, and confessing a name before the Father. Mosiah 26 performs both, in reverse order and with the polarity flipped — the Lord confesses to the strangers that he never knew them (26:27), and the unrepentant have their names blotted out (26:36). Read against Revelation, Alma's register is the negative image of the book of life: what the church strikes from its roll is what heaven promises the faithful will never lose, and the confession Revelation makes a reward is here made a sentence.

links.note: ‘Their names were blotted out.’ Two KJV verses blot out a name and only one of them is about church membership. The link is moderate and conceptual — Mosiah shares no clause with Revelation 3:5 — but the pairing of a struck name with a confessed name is distinctive enough to be worth recording, and Mosiah 26 has both, nine verses apart. That the record Alma keeps is a physical one he ‘wrote down’ (26:33) makes the analogy to a book with names in it exact rather than metaphorical.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Alma did regulate all the affairs of the church; and they began again to have peace, and to prosper exceedingly in the affairs of the church; walking circumspectly before God; receiving many, and baptizing many.

links.text: See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,

provenance.other: “circumspectly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:15, and its collocation with the verb walk is that verse's whole point. The word is otherwise absent from English scripture.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:15-16 tells a congregation to walk circumspectly and to redeem the time ‘because the days are evil’. Mosiah 26:37 uses the phrase for a church that has just come through a disciplinary crisis and is prospering again — walking circumspectly before God, receiving many, baptizing many. The borrowed adverb carries the reason with it: circumspection is what Ephesians prescribes for a community surrounded by danger, and Mosiah 26:38 immediately supplies the danger, ‘being persecuted by all those who did not belong to the church of God’.

links.note: A single word, but one that exists in exactly one KJV verse and appears here in the same construction as there. Verses 37 and 38 together reproduce Ephesians 5:15-16's pairing of circumspect walking with an evil surrounding age, which is what raises this above a lexical coincidence.

pericopes.text: And now all these things did Alma and his fellow-laborers do, which were over the church; walking in all diligence; teaching the word of God in all things; suffering all manner of afflictions; being persecuted by all those who did not belong to the church of God.

And they did admonish their brethren; and they were also admonished, every one, by the word of God, according to his sins, or to the sins which he had committed; being commanded of God to pray without ceasing, and to give thanks in all things.

links.text: Pray without ceasing.

provenance.other: “pray without ceasing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 5:17, and “in every thing give thanks” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 5:18. They are consecutive.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 26:39 takes two consecutive KJV verses in their KJV order and joins them with ‘and’: ‘being commanded of God to pray without ceasing, and to give thanks in all things’. The second is loosened — 1830 has ‘in all things’ where Paul has ‘in every thing’ — but the pairing is not available anywhere else in English scripture, and it is a pairing rather than a single phrase, which is what makes the borrowing demonstrable rather than lexical. The chapter that opened with a church having to invent a disciplinary procedure ends by putting its officers under the shortest two commandments Paul ever wrote.

links.note: Three words, reproduced whole, from a verse that is only three words long — one of the KJV's shortest — followed immediately by a paraphrase of the verse that follows it. Catalogued as a quotation on the completeness of the clause rather than its length, and well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold (CONVENTIONS §2). The looser second half, ‘in all things’ for ‘in every thing’, is the mark of a writer working from memory of the pair rather than copying it.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that the persecutions which was inflicted on the church by the unbelievers, became so great, that the church began to murmur, and complain to their leaders concerning the matter; and they did complain to Alma. And Alma laid the case before their king, Mosiah. And Mosiah consulted with his priests.
And it came to pass that king Mosiah sent a proclamation throughout the land round about, that there should not any unbeliever persecute any of those which belonged to the church of God;
and there was a strict command throughout all the churches, that there should be no persecutions among them; that there should be an equality among all men;
that they should let no pride nor haughtiness disturb their peace; that every man should esteem his neighbor as himself, laboring with their own hands for their support;

links.text: Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.

provenance.route: Philippians 2:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Leviticus 19:18's object substituted
provenance.other: “esteem other better” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 2:3, and it is the KJV's only use of ‘esteem’ to govern the regard of one member of a congregation for another. The object Mosiah gives it — ‘his neighbor as himself’ — is Leviticus 19:18's, which the KJV always attaches to ‘love’.
provenance.significance: The verse is a graft. Mosiah 27:4 takes the verb of Philippians 2:3 and the object of Leviticus 19:18 and makes a sentence neither has: ‘every man should esteem his neighbor as himself’. What that does is convert the second great commandment into a measurable standard of civic equality — the surrounding clauses are about pride, haughtiness and a levelled priesthood — because ‘love thy neighbour’ names an affection and ‘esteem’ names a valuation. Philippians 2:3's own subject is the same, a congregation ordered against strife and vainglory, and 2:4-8 goes on to ground it in Christ emptying himself; Mosiah grounds it instead in priests working with their own hands.

links.note: ‘That they should let no pride nor haughtiness disturb their peace; that every man should esteem his neighbor as himself.’ The prohibition matches Philippians 2:3's ‘strife or vainglory’ in function and the verb is that verse's alone in the KJV, but the object comes from the Levitical commandment. Filed high because the substitution is the argument: an ordinary writer reaching for Leviticus 19:18 reproduces ‘love’, and this one does not.

pericopes.text: yea, and all their priests and teachers should labor with their own hands for their support, in all cases save it were in sickness, or in much want: and doing these things, they did abound in the grace of God.

links.text: And labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it:

provenance.other: “with our own hands” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, and only 1 Corinthians 4:12 joins the phrase to labour as a minister's self-support; the other is Deuteronomy 32:27, of enemies boasting. The KJV's other self-support texts read ‘work with your own hands’ (1 Thessalonians 4:11) and ‘working with his hands’ (Ephesians 4:28).
provenance.significance: The clause Mosiah borrows is followed immediately in Paul by ‘being persecuted, we suffer it’ — and Mosiah 27 opens on persecution (27:1-3) and closes on it (27:32, ‘being greatly persecuted … being smitten by many of them’). So the chapter's frame and its economic rule come from the same sentence of 1 Corinthians 4. What Mosiah adds is a clause Paul never needed: ‘in all cases save it were in sickness, or in much want’, which turns an apostolic boast into an administrative exemption. That is this chapter's habit throughout — the New Testament supplies a posture and the Book of Mormon supplies the by-law.

links.note: ‘All their priests and teachers should labor with their own hands for their support.’ The pairing of labour with a possessed pair of hands is Pauline in three places and 1 Corinthians 4:12 is the one that has the possessive Mosiah has, the plural subject Mosiah has, and the persecution setting Mosiah 27 has. The verse before it, 27:4, applies the same rule to every man, which is why the recurrence is filed rather than a second link.

links.text: Therefore, as ye abound in every thing, in faith, and utterance, and knowledge, and in all diligence, and in your love to us, see that ye abound in this grace also.

provenance.other: “abound in this grace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 8:7. The verb and the noun meet in only one other place, 2 Corinthians 9:8, ‘God is able to make all grace abound toward you’, where grace is the subject rather than the thing abounded in.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 8 is Paul's collection letter: the grace the Corinthians are to abound in is money for Jerusalem, and the argument runs from a congregation's material generosity to the grace of Christ who became poor. Mosiah 27:5 ends its own paragraph about material arrangements — priests supporting themselves, exceptions for the sick and the destitute — with ‘doing these things, they did abound in the grace of God’. The borrowing is exact in its subject matter, which is what recommends it: both texts use the phrase of a community whose grace is demonstrated by how it handles money and labour.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 9:8, which is the more familiar verse but has the wrong grammar.

links.note: ‘And doing these things, they did abound in the grace of God.’ A KJV singleton, in a verse about congregational finance, closing a Book of Mormon paragraph about congregational finance. Moderate rather than high because ‘abound’ and ‘grace’ are both ordinary and the sentence could be assembled without a source. Note that the exclusion register rejects this same KJV verse at Mosiah 26:38, where the n-gram-friendly ‘in all diligence’ pointed at it for no reason; the real contact with 2 Corinthians 8:7 in this book is here, one chapter later, and it is with a different phrase.

pericopes.text: And there began to be much peace again in the land; and the people began to be very numerous, and began to scatter abroad upon the face of the earth; yea, on the north and on the south, on the east and on the west, building large cities and villages in all quarters of the land.
And the Lord did visit them and prosper them, and they became a large and a wealthy people.

Now the sons of Mosiah was numbered among the unbelievers; and also one of the sons of Alma was numbered among them, he being called Alma, after his father; nevertheless he became a very wicked and an idolatrous man. And he was a man of many words, and did speak much flattery to the people; therefore he led many of the people to do after the manner of his iniquities.

And he became a great hinderment to the prosperity of the church of God; stealing away the hearts of the people; causing much dissention among the people; giving a chance for the enemy of God to exercise his power over them.

links.text: And on this manner did Absalom to all Israel that came to the king for judgment: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

provenance.other: “stole the hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 15:6. Hearts are hardened, turned, enticed and won elsewhere in the KJV, but stolen only by Absalom.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one heart-thief is a king's son who flatters his way into a following and rebels against his father. Mosiah 27:8-9 has just told us that this Alma is ‘called Alma, after his father’, that he is ‘a man of many words’ who ‘did speak much flattery to the people’, and that he goes about stealing away their hearts. Absalom's method in 2 Samuel 15:1-6 is exactly that — standing in the gate, telling every suitor his cause is good, kissing the men who bow to him. Recover the rest of the Absalom narrative and the borrowing carries a threat the chapter then declines to execute: Absalom's father prays against his son's counsel and weeps for him, and the son dies in his rebellion. Alma's father prays for his son (27:14) and the son is knocked down and raised. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's story of a rebellion that could only end in a father's grief and given it the other ending.

links.note: ‘Stealing away the hearts of the people.’ One KJV verse contains the idiom and it belongs to the archetypal rebellious son, which is what Mosiah 27:8 has just gone out of its way to establish this Alma is — named for his father, working against his father's church. The flattery of 27:8 is Absalom's technique in 2 Samuel 15:2-4 and the phrase in 27:9 is Absalom's summary verse. Note too that ‘much flattery’ at 27:8 reuses the ‘flattering words’ of 26:6, so the chapter is carrying its predecessor's vocabulary as well as its own source.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that while he was going about to destroy the church of God: for he did go about secretly with the sons of Mosiah, seeking to destroy the church, and to lead astray the people of the Lord, contrary to the commandments of God, or even the king;

links.text: For ye have heard of my conversation in time past in the Jews’ religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the church of God, and wasted it:

provenance.other: “persecuted the church of God” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Galatians 1:13 and 1 Corinthians 15:9, and both are Paul on himself before Damascus. Galatians 1:23 supplies the verb Mosiah actually uses: ‘he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed.’
provenance.significance: Mosiah 27:10 has Alma ‘going about to destroy the church of God’ and 27:13 has the angel ask ‘why persecuteth thou the church of God?’ — the two verbs the KJV attaches to Saul's pre-conversion career, in the KJV's own object phrase, four verses apart. Galatians 1:23 is where they meet: persecuted, then destroyed, then preached. Mosiah 27 completes the same triad — destroys (10), is confronted (13), and by 27:32-35 is ‘publishing to all the people the things which they had heard and seen’ and repairing what he wrecked. Galatians 1:14, the ‘traditions of my fathers’ verse, is already the source behind Mosiah 26:1, so this chapter is the second stop in the same paragraph of Galatians.

links.note: ‘While he was going about to destroy the church of God … seeking to destroy the church.’ The object phrase is Paul's autobiographical formula and the verb is the one Galatians 1:23 pairs with it. What raises the link above vocabulary is that Mosiah 27 goes on to run the whole Galatians 1 sequence — destroyer, confronted by a revelation, preacher of the faith he destroyed — and that the immediately preceding chapter had already drawn on Galatians 1:14.

pericopes.text: and as I said unto you, as they were going about rebelling against God, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared unto them; and he descended as it were in a cloud; and he spake as it were with a voice of thunder, which caused the earth to shake upon which they stood;
and so great was their astonishment, that they fell to the earth, and understood not the words which he spake unto them.

links.text: And they that were with me saw indeed the light, and were afraid; but they heard not the voice of him that spake to me.

provenance.route: Acts 22:9 (with Acts 9:7) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV gives the Damascus companions twice and inconsistently: at Acts 9:7 they stand speechless, ‘hearing a voice, but seeing no man’; at Acts 22:9 they see the light ‘but they heard not the voice of him that spake to me’. Mosiah 27:12 takes the Acts 22 side — they fell, and ‘understood not the words which he spake unto them’.
provenance.significance: The difference between Acts 9:7 and Acts 22:9 is the classic crux of the Damascus narratives, and Mosiah 27:12 resolves it in the direction Acts 22 does, then softens it further: the companions do not fail to hear, they fail to understand. That is the harmonizing reading — the voice was audible but not intelligible — which is how the two Acts accounts have long been reconciled. The Book of Mormon verse takes a side in a New Testament textual problem, and the side it takes is the one that makes both KJV verses true at once.

links.note: ‘They fell to the earth, and understood not the words which he spake unto them.’ The falling is Acts 9:4's, the not-perceiving is Acts 22:9's, and the substitution of understanding for hearing is the standard harmonization of the two. High confidence: the wording is not distinctive on its own — ‘fell to the earth’ occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — but a Damascus-road scene that lands precisely on the point where the KJV's two accounts disagree is not doing so by accident.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless he cried again, saying, Alma, arise, and stand forth, for why persecuteth thou the church of God? For the Lord hath said, This is my church, and I will establish it; and nothing shall overthrow it, save it is the transgression of my people.

links.text: And he fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?

provenance.route: Acts 9:4 (with Acts 26:16) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “why persecutest thou” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses — Acts 9:4, 22:7 and 26:14 — which are the three tellings of one event. The KJV asks the question nowhere else. ‘Arise, and stand forth’ is not a KJV phrase; Acts 26:16's ‘But rise, and stand upon thy feet’ is the same command in the third telling, and Acts 9:6's ‘Arise, and go into the city’ supplies the verb.
provenance.significance: Everything is transposed by one step. The heavenly voice names the persecutor twice in Acts and once here; it asks why he persecutes ‘me’ in Acts and ‘the church of God’ here; and the speaker is the Lord in Acts and an angel here, sent by a Lord who is then quoted at second hand — ‘For the Lord hath said, This is my church.’ The last of those is the substantive change. Acts 9:4 identifies the church with Christ so completely that persecuting it is persecuting him, and Mosiah 27:13 declines the identification and replaces it with a possessive claim, ‘This is my church, and I will establish it’, which is the same claim the voice made to Alma's father at 26:22. The Book of Mormon keeps the Damascus question and answers it institutionally.
provenance.alternative: Acts 22:7 or 26:14, the parallel tellings; 9:4 is named because Mosiah 27:12-13 also has the falling to the earth, which 26:14 shares but 22:7 words differently.

links.note: The chapter's anchor. A KJV question asked in three verses about one man is asked here of another, in the same words but for a different object, and the whole scene around it — the light, the falling, the companions who do not understand, the days of helplessness, the raising up to preach — is the Damascus narrative. The 1830 reading is worth keeping in view: it has ‘why persecuteth thou’, which is not the KJV's grammar, and 1920 corrected it to ‘persecutest’, which is. That is the direction of change CONVENTIONS §8 flags — a later edition moving the text back toward its source — and it means the first edition shows the borrowing slightly less exactly than the modern text does.

links.text: He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.

provenance.other: “the transgression of my people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 53:8, and Mosiah 27:13 reproduces the five words entire. Isaiah 53 is transcribed whole into this book at Mosiah 14, and 53:8 is Mosiah 14:8.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 53:8 makes the transgression of my people the reason the servant was stricken. Mosiah 27:13 makes it the one thing that can overthrow the church: ‘nothing shall overthrow it, save it is the transgression of my people.’ The phrase has been moved from a cause of atonement to a cause of institutional collapse, and the speaker is an angel addressing a man in the act of trying to overthrow that church from outside — the verse's point being that he cannot, and that only the members can. This is the second of the batch's Isaiah 53 borrowings routed through Abinadi's transcription: Mosiah 26:14 took ‘poured out his soul’ from 53:12, and this takes ‘the transgression of my people’ from 53:8.
provenance.alternative: Direct dependence on Isaiah 53:8; nothing in the wording distinguishes Isaiah 53:8 from Mosiah 14:8, which reproduces it. The route is argued from the book's own contents, not from the words.

links.note: A five-word KJV singleton inside the angel's speech, taken from the Isaiah chapter this book has already transcribed twelve chapters earlier and put to a use Isaiah does not have. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is short, ordinary in its components, and its new sense is remote from Isaiah's; what recommends it is the absolute rarity and the established channel — Abinadi's Isaiah 53 is demonstrably in this narrator's hands, and Alma is the character whose whole standing derives from having believed it.

pericopes.text: And again: The angel saith, Behold, the Lord hath heard the prayers of his people, and also the prayers of his servant Alma, which is thy father: for he hath prayed with much faith concerning thee, that thou mightest be brought to the knowledge of the truth; therefore for this purpose have I come to convince thee of the power and authority of God, that the prayers of his servants might be answered according to their faith.

links.text: Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.

provenance.other: “the knowledge of the truth” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses: 1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Timothy 3:7 and Hebrews 10:26. Only 1 Timothy 2:4 uses it of a destination God wills people to reach; the other two use it of people who never arrive or who sin after arriving.
provenance.significance: 1 Timothy 2:1-4 is the KJV's argument that intercessory prayer for others is good and acceptable because God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Mosiah 27:14 is an angel explaining that a father's intercessory prayer has been heard, ‘that thou mightest be brought to the knowledge of the truth’. The source verse is the warrant for the very practice the angel has come to vindicate, and the chapter ends by reporting that the converts brought ‘many to the knowledge of the truth’ (27:36) — the prayed-for man becomes the answer to other people's prayers.

links.note: The phrase is not rare enough by itself to settle a source, but only one of its three KJV occurrences is about God's will that people arrive at it, and that occurrence sits inside the KJV's chief defence of praying for other people — which is exactly what Mosiah 27:14 is about. Moderate: real contact, short phrase, no clause reproduced.

pericopes.text: And now behold, can ye dispute the power of God? For behold, doth not my voice shake the earth? And can ye not also behold me before you? And I am sent from God.—

Now I say unto thee, Go, and remember the captivity of thy fathers in the land of Helam, and in the land of Nephi; and remember how great things he hath done for them: for they were in bondage, and he hath delivered them. And now I say unto thee, Alma, Go thy way, and seek to destroy the church no more, that their prayers may be answered, and this even if thou wilt of thyself be cast off.

links.text: Only fear the LORD, and serve him in truth with all your heart: for consider how great things he hath done for you.

provenance.other: “how great things he hath done for” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 12:24, and Mosiah 27:16 reproduces all seven words. The other KJV form of the idiom, “how great things the Lord hath done”, also occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 5:19, and inserts the divine name where Mosiah has none.
provenance.alternative: Mark 5:19, the Gadarene demoniac's commission, which the ranked machine stream and the memory of 1 Nephi 7:11 both pull toward. It loses on two words: Mark has ‘the Lord’ inside the run and Mosiah does not, while 1 Samuel 12:24 matches the run exactly.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 12 is Samuel's farewell at the making of the monarchy, and the ‘great things’ he tells Israel to consider are enumerated a few verses earlier: the LORD ‘brought forth your fathers out of the land of Egypt’ (12:6-11), a recital of bondage and deliverance. Mosiah 27:16 issues the same command with the same content — ‘remember the captivity of thy fathers in the land of Helam, and in the land of Nephi … for they were in bondage, and he hath delivered them.’ The angel is not merely using a biblical idiom; he is using the one KJV verse where that idiom means precisely what he wants it to mean, in a chapter of the KJV about a people who have just asked for a king and must now be told what their national deliverance obliges. Mosiah 27 is a chapter about a king's sons and a high priest's son, and the KJV verse behind its central command is Samuel's warning to a nation about its kings.

links.note: ‘Remember how great things he hath done for them: for they were in bondage, and he hath delivered them.’ A seven-word run from a KJV singleton, and the source's own context is a recital of deliverance from bondage. Mark 5:19 is the more famous home of the idiom and was adjudicated at 1 Nephi 7:11, where the 1830 ‘how’ preserved a reading 1920 removed; that argument is not restated here, because the run at Mosiah 27:16 matches 1 Samuel 12:24 word for word and Mark only with an insertion. The row is filed at high confidence on the exact run and the coinciding subject matter.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that these were the last words which the angel spake unto Alma, and he departed.

And now Alma, and those that were with him, fell again to the earth, for great was their astonishment: for with their own eyes they had beheld an angel of the Lord; and his voice was as thunder, which shook the earth; and they knew that there was nothing save the power of God, that could shake the earth and cause it to tremble, as though it would part asunder.

And now the astonishment of Alma was so great, that he became dumb, that he could not open his mouth; yea, and he became weak, even that he could not move his hands; therefore he was taken by those that were with him, and carried helpless, even until he was laid before his father.
And they rehearsed unto his father all that had happened unto them; and his father rejoiced, for he knew that it was the power of God.
And he caused that a multitude should be gathered together, that they might witness what the Lord had done for his son, and also for those that were with him.

And he caused that the priests should assemble themselves together; and they began to fast, and to pray to the Lord their God, that he would open the mouth of Alma, that he might speak; and also that his limbs might receive their strength, that the eyes of the people might be opened to see and know of the goodness and glory of God.

links.text: To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.

provenance.other: Acts 26:18 is the commission the risen Christ gives Paul in the third and fullest Damascus telling, and it is the only place in the KJV where opened eyes, a turn from darkness to light, and a rescue from Satan's power are one sentence.
provenance.significance: The chapter distributes Acts 26:18's four clauses across its second half. The priests pray ‘that the eyes of the people might be opened to see and know of the goodness and glory of God’ (27:22); Alma reports being taken out of ‘the darkest abyss’ into light (27:29); the enemy of God whose power he had served is named at 27:9; and the forgiveness and inheritance come at 27:24 and 27:26. Acts 26:18 is Paul's own summary of what his conversion was for, and Mosiah 27 uses it as the summary of what Alma's was for — but redirects the opened eyes from the future audience to the present congregation, who are watching.

links.note: Conceptual rather than verbal, and marked so. The argument is that the chapter is already demonstrably working from the Damascus narratives (27:12, 27:13) and that this verse and 27:29 take up the commission clause of the fullest of them, in its order. kjvSpecific ‘uncertain’ because no phrase here is distinctive enough to test against another English version.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass after they had fasted and prayed for the space of two days and two nights, the limbs of Alma received their strength, and he stood up and began to speak unto them, bidding them to be of good comfort:

links.text: And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.

provenance.other: “fasted and prayed” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Nehemiah 1:4 and Acts 13:3; only Acts 13:3 has the plural subject and the pluperfect Mosiah 27:23 has, ‘when they had fasted and prayed’.
provenance.significance: Acts 13:1-3 is the church at Antioch fasting and praying, laying hands on Barnabas and Saul, and sending them away — the commissioning of the persecutor-turned-preacher for his first journey. Mosiah 27:22-23 has the priests assemble, fast and pray, and Alma rise; 27:32-35 sends him and the four sons of Mosiah travelling round about through all the land. The source verse is the sending of Saul, which is the event Mosiah 27 has been reproducing since verse 10, and it arrives at the same point in the sequence: after the conversion, before the journey.

links.note: ‘After they had fasted and prayed for the space of two days and two nights.’ Five words of a two-verse KJV phrase, in the construction only Acts 13:3 has, at the point in a Damascus-shaped narrative where Acts 13 falls. Moderate: the phrase is short and the act is unremarkable, but the position in the sequence is not, and the chapter's dependence on Acts is established elsewhere at much higher confidence.

pericopes.text: for, said he, I have repented of my sins, and have been redeemed of the Lord; behold, I am born of the spirit.

And the Lord said unto me, Marvel not that all mankind, yea, men, and women, all nations, kindreds, tongues and people, must be born again; yea, born of God, changed from their carnal and fallen state, to a state of righteousness, being redeemed of God, becoming his sons and daughters;

links.text: Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.

provenance.other: “born again” occurs in exactly 3 KJV verses, John 3:3, 3:7 and 1 Peter 1:23. Only John 3:7 puts it after ‘Marvel not that’, which occurs in exactly 4 KJV verses and nowhere else with this predicate.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 27:25 keeps John 3:7's opening and its close and replaces its middle: ‘Marvel not that I said unto thee’ becomes ‘Marvel not that all mankind, yea, men, and women, all nations, kindreds, tongues and people, must be born again’. What has been inserted is the universalizing catalogue, which is Revelation's list of the redeemed, and what has been displaced is Nicodemus. John 3:7 is a rebuke to one man's incredulity; Mosiah 27:25 turns the same sentence into a doctrine about every human being. The rest of the paragraph then supplies John 3's other terms in order — born of God, changed, becoming his sons and daughters (John 1:12-13), new creatures, and the kingdom of God that John 3:5 says the unborn-again cannot enter.

links.note: Six of John 3:7's eight words, in order, with the addressee replaced by a universal catalogue. The chapter's conversion narrative is Pauline and its conversion doctrine is Johannine, which is the division of labour this verse marks: Alma has just been knocked down like Saul and now explains what happened to him in the vocabulary of Nicodemus. Catalogued as a quotation because the borrowed frame is complete, though it is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold (CONVENTIONS §2).
bibliography: Frederick 2016 — his index of co-occurrence (data/frederick-refs.json, from tools/parse-frederick.py) places Mosiah 27:25 within 1500 characters of his discussion of John 1:12-13; that index records proximity in his argument about the Gospel of John, not a proposed source.

links.text: And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty.

provenance.other: “my sons and daughters” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 6:18. The phrase elsewhere in the KJV is always ‘thy sons and thy daughters’ or ‘your sons and your daughters’, addressed to parents about their children rather than by God about his people.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 6:18 is the KJV's one divine adoption formula in this exact form, and it closes a paragraph demanding separation from unbelievers — ‘come out from among them, and be ye separate’. Mosiah 27:25 uses it of people ‘changed from their carnal and fallen state’, and the chapter's opening problem was precisely a church surrounded by unbelievers it could not separate from. This is the third Corinthian borrowing in the chapter, after 27:5's two.

links.note: ‘Becoming his sons and daughters.’ A KJV singleton in the exact possessive Mosiah needs, and the only place English scripture lets God speak of a people as his sons and daughters. Moderate because the phrase is short and the idea of divine adoption has many KJV homes; what makes it worth a row is that this particular wording has only one.

pericopes.text: and thus they become new creatures; and unless they do this, they can in no wise inherit the kingdom of God.

links.text: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.

provenance.other: “new creature” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Galatians 6:15, both Pauline and both singular. Mosiah 27:26 pluralizes: ‘thus they become new creatures’.
provenance.significance: Both KJV occurrences make the new creature a description of a state — if any man be in Christ, he is one — and neither makes it a requirement. Mosiah 27:26 makes it one: ‘unless they do this, they can in no wise inherit the kingdom of God.’ Paired with John 3:5 in the same sentence, this is the chapter's move again: a New Testament indicative converted into a Book of Mormon condition, in the same way 26:21 converted John 10:27's description of sheep into a rule of admission.

links.note: The pluralized phrase and the kingdom-of-God consequence come from two different sources fused in one clause — Paul's new creature and John 3:5's kingdom no one enters unborn. Moderate: two words, but they are two words the KJV uses twice, and the fusion with John 3 is already established four verses earlier.

pericopes.text: I say unto you, unless this be the case, they must be cast off: and this I know, because I was like to be cast off.
Nevertheless, after wandering through much tribulation, repenting nigh unto death, the Lord in mercy hath seen fit to snatch me out of an everlasting burning, and I am born of God;

links.text: Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.

provenance.other: “much tribulation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 14:22. Tribulation is ‘great’ in Matthew 24:21 and Revelation, and it is ‘much’ only here.
provenance.significance: Acts 14:22 has three clauses and Mosiah 27 uses all three within eight verses, out of order but complete: the kingdom of God that must be entered (27:26, ‘can in no wise inherit the kingdom of God’), the much tribulation one passes through to reach it (27:28, ‘after wandering through much tribulation’; 27:32, ‘preaching the word of God in much tribulation’), and the confirming and exhorting of disciples (27:33, ‘confirming their faith, and exhorting them with long suffering’). The source verse describes Paul and Barnabas returning to congregations they had planted in cities that had stoned them; Mosiah 27:32-33 describes converts returning to a church they had persecuted, in cities where they are now smitten. The parallel is doing structural work, not decorative.

links.note: A KJV singleton phrase at 27:28, and the other two clauses of the same KJV verse at 27:26 and 27:33. One link rather than three, on the rule that a phrase adopted within a book is recorded in recurrenceRefs rather than re-argued (ADJUDICATING §4); but the distribution is the evidence here, because a writer borrowing only ‘much tribulation’ would not also have ‘kingdom of God’ two verses before it and ‘confirming … and exhorting’ five verses after it.

links.text: The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?

provenance.other: “everlasting burnings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 33:14, in the plural; Mosiah 27:28 has the singular, ‘an everlasting burning’. The snatching has its own KJV background in the firebrand ‘plucked out of the burning’ of Amos 4:11 and Zechariah 3:2.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 33:14 asks the question as an unanswerable one — who among us can live with everlasting burnings? — and its speakers are the sinners in Zion, frightened. Mosiah 27:28 answers it in the first person and in the past tense: one of the sinners in Zion has been snatched out. The verse the KJV leaves as a rhetorical question about the impossibility of survival is turned into a report of a survival, which is the whole rhetorical situation of Alma's speech.

links.note: ‘The Lord in mercy hath seen fit to snatch me out of an everlasting burning.’ The noun phrase exists once in the KJV and Mosiah has it singular; the verb is not Isaiah's, and the firebrand-plucked-from-the-burning idiom of Amos 4:11 and Zechariah 3:2 lies behind it. Moderate rather than high because the two elements come from different places and neither clause is reproduced.

pericopes.text: my soul hath been redeemed from the gall of bitterness and bonds of iniquity. I was in the darkest abyss; but now I behold the marvellous light of God. My soul was wrecked with eternal torment; but I am snatched, and my soul is pained no more.

links.text: For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.

provenance.other: “gall of bitterness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “bond of iniquity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse, Acts 8:23. The two phrases exist in English scripture only in each other's company, and Mosiah 27:29 has them in Acts's order, with ‘bonds’ pluralized.
provenance.significance: Acts 8:23 is Peter's sentence on Simon Magus, who tried to buy the power of the Holy Ghost — a man inside the church, baptized, who wanted its authority for himself. That is the diagnosis Alma applies to his own former state, and it is a sharper self-accusation than the chapter has otherwise made: Alma has been described as a persecutor, an idolater and a flatterer, but the phrase he chooses for himself is the one the KJV reserves for a baptized man who wanted the priesthood on his own terms. Simon's story ends unresolved — ‘Pray ye to the Lord for me’ — and Mosiah 27's ends with the prayers answered. The link supplies the outcome Acts 8 withholds.

links.note: Two KJV singletons from one verse, adjacent and in order. This is the chapter's most secure borrowing after Acts 9:4, and unlike that one it is not part of the Damascus material — it comes from four chapters earlier in Acts and from a very different kind of sinner. That Alma's self-description reaches past his own Saul-shaped conversion to Simon Magus is the finding worth keeping.

links.text: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light;

provenance.other: “marvellous light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 2:9, and the 1830 text spells it with the KJV's double l. The 1920 edition modernized it to ‘marvelous’, which is the spelling the current text carries.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 2:9's darkness-to-light is said of a whole people and in the passive — you were called out. Mosiah 27:29 says it of one man and in the active present: ‘I was in the darkest abyss; but now I behold the marvellous light of God.’ The change from being called into light to beholding it is what makes the sentence a testimony rather than a doctrine, which is what the verse is for; and coming three verses after Alma has described himself as Simon Magus, it moves him from Acts 8 to 1 Peter 2 — from the man who wanted the priesthood illegitimately to the people who are one.

links.note: A KJV singleton, and one whose 1830 spelling is the KJV's own. This is a textbook case of CONVENTIONS §8: the first edition preserves an orthography that the modern text has erased, so the borrowing is fractionally more visible in the running text than in the book a reader owns. The 1830 also reads ‘My soul was wrecked with eternal torment’ where 1920 has ‘racked’ — not a KJV question, but worth noting alongside.

pericopes.text: I rejected my Redeemer, and denied that which had been spoken of by our fathers; but now that they may foresee that he will come, and that he remembereth every creature of his creating, and he will make himself manifest unto all;
