yea, every knee shall bow, and every tongue confess before him. Yea, even at the last day, when all men shall stand to be judged of him, then shall they confess that he is God; then shall they confess, who live without God in the world, that the judgment of an everlasting punishment is just upon them; and they shall quake, and tremble, and shrink beneath the glance of his all-searching eye.

links.text: I have sworn by myself, the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and shall not return, That unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.

provenance.route: Isaiah 45:23 → Romans 14:11 / Philippians 2:10-11 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “every knee shall bow” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Isaiah 45:23 and Romans 14:11. The word that separates the Old Testament form from the New is the second verb: Isaiah's tongue shall SWEAR, and both New Testament forms have it CONFESS (Romans 14:11 ‘every tongue shall confess to God’; Philippians 2:11 ‘every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord’). Mosiah 27:31 reads ‘every tongue confess before him’, and then twice more, ‘then shall they confess that he is God’.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's decidable mediation case and it decides cleanly on one word. The Book of Mormon has Isaiah's couplet with the New Testament's verb, so the route runs through Romans or Philippians rather than straight from Isaiah 45. Which of the two is the proximate witness cannot be settled: Romans 14:11 supplies the couplet's shape and Philippians 2:11 supplies the construction Mosiah actually uses twice in the next clause, ‘confess that he is God’ against ‘confess that Jesus Christ is Lord’. Philippians is marginally favoured on that construction, and Philippians 2:10-11's setting — the last-day acknowledgement by every creature, including the unwilling — is the setting Mosiah 27:31 builds out at length. Note that tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence for either New Testament witness, because Mosiah's clause diverges from both after the shared words; the swear/confess substitution has to be read by eye.

links.note: ‘Every knee shall bow, and every tongue confess before him.’ Isaiah's couplet with Paul's verb — the single substitution that distinguishes the New Testament citations of Isaiah 45:23 from Isaiah 45:23 itself. Mosiah then does what neither source does and extends the confession into a formal admission of the justice of one's own sentence, ‘that the judgment of an everlasting punishment is just upon them’, which is the chapter's characteristic turn of a doctrine into a procedure.

links.text: That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:

provenance.other: “without God in the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 2:12, where it is the last of four descriptions of the Gentiles' former condition.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 2:12's whole force is that it is past tense — ‘at that time ye were’ — and 2:13 immediately cancels it: ‘but now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh.’ Mosiah 27:31 uses the phrase for people whose condition is not cancelled: ‘then shall they confess, who live without God in the world, that the judgment of an everlasting punishment is just upon them.’ Alma is the man for whom Ephesians 2:13 has just happened — two verses earlier he was in the darkest abyss and now beholds the light — and he applies the uncancelled half of the same sentence to everyone else. The present tense ‘who live’ is doing all the work.

links.note: A five-word KJV singleton, unaltered. Its interest is entirely in the tense: Ephesians uses it of a past state that grace has ended, and Mosiah 27:31 of a present state that judgment will end differently. The link is high because the phrase is exact and unique; the argument is about what has been done to it.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that Alma began from this time forward, to teach the people, and those which were with Alma at the time the angel appeared unto them; travelling round about through all the land, publishing to all the people the things which they had heard and seen, and preaching the word of God in much tribulation, being greatly persecuted by those which were unbelievers, being smitten by many of them;
but notwithstanding all this, they did impart much consolation to the church, confirming their faith, and exhorting them with long suffering and much travail, to keep the commandments of God.
And four of them were the sons of Mosiah; and their names were Ammon, and Aaron, and Omner, and Himni: these were the names of the sons of Mosiah.

And after they had travelled throughout all the land of Zarahemla, and among all the people which was under the reign of king Mosiah, zealously striving to repair all the injuries which they had done to the church; confessing all their sins, and publishing all the things which they had seen, and explaining the prophecies and the scriptures to all who desired to hear them:
and thus they were instruments in the hands of God, in bringing many to the knowledge of the truth, yea, to the knowledge of their Redeemer.
And how blessed are they! For they did publish peace; they did publish good tidings of good; and they did declare unto the people that the Lord reigneth.

links.text: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

provenance.route: Isaiah 52:7 → KJV → Mosiah 12:21 (Abinadi's transcription) → Mosiah 15:14-18 (his exposition) → Mosiah 27:37
provenance.other: “good tidings of good” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:7. Nahum 1:15 has the mountains, the feet, the good tidings and the published peace but not the doubled ‘good tidings of good’, and Romans 10:15, the New Testament citation, has neither: it reads ‘preach the gospel of peace’ and ‘glad tidings of good things’.
provenance.alternative: Romans 10:15, ruled out by tools/mediation-check.py and by the wording — Mosiah has Isaiah's verb (publish, not preach) and Isaiah's unique phrase (good tidings of good, not glad tidings of good things).
provenance.significance: Two mediation questions, and they answer in opposite directions. Against Romans 10:15 the verse is decisively Isaiah's, on the verb and on a KJV singleton. But it is not Isaiah's directly: Isaiah 52:7 has participles governed by a construct — him that publisheth peace, that bringeth good tidings of good — and Mosiah 27:37 has finite verbs with a plural subject, ‘they did publish peace; they did publish good tidings of good’. That conversion has already been performed in this same book, by Abinadi at Mosiah 15:14, ‘these are they which hath published peace, that hath brought good tidings of good’. So Mosiah 27:37 is following the Book of Mormon's own exposition of Isaiah rather than Isaiah, and it takes the conversion one step further by making both clauses use ‘publish’ where Isaiah and Mosiah 15 alike use ‘bringeth’ or ‘brought’ for the second. The chapter that began with a man destroying the church ends by giving him and his companions Isaiah's title for the messenger — and it gives it to them in the words the prophet he had grown up hearing about had already put it in.

links.note: ‘They did publish peace; they did publish good tidings of good; and they did declare unto the people that the Lord reigneth.’ Isaiah 52:7's three clauses in Isaiah's order, with the participles finite and the addressee changed from Zion to the people. The KJV singleton settles the source against Romans 10:15; the grammar settles the route through Mosiah 12:21 and 15:14, where Isaiah 52:7 is transcribed and then re-cast in exactly this way. Mediation is therefore OT-via-earlier-BoM rather than direct-OT.

pericopes.text: Now it came to pass that after the sons of Mosiah had done all these things, they took a small number with them, and returned to their father, the king, and desired of him that he would grant unto them, that they might, with these whom they had selected, go up to the land of Nephi, that they might preach the things which they had heard, and that they might impart the word of God to their brethren, the Lamanites,

links.text: And desired of him letters to Damascus to the synagogues, that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “desired of him” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, Acts 9:2 and 1 John 5:15. Only Acts 9:2 has it of a man asking an authority for leave to make a journey to another city on a religious errand, which is Mosiah 28:1's exact construction.
provenance.significance: Acts 9:1-2 is two verses before Acts 9:4, which Mosiah 27:13 quotes. Saul goes to the high priest and desires of him letters to Damascus, so that he may travel to another city and bring believers back bound; the sons of Mosiah go to the king and desire of him leave to travel to the land of Nephi and bring unbelievers to the knowledge of the Lord. The same request, to the same kind of authority, for the opposite errand — and made by the men who, at Mosiah 27:8-10, were the ones going about to destroy the church. Where Mosiah 27 gave Alma the persecutor's conversion, Mosiah 28 gives his companions the persecutor's journey, with its direction reversed. Nothing in the chapter says this; the borrowed request formula is the only thing that points at it.

links.note: ‘Returned to their father, the king, and desired of him that he would grant unto them … go up to the land of Nephi, that they might preach.’ The four-word run is one of two KJV occurrences, and the situation matches only the Acts one. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is short and unremarkable in isolation; what makes it worth a row is that the preceding chapter has already established this narrative's dependence on Acts 9 at the level of quotation, and this is the verse two before the one it quoted.

pericopes.text: that perhaps they might bring them to the knowledge of the Lord their God, and convince them of the iniquity of their fathers; and that perhaps they might cure them of their hatred towards the Nephites, that they might also be brought to rejoice in the Lord their God, that they might become friendly to one another, and that there should be no more contentions in all the land which the Lord their God hath given them.

Now they were desirous that salvation should be declared to every creature, for they could not bear that any human soul should perish; yea, even the very thoughts that any soul should endure endless torment, did cause them to quake and tremble.

links.text: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

provenance.other: “that any should perish” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 3:9. The KJV's other perishing clauses are all conditional or particular — that whosoever believeth should not perish, that one of these little ones should perish — and none of them makes the perishing of anyone at all the thing not willed.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 3:9 says this of God: he is not willing that any should perish. Mosiah 28:3 says it of four young men: ‘they could not bear that any human soul should perish.’ The transfer is the finding. The KJV's one universalist sentence about who may be lost is a statement of divine patience, offered as the reason the day of the Lord is delayed; the Book of Mormon gives the same unwillingness to human missionaries as a motive for setting out, and makes it a physical distress — ‘did cause them to quake and tremble’. A doctrine about God's forbearance has become a description of a missionary's nerves.

links.note: ‘They could not bear that any human soul should perish.’ Five words from a KJV singleton, with the subject moved from God to men. The chapter's whole missionary rationale is built out of this verse and Mark 16:15's commission, and the two are used the same way: a divine disposition and a divine command are both re-read as things the sons of Mosiah personally felt.

links.text: And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.

provenance.route: Mark 16:15, with Colossians 1:23 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: ‘Every creature’ occurs in 6 KJV verses, of which two are about preaching: Mark 16:15's “preach the gospel to every creature”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Colossians 1:23's “to every creature which” — also exactly one KJV verse — where the gospel ‘was preached to every creature which is under heaven’. Mosiah 28:3 has ‘declared to every creature’ and Mosiah 28:15 has ‘to every creature which should possess the land’, which is Colossians' relative construction.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 28:3 does not reproduce Mark's clause; it reproduces Mark's scope. The interest is in what the chapter then does with that scope twelve verses later: 28:15 says the interpreters were preserved so that the Lord ‘should discover to every creature which should possess the land, the iniquities and abominations of his people’. Colossians 1:23's universal preaching is under heaven; Mosiah 28:15's is under a land grant. Between them the chapter takes the New Testament's two universal-preaching formulas and localizes both — first to the Lamanites, then to whoever holds this particular continent — which is the Book of Mormon's characteristic narrowing of a catholic claim to a hemispheric one.

links.note: ‘They were desirous that salvation should be declared to every creature.’ The verb is not Mark's and the phrase alone is too common to settle a source; the link is filed at moderate because the sentence is a missionary commission and the KJV has exactly two commission formulas using this scope, and because the second of them, Colossians 1:23's relative clause, turns up at 28:15 in the same chapter. Marked conceptual, since the shared wording is a scope rather than a clause.

pericopes.text: And thus did the spirit of the Lord work upon them, for they were the very vilest of sinners. And the Lord saw fit in his infinite mercy to spare them; nevertheless they suffered much anguish of soul, because of their iniquities; and suffering much, fearing that they should be cast off forever.

links.text: This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.

provenance.other: The KJV's one superlative self-description by a sinner is 1 Timothy 1:15, ‘of whom I am chief’, and its setting is 1:13's ‘who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy’. Mosiah 28:4's ‘the very vilest of sinners’ uses a different superlative; the adjective's only KJV occurrence, Psalm 12:8's ‘vilest men’, is of the wicked in power and not of a penitent.
provenance.significance: 1 Timothy 1:13-16 is the New Testament's set piece on the converted persecutor: he was a blasphemer and a persecutor, he obtained mercy, and he was spared to be ‘a pattern to them which should hereafter believe’. Mosiah 28:4 gives all three moves to the sons of Mosiah in one sentence — they were the very vilest of sinners, the Lord in his infinite mercy saw fit to spare them, and the next verses send them out as the pattern for everyone else's belief. The link is filed here rather than at Mosiah 27:29 because 27:29's self-accusation is verbally Acts 8:23's, Simon Magus's, and this one is not verbal at all: it is the same argument in a different vocabulary.

links.note: Conceptual and marked so — the wording is not Paul's and the superlative is not the KJV's. What is Pauline is the three-part shape, chief of sinners / obtained mercy / spared as a pattern, which no other KJV passage has and which Mosiah 28:4-9 has entire. Moderate confidence and kjvSpecific ‘uncertain’, since there is no phrase here to test against another English version. Recorded because the chapter's neighbours are demonstrably working from Acts 9 and Galatians 1, and 1 Timothy 1 is the third of the New Testament's accounts of the same man.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they did plead with their father many days, that they might go up to the land of Nephi.
And it came to pass that king Mosiah went and inquired of the Lord, if he should let his sons go up among the Lamanites to preach the word.
And the Lord said unto Mosiah, Let them go up, for many shall believe on their words, and they shall have eternal life; and I will deliver thy sons out of the hands of the Lamanites.

links.text: Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word;

provenance.other: “believe on me through their word” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 17:20. It is the KJV's only construction in which people believe by way of somebody else's word, and Mosiah 28:7's ‘many shall believe on their words’ compresses it by dropping the object of belief.
provenance.significance: John 17:20 is the point in the high-priestly prayer where Jesus stops praying for the eleven and starts praying for everyone who will believe through their preaching. Mosiah 28:6-7 is a king inquiring of the Lord whether to let his sons go, and the answer he gets is a guarantee in that same idiom — many shall believe on their words, and they shall have eternal life, and I will deliver thy sons. What John 17 offers as intercession, Mosiah 28 receives as a promise with terms: the converts get eternal life and the missionaries get physical protection, which is the addition and is not John's.

links.note: ‘Many shall believe on their words, and they shall have eternal life.’ The idiom of believing through another's word exists once in the KJV and this is its shape, with the possessive pluralized. Moderate: the compression drops the phrase's most distinctive element, ‘on me’, so what remains is short. The pairing with eternal life in the next clause is John's too — John 17:2-3 defines eternal life four verses earlier — which is what keeps the row.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Mosiah granted that they might go, and do according to their request;
and they took their journey into the wilderness, to go up to preach the word among the Lamanites: and I shall give an account of their proceedings hereafter.
Now king Mosiah had no one to confer the kingdom upon, for there was not any of his sons which would accept of the kingdom;

therefore he took the records which were engraven upon the plates of brass, and also the plates of Nephi, and all the things which he had kept and preserved, according to the commandments of God, and after having translated and caused to be written the records which were on the plates of gold, which had been found by the people of Limhi, which was delivered to him by the hand of Limhi:
and this he done, because of the great anxiety of his people, for they were desirous beyond measure, to know concerning those people which had been destroyed.
And now he translated them by the means of those two stones which was fastened into the two rims of a bow.
Now these things was prepared from the beginning, and was handed down from generation to generation, for the purpose of interpreting languages;
and they have been kept and preserved by the hand of the Lord, that he should discover to every creature which should possess the land, the iniquities and abominations of his people:
and whosoever has these things, is called seer, after the manner of old times.

links.text: (Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.)

provenance.other: “called a seer” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 9:9, and “beforetime called a seer” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The KJV's whole apparatus for the word — that it is an older title, that it needs glossing for a later reader — is confined to this one parenthesis.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 9:9 is a parenthetical gloss inserted by a later editor to explain an obsolete word to his own readers: what you call a prophet, they used to call a seer. Mosiah 28:16 does the identical editorial thing in the identical grammar — ‘whosoever has these things, is called seer, after the manner of old times’ — and ‘after the manner of old times’ is the Book of Mormon's rendering of the KJV's ‘beforetime’. The borrowing is not of a phrase but of an editorial gesture: a narrator stepping out of the story to date a term. What makes it more than pastiche is that Mosiah 28:16 uses the gloss to attach the title to an object rather than a person — whoever holds the interpreters is a seer — which is a definition 1 Samuel 9:9 does not supply and could not.

links.note: The KJV names a seer often and explains the title once. Mosiah 28:16 explains it in the same breath and with the same temporal gesture, and does so in a chapter that has just described the two stones and their history. High confidence: the KJV has exactly one home for this construction, and the Book of Mormon verse is doing the same job as the parenthesis it comes from.

pericopes.text: Now after Mosiah had finished translating these records, behold, it gave an account of the people which was destroyed, from the time that they were destroyed, back to the building of the great tower, at the time the Lord confounded the langauge of the people; and they were scattered abroad upon the face of all the earth, yea, and even from that time until the creation of Adam.

links.text: Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.

provenance.other: “confound the language” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 11:9, and “abroad upon the face of all the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Genesis 11:4 has the near-miss, “scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse and differs by a word; Mosiah 28:17 reads ‘all the earth’, which is 11:9's, not 11:4's.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons from one verse, and the choice between ‘all the earth’ and ‘whole earth’ settles which verse of Genesis 11 the writer had. That distinction is the kind of thing this catalogue exists to record: Genesis 11:4 and 11:9 say almost the same thing five verses apart, the Book of Mormon has one of them and not the other, and no reader could see that without counting. Note also what Mosiah 28:17 does with the borrowed sentence — it uses Babel as a terminus for a record that runs backward, from the destruction of the Jaredites ‘back to the building of the great tower … yea, and even from that time until the creation of Adam’. Genesis 11 is a hinge in Genesis's own forward narrative; here it is a milestone on a chronology being read in reverse, which is how the plates are described throughout this chapter.
provenance.alternative: Genesis 11:4 and 11:8, both of which have the scattering; 11:9 is named because it alone has the confounding and the ‘all the earth’ form together.

links.note: ‘At the time the Lord confounded the langauge of the people; and they were scattered abroad upon the face of all the earth.’ Two phrases, each a KJV singleton, each from Genesis 11:9, in Genesis's order. The 1830 misprint ‘langauge’ is a compositor's transposition and carries no weight. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 11:1-9 at this verse; the chapter-level reference is right and the link is filed on 11:9 specifically, on the ‘all the earth’ reading.

pericopes.text: Now this account did cause the people of Mosiah to mourn exceedingly; yea, they were filled with sorrow; nevertheless it gave them much knowledge, in the which they did rejoice.
And this account shall be written hereafter: for behold, it is expedient that all people should know the things which are written in this account.

And now, as I said unto you, that after king Mosiah had done these things, he took the plates of brass, and all the things which he had kept, and conferred them upon Alma, which was the son of Alma; yea, all the records, and also the interpreters, and conferred them upon him, and commanding him that he should keep and preserve them, and also keep a record of the people, handing them down from one generation to another, even as they had been handed down from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem.
Now when Mosiah had done this, he sent out throughout all the land, among all the people, desiring to know their will concerning who should be their king.
And it came to pass that the voice of the people came, saying: We are desirous that Aaron, thy son, should be our king, and our ruler.

provenance.other: “voice of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:7. This is not the KJV’s ordinary way of saying popular consent: within 1 Samuel 8 itself the idiom is “their voice” (8:9, 8:22) and “the voice of Samuel” (8:19), and 1 Samuel 12:1 has “your voice”. The definite, collective form the Book of Mormon adopts as the name of its constitution exists once in the English Bible.
provenance.significance: Recover the rest of the verse and the borrowing turns on its author. The KJV’s one authorisation to hearken to the voice of the people is God conceding a rejection of himself: “they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.” Mosiah takes that phrase, which in its own context licenses a monarchy God did not want, and makes it the instrument for abolishing monarchy — and then at 29:12 gives the reason in the terms of the same episode, that it is better to be judged of God than of man. The chapter is not quoting 1 Samuel 8 so much as reversing it: the people ask for a king (29:2), the ruler sends a written warning about what a king does (29:22-23, which is the office of Samuel’s “manner of the king”), and at 29:37 they are convinced, where Israel refused. Mosiah keeps the phrase and cancels the outcome. The counter-current is 29:27, where the voice of the people may itself “choose iniquity” — which is what 1 Samuel 8 records it doing.

links.note: “And it came to pass that the voice of the people came, saying: We are desirous that Aaron, thy son, should be our king.” The situation is 1 Samuel 8’s to the detail — a people petitioning an ageing ruler for a king to be drawn from his own sons — and the noun phrase that carries it exists in exactly one KJV verse, the verse in which God tells Samuel to give in. The phrase is first adjudicated in this book at Mosiah 7:9, where Limhi uses it of Zeniff’s accession, and by ADJUDICATING §4 a repeat inside one book is normally discharged in the exclusion register. The row is written out again here because this is not the formula recurring: it is the phrase returning to the scene it came from, with the petition, the sons, the written protest and the people’s answer all present, and because from this verse forward it is the name of a form of government rather than a description of an accession. Wilson’s ruling is wanted on whether a case of that kind takes a second row or an exclusion; the argument at 7:9 is not restated here, only extended.
links.text: And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.

pericopes.text: Now Aaron had gone up to the land of Nephi, therefore the king could not confer the kingdom upon him; neither would Aaron take upon him the kingdom; neither was any of the sons of Mosiah willing to take upon them the kingdom;

provenance.route: Judges 8:22-23 and Judges 9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: Judges 8:22-23 is the KJV’s one scene of a deliverer refusing an offered crown for himself and for his son, and its stated ground — “the LORD shall rule over you” — is the ground Mosiah gives at 29:12. What makes the parallel worth writing is the sequel. Judges 9 is what happens when one son does not refuse: Abimelech draws the men of Shechem after him, slays his seventy brethren on one stone, and the kingdom he seizes ends in civil war. Mosiah 29:7-9 states that sequel as a fear rather than a history — a son who will “turn to be angry, and draw away a part of this people after him”, causing “wars and contentions” and “shedding much blood” — and 29:8’s odd insistence that “we have no right to destroy my son” is the Abimelech remedy explicitly declined. Gideon refuses and his son takes it anyway; Mosiah refuses on behalf of sons who have already refused, and closes the succession instead of trusting it.

links.note: Aaron has gone up to the land of Nephi and none of the sons of Mosiah will take the kingdom. No clause of Judges is reproduced, but the shape is exact and it is a shape the KJV supplies once: the household of a deliverer declining a crown the people have offered it. The reason for proposing it rather than passing over it is 29:7-9, where the chapter narrates the Abimelech aftermath as the danger it is legislating against — an angry son, a party drawn away, blood shed — without naming it.
links.whyNot: This is a link at the level of narrative form with almost no verbal contact; “rule over you” occurs in five KJV verses and Mosiah does not use it. A reader who declines typological arguments has nothing here to hold on to, and the succession crisis of 29:1-9 is adequately explained by the Book of Mormon’s own dynastic narrative without any Judges behind it.
links.text: And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you.

pericopes.text: therefore king Mosiah sent again among the people, yea, even a written word sent he among the people. And these were the words that were written, saying:
Behold, O ye my people, or my brethren, for I esteem you as such; for I desire that ye should consider the cause which ye are called to consider; for ye are desirous to have a king.

provenance.other: “have a king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 8:19. The KJV’s usual constructions are “set a king over” (Deuteronomy 17:14-15), “make them a king” (1 Samuel 8:22) and “reign over us” (seven verses); the Book of Mormon uses the one form the Bible uses once, and uses it four times in this chapter.
provenance.significance: The KJV’s single “have a king” is a refusal: “Nevertheless the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel; and they said, Nay; but we will have a king over us.” Mosiah 29 is that verse run forward with the opposite result. The written word he sends is Samuel’s protest delivered a second time, and 29:37-38 reports the outcome 1 Samuel 8:19 denied: “they were convinced of the truth of his words; therefore they relinquished their desires for a king.” The borrowed phrase carries the refusal with it, which is why the chapter keeps repeating it — at 29:13 as the concession, at 29:16 as the verdict, and at 29:30 as the command “that ye have no king.”

links.note: “For ye are desirous to have a king.” Three ordinary words, but the collocation is a KJV singleton and it belongs to the one biblical scene this whole chapter is rewriting. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold by a wide margin and not one of his passages; the case rests on rarity and on the density of 1 Samuel 8 contact across the chapter (see 29:2, 29:23, 29:40) rather than on length.
links.text: Nevertheless the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel; and they said, Nay; but we will have a king over us;

provenance.other: “lifted up above his brethren” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 17:20, and “multiply to himself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 17:17. Neither string is reproduced; what is shared is their content.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 17:14-20 is the Torah’s law of the king, and its three prohibitions are the three things Mosiah is praised for not doing: his heart is not lifted up above his brethren (29:5, and 29:32’s “every man may enjoy his rights and privileges alike”), he did not multiply silver and gold to himself (29:40, “he had not exacted riches of them”), and he wrote out the law rather than ruling above it (17:18-19, and Mosiah’s “written word” at 29:4). The law of the king anticipates a king who will behave as Mosiah does; Mosiah’s conclusion is that no institution can guarantee it, which is 29:13 and 29:16 in a sentence.

links.note: “Behold, O ye my people, or my brethren, for I esteem you as such.” The self-correction is the point: a king addresses his people and immediately declines the relation the word implies. Deuteronomy 17:20’s one requirement of an Israelite king is that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, and the KJV says that in exactly those words once. The wording is not reproduced and the argument is a conceptual one, offered under CONVENTIONS §0a as worth putting on the table because the law of the king governs the rest of the chapter whether or not this verse alludes to it.
links.whyNot: “Brethren” is the Book of Mormon’s standard address and appears in this position throughout the corpus; no distinctive wording of Deuteronomy 17 is present, and the sentiment is available from Mosiah 2:26, King Benjamin’s “I am as ye are”, without any Deuteronomy in the room.
links.text: That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, and that he turn not aside from the commandment, to the right hand, or to the left: to the end that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he, and his children, in the midst of Israel.

pericopes.text: Now I declare unto you, that he to whom the kingdom doth rightly belong, hath declined, and will not take upon him the kingdom.

And now if there should be another appointed in his stead, behold I fear there would rise contentions among you; and who knoweth but what my son, to whom the kingdom doth belong, should turn to be angry, and draw away a part of this people after him, which would cause wars and contentions among you; which would be the cause of shedding much blood, and perverting the way of the Lord; yea, and destroy the souls of much people.

provenance.other: “draw away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:30, where it governs the same preposition and the same construction: “to draw away disciples after them” against Mosiah’s “draw away a part of this people after him.” The pervert-word is in both sentences as well — Acts has “speaking perverse things”, and Mosiah 29:7 continues “perverting the way of the Lord”.
provenance.significance: Acts 20 is Paul’s farewell at Miletus, and its argument is that the schism to come will not be imported: “of your own selves shall men arise.” Mosiah 29 is a farewell of the same genre — a ruler who says at 29:11 that he will serve out the remainder of his days and who is dead by 29:46 — and the danger he names is likewise domestic, a son of his own house drawing a party after him. Borrowing the phrase brings the genre with it. It also brings the sequel: the formula recurs at Alma 2:3, where the first crisis of the reign of judges is a people “drawn away after the persuasions of Amlici”, a man who wants to be king. What Mosiah forecasts in Paul’s words happens to the system he is founding within three chapters.

links.note: “Who knoweth but what my son … should turn to be angry, and draw away a part of this people after him.” The verb is a KJV singleton, it is here with its own preposition and its own object-construction, and the perversion language of Acts 20:30 shows up in the next clause of the same Book of Mormon sentence. That is two independent points of contact on a phrase that occurs once in the English Bible, which is why this is high rather than moderate.
links.text: Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.

provenance.other: “destroy souls” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 22:27, and the same verse supplies the two clauses on either side of the Book of Mormon’s: “to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain.” Mosiah 29:7 reads “the cause of shedding much blood … yea, and destroy the souls of much people”, and the third element arrives at 29:40 in the tyrant “who was seeking for gain”. mediation-check.py was run on this verse against Proverbs 1:16 and Romans 3:15 and returned a decisive call for both, which inspection shows to be an alignment artifact: the tool lost the phrase because Mosiah reads “destroy THE souls” and the intervening article broke its window. Ezekiel 22:27 is the only KJV verse that has the phrase at all, so there is nothing for the diff to mediate.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 22:27 is an indictment of rulers as a class — “her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey” — and it is the one KJV verse that puts bloodshed, the destruction of souls, and the pursuit of gain into a single charge against them. Mosiah 29 distributes that charge across the chapter and then acquits the last king of every count of it (29:40). The prophetic indictment of princes becomes a constitutional argument: what Ezekiel says of the princes of Jerusalem, Mosiah says is what the office does to whoever holds it.

links.note: “Which would be the cause of shedding much blood … yea, and destroy the souls of much people.” Two words, but they are two words that occur together nowhere else in the KJV and they arrive with their neighbour clause attached. Proposed at moderate rather than high because the phrase is short and the sense (killing people) is the obvious one; the argument is the company it keeps.
links.whyNot: “Destroy” and “souls” are both common and their combination is not a difficult thing for an English writer to reach independently. Mosiah shows no other contact with Ezekiel 22, and the bloodshed language of the verse is the chapter’s own from 29:21 onward.
links.text: Her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain.

pericopes.text: Now I say unto you, let us be wise and consider these things, for we have no right to destroy my son, neither should we have any right to destroy another, if he should be appointed in his stead.

And if my son should turn again to his pride and vain things, he would recall the things which he had said, and claim his right to the kingdom, which would cause him and also this people to commit much sin.
And now let us be wise, and look forward to these things, and do that which will make for the peace of this people.

Therefore I will be your king the remainder of my days; nevertheless, let us appoint judges, to judge this people according to our law, and we will newly arrange the affairs of this people; for we will appoint wise men to be judges, that will judge this people according to the commandments of God.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 1:13-17 (with Exodus 18:21-26) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “wise men” is in 42 KJV verses and cannot identify a source by itself. The distribution is the argument: of those 42, only Deuteronomy 1:13 and 1:15 make wise men into judges of Israel, and they are the KJV’s account of how a people that had one leader came to have many. “respect persons in judgment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 1:17, which is also the source of the appellate provision behind Mosiah 29:28.
provenance.significance: Moses at Deuteronomy 1:9 says “I am not able to bear you myself alone” and delegates; Mosiah at 29:11 delegates without the excuse, while still alive and competent, and permanently. The Mosaic precedent is for a judiciary that relieves a single leader, and the leader remains at its head. What Mosiah does with the same machinery is remove the head, which is why 29:29 has to invent something Deuteronomy does not have (see the row at 29:28).

links.note: “We will appoint wise men to be judges, that will judge this people according to the commandments of God.” The verbal contact is thin — two very common words — but the act is the specific act the KJV narrates twice, in Exodus 18 and Deuteronomy 1, and Mosiah’s chapter goes on to reproduce that passage’s appellate structure at 29:28 and its charge-formula at 29:30. Recorded here so that the reader meets the Mosaic precedent at the verse that enacts it.
links.whyNot: “Wise men” as judges is a natural English phrase and 42 KJV verses contain it. Nothing in 29:11 reproduces Deuteronomy 1 and the link would not stand at all if the surrounding verses did not carry the rest of the passage.
links.text: Take you wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes, and I will make them rulers over you.

pericopes.text: Now it is better that a man should be judged of God than of man, for the judgments of God are always just, but the judgments of man are not always just;

provenance.other: “should be judged of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 4:3, and it occurs there inside the identical antithesis: to be judged of man on one side and “he that judgeth me is the Lord” (4:4) on the other. Two Old Testament verses stand behind the thought without supplying the words: “take heed what ye do” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 19:6 — “ye judge not for man, but for the LORD”, the charge Jehoshaphat gives the judges he sets in the land — and “the judgment is God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 1:17. mediation-check.py was run on Psalm 19:9 against Revelation 16:7 and 19:2 for the second half of the verse (“the judgments of God are always just” against “true and righteous are thy judgments”) and found no decisive divergence; the Book of Mormon reproduces neither form, so that clause cannot settle its own mediation.
provenance.significance: The KJV’s wording is what makes the sentence available. 1 Corinthians 4:3 renders Paul’s “human day” as “man’s judgment”, and it is that translator’s choice — not the Greek — that produces a clean English antithesis between being judged of God and being judged of man. Mosiah’s argument for a judiciary rests on the antithesis the King James translators created. The metalepsis is sharper still: Paul is refusing to let a congregation sit in judgment on him, and the ground of his refusal is that a human tribunal is not the tribunal that matters. Mosiah borrows the refusal in order to build a human tribunal with it, and 29:29 will end by letting the people judge their judges after all.

links.note: “Now it is better that a man should be judged of God than of man, for the judgments of God are always just, but the judgments of man are not always just.” The four-word run is a KJV singleton and it comes out of the one New Testament passage that argues the same antithesis in the same direction. Behind it, and supplying the setting rather than the words, is Jehoshaphat’s charge at 2 Chronicles 19:6 — the only place in the KJV where a king institutes judges and tells them whose judgment they are exercising. This chapter reaches that passage again at 29:30 and, structurally, at 29:42.
links.text: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self.

pericopes.text: therefore, if it were possible that ye could have just men to be your kings, which would establish the laws of God, and judge this people according to his commandments; yea, if ye could have men for your kings, which would do even as my father Benjamin did for this people; I say unto you, if this could always be the case, then it would be expedient that ye should always have kings to rule over you.

And even I, myself have labored with all the power and faculties which I have possessed, to teach you the commandments of God, and to establish peace throughout the land, that there should be no wars nor contentions, no stealing, nor plundering, nor murdering, nor no manner of iniquity;
and whosoever hath committed iniquity, him have I punished according to the crime which he hath committed, according to the law which hath been given to us by our fathers.
Now I say unto you, that because all men are not just, it is not expedient that ye should have a king or kings to rule over you.
For behold, how much iniquity doth one wicked king cause to be committed! yea, and what great destruction!—

Yea, remember king Noah, his wickedness and his abominations; and also the wickedness and abominations of his people. Behold what great destruction did come upon them; and also because of their iniquities, they were brought into bondage.
And were it not for the interposition of their all-wise Creator, and this because of their sincere repentance, they must unavoidably remained in bondage until now.

But behold, he did deliver them because they did humble themselves before him; and because they cried mightily unto him, he did deliver them out of bondage: and thus doth the Lord work with his power in all cases among the children of men, extending the arm of mercy towards them that put their trust in him.

provenance.other: “them that put their trust in him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 30:5 — a seven-word run reproduced without alteration. The near-parallels are not close: 2 Samuel 22:31 and Psalm 18:30 read “a buckler to all those that trust in him”, without “put” and without “them that”. mediation-check.py was run on all three and reported no decisive divergence, which is wrong on inspection — Mosiah plainly has “put their”, which Psalm 18:30 and 2 Samuel 22:31 lack. Decided by eye against the tool: the Book of Mormon has the Proverbs form.
provenance.significance: The half of Proverbs 30:5 that is not borrowed is “Every word of God is pure”, and the trust-formula is its consequent — the verse is about the reliability of what God has said. Mosiah 29 works entirely by a document: a written word sent among the people (29:4), more things written (29:33), and a people who at 29:37 “were convinced of the truth of his words.” The one KJV verse that promises shelter to those who put their trust in him promises it on the ground of a trustworthy word, in a chapter whose whole instrument is one.

links.note: “Extending the arm of mercy towards them that put their trust in him.” Seven words, verbatim, from the only KJV verse that contains them, and the near-misses in 2 Samuel and Psalms differ in exactly the words that would have made them candidates. The clause the phrase hangs on — the extended arm of mercy — is not from the KJV at all but is this book’s own formula (see the exclusion at this verse), which is what makes the Proverbs half of the sentence stand out.
links.text: Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.

provenance.route: 2 Chronicles 7:14 with Jonah 3:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Two singletons in one sentence: “humble themselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 7:14, and “cry mightily” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jonah 3:8. Mosiah 29:20 has both, in the order the sources give them — humbling, then crying, then deliverance — with 29:19’s “sincere repentance” standing where Jonah 3:8 has “let them turn every one from his evil way” and 2 Chronicles 7:14 has “turn from their wicked ways”.
provenance.significance: Both sources are about deliverance granted to a people with no help from their king. 2 Chronicles 7:14 is God’s answer to Solomon at the dedication of the temple, and its conditions are laid on “my people”, not on the monarch; Jonah 3 is the one city in the Bible whose king can do nothing but put on sackcloth with everybody else. Mosiah cites them of Limhi’s and Alma’s people in bondage — people whose kings were the cause of the bondage — and the point of the citation is the argument of the whole chapter: what saved them was not the office. The verse then generalises it into a rule of providence, “thus doth the Lord work with his power in all cases among the children of men.”

links.note: “Because they did humble themselves before him; and because they cried mightily unto him, he did deliver them out of bondage.” Each phrase is a KJV singleton on its own; having both in one sentence, in sequence, with the repentance clause of 29:19 in front of them, is well past what coincidence covers. The two sources are unrelated to each other in the Bible and are fused here, which is the signature of composition out of remembered phrases rather than of quotation.
links.whyNot: Both phrases are short and each names an ordinary religious act; “humble themselves” in particular is a formula the Book of Mormon uses constantly, so its KJV rarity may say more about the KJV’s preference for “humble thyself” and “humbled himself” than about this verse’s source.
links.text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.

pericopes.text: And behold, now I say unto you, Ye cannot dethrone an iniquitous king, save it be through much contention, and the shedding of much blood.

For behold, he hath his friends in iniquity, and he keepeth his guards about him; and he teareth up the laws of those which have reigned in righteousness before him; and he trampleth under his feet the commandments of God;

provenance.route: Isaiah 32:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon; Matthew 7:6 for the second clause
provenance.other: “reign in righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 32:1. “trample them under” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:6, and “trample” in any form is in only three (Psalm 91:13, Isaiah 63:3, Matthew 7:6) — so the verb Mosiah chooses for what a king does to the commandments of God is a rare one, and the one KJV verse that uses it of contempt for something holy is the pearls-before-swine saying.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 32:1 is the KJV’s one promise of the good king — “Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment” — and Mosiah 29:22 makes the wicked king’s first act the tearing up of that king’s laws. The messianic guarantee is being cited as the thing a successor can destroy: righteousness reigned once and left statutes behind, and the next man repeals them. Isaiah’s promise is the premise of 29:13 (“if ye could have men for your kings, which would do even as my father Benjamin did”) and 29:16 is the refusal to build on it. If Matthew 7:6 is in the second clause, the commandments of God are the holy thing thrown to the swine.

links.note: “He teareth up the laws of those which have reigned in righteousness before him; and he trampleth under his feet the commandments of God.” The first phrase is a KJV singleton and it is the singleton about the ideal king; the second uses a verb the KJV reserves for three verses. Moderate rather than high because neither clause reproduces its source’s syntax — Isaiah has the future and a singular king, Mosiah a perfect and a plural — and because both phrases are short.
links.text: Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment.

pericopes.text: and he enacteth laws, and sendeth them forth among his people; yea, laws after the manner of his own wickedness; and whosoever doth not obey his laws, he causeth to be destroyed; and whosoever doth rebel against him, he will send his armies against them to war, and if he can, he will destroy them: and thus an unrighteous king doth pervert the ways of all righteousness.

provenance.other: Both halves of the Book of Mormon clause are KJV singletons and both are the same verse. “pervert the right ways of the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “enemy of all righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Acts 13:10 is that verse in each case. Mosiah 29:23’s “doth pervert the ways of all righteousness” fuses them, taking the verb and object from one clause of Acts 13:10 and the “all righteousness” from the other; 29:7 has the first half plain, “perverting the way of the Lord”. The verse also holds two further rarities: “the manner of the king” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, both in the Samuel passage this chapter is rewriting (1 Samuel 8:9, 8:11 — 10:25 reads “the manner of the kingdom”, a different noun, not a third instance), against Mosiah’s “laws after the manner of his own wickedness”; and “sent forth his armies” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 22:7, where an offended king destroys those who would not come.
provenance.significance: Two things follow from recovering Acts 13. The scene is a corrupt counsellor at a ruler’s elbow — Elymas beside Sergius Paulus — which is 29:22’s king who “hath his friends in iniquity, and he keepeth his guards about him”; and it ends with the ruler believing, as Mosiah’s people do at 29:37. More striking is what the same chapter of Acts contains eleven verses later: “and afterward they desired a king: and God gave unto them Saul” — “they desired a king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — which is the New Testament’s only retelling of 1 Samuel 8. The chapter of the Bible that supplies Mosiah’s formula for a ruler who perverts righteousness is also the chapter that summarises the episode Mosiah 29 exists to reverse. Whether that is design or accident, it is worth the reader knowing.

links.note: “And thus an unrighteous king doth pervert the ways of all righteousness.” The sentence is built out of one KJV verse used twice: Acts 13:10 supplies both “pervert the … ways of the Lord” and “all righteousness”, each a singleton, and the Book of Mormon has welded them into a single predicate about kingship. That is more than a phrase in common; it is a small piece of composition on a source, and it is repeated in weaker form at 29:7. The 1830 and 1920 texts agree here, so the reading does not depend on the first edition.
links.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

pericopes.text: And now behold I say unto you, It is not expedient that such abominations should come upon you;

therefore choose you by the voice of this people, judges, that ye may be judged according to the laws which hath been given you by our fathers, which are correct, and which was given them by the hand of the Lord.

Now it is not common that the voice of the people desireth any thing contrary to that which is right; but it is common for the lesser part of the people to desire that which is not right; therefore this shall ye observe, and make it your law to do your business by the voice of the people.

And if the time cometh that the voice of the people doth choose iniquity, then is the time that the judgments of God will come upon you; yea, then is the time he will visit you with great destruction, even as he hath hitherto visited this land.
And now if ye have judges, and they do not judge you according to the law which has been given, ye can cause that they may be judged of a higher judge;

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 1:17 and Exodus 18:22-26 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “small as well as the great” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 1:17, and so does “respect persons in judgment”. Neither is reproduced; the shared thing is the appellate machinery, and the KJV builds it in exactly two places — Exodus 18:22 (“every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge”) and Deuteronomy 1:17 (“the cause that is too hard for you, bring it unto me”).
provenance.significance: This is the chapter’s one genuinely unbiblical move, and it is made in biblical vocabulary. Jethro’s pyramid and its Deuteronomic restatement exist to route hard cases upward and end at one man; nothing in the KJV provides for judging the man at the top, because Moses is the top. Mosiah keeps the upward appeal at 29:28 — “ye can cause that they may be judged of a higher judge” — and then at 29:29 turns the structure over: “a small number of your lower judges” shall be gathered to judge the higher, “according to the voice of the people.” The apex is made answerable to the base. Deuteronomy 1:17’s ground for hearing the small as well as the great is that “the judgment is God” — a phrase that occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and Mosiah has already used that principle at 29:12. He then draws from it a conclusion Deuteronomy does not: if judgment belongs to God rather than to the office, the office can be reviewed from below.

links.note: “Ye can cause that they may be judged of a higher judge.” No wording of Exodus 18 or Deuteronomy 1 survives into the verse, so this is a figural link and is offered as one; what recommends it is that 29:11 has already appointed the wise men of Deuteronomy 1:13, 29:12 has already argued from Deuteronomy 1:17’s principle, and 29:30 will close with 2 Chronicles 19:9’s charge-formula. The Mosaic judiciary is demonstrably in the chapter; this is the verse where the Book of Mormon departs from it, and the departure is the finding.
links.whyNot: A tiered appeal is what any working court system needs and does not have to be borrowed from anywhere. The verse shares no distinctive language with either source, and a reader could reasonably hold that the Mosaic material is present in the chapter without being present in this verse.
links.text: Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God’s: and the cause that is too hard for you, bring it unto me, and I will hear it.

pericopes.text: if your higher judges doth not judge righteous judgments, ye shall cause that a small number of your lower judges should be gathered together, and they shall judge your higher judges, according to the voice of the people.

provenance.other: “judge righteous judgment” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 7:24, where it is an imperative. Mosiah has it twice in this chapter, both times as the standard against which a judge is measured — 29:29’s “if your higher judges doth not judge righteous judgments” and 29:43’s “he did judge righteous judgments” of Alma — and pluralises the object, which the KJV never does with this phrase.
provenance.significance: John 7:24 is spoken in a quarrel about whether the men who administer the law keep it: five verses earlier, “Did not Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keepeth the law?” The Nephite constitution takes Jesus’s rule for judging a case and makes it the test for removing a judge from office — an ethical imperative converted into a procedural standard, and then applied at 29:43 to Alma, who holds the judgeship and the high priesthood together. The clause that supplies the criterion comes from a scene in which the priestly authorities are the ones failing it.

links.note: “If your higher judges doth not judge righteous judgments … they shall judge your higher judges, according to the voice of the people.” A KJV singleton doing constitutional work: the removal standard for a Nephite judge is a phrase that exists in one verse of the English Bible. Adjudicated here rather than at 29:43 because this is its first occurrence in the chapter; the 1830 keeps the non-standard concord “judges doth” which 1920 corrected to “do”, a change that touches the grammar and not the borrowing.
links.text: Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.

pericopes.text: And I command you to do these things in the fear of the Lord; and I command you to do these things, and that ye have no king: that if these people commit sins and iniquities, they shall be answered upon their own heads.

provenance.other: Three singletons from four consecutive verses. “ye do in the fear of the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 19:9 (“Thus shall ye do in the fear of the LORD”), against Mosiah’s “to do these things in the fear of the Lord”; “take heed what ye do” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 19:6; “set judges in the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 19:5. The n-gram stream instead proposed Deuteronomy 11:22 here on “I command you to do”, which is connective boilerplate and is filed in the exclusion register.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 19:5-11 is the only narrative in the KJV of a king instituting a system of judges throughout his land, and every structural element of Mosiah 29 is in it. Jehoshaphat sets judges city by city (19:5, Mosiah 29:11, 29:41); he charges them that they judge not for man but for the LORD (19:6, Mosiah 29:12); he places priests and Levites over the appellate cases (19:8, Mosiah 29:28-29); he tells them to do it in the fear of the LORD (19:9, this verse); and he puts a chief priest over all matters of the LORD alongside a civil ruler for the king’s matters (19:11, and Mosiah 29:42’s Alma, who is given both). The difference is the one that matters: Jehoshaphat’s judges answer to Jehoshaphat, and after 29:30 the Nephite judges answer to nobody but each other and the people. Mosiah reproduces the biblical reform and removes its king, which is why the same verse that borrows the charge-formula also contains “that ye have no king”.

links.note: “And I command you to do these things in the fear of the Lord … and that ye have no king.” The charge-formula is a KJV singleton, and it belongs to the one royal judicial reform the Bible narrates — a passage whose other three verses this chapter has also been drawing on, at 29:12 and again at 29:42. That a single sentence carries both the borrowed charge and the abolition of the office that gave the charge is the chapter in miniature.
links.text: And he charged them, saying, Thus shall ye do in the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart.

provenance.other: “upon their own heads” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 11:21. mediation-check.py was run on Ezekiel 11:21 against Ezekiel 33:4, Acts 18:6 and 1 Kings 2:32 and reported a decisive result for Ezekiel 33:4; that is an alignment artifact, produced by matching the tool’s “head” inside the Book of Mormon’s “heads”. Decided by eye, the case is not close: Mosiah has the plural noun and the third-person plural possessive, which is Ezekiel 11:21’s exact four words, where Ezekiel 33:4 and 1 Kings 2:32 read “his own head” and Acts 18:6 “your own heads”. CONVENTIONS §4’s warning about pronouns applies to number as well.
provenance.significance: In Ezekiel the formula is God’s and the recompense is eschatological: “I will recompense their way upon their own heads.” Mosiah legislates it. What the prophet says God will do at the end, the constitution arranges for now — which is why the next verse has to supply the corollary, that under a king the arrangement fails and “their iniquities are answered upon the heads of their kings”. Behind both stands Ezekiel 18:20, whose doctrine that the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father is here used, unusually, as an argument about political structure rather than about individuals: monarchy is objectionable because it makes one head bear a nation’s account, and 29:38’s “every man expressed a willingness to answer for his own sins” is the people accepting Ezekiel 18’s terms as a form of government.

links.note: “That if these people commit sins and iniquities, they shall be answered upon their own heads.” Four words from the only KJV verse that has them, in the right number and the right person, and doing at 29:30-31 exactly the theological work Ezekiel 18 does — which is what raises this above a lucky match on a common idiom. The verb is not Ezekiel’s (“recompense” becomes “answered”), so this is an allusion and not a quotation.
links.text: But as for them whose heart walketh after the heart of their detestable things and their abominations, I will recompense their way upon their own heads, saith the Lord GOD.

pericopes.text: For behold I say unto you, The sins of many people have been caused by the iniquities of their kings; therefore their iniquities are answered upon the heads of their kings.

And now I desire that this inequality should be no more in this land, especially among this my people; but I desire that this land be a land of liberty, and every man may enjoy his rights and privileges alike, so long as the Lord seeth fit, that we may live and inherit the land; yea, even as long as any of our posterity remaineth upon the face of the land.

provenance.other: “live and inherit the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 16:20, and the Book of Mormon reproduces it whole: “that we may live and inherit the land”. The same short passage yields two further singletons — “judges and officers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 16:18, and “which is altogether just” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 16:20 — and the liberty language of the verse has its own: “liberty throughout all the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 25:10, the jubilee, which likewise returns every man to his possession. This is the chapter’s single longest verbatim run and the machine found it.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 16:18-20 is the Torah’s law for appointing judges, and 16:20 is the promise attached to obeying it: follow what is altogether just, “that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.” Mosiah’s peroration on a land of liberty closes with that clause, in a chapter whose whole business is appointing judges — so the reward the KJV attaches to a judiciary is the reward Mosiah attaches to his. Two texts, separated by everything, agree that what a people gets for judging justly is tenure of its land. The KJV sequence is also the chapter’s sequence: 16:18 appoint judges (Mosiah 29:11, 29:25), 16:19 take no gift (29:40, the king who did not exact riches), 16:20 and you shall keep the land (here). The 1830 preserves “seeth” and “remaineth” where 1920 prints “sees” and “remains”, so the first edition sits closer to the source’s register than the modern text does.

links.note: “That we may live and inherit the land; yea, even as long as any of our posterity remaineth upon the face of the land.” Five words reproduced exactly from the one KJV verse that contains them, and that verse is the conclusion of the Bible’s law about appointing judges. Of everything in this chapter this is the cleanest case: the rarest run, from the most contextually apt source, at the rhetorical summit of Mosiah’s argument. It is well below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his passages; the count is what carries it.
links.text: That which is altogether just shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.

pericopes.text: And many more things did king Mosiah write unto them, unfolding unto them all the trials and troubles of a righteous king; yea, all the travails of soul for their people, and also all the murmurings of the people to their king; and he explained it all unto them.

provenance.other: “travail of his soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 53:11, and “travail of” in any continuation occurs in exactly one KJV verse as well. The mediation cannot be settled by divergence, because there is no divergence to test: Mosiah 14 transcribes Isaiah 53 continuously and Mosiah 14:11 reproduces Isaiah 53:11 word for word. It is decided instead on proximity — the phrase re-enters the book fifteen chapters after the book itself has put it on the page, in the same authorial hand, which is the situation CONVENTIONS §7 has OT-via-earlier-BoM for. A reader who prefers direct-OT here is not making an error, only a different judgment about what ‘proximate model’ means when the two candidates are textually identical.
provenance.significance: The Servant’s travail is transferred to the office of a righteous king — and then, in the very next verse, refused. Isaiah 53:11 promises that the righteous servant “shall bear their iniquities”; Mosiah 29:34 answers that “the burdens should come upon all the people, that every man might bear his part”, and 29:30 has just legislated that sins are answered on the heads of those who commit them. So the chapter names the good king as a suffering servant in order to argue that nobody should be asked to be one. The substitution that is redemptive in Isaiah 53 is, as a political arrangement, precisely what Mosiah is abolishing. That reading is only available if the Isaiah is heard, which is what the singleton makes possible; compare Hays on metalepsis, where the meaning lies in what the two texts do not say to each other.

links.note: “All the travails of soul for their people”, said of a righteous king. The phrase belongs to one KJV verse, and this book has already printed that verse verbatim at Mosiah 14:11 as part of Abinadi’s Isaiah 53. Mosiah pluralises it and drops the possessive, which is how a remembered phrase behaves rather than a copied one. The argument for the row is not the two words but what 29:34 immediately does with them.
links.text: He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.

pericopes.text: And he told them that these things had not ought to be; but that the burdens should come upon all the people, that every man might bear his part.

provenance.route: Galatians 6:2 and 6:5 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “shall bear his own burden” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 6:5. mediation-check.py was run on Ezekiel 18:20 against Galatians 6:5 and 6:2 and found no decisive divergence — correctly, since the Book of Mormon reproduces none of the three verbatim. Decided on vocabulary instead: the words Mosiah shares (“burdens”, “every man”, “bear”) are Galatians’, and Ezekiel supplies only the doctrine, so mediation is direct-NT with Ezekiel 18 as a composite.
provenance.significance: Galatians 6:2 and 6:5 are the KJV’s famous unresolved pair — bear ye one another’s burdens, and every man shall bear his own burden — and Mosiah 29:34 holds both at once: the burdens fall on all the people, and each man carries his part of them. What is a puzzle in Paul is a constitutional principle here. Note the 1830 reading (CONVENTIONS §8): the first edition has “burdens” plural, which is Galatians 6:2’s form, and 1920 prints “burden” singular, which is 6:5’s. Whichever way the change is read, both readings are the KJV’s, and the modern text has moved from one verse of Galatians 6 to its neighbour.

links.note: “The burdens should come upon all the people, that every man might bear his part.” Galatians 6:5 is the only KJV verse with the construction, and Mosiah 29 has just spent four verses on the doctrine that Galatians 6:5 and Ezekiel 18:20 share — that accounts are individual and not transferable, which is the reason given for having no king. The substitution of “his part” for “his own burden” is what keeps this an allusion; the sentence is Paul’s two maxims combined rather than either one quoted.
links.text: For every man shall bear his own burden.

pericopes.text: And he also unfolded unto them all the disadvantages they labored under, by having an unrighteous king to rule over them;

yea, all his iniquities and abominations, and all the wars, and contentions, and bloodshed, and the stealing, and the plundering, and the committing of whoredoms, and all manner of iniquities, which cannot be enumerated; telling them that these things ought not to be; that they was expressly repugnant to the commandments of God.
And now it came to pass, after king Mosiah had sent these things forth among the people, they were convinced of the truth of his words;

therefore they relinquished their desires for a king, and became exceedingly anxious that every man should have an equal chance throughout all the land; yea, and every man expressed a willingness to answer for his own sins.

Therefore it came to pass that they assembled themselves together in bodies throughout the land, to cast in their voices concerning who should be their judges, to judge them according to the law which had been given them; and they were exceedingly rejoiced, because of the liberty which had been granted unto them.

And they did wax strong in love towards Mosiah; yea, they did esteem him more than any other man: for they did not look upon him as a tyrant, who was seeking for gain, yea, for that lucre which doth corrupt the soul, for he had not exacted riches of them, neither had he delighted in the shedding of blood; but he had established peace in the land, and he had granted unto his people that they should be delivered from all manner of bondage; therefore they did esteem him, yea, exceedingly, beyond measure.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 8:3, with the pastoral “filthy lucre” verses → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “lucre” occurs in exactly 6 KJV verses, and the distribution is the whole argument. Five are the qualification for a church officer — 1 Timothy 3:3 and 3:8, Titus 1:7 and 1:11, 1 Peter 5:2, all “filthy lucre” — and the sixth is 1 Samuel 8:3, of Samuel’s sons: “his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment.” Separately, “exacted” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 2 Kings 15:20 and 23:35, both of kings taking money of their people, against Mosiah’s “he had not exacted riches of them”.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 8:3 is the cause of the whole episode: Israel asks for a king because the judges have gone after lucre. Mosiah 29 ends by praising the last king for not going after lucre, and then — two verses later — installs judges. The KJV’s one non-ecclesiastical “lucre” names the exact failure that made monarchy look necessary, in the chapter that undoes the monarchy by restoring the office that failed. Read with the other five verses, the sentence is stranger still: the vocabulary in which Mosiah is cleared of avarice is the vocabulary in which the KJV screens candidates for the office of bishop and elder, and 29:42 immediately makes Alma chief judge and high priest at once. The two halves of the KJV’s “lucre” — the corrupt judge and the disqualified bishop — are the two halves of the office this chapter creates.
provenance.alternative: The five pastoral verses alone would account for the word, in which case the mediation is direct-NT and the significance is only that a civil ruler is measured by an ecclesiastical standard. That reading is weaker only because it has to ignore how thoroughly 1 Samuel 8 governs the rest of the chapter.

links.note: “They did not look upon him as a tyrant, who was seeking for gain, yea, for that lucre which doth corrupt the soul.” One word, and six KJV verses have it — which is why this is moderate and not high. The case is not the count but the split: one of the six is the verse that causes Israel to demand a king, in a chapter that has been rewriting that demand from its second verse, and the other five legislate the office Alma is about to receive alongside the judgeship. The nearest supporting rarity is “exacted”, whose only two KJV occurrences are both of kings extracting money from their subjects.
links.whyNot: A single content word cannot establish dependence, and “lucre” is simply the KJV’s word for ill-got money; a writer steeped in the English Bible would produce it without any particular verse in mind. The distributional argument is suggestive rather than demonstrative, and a cautious editor would decline it. It is written up because CONVENTIONS §0a asks for the risk to be taken openly.
links.text: And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they did appoint judges to rule over them, or to judge them according to the law; and this they done throughout all the land.

And it came to pass that Alma was appointed to be the chief judge; he being also the high priest; his father having conferred the office upon him, and had given him the charge concerning all the affairs of the church.

provenance.other: “chief priest is over you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 19:11, and “ruler of the house of Judah” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. Neither is reproduced, so this row is figural and stands on the arrangement rather than the words.
provenance.significance: Jehoshaphat’s reform ends by naming two men: Amariah the chief priest over all matters of the LORD, and Zebadiah the civil ruler for all the king’s matters. The Book of Mormon collapses them into one person in a single sentence — “Alma was appointed to be the chief judge; he being also the high priest” — at the end of a chapter that has taken the charge-formula (29:30), the not-for-man principle (29:12) and the city-by-city appointment (29:41) from the same eleven verses of 2 Chronicles. Where the biblical reform separates the sacred and civil apexes under a king, the Nephite one fuses them and removes the king. That is a structural inversion of a specific passage and it is worth recording as such, whatever a reader concludes about dependence.

links.note: “Alma was appointed to be the chief judge; he being also the high priest.” The double office is the chapter’s last constitutional act and it has an exact biblical counterpart, in the passage this chapter has already used three times: 2 Chronicles 19 divides the two offices between two named men, and Mosiah 29 unites them in one. Proposed as a figural link because there is no shared wording at all; its warrant is the accumulation of contact with 2 Chronicles 19:5-11 elsewhere in the chapter, and it should be withdrawn if that contact is judged to fail.
links.whyNot: No verbal contact whatever, and the Book of Mormon has its own reasons for the fusion — Alma is high priest because his father made him so (Mosiah 26:8), which the verse itself says. A reader may hold that the priest-and-judge arrangement of Mosiah 29:42 is fully explained by Mosiah 25-26 and owes 2 Chronicles nothing.
links.text: And, behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, for all the king’s matters: also the Levites shall be officers before you. Deal courageously, and the LORD shall be with the good.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that Alma did walk in the ways of the Lord, and he did keep his commandments, and he did judge righteous judgments; and there was continual peace through the land;
and thus commenced the reign of the judges throughout all the land of Zarahemla, among all the people which was called the Nephites: and Alma was the first and chief judge.
And now it came to pass that his father died, being eighty and two years old, having lived to fulfil the commandments of God.

And it came to pass that Mosiah died also, in the thirty and third year of his reign, being sixty and three years old; making in the whole, five hundred and nine years from the time Lehi left Jerusalem;
and thus ended the reign of the kings over the people of Nephi; and thus ended the days of Alma, who was the founder of their church.
